    `w3.org` namespace URIs exist in the tree); one is added to the grep, never to the sources, if a
    namespace URI ever appears. The §16.1 `check.sh` listing gains this stage between the jget
    self-test and the test build.
28. **`SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` is validated at boot** (`internal/config/config.go` `cookieName`): the value
    must be an RFC 6265 cookie-name token (letters, digits and ``!#$%&'*+-.^_`|~``); anything else —
    a space, `"` (a quoted `.env` value handed over verbatim), `;`, `,`, `=`, `:`, `/`, a non-ASCII
    rune — fails `config.Load` with a one-line reason naming the variable and the rule. `net/http`
    drops a `Set-Cookie` with such a name silently, so the process would otherwise boot, answer 201/200
    to register/login while inserting session rows, set no cookie and log nothing — exactly the
    "working-looking server nobody can stay logged in to" §4's fail-fast rule exists to prevent. The
    §4 table row gains this note; the default is unchanged.
29. **Text-validation messages name the rule that failed** (`internal/httpapi/dto.go` `cleanText`,
    `writeInvalidText`). The status and the stable `error` code are unchanged (400 `invalid_request`);
    the human `message` — which `app.js` surfaces verbatim and capture-tool integrators read — is now
    true. A text field (`title`, `description`, token `name`) holding a control character other than
    tab/newline/CR answers "`<field>` must not contain control characters" instead of the length
    message (a five-character title was told it exceeded 200 characters); the length message is kept
    for the length rule (`at most 200 characters`, `1-200 characters`, `1-64 characters`, an empty
    trimmed value included). `cleanText` returns the reason as an error (`errTextTooLong` /
    `errTextControl`) and the three callers route it through `writeInvalidText`.
30. **Type-mismatched JSON fields are named** (`internal/httpapi/dto.go` `decodeJSON`,
    `jsonShapeMessage`, `jsonKind`; `upload.go` `readMetadata`): a body or metadata part that *is* an
    object but carries a field of the wrong JSON type answers 400 `invalid_request` with "field
    `<name>` must be a `<boolean|string|number|array|object>`, got `<what was sent>`"
    (`*json.UnmarshalTypeError` with a field path — `{"unlisted":1}` → "field unlisted must be a
    boolean, got number") instead of the false "body must be a JSON object" / "metadata is not a JSON
    object". Those generic messages stay for what they describe: a syntax error, a truncated body, or a
    document that is not an object (the same error type with no field path). `ttl_days` keeps its own
    400 `invalid_ttl` (§8.2). Codes and statuses are unchanged; only the human text moved.
31. **The public probes print a storage failure's CLASS, not its message** (`internal/store/store.go`
    `PingError`, `minio.go` `pingClass`, `internal/httpx/health.go` `storageClass`): §15 says
    `/healthz` exposes no config values, but `Ping` wrapped minio-go's error with `%w` and
    `StorageHealth.Get()` rendered it verbatim into the anonymous, cached, unmetered `/healthz`
    `storage` field (and `/readyz`'s). On a dial/DNS/TLS failure minio-go hands back net/http's
    `*url.Error`, whose text is the whole request URL — `S3_ENDPOINT` (for R2 the account id) and
    `S3_BUCKET` — and the not-exists branch named the bucket outright, so a scanner polling during a
    storage outage learned the operator's endpoint and bucket. `Ping` now returns a
    `*store.PingError{Class, Err}`: `Err` keeps every detail (the boot ping loop's WARN and
    `/readyz`'s `storage_error` access-log field are unchanged, so the operator loses nothing) and
    `Class` is one of `unreachable` / `timeout` / `denied` / `bucket missing` / `unavailable`.
    `StorageHealth.Get()` renders `"error: " + class` through a duck-typed `HealthClass() string`
    (no `httpx`→`store` dependency) and falls back to `unavailable` for any error that does not
    classify itself — the leak is closed by default, not by enumerating leaky shapes. §8.1's
    `"storage":"pending"|"ok"|"error: …"` shape and §8.7 are unchanged; only what fills the `…` is.
32. **At most one live run per clip id** (`internal/worker/worker.go` `runRegistered`): `fail()` and
    `release()` commit the DB transition that lets another loop re-claim the job — `FailAttempt`
    setting clip `failed` (which `POST /retry` needs) or `ReleaseJob` re-queueing it — and only
    afterwards walk their exit path: `deleteKeys` (up to three `DeletePrefix` calls under the 10s exit
    budget), `os.RemoveAll($SCRATCH/{id})` and the forced terminal progress write. Everything that path
    touches is keyed by the CLIP id, not by the attempt, so with `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY` ≥ 2 the
    successor (a retry, or a re-claim after a transient requeue) ran *under* its predecessor's cleanup:
    its scratch dir removed while ffmpeg was writing into it — a spurious environment failure that
    burns a `transient_failures` count — and its live progress entry overwritten with the stale
    `failed`. A run now waits in `runRegistered` until no run is registered for its clip id (the
    unregister happens after `execute()` has fully returned), so a superseded run can never touch a
    successor's dir or registry entry. The wait is bounded by the predecessor's exit budget, costs
    nothing on the common path (no predecessor), and `Cancel`/`Stop` are unchanged — §10.1's "Cancel
    blocks until that clip's job goroutine has exited" now has one goroutine to wait for by
    construction.
33. **`MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` is bounded at boot** (`internal/config/config.go` `int64Range`,
    `maxUploadCeiling` = 2^62; `internal/httpapi/upload.go` `uploadLimit`): the §4 row invites
    "no arbitrary caps — this is your disk", so an operator meaning "unlimited" plausibly sets
    `9223372036854775807`. `Load` accepted it, `upload` then computed `MaxUploadBytes +
    uploadSlackBytes` (1 MiB) in int64 → wrapped negative, and `http.MaxBytesReader` (which clamps
    `n < 0` to 0) failed the FIRST read — the metadata part — so every `POST /api/clips` answered 413
    `too_large` whatever its size, with nothing logged to explain it. `Load` now rejects a value above
    2^62 (4 EiB, past any disk) with the usual one-line reason, and `uploadLimit` saturates instead of
    wrapping so the arithmetic cannot produce a negative limit however the Config was built. The §4
    row gains the bound; the 413 contract is unchanged.
34. **compose interpolates every `S3_*` value** (`compose.yaml`, `.env.example`): `.env.example` told
    the operator to "set `S3_ENDPOINT` / `S3_REGION` / `S3_ACCESS_KEY` / `S3_SECRET_KEY` directly"
    for R2/B2, but the app service hard-coded `S3_ENDPOINT: http://minio:9000`, derived the
    credentials from `MINIO_ROOT_USER`/`MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD` and pinned `S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE: "true"`
    — only `S3_REGION` and `S3_BUCKET` passed through. An operator following the file got a stack
    still talking to the local MinIO with MinIO credentials, an R2 bucket name and `S3_REGION=auto`:
    a working-looking dev stack instead of R2, with no error anywhere, and §4's provider matrix goes
    verbatim into the Phase 5 README. All six now interpolate with the dev stack as the fallback —
    `S3_ACCESS_KEY: ${S3_ACCESS_KEY:-${MINIO_ROOT_USER:-clippet}}` (same for the secret), so an
    unset `.env` renders byte-for-byte what it rendered before and `check.sh`/`e2e.sh` are unaffected.
    `.env.example` lists the four override variables commented out and records that an external bucket
    leaves the `minio` and `bucket-init` services unused (the bucket must already exist) and that the
    MinIO-only test helpers stop applying.
35. **A `__Host-`/`__Secure-` cookie name requires an https base** (`internal/config/config.go`
    `cookiePrefix`): both prefixes are ordinary RFC 6265 tokens, so erratum 28's charset rule accepts
    them, but §14 derives the cookie's `Secure` flag from `PUBLIC_BASE_URL`'s scheme alone and RFC
    6265bis makes a client DISCARD a `__Host-`/`__Secure-` cookie that arrives without `Secure`.
    `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME=__Host-clippet_session` on an `http://` base therefore booted, answered
    200 to login while inserting session rows, and left every browser — and curl, which enforces the
    same rule — permanently logged out with nothing in the log: erratum 28's exact failure mode
    reached through the client's prefix rule instead of net/http's parser. `Load` now rejects the
    combination with a one-line reason naming the variable, the prefix and the rule; the same name on
    an `https` base is accepted unchanged. The §4 row records both rules, and the erratum-28 test's
    `__Host-` case moved to an https fixture.
36. **E2E cleans up after itself** (`scripts/e2e.sh` step 17): steps 12/14/15 remove D (owner DELETE),
    A and F (forced expiry), but B, C and E are uploaded with ttl `never` and were never removed, and
    the run's user stayed logged in — so every run left three clips, their objects and a live session
    on the SHARED stack (41 users and rows titled "E2E noaudio"/"E2E vertical"/"E2E dual" from earlier
    runs were the evidence). A new step 17 DELETEs B, C and E with the cookie jar and logs out. It is
    strictly best effort — every call is `|| echo 000`, nothing in it can fail a run that has already
    passed — and it runs AFTER the step-16 log gate so its own lifecycle log lines are never inside
    the window the gate reads. The §16.3 step list gains step 17; the E2E user (registration is the
    thing under test) is not deleted, only logged out — no route deletes a user.
37. **Session-gated 303s carry the private headers too** (`internal/web/server.go`
    `redirectPrivate`): `GET /` and `/settings/tokens` answer `303 /login?next=…` for a session-less
    caller while `/login` and `/register` answer `303 /` for a logged-in one, and the invalid-cursor
    bounce exists only inside a session — WHICH response a URL produces depends on the cookie, exactly
    like the pages erratum 17 marked `private, no-store` + `Vary: Cookie`. Those five redirects were
    bare `http.Redirect` calls with no cache headers at all, so a shared cache in front of the app
    could store the anonymous bounce and loop a logged-in user through `/login` (or hand a logged-in
    user's bounce to an anonymous one). They now go through `redirectPrivate`, which sets the same
    headers before redirecting. §9.1's page-header table is unchanged; this closes the redirect
    branches it never described. (Erratum 246: `/` now renders the front door for a session-less
    caller instead of bouncing it; the private-headers rule is unchanged for the other four redirects.)
38. **A zero-length suffix range answers 416** (`internal/httpapi/media.go` `zeroSuffixRange`):
    `Range: bytes=-0` selects no bytes, which RFC 9110 §14.1.2 makes unsatisfiable, but
    `http.ServeContent`'s parser computes `start = size, length = 0` (its no-overlap guard covers only
    the explicit first-byte-pos branch) and answers **206** with an INVALID `Content-Range: bytes
    {size}-{size-1}/{size}` — last-byte-pos below first-byte-pos — under the media routes' cacheable
    `public, max-age=3600`; `bytes=-0,-0` produced the same header inside each multipart part.
    §8.5 already states the rule ("unsatisfiable → 416 with `Content-Range: bytes */size`, zero
    GETs") and this package already owns the range surface (`rangeErrorWriter` reshapes stdlib's own
    416, `maxRanges` pre-empts `ServeContent` — erratum 23), so `serveObject` now rejects a Range
    header listing a zero-length suffix spec beside the count gate: 416 `range_not_satisfiable`,
    message "a suffix range of zero length is not satisfiable", `bytes */size`, `no-store`, zero
    storage calls, GET and HEAD alike, on all four media routes. The shapes net/http parses
    identically (`-00`, `- 0`) go the same way; `bytes=-100` and `bytes=0-0` are untouched. E2E step 8
    asserts both.
39. **A non-quarter rotation is reported as 0, not snapped to 90** (`internal/transcode/probe.go`
    `normalizeRotation`, `rotationEpsilon`): the normalizer took `round(r/90) % 4`, so a Display
    Matrix rotation of 45° became 90°, `displayDims` swapped 640×360 to 360×640 and `MakePlan` built
    `scale=360:640`. Because the angle came from side data, `Plan.PreRotate` stayed 0 and the graph
    emitted no rotate filter — the design relies on ffmpeg autorotating so "output geometry matches
    the display dims" — but ffmpeg does NOT turn an odd angle into a swapped frame: it warns "Odd
    rotation angle" and rotates in place on the original canvas, so the pipeline scaled an unrotated
    landscape into a portrait box and produced a squished rendition and poster. Rotation exists here
    only to swap the display dims, so an angle further than `rotationEpsilon` (1°, room for the 16.16
    fixed-point slop that makes a real 90 arrive as 89.9998) from a quarter turn is now 0: no swap, no
    filter, output geometry equal to the decoded frame. The §10 rotation rule records the tolerance;
    the probe table's `46 → 90` row becomes `46 → 0`. The trigger is exotic (no camera writes a
    non-quarter matrix) but trivial to produce with `ffmpeg -display_rotation 45`.
40. **The video part's Content-Type is bounded like its filename** (`internal/store/keys.go`
    `MaxContentTypeLen`, 127): `ContentTypeFor` returned `mime.ParseMediaType`'s media type verbatim
    for anything starting with `video/`, with no length bound — the exact hole erratum 26 closed for
    the sibling field read two lines away from the same untrusted multipart part header (Go's
    `mime/multipart` accepts up to 10 MiB of part headers). Unbounded, one authenticated
    `POST /api/clips` stored a multi-KB `source_content_type` that every `ClipDTO` echoed — the
    shared `GET /api/clips` library every user fetches included — and that `GET /original` emitted
    verbatim as its `Content-Type` **response header**. Past the object store's own metadata limit
    (~4–8 KiB on MinIO) `PutFile` then failed, so a permanently malformed request was answered
    **503 `storage_unavailable`** + `Retry-After: 5` — a §11 misclassification (file/client faults are
    the 4xx class) — under two WARN lines per attempt whose text blamed the operator's bucket, one of
    them the access log's `storage_error` field that erratum 31 deliberately kept as the operator's
    storage signal: an alarm any account could forge at will, 60 uploads/hour, with `REGISTRATION=open`
    by default. The part's type is now honoured only when it is at most 127 bytes; anything longer
    falls through to §6's extension map and finally `application/octet-stream`, exactly like a
    non-`video/` type. Real clients are untouched (the longest registered `video/*` type is far under
    the bound, and arbitrary `video/x-…` subtypes still pass), nothing oversized can reach
    `PutObject`, and §15's "the original's stored type is derived server-side (§6), never trusted
    blindly" holds in the dimension that was missing. §6's `ContentTypeFor` rule gains the bound.
41. **The media seeker survives a Close that races its reader** (`internal/store/seeker.go`,
    `internal/httpapi/media.go` `readRecorder`): for a Range header listing 2–8 specs
    `http.ServeContent` writes the `multipart/byteranges` body from a goroutine it starts and
    **never joins** — closing its pipe only fails that goroutine's next pipe *write*, it cannot
    interrupt a read already inside `content.Read`. So whenever the copy into the client ends early
    (a disconnect, a seek-away, a tab close, any `ResponseWriter` write error) `serveObject` returned
    while that goroutine was still inside `store.(*seeker).Read`, and then read `rs.err` and ran
    `defer rs.Close()` on top of it. `seeker` had no synchronisation at all: `body`, `pos` and
    `bodyErr` were written by `Close` and read/written by that `Read`, and `readRecorder.err` was
    written by it while the handler read the field — a genuine data race (`-race` reports it on the
    pair `closeBody` ← `Close` ← `serveObject.deferwrap1` vs `seeker.Read` ← `readRecorder.Read` ←
    `net/http.serveContent.func1`), with a post-`Close` read free to open a **fresh `GetRange` for a
    request that had already ended** — the one thing §8.5 says never happens — and a torn `rs.err`
    free to mislead the §8.5 INFO/WARN/ERROR split. Erratum 23's cap bounds the amplification, not
    the race: two range-specs suffice, on the anonymous media routes. `seeker` now guards its fields
    with a mutex that is never held across a storage call or a body read — so `Close` closes the open
    body (which is what unblocks a read parked on the network) instead of queueing behind it — plus a
    `closed` flag: a later `Read`/`Seek` answers `errSeekerClosed`, and a body that `GetRange`
    returns after the close is closed at once and never recorded. `readRecorder` takes its record
    under a mutex and stops recording at `Close`, so an error that belongs to the teardown is never
    reported as the response's outcome; `serveObject` closes explicitly before classifying, keeping
    the deferred `Close` for the panic path. Nothing about the served bytes changes.
    CI gained the pass that catches this class: the `test` stage installs `gcc musl-dev` and runs
    `CGO_ENABLED=1 go test -race -count=1 ./...` after the tagged suite (§16.1); the aborted
    multi-range copy is pinned by `internal/httpapi.TestMediaMultiRangeAbortedCopy` and the seeker's
    half by `internal/store.TestSeekerClosedStopsReading` / `TestSeekerCloseDuringRead`.
42. **The pre-encode scratch guard is sized from the plan, not only from the source**
    (`internal/worker/pipeline.go` `checkOutputRoom`, `plannedOutputBytes`, `outputBitsPerPixel`):
    §10.2's rule was `free ≥ 2×source_size + SCRATCH_MIN_FREE_BYTES`, whose premise — output ≈
    source — the encode does not honour. `EncodeArgs` always emits `-r {fps} -fps_mode cfr` and
    nothing bounds `Plan.DurationUS`, so a container that declares a long duration over a couple of
    frames (one big presentation-timestamp gap) makes ffmpeg duplicate frames to fill it: the output
    size and encode time scale with the DECLARED duration, not with the uploaded bytes
    `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` bounds. Measured: a 112,919-byte 2-frame `.mkv` declaring one hour produced an
    81,197,450-byte rendition in 7 s (719×) and reached `ready`; at ten hours it produced 811 MB
    while the guard asked for only `2×112,920 + 512 MiB` free. It is not a hostile-only shape either
    — a screen recorder that pauses or drops frames writes real timestamp gaps, and any long
    low-bitrate source encodes past twice its size. Blast radius was the SHARED scratch volume:
    filling it fails unrelated in-flight jobs with ENOSPC, which surfaces as a non-zero ffmpeg exit
    and is therefore classified PERMANENT (`failed`, not requeued), and ingest spools there too
    (erratum 14). The encode stage now runs a second `statfs` against what the plan schedules —
    `W·H·fps·duration·0.2/8` bytes, the bits-per-pixel ceiling measured for libx264 CRF 23 at
    `veryfast` with headroom — plus `SCRATCH_MIN_FREE_BYTES`, and refuses to start above it with the
    same transient `insufficient scratch` §10.2 already specifies (`encode:` prefix, requeued with
    backoff, runner never invoked). The encode therefore cannot write more than the disk the guard
    reserved, which also bounds what one upload can put in the operator's bucket. A plan with no
    usable duration, frame rate or dimensions has nothing to size from and falls back to the
    source-based guard alone — a fallback, not a bound: this check only PREDICTS, and what actually
    stops an unsizeable (or a lying) source is the runtime cap of erratum 46. Deliberately an
    over-estimate: refusing to start is a clean transient failure, ENOSPC mid-encode is not. §10.2's
    rule records the second check.
43. **The range gates stand aside when a precondition pre-empts the Range** (`internal/httpapi/media.go`
    `rangeBinding`): erratum 23's count cap and erratum 38's zero-length-suffix gate read
    `r.Header.Get("Range")` and answered 416 straight off it, BEFORE `http.ServeContent` evaluates
    `If-Range` / `If-None-Match` / `If-Match`. RFC 9110 §13.1.5 requires a server to IGNORE the Range
    when the `If-Range` validator does not match — the answer is 200 with the full representation —
    and §13.2.2 resolves `If-None-Match` → 304 and `If-Match` → 412 before Range is looked at. Both
    invariants held on the plain `ServeContent` path (`TestMediaRoutes` already pinned "If-Range with
    a stale validator ignores the Range (200), never 416"), so the same request shape answered 200 or
    416 depending on which check saw it first, and a client owed the whole representation got a hard
    error instead. `serveObject` now runs the two gates only when the Range is actually binding:
    `rangeBinding` mirrors net/http's own precondition order (If-Match / If-Unmodified-Since →
    If-None-Match / If-Modified-Since → If-Range, with a strong comparison for If-Match and If-Range
    and a weak one for If-None-Match, via `scanETag`/`etagListMatches`) and errs toward binding —
    anything unparsable or unknown leaves the gates in force. Standing aside costs nothing the gates
    exist to prevent: an ignored Range is served as one full-body GET, a 304 and a 412 as zero. The
    416s themselves are unchanged wherever the Range really applies, `bytes=-0` and a nine-spec
    header included.
44. **An unrecognised range unit is ignored, not refused** (`internal/httpapi/media.go`
    `normalizeRangeUnit`): RFC 9110 §14.2 — "An origin server MUST ignore a Range header field that
    contains a range unit it does not understand" — so `Range: items=0-1` is owed the full
    representation. All four media routes answered **416** `range_not_satisfiable` with
    `Content-Range: bytes */size` instead: `http.ServeContent`'s parser tests for a literal `bytes=`
    prefix and rejects anything else as an invalid range, and `rangeErrorWriter` then dressed that
    stdlib 416 up as this package's own considered answer. The same literal prefix test also breaks
    §14.1's "all range unit names are case-insensitive": `Range: BYTES=0-99` was refused a range it
    fully understands. `serveObject` now settles the unit before anything reads the specs — a
    `bytes` unit in any case is canonicalised so its ranges are honoured (`BYTES=0-99` → 206), an
    unrecognised unit is dropped so the response is a normal 200, and a value with no `=` at all
    (`bytes 0-1`) keeps its 416, being an invalid ranges-specifier §14.1.1 lets a server reject. The
    count and zero-suffix gates then see the normalised header, so `BYTES=-0` is still 416. §8.5's
    range rules record the unit. Practical impact is nil — nothing on the wire sends a non-`bytes`
    unit — but this package already owns the range surface (errata 23, 38, 43) rather than
    inheriting the stdlib's answer, and 416 for a unit is not what §8.5 reserves 416 for.
45. **The HTML pages are bounded by `SSR_TIMEOUT`, not by `TimeoutHandler`** (documentation only;
    `cmd/clippet/serve.go`, `internal/web/server.go`): §8's conventions bullet said the 15 s
    `http.TimeoutHandler` wraps "the JSON … routes **and the HTML pages**", but §18.1's root-mux
    wiring — `Handle("/", pages)` under `RequestID → AccessLog → Recover` only, restated by erratum 8
    and frozen with `serve.go` — never wrapped them, and `internal/web`'s `handler()` adds no wrap of
    its own. The code is right and the conventions line was stale: a page HANDLER's only blocking
    work is a DB read already bounded by `ssrContext` (`SSR_TIMEOUT`, 5 s, §9), whose deadline renders
    the styled 503 + `Retry-After: 30` page that §9.1 specifies — where `TimeoutHandler` would replace
    it with the stdlib's stock body — and `writeHTML` renders into a buffer with an explicit
    `Content-Length`, so the observable response shape is what a wrapped one would be anyway. (Amended
    for accuracy: one blocking DB call on the page path is NOT the handler's and NOT bounded by
    `ssrContext` — `auth.Resolver.Middleware` runs OUTSIDE the handler, so its `GetSession` and its
    once-a-minute `TouchSession` use the bare request context. That is accepted, not an oversight: it is
    shared with every `long` JSON route, `DELETE /api/clips/{id}` and `GET /api/clips/{id}/original`
    among them; it is skipped entirely for an uncredentialed request, which is the only traffic an
    attacker can generate at scale; reads take the 4-connection read-only pool under WAL with
    `busy_timeout(5000)`, the one write is a single short `UPDATE` at most once per minute per session,
    and a client disconnect cancels the context. Wrapping the Resolver in an `SSR_TIMEOUT` child was
    considered and REJECTED: it would change the slide-cookie and 503 paths for a stall nobody has
    shown to be reachable.) The
    conventions bullet now names the JSON routes only and points at the page bound; nothing about
    the served pages changes. Recorded because §20 is where a divergence between the frozen wiring
    and an earlier section belongs, and because a future page handler that adds an unbounded call
    must know its bound is the context deadline, not an outer wrapper.
46. **The encode is capped by a byte budget it cannot talk its way out of** (`internal/worker/pipeline.go`
    `outputBudget`, `checkOutputSize`; `internal/transcode/encode.go` `EncodeOptions.MaxOutputBytes`):
    erratum 42 cured the instance it measured — a container that DECLARES a long duration — and left
    the cause. `plannedOutputBytes` returns 0 whenever `HasDuration` is false, and `checkOutputRoom`
    then reserves nothing at all, falling back to acquire's `2×source_size`, the very rule shown to be
    off by three orders of magnitude; and `HasDuration` comes only from `format.duration` / a stream
    duration — uploader-written container metadata — while the CFR fill follows the FRAME timestamps
    nothing measures, `EncodeArgs` setting no `-t`. Both halves are reachable without hostility: any
    mkv/webm muxed to a non-seekable output carries no Duration element (a browser `MediaRecorder`
    clip, ffmpeg or OBS piping), and an mp4's `mvhd`/`mdhd` or an mkv's Duration can state a lie in
    either direction, which ffprobe reports verbatim. Measured on 7.1.1 with the pipeline's own argv:
    `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i color=c=red:s=640x360:r=30 -frames:v 2 -vf setpts=N*107970 -c:v libx264 -f matroska pipe:1`
    writes 1,377 bytes with no duration ffprobe can see; encoding it produced dup_frames=215,940 — a
    215,942-frame, 3599 s, 6,784,049-byte rendition in 28 s — with the plan guard waved through on
    `need=0` and only `TRANSCODE_HARD_TIMEOUT` (6 h) above it. Every extra source frame is another gap
    to fill, and at the plan's ceiling dims with textured content the per-frame cost is far larger, so
    one upload still writes gigabytes into the SHARED scratch volume and the bucket.
    The fix stops predicting and enforces instead. `Encode` takes `MaxOutputBytes`, and the progress
    tracker already parses `total_size` from `-progress pipe:1`: the first block past the budget
    cancels the run with its own cause and it ends as a **permanent** `output_too_large` — checked
    BEFORE the exit status, so a run that raced to exit 0 is caught too — and `checkOutputSize` then
    stats the file that survived, so a muxer that reports no `total_size` cannot slip past either. The
    budget is the largest of the three bounds this clip has already been granted: what the plan
    schedules (erratum 42 found the room for it), `2×source_size` (acquire found the room for it) and
    `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` (the operator's own statement of what one clip may cost). No honest rendition
    can reach it — a false positive needs more than 0.2 bits/pixel AND more than twice its source AND
    more than a whole upload's worth of bytes — while the shapes above hit it in seconds and die
    permanently, un-retried. `checkOutputRoom` is deliberately unchanged: reserving a fixed ceiling up
    front would refuse honest unsized uploads on small scratch volumes, so the unsizeable case is
    bounded at the cap rather than at the prediction. `-t {DurationUS}` was considered for the
    declared-duration half and REJECTED — a container that under-reports its duration is a real shape
    (a stale `mvhd`, an interrupted recording) and `-t` would silently truncate it, trading a bounded
    resource bug for unbounded data loss, while the cap already covers a lie in either direction.
    Pinned by `internal/transcode.TestEncodeOutputBudget` and `TestEncodeOutputBudgetBoundary` (the cap
    is a ceiling, not a target; zero disables it), `TestFFmpegNoDurationGapFillIsCapped` (the real
    pipe-muxed two-frame mkv, under `-tags ffmpeg`), and `internal/worker.TestOutputBudgetCapsAnUnsizedPlan`
    / `TestOutputBudget`. §10.2 and §10.3 record the cap.
47. **A Display Matrix rotation is classified the way ffmpeg's autorotate classifies it, from the
    matrix itself** (`internal/transcode/probe.go` `matrixRotation`, `autorotateQuarter`): erratum 39
    stopped an odd angle (45°) from swapping the display dims and left a band inside its own
    tolerance where the pipeline and ffmpeg still disagreed. ffprobe prints the Display Matrix angle
    under `"rotation"` through a C cast — `print_int(av_display_rotation_get(...))` — so it is
    TRUNCATED: 89.4 and 89.6 both print `89`. ffmpeg's `get_rotation` instead ROUNDS the raw angle
    (`-round(av_display_rotation_get(...))`, normalized into [0, 360)) and inserts a transpose only on
    an exact quarter (`|θ−90k| < 1` over a whole number means equality), so 89.6 is transposed and
    89.4 is turned in place by a `rotate` filter on the untouched canvas. Classifying from the
    truncated key put both on the same side (`|89−90| = 1`, not `> rotationEpsilon`), so an 89.4°
    source planned a swapped 720×1280 over a frame ffmpeg never transposed and `scale=W:H` — which
    preserves no aspect — squeezed the rendition AND its poster: the erratum-39 failure mode,
    reproduced from inside the tolerance. Measured on 7.1.1 with the pipeline's own argv against a
    1280×720 source: the 89.4° remux scored SSIM 0.49 versus the correct picture and 0.995 versus
    `rotate=271*PI/180`, i.e. ffmpeg had rotated in place while the plan had swapped. The tolerance
    could not simply be tightened — on a truncated integer, refusing `89` would also un-swap a real
    90 arriving as 89.9998 — so the fix reads the angle from where it survives: ffprobe emits the nine
    16.16 fixed-point coefficients as `"displaymatrix"`, and `matrixRotation` reproduces
    `av_display_rotation_get` from them exactly (the /65536 is a power of two, so no rounding
    changes), after which `autorotateQuarter` mirrors ffmpeg's round-then-exact-match. The mismatch
    band was wider than the one angle: raw ∈ [89.0, 89.5) ∪ (90.5, 91.5) and the 179/181, 269/271
    mirrors all resolved wrong before, all resolve with ffmpeg now. `rotationEpsilon` survives for the
    two paths where a number, not a matrix, is all there is: the legacy `rotate` tag (whose turn this
    package emits itself, so any tolerance is self-consistent) and a side data entry carrying no
    coefficients. Pinned by `internal/transcode.TestDisplayMatrixRotationMirrorsAutorotate` (the raw
    angle out of ffprobe 7.1.1's verbatim coefficient dumps; the quarter-turn table; equal `"rotation": 89`
    inputs planning 640×360 and 360×640) and the `-tags ffmpeg` matrix cases `rotated-89.4-sidedata` /
    `rotated-89.6-sidedata`, which run the real remuxes end to end and score both against their own
    reference and the squish control. Severity nit — the angle needs a hand-written sub-degree matrix
    (`ffmpeg -display_rotation 89.4`), no camera writes one — and the blast radius is one distorted
    rendition of the uploader's own clip. The §10.3 rotation rule records the classifier.
48. **An absurd declared duration cannot overflow the guards that exist to bound it**
    (`internal/worker/pipeline.go` `satAdd`, `checkOutputRoom`, `outputBudget`): errata 42 and 46 stop a
    container that declares a long duration over a couple of frames from making the CFR gap fill write a
    runaway rendition into the SHARED scratch volume — and both were defeated by int64 overflow at the
    top of the range they bound. `plannedOutputBytes` saturates at `math.MaxInt64` once
    `W·H·fps·duration·0.2/8` runs past int64, which at the default 1280×720@60 ceiling is a declared
    `format.duration` of about 6.7e12 s — a number an uploader writes into an `mvhd` or an mkv Duration
    element and ffprobe reports verbatim, there being no maximum-duration gate anywhere. From there:
    `checkOutputRoom` did `need += SCRATCH_MIN_FREE_BYTES`, which WRAPPED to −9223372036317904897, and
    `free >= 0 && free < need` is false for every non-negative free space, so the encode started with
    nothing reserved; and `outputBudget`'s `max(...)` returned `math.MaxInt64`, so erratum 46's runtime
    `n > MaxOutputBytes` could never fire and `checkOutputSize` could never fail. The guards inverted:
    a moderate lie (35 990 s) was correctly refused while the extreme one sailed through with only
    `TRANSCODE_HARD_TIMEOUT` (6 h) above it — and with `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY` at 1 that runaway also
    blocks every other transcode for those six hours. Confirmed against the live stack: the same 7e12 s
    declaration was REFUSED at 320×240@30 ("the planned output … needs 403200000536870912") and reached
    `ready` at 1280×720@60, the smaller predicted output refused while the larger one passed.
    The fix is arithmetic that cannot lie about its own failure. `satAdd` saturates instead of wrapping
    (applied to acquire's `2×source_size` sum as well, which had the same shape with physically
    unreachable inputs), so an absurd plan now refuses with `insufficient scratch` like any other plan
    too big for the disk — transient, requeued, capped by `MAX_TRANSIENT_FAILURES` exactly as the
    35 990 s case already was. And a saturated estimate is no longer a grant: `outputBudget` drops it and
    falls back to `max(2×source_size, MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES)`, the two bounds this clip really was granted, so
    the runtime cap stays armed even where the reservation is skipped (a filesystem whose free space
    cannot be read reports −1). The exploitable window had an upper edge too — past ~9.22e12 s the
    float→int64 conversion in `secondsToUS` goes out of range, `DurationUS` lands ≤ 0 and the plan takes
    the safe unsized path — which is precisely why the fix belongs in the arithmetic rather than in a
    duration ceiling: the guards must hold for every number that reaches them. Pinned by
    `internal/worker.TestSaturatingPlanDoesNotDisableTheOutputGuards` (the saturating plan is refused,
    its budget is finite, and both a representable lie and an honest plan keep their existing outcomes)
    and `TestSatAdd`. §10.2 records the saturation.
49. **`Forget` voids the run it interrupts, so an evicted progress entry stays evicted**
    (`internal/worker/worker.go` `Forget`, `run.progressVoid`; `internal/worker/pipeline.go`
    `setProgress`): erratum 18 made `POST /retry` call `Worker.Forget` before `Wake` so `/progress`
    stops reporting the previous run's failure — and `Forget` only cleared what was in the registry at
    that instant. `fail()` commits `FailAttempt` FIRST, which is the moment `clips.state` becomes
    `failed` and every caller can see it and offer Retry, and only THEN walks its exit path: up to three
    `DeletePrefix` round trips against a remote bucket sharing one 10 s exit budget, an `os.RemoveAll`
    of a scratch dir holding a multi-GB source, and last of all the forced terminal registry write. A
    retry landing anywhere in that window had its eviction undone — the superseded run force-wrote
    `{failed, <old reason>}` into the entry `Forget` had just deleted, `httpapi.progress` prefers the
    registry over the row (§8.4), and §9.3's poller stops on `failed`, so the user saw the retry
    instantly re-fail with a stale message and had to reload. Erratum 32 widens the window rather than
    closing it: the successor cannot register, and therefore cannot overwrite the entry, until the
    predecessor has fully unregistered — which happens after that write. Reproduced deterministically
    by parking a failed run in `DeletePrefix` and retrying: `{State:failed Stage:store Percent:97
    Error:"store: upload poster: …"}` for a row reading `queued`.
    Writing the terminal entry earlier — adjacent to the `FailAttempt` commit — was considered and
    REJECTED as a symptom patch: it shrinks the window to the microseconds between the commit and the
    write without closing it, and leaves `release()`'s trailing `queued` write with the same shape. The
    fix instead makes the eviction mean what it says. `Forget` takes `worker.mu`, marks the clip's
    registered run `progressVoid` and evicts under that lock; every registry write a run makes now goes
    through `jobRun.setProgress`, which takes the same lock and drops the write when its run is voided.
    So a check and a write can never straddle a `Forget`, and a run whose view of the clip has been
    declared obsolete resurrects nothing — terminal write, stage write or `release()`'s `queued` alike.
    The void is per RUN, not per clip: a run registered after the `Forget` (every successor, since at
    most one run per clip id is live) writes normally, which is what keeps erratum 32's
    `TestSupersededRunNeverRacesItsSuccessor` reporting `ready` after its retry. `Cancel` now routes its
    own eviction through `Forget` for one code path; it waits for the run to exit first, so it voids
    nothing. Pinned by `internal/worker.TestRetryEvictionSurvivesTheFailedRunsExitPath` (the row says
    queued and the registry stays empty through the whole exit path) and
    `TestForgetVoidsOnlyTheRunItInterrupts`. §12 step 5 and §8.4 are unchanged in substance: the
    registry is still the source of truth for progress; it can no longer be stale-terminal for a clip
    the row says is queued.
50. **A non-ASCII download name keeps a plain `filename=` beside the encoded one**
    (`internal/httpapi/media.go` `contentDisposition`, `asciiFilename`, `encodeRFC5987`): §8.1 promises
    `GET /api/clips/{id}/original` answers `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="<sanitized>"`,
    and `contentDisposition` handed the name to `mime.FormatMediaType` as its one `filename` parameter.
    Go emits the RFC 2231/5987 extended form — `filename*=utf-8''…` — and NO plain parameter as soon as
    the value carries a byte outside printable ASCII, so a clip uploaded as `vidéo été — clip.mp4` came
    back with no `filename=` at all. Browsers are fine; a client that implements only `filename=` is
    left with nothing and falls back to the URL's last path segment, so `curl -OJ` saved the file as
    `original` — no name, no `.mp4`. Verified live at :8481 against curl 8.18.0, with an ASCII control
    clip in the same session saving under its real name. RFC 6266 §4.3 recommends sending both
    parameters for exactly this reason, and the promise in §8.1 is the plain one.
    So a name outside printable ASCII now renders both: `filename=` carrying an ASCII fallback (every
    such rune mapped to `_`, which keeps the extension — the half that decides what opens the file) and
    `filename*=utf-8''…` carrying the name exactly. `mime.FormatMediaType` renders the pair itself —
    the extended value is all RFC 2045 token characters, so it is emitted unquoted, and `filename` sorts
    first — with `encodeRFC5987` doing the percent-encoding down to RFC 5987's attr-char set, which
    excludes `%`, `'` and `*` where a URL escaper would keep them. A pure-ASCII name keeps byte for byte
    the header it had. Pinned by `internal/httpapi.TestContentDispositionCarriesAnASCIIFallback` (exact
    headers for the ASCII and non-ASCII shapes, and a parse-back asserting the plain parameter is
    present, ASCII and still carries the extension — `mime.ParseMediaType` itself cannot see the bug,
    since it prefers `filename*`, which is precisely the reader this is not for). The stored
    `source_filename` is untouched: this is presentation, bounded by erratum 26's 255-rune cap.
51. **A clip deferred by the sweep grace is logged as deferred, not as "no longer expired"**
    (`internal/lifecycle/lifecycle.go` `DestroyExpired`, `stillExpired`): `MarkDeletingIfDue` answers
    `ErrStateMismatch` for every candidate that stops matching the §12 predicate under the tick's
    `(now, grace)`, and `destroy` logged all of them with erratum 15's note — "no longer expired;
    skipped" — which is true of exactly one of the two ways it happens. The other is a candidate the
    worker CLAIMS between `SweepCandidates` and its turn in the tick's loop (a real wall-clock window:
    the loop does a blocking `Worker.Cancel` and a multi-round-trip `DeletePrefix` per candidate ahead
    of it): the clip becomes `processing`, so rule (b) — restricted to `queued`/`ready`/`failed` — stops
    matching, while rule (c) needs `expires_at <= now - grace` and does not match yet. That clip is not
    rescued. It is still past its expiry, inside the `SWEEP_GRACE` window §12 grants a clip that is
    mid-encode at its expiry, and the first tick past that window destroys it. Reachable through
    `clippet admin expire <id>` on a queued clip (§8.8, and the project's own fixtures use it that way)
    and after downtime that outlived some TTLs, when the boot tick's candidate list and the worker's
    first claims run concurrently.
    `DestroyExpired` now re-reads the row on a mismatch and, when `expires_at` is still set and still
    past, logs `note="in grace; deferred"`. Nothing else moves: the level stays INFO, the outcome stays
    `Result{Skipped: true}` counted in the sweep line as `skipped` — whose documented meaning, "no
    longer due on this tick", is true of a deferral as much as of a rescue, and erratum 15 requires only
    that the rescue be recorded that way — and a row that cannot be read keeps the generic note. This is
    the errata-29/30 class: a message that named the wrong cause. Pinned by
    `internal/sweeper.TestDestroyExpiredTellsAGraceDeferralFromARescue` (a claimed candidate is deferred
    with the new note, its objects untouched, and destroyed by the next tick past the grace; a rescued
    clip keeps erratum 15's note).
52. **`safeNext` validates the string net/http will send, not the one it was handed** (`internal/web/server.go`
    `safeNext`, `web/static/app.js`): §9's post-login bounce is "`next` (same-origin path only)", and the
    guard rejected a value that already began `//` or `/\`. But `redirectPrivate` hands the accepted value
    to `http.Redirect`, which — for a target with no scheme and no host — writes `path.Clean(path)+query`
    rather than the string it was given. `path.Clean` treats `\` as an ordinary path rune while collapsing
    `.` and `..` segments, so it can MANUFACTURE the exact prefix the guard exists to block:
    `path.Clean("/./\/evil.example") == "/\/evil.example"` and `path.Clean("/a/../\evil.example") ==
    "/\evil.example"`. Every browser's URL parser folds `\` to `/` for a special scheme, so
    `Location: /\/evil.example` resolves against `https://clips.example/login` as `https://evil.com/` — a
    cross-origin bounce off the operator's own trusted origin, over a plain GET, reached by a logged-in
    victim opening `/login?next=%2F.%2F%5C%2Fevil.com` (or the same on `/register`, the other handler that
    redirects to a caller-supplied target). That is a CWE-601 open redirect: a phishing primitive today and
    a redirect-chain laundering step for any Phase 4 OAuth/webhook work.
    `safeNext` now admits a value only when (a) it is rooted at exactly one `/`, (b) it carries no control
    character and no backslash anywhere — no route of this app holds one, in path or query — and (c) it is
    already its own normal form, i.e. `path.Clean` of the path half, with a trailing slash preserved the
    way `Redirect` preserves it, equals that half. (c) is the load-bearing clause: requiring the value to
    be what `Redirect` will send makes the check total instead of a list of the shapes `Clean` can
    synthesise, and it is what rejects `/x/../ok` and `/x/..//evil.example` — same-origin either way, but
    not the string we approved. `app.js`'s twin adds only the backslash rejection: a browser resolving the
    UNCLEANED relative value stays same-origin (`/./\/evil.example` → `https://clips.example//evil.example`),
    so the hole is created purely by Go's server-side `Clean`, and the client copy is a second line over
    values the server already normalised. Pinned by `internal/web.TestLoginAndRegisterPages`, whose `next`
    table gained the Clean-manufactured cases and now asserts the logged-in **303 `Location`** — the header
    the bug lived in — as well as the hidden input, which by construction could never see it.
53. **A malformed multipart body is a body-validation failure, not a client disconnect**
    (`internal/httpapi/upload.go` `spoolVideo`): the `io.Copy` switch in §8.3 step 5 typed only
    `*http.MaxBytesError` (413) and `*diskError` (507) and swept everything else into a catch-all that set
    `client_disconnected=true` and answered 400 `upload_interrupted`. A well-formed, `Content-Length`-framed
    request whose video part simply never reaches its closing boundary — a truncating proxy, a broken
    capture tool, a hand-rolled uploader — makes `mime/multipart` return `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF` from
    `Part.Read` and landed there. The client is still on the connection and reads that reply, so the app was
    asserting a network failure that provably did not happen (the request context is not cancelled on this
    path), both to the caller and in the structured access-log field an operator later trusts to tell a
    flaky link from a flaky uploader. That is the same class as errata 29 and 30 — a message naming the
    wrong cause — and it defeats erratum 18, whose whole point is that upload failure classification is
    honest: `upload_interrupted` is the disconnect class, and the two neighbouring steps in this very
    handler (`probeGate`, and the `PutFile` error path) already gate it on `clientGone(r, err)`.
    `spoolVideo` now gates it the same way: `clientGone` keeps 400 `upload_interrupted` +
    `client_disconnected=true`, and every other framing error becomes 400 `invalid_request` —
    already one of §8.1's `POST /api/clips` codes — with `reject=malformed_multipart`,
    `multipart_error=<err>` and the message "the multipart body ended before the video part was complete".
    On a real abort net/http cancels the request context inside the failing read, so the honest case is
    unchanged. Pinned by `internal/httpapi.TestUploadMalformedMultipartIsNotAClientDisconnect`, which drives
    a hand-built unterminated body and a body that fails mid-part through `httpx.AccessLog` and asserts both
    answers and both log annotations (`SetLogField` is a no-op without that middleware, and the false field
    is half the defect).
54. **A cancelled request keeps the handler's own answer** (`internal/httpapi/router.go` `timeout`,
    `cancelable`): `http.TimeoutHandler`'s `<-ctx.Done()` arm branches on the error — `DeadlineExceeded`
    writes 503 plus the `timeoutBody` envelope, and *anything else* writes a bodyless
    `WriteHeader(503)` and discards whatever the inner handler had already buffered. net/http cancels
    the request context inside `connReader.handleReadError` the moment the client FINs or its body comes
    up short, so every short JSON route (`json` in the §8.1 table: register, login, logout, me, tokens,
    tokens/{tid}, the clip GET/PATCH/retry/progress/view, healthz, readyz) answered an ordinary client
    abort with a **503 carrying `Content-Length: 0`** under a `Content-Type: application/json` label and
    no `Retry-After`, which `httpx.AccessLog` then recorded at **WARN**. §12's doctrine is explicit and
    binding — "a client disconnect mid-upload or mid-stream, `context.Canceled` **anywhere**" is INFO —
    and `writeClientGone`, written for exactly this, could never run: TimeoutHandler won the race before
    the handler's 4xx reached the wire. A client that half-closes its write side after a short body is
    still reading, so it was told the *server* was unavailable for what is a client-side framing error,
    with an unparseable body. This is erratum 53's twin — the multipart half of the same surface was
    fixed there, and it is on the `long` chain, so the two halves disagreed.
    `timeout` now hands `http.TimeoutHandler` a context that can only EXPIRE
    (`context.WithoutCancel` of the request's, so no cancel can reach that arm) with the client's own
    context stashed as a value, and `cancelable`, immediately below TimeoutHandler, gives the handler a
    context that is a child of TimeoutHandler's (keeping its deadline) and is also cancelled — via
    `context.AfterFunc`, plus an eager check for a client already gone — when the client's is. Nothing
    else moves: the deadline arm still writes the same envelope, no work outlives a disconnect, and the
    handler's `r.Context().Err()` still reports it. So a disconnect now yields `writeClientGone`'s 400
    `client_disconnected` (+ the log field) or `decodeJSON`'s 400 `invalid_request` for a truncated
    body — both at INFO, both a real envelope. Pinned by
    `internal/httpapi.TestCancelledRequestKeepsTheHandlerAnswer`, which drives both shapes through
    `httpx.AccessLog` and asserts the status, the envelope and the absence of a WARN line;
    `TestJSONRoutesAreTimeBounded` still pins the expiry 503.
55. **`/original`'s 403 and 404 carry a cache directive** (`internal/httpapi/router.go`, the
    `privateNoStore` middleware — erratum 17's `privateJSON`, renamed now that it also guards bytes):
    erratum 25 ships the sliding session cookie on the once-a-minute touch and justifies it with "every
    route under the Resolver already answers `no-store` or `private`". `GET /api/clips/{id}/original`
    was the one route that made that false. It is the only Resolver-covered GET registered with `long`
    rather than `json`, so it gets none of `timeout`'s `Cache-Control: no-store` preset, and its two
    early exits set no cache directive of their own: `writeNotFound` (a malformed, unknown or deleting
    id) and `serveMedia`'s owner check (403) — unlike the `not_ready` branch beside it, and unlike
    `serveObject`, `writeRangeError` and the storage/DB 503s, which all set theirs. So a session whose
    touch was due (always so on the first authenticated request after login) got its raw cookie re-issued
    on a `404 not_found` with no `Cache-Control` and no `Vary`, and RFC 9110 §15.5.5 lists 404 among the
    statuses a cache may store heuristically, keyed on the URL alone. A shared cache in front of the app
    — the reverse proxy / cloudflared deployment §13 and §14 anticipate — is then permitted to replay
    that response, `Set-Cookie` included, to the next caller of the same URL; `SameSite=Lax` means a
    logged-in victim following a link to `/api/clips/<unknown-id>/original` is enough to populate the
    entry. Mainstream caches refuse to store a `Set-Cookie` response by default, so no default
    deployment is hit — what was wrong is the untagged credentialed response, and a binding invariant
    that the code did not hold. This is the errata-17/37 class, reached through the one route those
    enumerations missed (erratum 37 fixed bare `303`s on the same reasoning, and a 303 is not even
    heuristically cacheable).
    The route now carries `privateNoStore` (`private, no-store` + `Vary: Cookie, Authorization`) as its
    outermost handler middleware, exactly as `GET /api/clips` and `GET /api/clips/{id}` do. Nothing on
    the success path moves: `serveObject` overwrites both with `private, max-age=3600` + the same `Vary`
    (§8.5, erratum 17's decided media caching), `writeRangeError`'s 416 overwrites with `no-store` and
    `auth.reject`'s 401 with `no-store`, so only the two bare exits change. Pinned by
    `internal/httpapi.TestOriginalErrorsAreNotCacheable`, which asserts both headers on the 404 and the
    403 and first asserts the sliding cookie is on that very response, so the case cannot go vacuous;
    `TestOriginalRoute` still pins the 200/304 pair.
56. **E2E over a public https base** (`scripts/e2e.sh`; §16.3 rewritten to match; Phase 3). The brief's
    Phase 3 gate is "E2E green over public https; **tag URLs publicly resolvable**", and its documented
    command is `BASE=https://… bash scripts/e2e.sh` — but the script derived its origin as
    `BASE=${PUBLIC_BASE_URL:-$(envfile PUBLIC_BASE_URL)}`, which **overwrites** an explicitly exported
    `BASE`. The gate command therefore silently tested whatever `.env` said; it only appeared to work
    because Phase 3 sets both to the same tunnel URL. `BASE` now takes precedence over `PUBLIC_BASE_URL`
    and `.env`, a trailing slash is trimmed, and a `BASE` that differs from `.env`'s `PUBLIC_BASE_URL`
    prints a NOTE naming both (the app bakes its own value into every absolute card tag, so a mismatch
    can only fail, and it fails in step 10 with a confusing diff).
    `SECURE=1` (an `https://` base) gates four additions; an `http://` base skips all four and keeps
    passing unchanged, so `PUBLIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8481` still runs the suite it always ran.
    (Not *byte-identically*: two changes are unconditional — register's `Set-Cookie` gained an
    `expect_nonempty`, and `BASE` is now trimmed of a trailing slash. Neither can change a verdict on a
    run that was passing; the point of the clause is that no https-only ASSERTION fires on an http base.) (a) Step 3: register's
    `Set-Cookie` carries `Secure` + `HttpOnly`, and `POST /api/auth/login` — until now never exercised
    live — is driven into a second jar and asserted the same way, then logged out. (b) Step 10:
    `card_check` requires every URL-valued tag to be `https://` **on `$BASE`**, and the anonymous page
    body to contain no `http://` substring at all (mixed content is invisible: the browser drops the
    media and X drops the player, with the tags still looking correct). (c) Step 10, the gate condition
    itself: a new `card_urls` helper re-parses the ready share page for every URL a crawler or a player
    is handed — the URL-valued §9.1 tags, `<link rel=canonical>`, and the `<video>` `src`/`poster`. The
    last two are **root-relative** (only card tags must be absolute, §9.1), so they are absolutised with
    `urljoin` against `$BASE`; that is what brings `video.mp4` into the sweep, and skipping it would have
    left the player's own source unproven. `data-view-url` is deliberately excluded — POST-only, a GET is
    405. The five expected routes (`/clips/{A}`, `poster.jpg`, `social.mp4`, `/embed/{A}`, `video.mp4`)
    must all be present, and **every URL is fetched back from the public origin with the Discordbot UA
    and again with the Twitterbot UA, and must answer 200** — the only assertion in the suite that
    proves reachability from outside the host rather than from it. (d) Step 11: the embed body carries no
    `http://`, and no-XFO + `frame-ancestors *` are re-asserted on a Twitterbot `HEAD` through the public
    origin. The `E2E PASS` block gains a one-line https summary.
    Two mechanics worth recording. Python's `print` on Windows writes CRLF, so `card_urls > file` fed
    `read -r` a URL with a trailing `\r` and curl answered `URL rejected: Malformed input to a URL
    function`; the helper's output is piped through `tr -d '\r'` (the same discipline `hdr()` already
    uses). And the admin-CLI and bucket steps stay **local** (`dc exec` / `dc run`) at every `BASE`: one
    run drives the public origin over HTTP while reaching into the stack from the host, which is what
    makes forced expiry and the object-count assertions work over a tunnel at all.
    Operational finding from the same run, documented in `DEPLOY.md` §4 rather than changed in code:
    behind cloudflared every request's TCP peer is the Docker bridge gateway (`172.19.0.1` here), so
    without `TRUSTED_PROXIES` the auth and view limiters and the §13 view-dedupe key collapse the whole
    internet onto one client; and `TRUSTED_PROXIES` does **not** move the access log's `remote=` field,
    which is always `r.RemoteAddr` (`httpx.AccessLog`) — the resolved client address is used for limits
    and dedupe only. Correlate requests by `request_id=`.
57. **compose interpolates every §4 variable** (`compose.yaml`, the `app` service's `environment:`;
    §2's block amended in place). Erratum 34 made every `S3_*` value interpolate so `.env` could point
    the app at R2/B2, and `.env.example` plus DEPLOY.md §7 tell operators that `.env` is where values
    are set — but the app service only ever passed **14** of §4's variables through, hardcoding three
    and simply omitting the rest. `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`, `S3_KEY_PREFIX`, `LOG_FORMAT`,
    `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME`, every sweeper/transcode/timeout/session/rate-limit knob: setting any of them
    in `.env` was a **silent no-op**, since compose only substitutes variables that appear in the file
    and the container therefore never received them. Silent is the whole problem — `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`
    stays 4 GiB while the operator believes it is 200 MiB, and `SESSION_COOKIE_NAME=__Host-…`
    (an operator path which erratum 35 exists to make safe) appears to succeed while the
    process keeps the default name. Nothing in the app changed: `config.Load(os.Getenv)` was always
    ready to read them; the environment simply had a 14-key hole in it.
    All of §4 is now present as `${VAR:-<the §4 default>}` — 44 keys, with three deliberate rules.
    (1) `SESSION_SECRET` is **not** added: §4 records it as deliberately absent (nothing is signed), so
    an interpolation line would invite someone to set it. (2) `CLIPPET_LISTEN`, `DATA_DIR` and
    `SCRATCH_DIR` are interpolated for completeness but carry a comment that they are coupled to
    `ports:`, the named volumes and the healthcheck — changing one alone breaks the stack. (3) The
    `:-` (colon) form is kept throughout, including the pre-existing `S3_ACCESS_KEY:
    ${S3_ACCESS_KEY:-${MINIO_ROOT_USER:-clippet}}`, which treats an **empty** `S3_ACCESS_KEY=` exactly
    like unset: a blank credential line next to a live R2 endpoint hands the app the MinIO dev
    credentials, and every call fails authentication citing `clippet`. That is the real shape of the
    footgun DEPLOY.md §7 warns about (it said it backwards before this
    erratum: they claimed the empty value was passed through).
    Verified read-only with `docker compose config`: against an empty env file the 14 previously
    interpolated keys resolve **byte-identically** to before the change, and
    `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES=123 SESSION_COOKIE_NAME=x docker compose config` (and the same two in an
    `--env-file`) now show up in the resolved app environment.
58. **`POST /api/upload` shipped** (`internal/httpapi/upload.go`, `upload_capture.go`, `dto.go`, `router.go`;
    Phase 4 feature #1). The §8.1 row reserved for it is now implemented and its shape is binding:
    - **Auth and limits are literally the same code, not a copy.** `upload.go` is split into `beginUpload`
      (the multipart check, the `Content-Length` too-large and scratch gates, `MaxBytesReader`) and `ingest`
      (spool → ffprobe gate → `PutFile` → `CreateClipWithJob` → rename → `Wake`), and both routes call both.
      `POST /api/upload` runs the same middleware chain as `POST /api/clips` — `RequireUser`,
      `RequireScope("upload")`, the CSRF rule (cookie-authenticated mutations only; a Bearer request skips
      it, §14), the `uploadRate` limiter keyed by **user id**, and no `TimeoutHandler`. One budget, not two:
      spending the hourly upload allowance on `/api/clips` and then switching endpoints answers 429.
      A parity test table drives each failure class (413 `too_large`, 507 `insufficient_scratch`, 415
      `not_a_video`, 503 `unavailable` on a transient probe failure, 400 `empty_video`) through **both**
      routes and requires identical status and code.
    - **The multipart grammar.** Simple text fields `title`, `description`, `ttl_days`, `unlisted` in any
      order, each ≤ 16 KiB, at most 32 fields, all **before** the file part. The file part is the first part
      carrying a `filename`, and must be named **`file`** (what `clippet.sxcu` sends) or **`video`** (the name
      `POST /api/clips` uses; RePlays/OBS scripts differ) — a file part under any other name is 400
      `missing_video`, as is a body with no file part at all. Unknown **text** fields are ignored, so a tool
      that always sends extras still works. A text field **after** the file part is never seen: `ingest` is
      already streaming the body to scratch and answers without reading further, so `-F file=@… -F title=…`
      lands with the title defaulted from the filename. Field values follow §8.2 exactly: `title`/`description`
      go through the same `cleanText` (§20 errata 26/29 messages included), `ttl_days` must be one of
      `0|1|7|30|90` (else 400 `invalid_ttl`), `unlisted` accepts `true/false/1/0/on/off/yes/no`. An **empty**
      value means "not sent" for every field — a tool that always emits its arguments is not forced to invent
      a TTL — so an empty `title` still falls back to the filename without its extension (`Untitled` when
      nothing usable remains) and an empty `ttl_days` takes `DEFAULT_CLIP_TTL`.
    - **The response** is the five §8.1 fields and nothing else: `{"id","url","embed_url","state","expires_at"}`.
      `url` is the share page — the link the tool pastes and the one that unfurls as a player card — and
      `embed_url` the iframe player; both absolute from `PUBLIC_BASE_URL`. No owner-private field is in it
      (no `views`), so the body is safe for a token principal without the erratum-19 dance. Errors are the
      `POST /api/clips` envelopes, codes and statuses unchanged.
    E2E step 18 proves the whole path on the live stack; `TestCaptureUpload*` and `TestMintTokenCarriesSXCU`
    cover the grammar, the defaults, the sxcu shape and the shared pipeline.
59. **`clippet.sxcu` is minted, not served** (`internal/httpapi/sxcu.go`, `token_handlers.go`,
    `web/templates/tokens.html`, `web/static/app.js`). §17 offered "`GET /clippet.sxcu` / an `sxcu` object in
    the mint response"; only the second half can exist. A ShareX custom-uploader file is useful precisely
    because it carries the credential (`Headers.Authorization: Bearer ck_…`), and §14 shows the raw token
    **exactly once**, at mint. A `GET` route could therefore only serve a token-less template the user would
    have to hand-edit, or — far worse — put a live credential in a URL, where it lands in the access log, the
    browser history and any proxy in between. So:
    - `POST /api/auth/tokens` gains an additive `sxcu` object beside `token` (the §8.1 mint row now reads
      `{"id","name","prefix","scopes","token","created_at","last_used_at","sxcu"}`). It is the finished file:
      `Version`, `Name` "Clippet", `DestinationType` **`FileUploader`**, `RequestMethod` POST,
      `RequestURL` = `PUBLIC_BASE_URL + /api/upload`, `Headers.Authorization` = `Bearer <raw>`,
      `Body` MultipartFormData, `FileFormName` `file`, `URL` `{json:url}`, `ErrorMessage` `{json:message}`.
      `DestinationType` names **only** `FileUploader`: ShareX's import offers to activate the destinations a
      file declares, so adding `ImageUploader` would quietly make Clippet the screenshot destination and every
      screenshot would come back **415 `not_a_video`** from the ffprobe gate (§8.3 step 6) — verified against
      the live stack with a PNG. Clippet stores videos; a clip is a file, and that is the one destination it
      claims. `ThumbnailURL` is deliberately **absent** too: ShareX expects an image URL there and the only
      per-clip URLs this endpoint returns are HTML pages, so pointing it at the embed would give every upload
      a broken thumbnail. `Arguments` is absent as well — see erratum 60.
      `GET /api/auth/tokens` is untouched and carries neither `token` nor `sxcu`.
    - `/settings/tokens` reveals a "Download clippet.sxcu" link beside the token it already shows once.
      `app.js` builds the file from that one response — `JSON.stringify` into a `Blob`, `URL.createObjectURL`,
      `<a download="clippet.sxcu">` — and revokes the previous object URL on the next mint. The token
      therefore reaches the file **without a server round trip**: nothing is persisted server-side, no GET URL
      carries it, no access-log line records it. The CSP is untouched (no inline script or style; `app.js`
      only) and the anchor ships hidden with its download name, so the rendered HTML never contains a token.
    - **Amended by erratum 308 (2026-09-18).** There are now TWO mints and still ONE file.
      `clippet admin tokens mint <user> --sxcu` writes this same document to stdout for an operator who
      has no browser session — `newSXCU` became `NewSXCU` and the CLI calls it, rather than carrying a
      second generator that could drift a field. Everything above is unchanged and none of it is
      weakened: the file is still built only at MINT time, it still never exists as a server-side file
      and no GET route serves it; what is new is that the credential may be handed over through a shell
      as well as through a browser download, and the shell puts it on **stdout alone** so a redirect
      captures the file and nothing else does.
60. **A capture title that is exactly the filename is treated as absent** (`internal/httpapi/sxcu.go`,
    `upload_capture.go` `titleUnlessFilename`). The shipped `clippet.sxcu` carried
    `Arguments: {"title": "{filename}"}` — and ShareX expands `{filename}` **with the extension**, so every
    ShareX upload sent `title=2026-09-04_18-22-13.mp4`, `applyCaptureField` stored it verbatim as an explicit
    title, and the share page `<title>`, `og:title`, `twitter:title` and the Discord card all read "….mp4".
    The extension-stripping `defaultTitle` fallback of §8.1 only runs when **no** title is supplied, which is
    the one path the shipped file never took: the feature's own uploader defeated the feature's own naming
    rule. Both halves are fixed.
    - The `sxcu` sends **no `Arguments` at all** (the key is omitted, not emitted empty), so ShareX posts the
      file part alone and the server names the clip. There is nothing a title argument could add: the filename
      is already the only thing ShareX knows.
    - The capture path additionally drops a supplied title that, after the §8.2 trim, equals the
      **path-stripped filename** — the RePlays / OBS-script case, where the tool's title argument is filled
      from the file name and cannot be configured away. Such a title says nothing the filename did not already
      say, so it is treated as absent and the ONE shared `defaultTitle` names the clip (last path segment,
      extension dropped, 200 runes, `Untitled` when nothing usable remains). **Any other title is kept
      verbatim**, extension or not: `title=My clip.mp4` on a file called `raw-000123.mp4` stays `My clip.mp4`,
      because that is a choice the user made rather than an echo of the filename.
    The rule is the capture path's alone. `POST /api/clips` carries an explicit metadata document from the
    browser form, where a title equal to the filename is what the user typed and stays untouched. E2E step 18
    asserts `Arguments` is absent and that no `{filename}` appears in the mint response;
    `TestCaptureUploadTitleEqualToTheFilename` pins both directions of the rule and the `/api/clips` exemption.
61. **`POST /api/clips/{id}/touch` shipped** (`internal/db/clips.go` `TouchClip`, `internal/httpapi/clip_handlers.go`
    `touchClip`, `router.go`; Phase 4 feature #2). The §8.1 row reserved for it is now implemented and its shape
    is binding:
    - **One UPDATE, and its predicate is the whole semantics.**
      `UPDATE clips SET expires_at = ? + ttl_seconds, updated_at = ? WHERE id = ? AND state <> 'deleting' AND
      ttl_seconds IS NOT NULL`, then the row is read back inside the same transaction. The expiry is
      **recomputed from now**, never extended from the old value, so a clip touched a week late gets a fresh
      full TTL rather than a week plus a TTL — the same rule `PATCH {"ttl_days":n}` already followed (§8.2).
      `ttl_seconds` is never touched: a 7-day clip stays a 7-day clip.
    - **A clip kept forever is a 200 no-op.** `ttl_seconds IS NULL` fails the predicate, so `expires_at` stays
      null, `updated_at` is not even stamped, and the unchanged DTO is returned. There is no timer to reset and
      nothing to report as an error — a client (or a copy-link click) that touches a permanent clip is not
      wrong, it is simply asking for something already true.
    - **Every state but `deleting`.** A queued or processing clip's TTL runs exactly like a ready one's (§12
      rule (b) lists `queued` among the candidates), so it is touchable; a tombstone is not, and answers 404
      like every other public read of it. The handler's own 404 covers the clip destroyed between `ownedClip`'s
      lookup and the UPDATE.
    - **The rescue is the point.** `MarkDeletingIfDue` re-verifies expiry inside the tombstone write (erratum
      15), so a touch that lands after `SweepCandidates` has already listed the clip — but before
      `DestroyExpired` reaches it — wins: the tombstone is not written, the clip is `Skipped` (INFO, "no longer
      expired"), and the objects are never deleted. Without erratum 15 this route would be a lie on a 60s
      period; with it, a late touch is a rescue. `sweeper.TestTouchedClipSurvivesTheTick` drives that exact
      ordering — candidate list first, touch second — because only a unit test can place a write between those
      two calls. E2E step 19 proves the half a live stack can prove: a touched clip stops being a candidate and
      survives a full tick, with an identical untouched control destroyed by that same tick standing as the
      evidence the tick ran at all.
    - **Auth, CSRF and limits are the owner-route conventions, unchanged.** `RequireSession` + the CSRF rule +
      the 15s `TimeoutHandler`, i.e. literally the `PATCH`/`retry` chain: a capture token gets 403
      `token_not_allowed` (erratum 19), an anonymous caller 401, a stranger 403, and a bodiless POST needs no
      `requireJSON`. **No rate limiter of its own**, deliberately: the §14 hooks guard the routes that cost real
      work (bcrypt, an encode, a shared IP counter), and this is one indexed UPDATE behind a session and a CSRF
      check — the same exposure `PATCH` has always carried. A per-owner limiter here would only punish the
      behaviour the feature is built to encourage.
62. **The share page's lifetime controls are the owner's, and copying never costs the link**
    (`internal/web/pages.go` `clipModel`, `web/templates/clip.html`, `web/static/app.js`). Feature #2's UI half,
    stated as a contract because two of its rules are failure-mode rules:
    - **Copy link copies first, then touches.** `copyText` runs and the "copied" flash fires before the
      keep-alive request is even started, and `touchIfExpiring` swallows every failure. A network error, a 503,
      a revoked session — none of them may cost the owner the clipboard, because copying the link is what the
      click is for and the timer merely rides along. A failed touch simply leaves the clip on the expiry it
      already had; the next copy resets it.
    - **A clip kept forever is never touched.** The owner section carries `data-expires` only while
      `expires_at` is non-null, and the click sends nothing without it — no request, no log line, no 200 no-op
      round trip for the common permanent case.
    - **A late touch response never overrides a keep-forever.** The two controls sit side by side and the
      keep-alive is fire-and-mostly-forget, so a Copy link whose touch is still in flight when Keep forever's
      PATCH answers holds a DTO that is already stale by one write. `touchIfExpiring` therefore re-checks
      `data-expires` — which Keep forever has just removed — **after** awaiting its reply, and discards the
      response rather than repainting an expiry the server no longer has. (Ordering matters only in this
      direction: a keep-forever answering last is simply correct.) There is no JS test runner in this repo
      (`check.sh` builds Go and shell only), so this rule is pinned here rather than by a unit test.
    - **Keep forever is one click and no reload.** The button PATCHes `{"ttl_days":0}` and `applyLifetime`
      re-renders from the returned DTO: the `data-expiry` line (through the same "expires …"/"kept forever"
      wording the server renders), the button's own visibility, and the "copying the link resets the countdown"
      hint. The clip becomes permanent and the copy button stops touching, in the same tick.
    - **Everything above lives inside `{{if .IsOwner}}`** — `data-touch-url`, `data-expires`,
      `data-keep-forever`, `data-copy-note` — so the anonymous and non-owner page is byte-identical to what it
      rendered before this feature. `TestSharePageReadyAnonymous` asserts the absence of all four by name;
      E2E step 19 asserts the same four on the live anonymous page (`data-touch-url`, `data-keep-forever`,
      `data-expires`, `data-copy-note`) — it checked only the first two until the Phase 5 sweep.
      The **Lifetime** line itself stays where §9.1 put it, visible to everyone: it is a fact about a link
      someone was handed ("this stops working on the 11th"), not a private metric like the view count, and
      hiding it would have changed the public page this erratum promises is unchanged.
63. **`DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL` is validated at boot, and it is a secret** (`internal/config/config.go`
    `discordWebhook`, `DiscordWebhook`; `internal/notify/notify.go`; Phase 4 feature #4). The §4 row is
    binding and so is the reasoning behind its narrowness.
    - **The rules.** Empty (the default) = the feature is off. Non-empty must be: an absolute URL that
      parses; scheme **`https`**; host **exactly** one of `discord.com`, `discordapp.com`,
      `ptb.discord.com`, `canary.discord.com` — compared against `u.Host`, so a port, a subdomain
      (`cdn.discord.com`) or a lookalike (`discord.com.evil.example`) is rejected; **no userinfo**, **no
      query**, **no fragment** — and not a bare trailing `?` or `#` either, which `url.Parse` reports as
      `ForceQuery` and as an empty `Fragment` rather than as a query or a fragment, and which would
      otherwise survive into the value `internal/notify` appends `?wait=true` to (renaming that
      parameter to `?wait`, or swallowing it into a fragment); path exactly `/api/webhooks/{id}/{token}`
      with an all-digits `id` and a single-segment `token` matching **`[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+`** — Discord's
      own URL-safe alphabet. The charset is not decoration: it keeps the configured spelling and the
      spelling `net/url` puts on the wire byte-identical, which is what lets `internal/notify` scrub the
      token out of an echoed error by plain string match. The versioned form `/api/v10/webhooks/…` and
      Discord's alternate `…/slack` and `…/github` endpoints are rejected deliberately: the unversioned
      route is what the "Copy Webhook URL" button produces, and the alternates take a different body
      than the one this feature sends. Anything else is fatal at `config.Load` with a one-line reason.
    - **Why so narrow.** Three reasons, each on its own sufficient. (a) §15's no-call-home claim has to
      stay **auditable** — "outbound traffic goes to `S3_ENDPOINT` and to Discord" is something an
      operator can verify; "outbound traffic goes wherever this variable points" is not. (b) A **typo
      must not leak share links**: this value is pasted from a chat client into a `.env`, and a mistyped
      host would quietly start posting every ready clip's link to somebody else's server with nothing in
      the app looking wrong. (c) The **token is in the path**, so plain `http` would hand the webhook's
      credential to every hop in between.
    - **It is a secret, and it is treated like one.** The token is the last path segment; anyone holding
      it can post to that channel indefinitely. So the raw value lives behind `DiscordWebhook.URL()` and
      the type's `String()`/`LogValue()` render `host/id/(token redacted)` — a `Config` printed with `%v`
      or handed to slog cannot leak it. **No validation error echoes the value** (each one names the rule
      that failed instead). `internal/notify` unwraps `*url.Error` — whose `Error()` embeds the URL it
      failed on — to its cause before rendering any failure, and scrubs the endpoint and the token out of
      every string it returns anyway. Nothing about the webhook reaches `/healthz`, `/readyz`, the admin
      CLI or a job row. The **one** line that mentions it is at boot, INFO:
      `discord webhook configured host=<host> webhook_id=<numeric id>` — the id identifies which webhook
      is live without being usable on its own.
    - The allowed hosts are stored as **bare host names** and the path as a **path string**, so the
      binary still contains no `http(s)://` literal and erratum 27's grep needs no carve-out.
64. **An unlisted clip is never auto-posted, and that is the whole opt-out** (`internal/db/jobs.go`
    `enqueueNotifyTx`, `internal/worker/notify.go` `runNotify`). `unlisted` already means "do not surface
    this": §8.1 hides such a clip from the shared library and the link becomes its only authentication.
    Announcing it to a channel is precisely the surfacing the uploader declined, so the notify job is
    **not enqueued at all** for an unlisted clip. This is why feature #4 adds **no** API surface: no
    `notify` field on the upload DTO, no checkbox beside the TTL select, no per-clip override to
    document — the uploader has already said what they meant, in a field that exists, and one meaning is
    easier to explain than two.
    The rule is checked **twice**, deliberately. At enqueue, inside `FinalizeTranscode`'s transaction,
    reading `unlisted` from the row rather than from the caller — the owner may have flipped it during
    the encode, and the row at commit time is the one that counts. And again in `runNotify` immediately
    before the post, because the job can wait in the queue behind a backoff while the owner changes their
    mind; a clip unlisted since is `skipped: clip is unlisted` (job `done`, INFO). There is no third
    check and no way to re-drive a skipped job: the announcement is a one-shot event tied to becoming
    ready, not a state to reconcile.
    E2E step 20 keeps matrix clip **E** unlisted as the standing control, and `worker`'s
    `TestNotifyNeverEnqueuedForAnUnlistedClip` / `TestNotifySkippedWhenUnlistedSince` pin both checks.
65. **The `notify` job: one commit, three attempts, and never a mark on the clip**
