    (`internal/db/jobs.go` `FinalizeTranscode`/`CompleteJob`/`FailAttemptAfter`/`limitsFor`,
    `internal/worker/notify.go`, `internal/notify/notify.go`). The delivery contract, in full.
    - **Enqueued inside the ready transaction.** `FinalizeTranscode` gained a `notify bool` (the caller's
      one bit: "a webhook is configured"; `db` learns nothing about the URL) and inserts
      `jobs(kind='notify', state='queued', params_json='{}', run_after=now)` in the **same** transaction
      as the ready flip. A crash between "the clip is ready" and "the announcement is queued" is
      therefore impossible: either both happened or neither did. A lost-race finalize (the clip was
      tombstoned meanwhile) enqueues nothing, because it changes nothing.
    - **It never touches the clip** (§5, and the reason the kind list in §5 is now enforced rather than
      promised). `ClaimNonTranscodeJob` — the claim this kind is now reached by (erratum 67) — moves no
      clip at all; `FailAttempt` and `ReleaseJob` move no clip for this kind; `CompleteJob` — the generic terminal write a notify uses — **refuses a transcode job**
      so the coupling stays the exclusive property of `FinalizeTranscode`; `failAttemptTx` runs a
      non-transcode kind's caps through `limitsFor`; and `orphanedProcessingClips` now matches
      `kind='transcode'` so a leftover running notify cannot hide a `processing` clip from the boot
      repair. `db.TestNotifyJobNeverTouchesTheClip` drives all six exit paths (crash / permanent /
      transient `FailAttempt`, `ReleaseJob`, `CompleteJob`, `ReconcileOnStartup`) and requires the clip
      row to come out `reflect.DeepEqual` to what went in. **A failed announcement is not a failed clip.**
    - **The retry table.** Retryable — network error, timeout, **429**, **5xx** — is **crash-class**
      (`attempts++`, the existing `min(30s·2^(n−1), 10m)` backoff) capped at `db.NotifyMaxAttempts = 3`,
      a **constant, not config**: `TRANSCODE_MAX_ATTEMPTS` is a knob about re-running an *encode* on a
      file that may be what crashes the worker, and it has no business deciding how often a chat message
      is retried. A **429**'s `Retry-After` (delta-seconds, including Discord's fractional form, or an
      HTTP-date) becomes a **floor** under that backoff, capped at 5 minutes — `FailAttemptAfter` exists
      for exactly this and can only ever push a retry out, never pull it in. The header value is
      **range-checked before the cast** to a `time.Duration`: `+Inf` (which `ParseFloat` accepts from
      the text `Inf`), `NaN` and anything from ~9.2e9 seconds up would otherwise convert to an
      implementation-defined — in practice **negative** — Duration, and that number would reach a WARN
      line, `jobs.last_error` and the requeue floor. `NaN` and ≤ 0 give 0, anything above the cap gives
      the cap, so what leaves `retryAfter` is always within `[0, 5m]`. Permanent — **any other
      non-2xx**, 400/401/403/404 and **every 3xx** included — fails the job immediately at WARN with the
      status and up to 200 bytes of the response body (the body is Discord's error JSON and is not
      secret; the URL is — so the body is **scrubbed before it is cut**, on a window four times the
      snippet: cutting first leaves the prefix of a secret that straddled the cut in the output, and no
      later scrub can match half of its needle. The scrub itself matches every spelling the endpoint
      and the token can take — as configured, with `?wait=true`, and as `net/url` re-escapes them on
      the wire — longest needle first). Success is any **2xx** → job `done`, INFO
      `discord webhook delivered clip=<id> status=<code>`. Cancellation (shutdown mid-attempt) is **no
      failure**: `ReleaseJob`, counters untouched, retried after the restart. Nothing here is ever
      **ERROR** except a DB error — a rate-limited or misconfigured chat integration does not need a
      human at 3am, which is what ERROR means in §12 and what E2E step 16 gates on.
    - **Per-attempt timeout 10s**, and the run is cancelled by `Stop`, so a wedged Discord cannot hold
      shutdown. It runs on the worker's **non-transcode loop**, never on a transcode loop, so those
      10s are not taken from the encode queue (erratum 67). The run is deliberately **not** in the
      §10.1 run registry: everything `Cancel` waits for
      (ffmpeg reaped, no `PutFile` in flight, no scratch I/O) is absent from a notify job, and
      registering it would make an unrelated retry of the same clip queue behind it (erratum 32). The
      only exposure that trades away is a post landing microseconds after a delete — covered by the
      pre-post re-read and, beyond it, by the `deleting` tombstone 404ing the link immediately anyway.
    - **The client.** Built **only** when the URL is configured (`notify.New` returns nil for an empty
      endpoint), so unset means no `http.Client` exists in the process. It does **not follow redirects**
      (`CheckRedirect` → `http.ErrUseLastResponse`): a 3xx off the validated endpoint is exactly the
      laundering the host allowlist exists to prevent, so it is a permanent failure instead. The request
      is `POST …?wait=true` (Discord answers 200 with the message instead of 204; both are success), with
      a static `User-Agent: Clippet` carrying no version and nothing that identifies the deployment.
    - **The payload** is `{"content": "<title>\n<share URL>", "allowed_mentions": {"parse": []}}` and
      nothing else. No `embeds` object: the share URL unfurls into the **player** card §9.1 already
      builds, which is the entire product promise — an embed object would replace it with a worse one.
      `allowed_mentions.parse` is an **empty list, never `null`** (`null` means "apply the default", i.e.
      everything may be pinged), because the title is user text and a clip called `@everyone gg` must not
      ping a server. The title is additionally neutralised, in two steps.
      (i) **Invisible characters become spaces**: control characters — including the tab/newline/CR
      §8.2's `cleanText` permits — plus the bidi overrides and zero-width characters
      (U+200B–U+200F, U+202A–U+202E, U+2066–U+2069, U+FEFF). One title is one line, the URL always
      stands alone on the second, and nothing rides along invisibly into every copy of the message or
      makes the line read as something other than what it is.
      (ii) **Every markdown metacharacter is backslash-escaped, anywhere in the title, not only at its
      start**: `\` (first, so it cannot re-open what follows), `` ` ``, `*`, `_`, `~`, `|`, `[`, `]`,
      `#`, `>` everywhere, and `-` when it is the first character (mid-title hyphens are ordinary and
      are left alone; the other old block starters are already in the everywhere set). The one that
      makes this a **security** rule rather than a cosmetic one is `[`: Discord renders `[text](url)`
      as a **masked link** in webhook- and bot-authored content — not in a message a human types — so
      an unescaped `[` in a user's title produces a link whose visible text lies about its destination,
      posted under the operator's webhook identity in the operator's channel. Backslash rather than a
      zero-width space because it neutralises a token *twice over*: Discord documents the backslash as
      its markdown escape, and even where that escape did not apply the line no longer *begins* with
      the character, which is what block markdown requires — a zero-width space has only the second
      property. Content is clamped to Discord's 2000-rune limit by trimming the **title** *after*
      escaping (escaping adds runes) and never leaves a **dangling backslash**, which would escape the
      newline and pull the URL onto the title's line; the URL is the payload and is never cut.
      What is **not** neutralised, and is documented rather than fixed: a title containing a URL will be
      auto-linked by Discord and may unfurl alongside the clip. It can no longer *lie* about where it
      points (that was the masked link, and it is escaped), so what is left is a visible link to a
      visible URL; stripping URLs from titles would mangle legitimate ones. The operator's controls are
      `REGISTRATION=closed` and the unlisted opt-out (DEPLOY.md §11).
    - **A job can outlive its configuration** — enqueued with a webhook set, claimed after the operator
      removed it. There is then no client to deliver with, which is the point: the job is resolved
      `skipped: webhook not configured` (INFO) rather than retried forever, and the "unset ⇒ zero
      outbound HTTP" rule holds for old rows too.
66. **`check.sh` asserts there is exactly ONE outbound HTTP call site** (`scripts/check.sh`, the stage
    immediately after erratum 27's URL-literal grep; §15 and §16.1 amended). Erratum 27 stops a *URL*
    from appearing in the binary, which was the whole story while the binary made no outbound request at
    all. Feature #4 changes that, and a rule that says "the only destinations are S3 and Discord" is worth
    only as much as its enforcement: the URL grep alone would happily pass a second `http.Client` pointed
    at a value read from somewhere else. So the new stage greps every non-test `*.go` under `internal`,
    `cmd` and `web` (**scope amended by erratum 96** — `web/static/embed.go` and `web/templates/embed.go`
    are compiled into the binary, and erratum 27's URL grep already covered `web`)
    for `net.Dial*`/`net.Dialer`, an `http.Client`/`http.Transport`/`http.Request` in any of its
    construction spellings (composite literal, `new(…)`, and the bare `http.Client` zero value),
    anything from `net/http/httputil`, `http.NewRequest*`, `http.Post`, `http.PostForm`, `http.Get(`,
    `http.Head(`, `http.DefaultClient` and `http.DefaultTransport`, and **fails unless every hit is
    under `internal/notify/`** — the package named in the grep. Moving the notifier means updating this
    line, which is the point: the exception is written down in one place.
    What this stage is, exactly: **a tripwire over the common call sites, not a proof**. A regex over
    Go source cannot be one — a type alias, an interface value built elsewhere, a `reflect` call or a
    dependency's own client all slip past it. The guarantee is the host allowlist in `internal/config`
    (erratum 63) and the single construction site in `cmd/clippet/serve.go`; this stage is what makes
    the *second* one fail CI instead of passing unnoticed. Two deliberate omissions: `net.Listen`,
    which is `serve.go`'s INBOUND listener and not an outbound call site at all, and the **minio
    module** that carries every S3 request — in scope by design (`S3_ENDPOINT` is the other allowed
    destination), out of reach of a grep over this repository's own packages, and pinned by go.sum
    rather than by this expression. Like erratum 27's grep it carries a planted-file self-test — an `a.go` with
    four spellings that must ALL be flagged (the zero value, `new(…)`, a dialer literal, an `httputil`
    call) and an `a_test.go` that must not be — so a broken expression fails loudly instead of passing
    vacuously. Tests are out of scope — `httptest` is how the notifier is tested without a network.
67. **The job queue is two queues: `transcode`, and everything else** (`internal/db/jobs.go`
    `ClaimJob`/`ClaimNonTranscodeJob`, `internal/worker/worker.go` `Start`/`claimLoop`/`Wake`; §10.1
    amended). Feature #4 put a second KIND of work on a queue built for one, and `ClaimJob`'s
    `ORDER BY j.id` over every kind made the two compete for the same goroutines. With
    `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY=1` — the default — a blackholed Discord then cost **3 × 10s of the only
    loop there is**, per ready clip, with `runNotify` executing inline on the claiming loop; and a
    `notify` queued while clip A finished was claimed *ahead* of the `transcode` of clip B that
    somebody uploaded afterwards, because it had the lower id. Neither is acceptable for a feature
    whose whole promise is "a failed announcement is not a failed clip" (erratum 65): a wedged chat
    integration must not slow the encode down either.
    So the claim is **kind-filtered** and the worker starts **one extra goroutine**: `ClaimJob` takes
    only `kind='transcode'`, `ClaimNonTranscodeJob` takes only the rest, and `Start` spawns
    `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY` loops on the first plus exactly ONE on the second. The two loops share the
    body (`claimLoop`), the stop channel, the `WaitGroup` — so `Stop` still cancels and waits for both
    — and the run registry; they differ only in which half of the queue they can see.
    Two details are load-bearing. (a) The second loop claims by **exclusion**, not by
    `kind='notify'`: every kind belongs to exactly one loop, so a future kind needs no new goroutine
    and an unrecognised kind is still claimed and failed loudly by `refuseKind` instead of sitting
    queued forever. (b) `Wake` nudges **both** channels (a buffered channel of one wakes one waiter,
    and a caller enqueueing work does not know which kind it enqueued), and a transcode that reaches
    `ready` nudges the other loop directly — the ready flip and the notify enqueue are one commit, so
    the announcement goes out at once rather than on the next 5s poll.
    `db.TestClaimIsPartitionedByKind` pins every claim, and
    `worker.TestNotifyDoesNotBlockTheTranscodeLoop` pins the property that matters: a delivery pinned
    in flight, its job older than the transcode's, does not delay the clip.
    **Amended after the #5 verifier: it is THREE queues, not two** (erratum 79). One "everything else" loop
    was right while everything else was a 200 ms HTTP POST; with `trim` and `gif` on it, a multi-minute
    ffmpeg run starved exactly the deliveries this erratum moved off the encode queue to protect. The
    classes are now `transcode` (`ClaimJob`), `media` = trim + gif (`ClaimMediaJob` /
    `ClaimJobOfKinds(MediaKinds())`, an INCLUSION filter) and `notify` (`ClaimNotifyJob` /
    `ClaimJobOtherThanKinds`, still EXCLUSION so an unrecognised kind is claimed and failed loudly rather
    than left queued for ever). `Wake` nudges all three channels; a transcode reaching `ready` nudges the
    notify one directly, as before.
68. **`POST` / `GET /api/clips/{id}/trim` shipped** (`internal/httpapi/trim.go`, `dto.go`, `router.go`,
    `internal/db/trim.go` `TrimParams`; Phase 4 feature #5). The §8.1 rows reserved for the trim are now
    implemented and their shape is binding:
    - **`POST` takes a window in milliseconds on the ORIGINAL's timeline** — `{"start_ms","end_ms"}`, 0
      being the first frame of the FILE THAT WAS UPLOADED, never of the rendition the owner happens to be
      looking at — and answers **202 `{"job_id","state":"queued"}`**. It never touches the clip: the answer
      says a job exists, nothing more, and every fact in the ClipDTO is still true when it lands.
      *(Amended after the #5 verifier; this sentence REPLACES the "clip's timeline" one it refutes. The
      window was validated against the RENDITION's `duration_ms` and then cut from the ORIGINAL at the same
      offsets, so a clip trimmed to 5s–9s and then to 0s–2s came back as the upload's first two seconds —
      footage the first cut had removed — and after one trim the reachable region had shrunk to what was
      left, for ever: re-extending was a 400. The original is retained for the life of the clip (§17,
      "non-destructive editing"), so its timeline is the only coordinate system that does not move under
      the owner, and it is now the one the API, the database and the share page all speak.)*
    - **The timeline is persisted, in three columns** (migration `0003_trim_window.sql`):
      `clips.source_duration_ms` (the original's container duration), `clips.trim_start_ms` and
      `clips.trim_end_ms` (the window the current rendition was cut from; both NULL = the whole original).
      `FinalizeTranscode` fills the length from the source probe and NULLs the window — a transcode renders
      the whole upload — and `SwapRendition` writes the window the run ACTUALLY cut plus, by `COALESCE`,
      the length its own probe measured. The migration backfills conservatively: a ready clip that has
      never completed a trim IS its own original (`source_duration_ms = duration_ms`), one that HAS keeps
      NULL, because its `duration_ms` describes a cut and a guess there would be this very bug.
      `db.TestMigrate0003UpgradesA0002Database` rehearses the live volume's upgrade with both rows in it.
    - **One 400 code, `invalid_trim`, with the rule that failed in the message.**
      `0 ≤ start_ms < end_ms ≤ source_duration_ms`, `end_ms − start_ms ≥ 500`, and **not the cut the clip
      already has**: a window equal to the CURRENT one (`trim_start_ms`..`trim_end_ms`, or
      `0..source_duration_ms` when untrimmed) is a 400 too, because trimming a clip to exactly itself would
      re-encode it and change every ETag for no change at all — the one outcome nobody asked for. A missing
      `start_ms` or `end_ms` is the same 400; there is no default window. When `source_duration_ms` is NULL
      — a row from before 0003 that has already been cut, the only way it can be — the handler stops
      guessing: anything under 24 h is accepted and the worker's probe of the original decides (erratum 78).
    - **The DTO carries both, owner-only.** `source_duration_ms` (int) and `trim` ({`start_ms`,`end_ms`})
      sit beside `views` and are ABSENT for every other caller, for the reason `views` is: together they
      say "this clip is a cut of something longer", which is the owner's editing history and nobody else's.
      Absent is also how "nothing to say" is spelled (an untrimmed clip has no `trim`, an unmeasured
      original no length) — no client has to tell absent from null.
    - **Preconditions are the database's, not a pre-read's.** `db.EnqueueTrim` checks `state='ready'`,
      counts the clip's queued-or-running trim jobs and INSERTs, all in ONE transaction on the
      single-writer `rw` pool — so two clicks (or two tabs, or a retrying client) produce exactly one job
      and the loser gets **409 `trim_in_progress`**; a clip that is not ready gets **409 `not_ready`**.
      `db.TestEnqueueTrimIsSerialisedUnderConcurrency` fires eight simultaneous enqueues and asserts one
      winner. The handler's pre-checks exist only to give a better message.
    - **`GET` reports the LATEST trim job**, not the clip:
      `{"job_id","state":"queued|running|done|failed|cancelled","stage","percent","error","start_ms",
      "end_ms","applied_start_ms","applied_end_ms"}`, `no-store`, and **404 `not_found`** when the clip
      has never been trimmed — a poller must not read "no job" as "finished", exactly as §8.4 forbids for
      progress. `percent` comes from the live registry while the row says `running` and from the persisted
      `stage`'s §10.3 band otherwise (`worker.StagePercent`), so the answer survives a restart. `error` is
      the job's `last_error` and is set only for `failed`. **`cancelled` is in that enum** because the row
      can hold it (§11's lost race: the clip stopped being ready under a running trim), and a poller that
      does not stop on it polls for ever. `start_ms`/`end_ms` are what was ASKED for; the `applied_*` pair
      appears once the job is `done` and is read from the CLIP — what was actually cut, which differs by
      design (a stream copy starts at the keyframe it can start at; a window past the video's end is
      clamped to it, erratum 78).
    - **Auth, CSRF and limits are the owner-route conventions.** `RequireSession` + the CSRF rule +
      `requireJSON` on the POST + the 15s `TimeoutHandler`, i.e. the `PATCH`/`touch` chain: anonymous 401,
      a stranger 403 `forbidden`, a capture token 403 `token_not_allowed` (erratum 19). The **`GET` is
      session-only too** — its `error` field is the operator-facing detail of a failed job, which is the
      owner's and nobody else's. The POST carries the **`upload` limiter**: a trim occupies a transcode
      slot, so it costs what an upload costs.
    - **`GET …/progress` is untouched.** It reports the CLIP, which is `ready` for the whole of a trim, and
      `ProgressDTO` is byte-identical to what it was. The two routes answer different questions and must
      not be confused; `httpapi.TestTrimStatus` asserts both in the same test.
69. **A stream copy is allowed only where it is indistinguishable from the re-encode, and its window is
    snapped to the keyframe** (`internal/transcode/trim.go` `DecideTrim`/`Copy`,
    `internal/transcode/encode.go` `EncodeOptions.Trim`/`Window`). Feature #5's one real decision.
    - **The copy conditions, and why each is there.** A trim is a stream copy only when the ORIGINAL is
      already the shape the pipeline produces — mp4/mov container, `h264`, `yuv420p`, no audio or exactly
      one `aac` track, no rotation, square pixels, and a plan that neither rescales the frame nor caps the
      frame rate — **and** both cut points land within one frame of a keyframe. Each condition is something
      the encode would otherwise have changed: two audio tracks are *merged* by §10.3 and a copy would
      silently drop one; a 1080p60 source copied unchanged would fail `CheckOutput`'s box; a rotated or
      anamorphic source would keep metadata the rendition never carries. Everything else re-encodes, which
      is slower and always right. The keyframe list is only demuxed once every cheap condition has passed
      (`DecideTrim` answers `ReasonNoKeyframes` for exactly that state, and the worker then asks).
    - **The window a copy uses starts at the KEYFRAME, never at the requested millisecond.** `-ss` in front
      of `-i` on a `-c copy` run seeks *backward* to a keyframe and decodes nothing, and because the output
      timestamps are then shifted to zero, `-t` still yields a clip of exactly the requested LENGTH. An
      unsnapped window therefore produces a perfectly plausible file that begins up to a whole GOP early —
      a wrong cut that **no downstream duration check can see**. `DecideTrim` returns the keyframe's own
      timestamp as `Window.Start`; `transcode.TestTrimCopySeekRewindsToTheKeyframe` measures the rewind
      with `-copyts` and pins the refusal.
    - **The re-encode uses the same `-ss` in front of `-i`, where it IS accurate**: since ffmpeg 2.1 the
      frames between the preceding keyframe and the requested point are decoded and discarded, so the cut
      is exact to the frame and still fast. The length is an output `-t`, not `-to`: input seeking shifts
      the output timeline to zero, so an output `-to` would mean the same thing while reading as if it were
      an absolute point in the source.
    - **Tolerance is one frame**, plus an epsilon for ffprobe's six printed decimals. The END may also sit
      at the end of the source, which is the same clean cut as a keyframe. A copy ends on a packet
      boundary, so its output may run a frame or two long; a re-encode is exact.
    - **`EncodeArgs` is unchanged for every transcode.** The window is an option (`EncodeOptions.Trim`,
      nil by default), so a transcode renders the argv it always rendered — asserted directly by
      `TestEncodeArgsCarryTheTrimWindow`.
    - *(Amended by errata 68 and 78.)* The `startMS`/`endMS` `DecideTrim` is given are on the **ORIGINAL's**
      timeline — it always probed the original, so nothing here changes — and they are the window
      `CoverTrim` has already CLAMPED to what the video stream holds, not the raw request. The window
      `DecideTrim` returns is therefore what is cut, what `verify` measures against and what
      `SwapRendition` persists as `trim_start_ms`/`trim_end_ms`: the snap to the keyframe is a real change
      to the result, so it must be a change to what the clip claims about itself. `TrimPlan.DropAudio`
      carries the third of `CoverTrim`'s verdicts into `CopyArgs` (the audio map is simply not emitted);
      the re-encode path expresses the same thing as `AudioMode = AudioNone`, i.e. `-an`.
70. **The trim commits with ONE UPDATE, and everything else follows from that** (`internal/db/trim.go`
    `SwapRendition`, `internal/worker/trim.go` `swap`/`lostRace`). The §5 Phase 4 rule made concrete.
    - **The swap.** `UPDATE clips SET rendition_*, poster_*, width, height, duration_ms, fps_*, has_audio,
      source_duration_ms = COALESCE(?, source_duration_ms), trim_start_ms, trim_end_ms, gif_* = NULL,
      updated_at WHERE id = ? AND state = 'ready'`, plus the job's `done`, in one transaction, guarded
      **also** by the job still being `running`. The window it records is the one that was APPLIED — the
      keyframe-snapped start of a copy, the clamped end of a window past the video (erratum 78) — because
      that is what the next trim, the DTO and the share page must agree about (erratum 68). `clips.state` is not in the SET list and neither is
      `failure_reason`, `ready_at` or either failure counter: the clip is `ready` before the statement,
      during it and after it. `SwapRendition` refuses a `transcode` job outright, so `FinalizeTranscode`
      remains the only writer of the state coupling (§5).
    - **Atomic from every viewer's side.** Every attempt writes to fresh `{r8}` keys (§6), so nothing it
      uploads is reachable until the commit points the row at it. Readers see the old rendition until that
      instant and the new one after it — never a half of either, and never a `ready` row with no object.
    - **Losing the race costs the ATTEMPT, not the clip.** `ok=false` (the clip was tombstoned, or the job
      was cancelled by `MarkDeleting`) means nothing changed; the run then deletes its own two objects and
      cancels the job at INFO, the §11 pattern the transcode's finalize already used. The clip keeps the
      rendition it had.
    - **The superseded keys are deleted after the commit, best effort.** `SwapRendition` returns them; the
      run removes them with a fresh 10s context and logs a WARN on failure. It is never retried — retrying
      a delete is how you delete the wrong thing — so a failure leaves two unreferenced objects under a
      LIVE clip's prefix. That is a **known orphan class**: `clippet admin orphans` reports prefixes with
      no row and rows whose objects are missing, and neither describes an extra object inside a live
      prefix. They are invisible to every route and removed with the clip; the log line
      (`delete attempt output`) is how an operator notices. Documented in DEPLOY §12.
    - **URLs stay, ETags change.** `/clips/{id}`, `/video.mp4`, `/social.mp4` (whose `COALESCE` still picks
      the rendition, `social_key` being NULL until #3) and `/poster.jpg` keep their addresses, so links and
      posted cards keep working; the ETag of each changes — and so does `Last-Modified`, because the
      derived routes date from `updated_at`, which this very UPDATE stamps (§8.5; the #6 verifier's F1):
      a cache that revalidates with `If-Modified-Since` ALONE must not be told 304 about bytes the trim
      replaced, and `ready_at`, which the swap deliberately leaves alone, would have said exactly that.
      With **`public, max-age=3600`** (§8.5's
      `mediaCacheControl` — *corrected after the #5 verifier: this text said `private`, which is what only
      the owner-only `/original` route sends*) already cached players and crawler cards catch up **within
      an hour**. `public` also means a SHARED cache — a CDN, a corporate proxy — may hand out pre-trim
      bytes for that hour, to callers this server never sees. The share page cache-busts the owner's own
      `<video>` so the person who asked for the change is not the one who waits for it.
      **When #3 ships**, `social_key` must be invalidated here too — a dedicated social rendition of the
      untrimmed clip would otherwise survive its own source.
    - **`meta/probe.json` is not rewritten.** It is the record of how the clip was first encoded, it is
      never served, and replacing it with a description of an edit would leave nothing describing the
      upload.
71. **A trim is REGISTERED in the run registry; a notify is not** (`internal/worker/worker.go`
    `runJob`/`withRun`, `internal/worker/trim.go`). Erratum 65 kept `notify` out of the registry because
    everything §10.1's `Cancel` waits for — ffmpeg reaped, no `PutFile` in flight, no scratch I/O — is
    absent from an HTTP POST. A trim is the opposite: it runs ffmpeg, writes scratch and uploads objects,
    which is that list exactly. Leaving it unregistered would let `lifecycle.Destroy` return from
    `Cancel` while our ffmpeg was still writing into a prefix it was about to delete, and the `PutFile`
    that landed afterwards would be an object with no row. So `runRegistered`'s bookkeeping was factored
    into `withRun` and both kinds go through it; `worker.TestTrimIsCancelledSynchronously` pins that
    `Cancel` blocks on an encode that ignores its context. The erratum-32 "at most one live run per clip"
    property extends to trims for free, and costs nothing: a trim only runs on a `ready` clip, which has
    no claimable transcode job to be queued behind it.
    **Its progress is a SECOND registry** (`worker.trimProg`, `Worker.TrimProgress`). §8.4's registry is
    the source of truth for `GET …/progress`, whose subject is the clip — and the clip is `ready`
    throughout a trim, so an encode percentage written there would make a ready clip poll as
    40 %-processing. The trim registry holds only live entries: every terminal outcome forgets its entry
    and leaves the job row as the truth, which is also what makes the API's answer survive a restart.
72. **A trim's caps are two, and a failed trim is not a failed clip** (`internal/db/jobs.go`
    `TrimMaxAttempts`/`limitsFor`, `internal/worker/trim.go` `fail`). `limitsFor` grows a `trim` arm
    pinning BOTH counters to `db.TrimMaxAttempts = 2`, for the reason erratum 65 gave for notify:
    `TRANSCODE_MAX_ATTEMPTS` is a knob about how often an operator will re-run the encode a clip cannot
    exist without, and it has no business deciding how often an *edit of an already-playable clip* is
    retried. Two — one retry — is the budget, and the fallback is better than a third machine attempt: the
    owner asks again from the share page.
    Everything else follows §11 unchanged: a permanent ffmpeg failure fails the job at INFO with the
    reason in `last_error`, a transient one backs off, a panic counts as crash-class, and a cancellation
    releases without counting. `db.FailAttempt` moves no clip for this kind, so at every one of those
    endings the clip is still `ready`, still on the rendition it had, still playable — which
    `worker.TestTrimFailurePreservesTheClip` and `db.TestTrimFailureNeverMarksTheClip` assert from both
    sides.
    **The ERROR sites of a trim run, and why a client cannot reach any of them** *(rewritten after the #5
    verifier, which reached one of them from a browser: this text used to say "the one ERROR … cannot
    happen by design", and the reader had to take that on trust)*:
    (a) `trim job panicked` — a bug in this program;
    (b) `trim exit path panicked` / `trim progress callback panicked` — the same, in the exit path;
    (c) `fail trim attempt` / `set trim job stage` / `cancel trim job after lost race` / `complete trim
    job` / `trim swap gave up` — the database refusing or failing a write that its own guards say must
    work;
    (d) `trim failed: bad_output from our own trim` — the output does not match the window, **over a window
    the source was MEASURED to cover** (`covered`, from `transcode.CoverTrim`'s `Verified`).
    (a)–(c) are ours by construction. (d) is the one an owner used to be able to provoke: a window past the
    end of a video stream that stops before its container does produced an output with no video in it, and
    the `bad_output` guard then blamed us at ERROR — with the raw ffmpeg text in the row the owner reads.
    Erratum 78 turns that case into a CLIENT failure at INFO before ffmpeg is ever run, and narrows this
    branch to the covered case, where the file really did contain what we asked for and did not produce it.
    Everything a FILE or a REQUEST is responsible for — an ffmpeg refusal, an empty window, an output past
    the byte budget — is INFO, and the clip is unharmed at every one of them.
73. **Migration 0002 is five nullable columns, and the upgrade path is the point**
    (`internal/db/migrations/0002_gif.sql`, `internal/db/types.go` `clipCols`/`scanClip`; Phase 4
    feature #6). `clips` gains `gif_key`, `gif_size`, `gif_etag`, `gif_width`, `gif_height`, all
    NULL, no index, no CHECK, no default. `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` is O(1) in SQLite and NULL is
    exactly what "this clip has no preview yet" means, so an installation that has been running on
    0001 upgrades by applying one file to a database full of rows — which is what the live stack's
    volume is, and what `db.TestMigrate0002UpgradesA0001Database` rehearses (it writes a ready clip
    with raw SQL, proves `GetClip` cannot scan it yet, migrates, and reads it back with the five
    fields nil and everything else untouched). E2E step 22 asserts the same on the live volume
    through `clippet admin stats`, which now prints `schema: applied=1,2,3` (0003 is erratum 68's).
    The GIF's dimensions are stored because they are MEASURED from the produced file (the plan says
    at most 480 wide; the height follows the aspect ratio), and its ETag is the hex sha256 computed
    while uploading, like every other object's — the media routes' ETag comes from the row, never
    from the bucket.
74. **The preview is cut from the RENDITION, and that is the one derived artefact not re-derived
    from the upload** (`internal/worker/gif.go`, `internal/transcode/gif.go`). Everything else in
    the system goes back to `original/` — the trim re-derives from it every time precisely so a clip
    cut three times is still one generation from its source (erratum 69). The GIF deliberately does
    not, for two reasons that point the same way: the rendition is already normalised and bounded
    (≤720p, ≤60 fps, faststart mp4), so the preview's cost is bounded by a file WE produced rather
    than by whatever a user uploaded; and a GIF of the clip people are actually watching is the
    honest preview of it, while one cut from a 4K 120 fps original would be a preview of something
    nobody can see. The generation loss is irrelevant — the output is 256 colours at 12 fps.
    **The bounds are the feature.** `transcode.PlanGIF` takes the first `min(6 s, duration)` at
    12 fps, scaled to `min(480, rendition width)` on an even height and never upscaled; `MakeGIF`
    runs `palettegen(stats_mode=diff)` then `paletteuse(dither=bayer:bayer_scale=5)`, with `-t` in
    FRONT of `-i` so a two-hour rendition costs what a six-second one does, and `-loop 0` so the
    result loops forever. Two passes because one is visibly worse (ffmpeg's built-in 216-colour web
    palette bands every gradient); `stats_mode=diff` spends the palette on what MOVES; ordered
    dithering rather than error diffusion because the latter puts different noise in every frame,
    which a GIF cannot compress. Around it: erratum 46's byte cap at **8 MiB** (the run is killed,
    not measured afterwards), a **60 s per pass** hard timeout — `runInstrumented` applies it to each
    of the two passes, so one attempt's ffmpeg ceiling is 2 × 60 s and the two attempts of erratum 75
    are ≤ 4 min of the media loop per clip worst case — and the operator's stall timeout. `Encode`'s
    body became `runInstrumented` so those three guards have ONE implementation for encodes, trims
    and previews; `Encode` renders byte-identical argv and byte-identical failure text
    ("encode_stalled", "output_too_large: the encode wrote past …"), with the label swapped for
    "gif" here.
    Verification is `ProbeGIF` + `CheckGIF`: ffprobe with **`-count_frames`**, because a GIF's
    stream carries no frame count and "did this actually animate" is the one question a preview must
    answer. Counting is cheap only because the plan bounds the file to a few dozen frames.
    **No overlay, no text, no branding, ever** — a watermark is a medal anti-feature, and
    `TestGIFArgsAreTheTwoPassPaletteChain` pins its absence in the argv.
75. **A `gif` job is registered, keeps no progress and cannot cost a clip anything**
    (`internal/worker/gif.go`, `internal/worker/worker.go` `runJob`, `internal/db/gif.go`). It runs
    on the non-transcode loop like `notify` and `trim`, and it is REGISTERED in the run registry for
    erratum 71's reason exactly: ffmpeg, scratch and a `PutFile` are the set of things §10.1's
    `Cancel` promises to have finished when it returns, so an unregistered one would let
    `lifecycle.Destroy` delete a prefix our ffmpeg was still writing into
    (`worker.TestGIFIsCancelledSynchronously`).
    It writes to **no progress registry at all** — not §8.4's, whose subject is the clip (`ready`
    throughout), and not the trim's second one: the job's only public state is `queued` / `running` /
    `failed` on the route, and a percentage nobody can ask for is a registry nobody can evict. Stages
    are persisted (`acquire`/`gif`/`verify`/`store`/`finalize`) so `admin ls` says where a failure
    happened.
    Its caps are `db.GIFMaxAttempts = 2` on BOTH counters, a constant for the reason
    `NotifyMaxAttempts` and `TrimMaxAttempts` are: `TRANSCODE_MAX_ATTEMPTS` is a knob about the
    encode a clip cannot exist without. `db.FailAttempt` moves no clip for this kind, so at every
    ending — permanent, transient cap, panic, cancellation — the clip is still `ready`, still on its
    rendition, still playable, and only the preview is missing. Scratch is per-attempt and the run
    removes only its own three files: unlike the transcode and the trim, a gif run does not own the
    clip's scratch dir.
76. **The commit is guarded by the rendition's ETag, and a trim throws the preview away**
    (`internal/db/gif.go` `SetGIF`, `internal/db/trim.go` `SwapRendition`). `SetGIF` writes the five
    columns of a clip that is still `ready` AND still on the rendition the job read when it started,
    in one UPDATE whose predicate carries that ETag. Without it a trim landing mid-run would publish
    a perfectly valid GIF of frames that no longer exist — and **nothing downstream could ever tell**:
    it is the right size, the right shape, and a picture of a clip nobody has any more. The refusal
    is not a failure: the attempt deletes its own object and resolves the job `done`/`skipped` with
    the reason, because there is nothing to retry and the route will queue a fresh job the next time
    somebody asks. For the same reason `SwapRendition` NULLs `gif_*` and returns the old key among
    the superseded ones, so the object goes with the row that referenced it (E2E step 22 watches the
    prefix shrink).
    **The card tags do not change.** `og:image` stays the poster JPEG: an animated `og:image` is not
    honoured by Discord or X for a video card — they render the player from `og:video` /
    `twitter:player` and use the still — so swapping it would trade a working card for a worse one.
    The preview is a thing the OWNER makes and hands out, not part of the unfurl.
    **`gif_url` is a fact, not an address** (§8.2), which is why it is a nullable top-level field
    rather than a member of `urls`: everything in `urls` answers at any time, while `null` here is
    how a client knows to ask the route to make one. It is the same absolute URL for every caller —
    a preview is as public as the poster.
    **The public route may start work, and two guards make that safe.** `db.EnqueueGIF` admits at
    most ONE live gif job per clip in a single `rw` transaction, so a hundred simultaneous first
    requests produce one job; and the job is bounded by construction (erratum 74). On top of that the
    route carries the **`view` limiter** (60/min/IP), so a stranger cannot spend an operator's queue
    by walking clip ids. A `gif` job that has already FAILED is REPORTED (503 `gif_failed` with the
    redacted reason), never re-enqueued — otherwise every visitor of a page linking the preview would
    re-run a doomed encode. The owner's `POST …/gif` is the retry, and 409 `gif_in_progress` is the
    conflict that separates it from the GET: the GET says "come back" to the same state because that
    caller wants the picture, while the POST asked to START one and did not. *(Amended after the #6
    verifier: `gif_in_progress` is not its ONLY 409 — `EnqueueGIF` refuses a clip that is not `ready`
    with `ErrStateMismatch`, which both routes answer 409 `not_ready`, so a POST on a `processing`,
    `failed` or `queued` clip gets that instead.)*
    **The preview's `Last-Modified` follows `updated_at`, not `ready_at`** (§8.5; the #6 verifier's
    F1). `SetGIF` stamps `updated_at` in the same UPDATE, so a regenerate that DID change the bytes
    moves the date with them — otherwise a cache revalidating with `If-Modified-Since` alone could be
    told 304 about a preview it no longer had. The deterministic case costs nothing either way: the
    ETag is identical, so `If-None-Match` still settles it in one 304.
    A regenerate of an unchanged rendition is **deterministic**: the bytes, and therefore the ETag,
    are identical, so no cache anywhere is churned — only the key changes (a fresh `{r8}` per
    attempt, §6). E2E step 22 asserts exactly that.
77. **Embed params are flipped on, and autoplay implies muted** (`internal/web/pages.go`
    `embedOptions.resolve`/`Preload`, `web/templates/embed.html`; Phase 4 feature #8). §9.2's
    parsed-and-ignored `autoplay`, `muted` and `loop` now render the `<video>` attributes of the same
    names. The implication is browser policy, not taste: Chrome, Safari and Firefox all refuse to
    start an unmuted video without a user gesture, so `?autoplay=1` alone would produce a player that
    silently does nothing — which looks like a bug from every side and is the one outcome a
    stable-since-Phase-1 URL shape must not suddenly produce. Autoplay also switches `preload` from
    `metadata` to `auto`: a player that is about to start by itself needs the media, not just its
    header.
    `parseEmbedOptions` is UNCHANGED and still reports exactly what the URL said (`1`, `true`, `yes`,
    `on` or an empty value are true; anything else is false) — the implication lives in `resolve()`,
    so the parser's table test keeps pinning the wire format and the template gets what the browser
    needs. Defaults are unchanged, the markup is otherwise identical, the CSP is untouched, and the
    SHARE page still ignores the same query: a person opening a link did not ask for autoplay.
78. **A trim window is checked against what the SOURCE HOLDS, and a window it cannot honour is the
    CLIENT's, not ours** (`internal/transcode/trim.go` `CoverTrim`/`ErrWindowEmpty`,
    `internal/transcode/probe.go` `extentOf`, `internal/worker/trim.go` `probeSource`; the #5 verifier's
    F2). A container routinely outlives its streams — two seconds of video muxed with eight of audio is a
    legal, ordinary file, and so is a screen capture whose encoder stopped early — so `HasDuration` /
    `DurationUS`, which describe the CONTAINER, cannot answer "is there any video in the seconds this
    owner asked for". A window past the video's end therefore reached ffmpeg and came back as an output
    with **no video stream at all**: `level=ERROR msg="trim failed: bad_output"` with a raw ffmpeg dump in
    the field the OWNER reads, from a request the API had every reason to accept. An owner could put an
    ERROR line in an operator's log at will, and the E2E's own log gate with it.
    `ProbeResult` now carries `Video` and `Audio` `StreamExtent` (each stream's `start_time` + `duration`;
    `Known` false when it declared none), and `CoverTrim` answers three things before ffmpeg is asked
    anything:
    - **no video in the window** (or under 100 ms of it) → `ErrWindowEmpty`, wrapped as `ErrPermanent`:
      the attempt fails at INFO with the plain sentence *"there is no video in the part of the original
      you asked for"*, no retry, no counter, no ERROR, and no ffmpeg run at all;
    - **video that stops INSIDE the window** → the window is CLAMPED to it, and the clamped window is what
      is cut, verified against and persisted. The owner gets the footage that exists rather than a file
      whose own duration guard then calls our output bad;
    - **audio that does not reach the window** → `DropAudio`: the map is dropped (`CopyArgs`) or the plan's
      `AudioMode` goes to `AudioNone` (`-an`), and the cut is silent, which is what that part of the source
      is.
    A stream with no measured extent constrains NOTHING: the window is used as asked and `Verified` stays
    false, which is precisely the flag that keeps a later `bad_output` from being blamed on this server
    (erratum 72's list). `transcode.TestCoverTrimAgainstRealStreamExtents` builds both mismatched shapes
    with ffmpeg and pins all three verdicts on real probes; `worker.TestTrimRefusesAWindowWithNoVideo` and
    `worker.TestTrimDropsAudioOutsideTheWindow` pin the run's behaviour, including that no ERROR is logged.
79. **`TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY` bounds ffmpeg PROCESSES, and the media kinds have a loop of their own**
    (`internal/worker/worker.go` `Start`/`acquireFFmpeg`/`sem`, `internal/db/jobs.go`
    `ClaimJobOfKinds`/`ClaimJobOtherThanKinds`; the #5 verifier's F4, amending erratum 67). Two things were
    wrong with putting `trim` and `gif` on erratum 67's single "everything else" loop.
    (a) **The limit stopped being a limit.** DEPLOY §7 tells an operator that `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY=1` —
    the default — means one ffmpeg at a time, and the verifier ran a trim and a transcode simultaneously on
    exactly that install. The number named the transcode LOOPS, and a second class of ffmpeg work had
    appeared beside them. Now a single `chan struct{}` of `max(1, TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY)` slots gates every
    stage that spawns ffmpeg: a transcode takes one for its whole run (behaviour unchanged — there are as
    many slots as transcode loops), a trim and a gif take one around cut/verify/poster and give it back
    before uploading, because moving bytes is not what an operator sized a CPU limit for. Holding it
    through `verify` and `poster` is deliberate: those read and write the very files the cut produced, so
    releasing earlier would let a second ffmpeg loose on scratch this attempt has not finished with.
    `worker.TestFFmpegSlotsBoundTrimAndTranscodeTogether` races a trim against a transcode and asserts the
    PEAK overlap, which is the only thing that can prove the promise.
    (b) **A trim starved every notify.** The loop that erratum 65 kept out of the run registry so a
    blackholed Discord could not cost the encode 30 s was now also the loop a three-minute trim sat on.
    Kinds are therefore claimed by CLASS: `MediaKinds()` = {`trim`, `gif`} on a media loop, everything else
    on the notify loop (still by exclusion, so an unknown kind is claimed and failed loudly). Media work
    can queue behind media work — it is nobody's blocking path — while a delivery, which is 200 ms of
    network, never waits on ffmpeg. `worker.TestTrimDoesNotStarveTheNotifyLoop` pins it with a trim held
    inside ffmpeg while the announcement goes out.
    A run waiting for a slot logs `waiting for an ffmpeg slot` at INFO, and a wait that Stop will never
    satisfy ends in the ordinary release path (`errStopping`), not a failed attempt.
80. **What the OWNER is told about a failed trim is a fixed vocabulary; the detail stays in the log**
    (`internal/worker/trim.go` `ownerReason`/`fail`; the #5 verifier's F2, second half). `jobs.last_error`
    of a trim is the one failure text this system shows a person who is not an operator (`GET …/trim`'s
    `error`, rendered on the share page), and it was carrying whatever the stage happened to say — an
    ffmpeg stderr tail, a byte count, a redacted-but-recognisable path. `ownerReason` maps every ending
    onto one of seven sentences (`msgNoWindow`, `msgTooLarge`, `msgBadOutput`, `msgMedia`, `msgDisk`,
    `msgStorage`, `msgInternal`), chosen from markers this codebase itself writes — `bad_output`,
    `output_too_large`, `insufficient scratch`, `ErrWindowEmpty` — with the STAGE as the fallback, so an
    error nobody anticipated still comes out as a sentence rather than as whatever it said.
    The detail is not lost: it is a `detail` field on the same log line the outcome writes (INFO for a
    permanent failure, WARN for a requeued one, ERROR only for erratum 72's (d)), with scratch paths
    redacted as before. An operator reads the log; a visitor reads a sentence.
81. **Tags are a grammar, a filter and a cursor — and deliberately not a surface** (`internal/db/tags.go`,
    `migrations/0004_tags_collections.sql`, `internal/db/clips.go` `ListClips`/`encodeCursor`/`decodeCursor`/
    `NewClip.Tags`/`ClipPatch.Tags`, `internal/httpapi/dto.go`/`clip_handlers.go`/`upload.go`/
    `upload_capture.go`, `internal/web/pages.go`, `web/templates/{index,clip}.html`, `web/static/app.js`;
    Phase 4 feature #9, first half). §17 sketched `clip_tags(clip_id, tag)` and `GET /api/clips?tag=`; this
    is what was built and it is binding.
    - **The grammar.** After `strings.TrimSpace` and an **ASCII-only** lower-casing, a tag must match
      `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,31}$`; at most **10** per clip; duplicates collapse; the stored set is sorted.
      Anything else is 400 `invalid_tags` and the message NAMES the offending value (Go-quoted and
      truncated, so client text cannot break out of the JSON string) — a rejected list is useless to
      somebody who cannot see which word in it was wrong. Two rules deserve their reasons.
      The lower-casing is ASCII-only *because* a full Unicode fold maps characters that look nothing like
      `a`–`z` onto `a`–`z` — U+212A KELVIN SIGN → `k`, U+0130 → `i̇` — so two visibly different tags would
      silently become one row, and `db.TestCleanTagGrammar` pins both of those as rejections. And the
      leading character may not be `-` so a tag can never be mistaken for a flag or for a path segment.
      The cap counts SURVIVING tags, applied after the collapse: sending the same word twelve times is a
      sloppy client, not a client asking for twelve tags.
    - **The stored form IS the wire form.** `clip_tags` holds only normalised values, so `WHERE tag = ?` is
      an exact match needing no `COLLATE` and no function index, and the `(tag, clip_id)` index
      (`clip_tags_tag`) is what the filter runs on — *as an uncorrelated IN-list; amended by erratum 84,
      which replaced the correlated `EXISTS` this entry originally described and under which that index was
      unreachable*. `SetClipTags`, `CreateClipWithJob` and `UpdateClipMeta` all re-clean rather than
      trust, and the last two write the tags in the SAME transaction as the row — a clip is never briefly
      visible without the tags it was uploaded with, and a rejected tag fails the whole create.
    - **`ClipDTO.tags` is always present, sorted, `[]` when none, and NOT owner-private.** It is not
      `views`: a tag is part of what the clip IS rather than a measurement of who watched it, and this DTO
      is already owner-or-link gated, so it renders for every caller the DTO reaches. `[]` rather than
      `null` keeps a client from needing a null check and keeps a `GET` round-tripped into a `PATCH`
      meaning what it said. Every route that answers with a ClipDTO carries them — `PATCH`, `touch` and
      `retry` included, so a client that re-renders from the reply never watches a clip lose its tags
      because somebody pressed "keep forever". The list route reads the whole page's tags in ONE
      `TagsForClips` query rather than one per row.
    - **Three write paths, one validator.** `PATCH {"tags":[…]}` replaces the WHOLE set (`[]` clears,
      absent leaves it alone — there is no add-one verb, because the editor driving it is a text field
      holding the whole list and a partial verb would need a merge rule nobody can see in the box they are
      typing into); `metadata.tags` on `POST /api/clips`; and a comma-separated `tags` field on
      `POST /api/upload`, where an empty field means "not sent" like every other capture field (erratum
      58). The capture 201 is still erratum 58's five fields exactly — a tool reads the set back from
      `GET /api/clips/{id}` if it wants it.
    - **The filter narrows; it never widens.** `?tag=` on `GET /api/clips` and on the library page applies
      an id IN-list over the tag index INSIDE the existing visibility clause (erratum 84), so a tag can no more reveal
      somebody else's unlisted clip than an empty filter can. **The cursor carries the filter it was minted
      under**: a page token from a filtered list spent without the filter (or under a different one) is
      `invalid_cursor`, because continuing with it would page through positions that mean nothing in the
      other list and silently skip rows. Unfiltered cursors keep their original two-field shape, so tokens
      minted before this feature still decode.
    - **The page rules differ from the DTO's, and that is §9.** The OWNER's share page carries a
      comma-separated editor that PATCHes and re-fills itself from the reply (the server normalises, so the
      reply is the authority). The ANONYMOUS share page carries **no tag markup at all** — not the editor,
      not a read-only chip, not the words — because a watch page is the clip and nothing else; an anonymous
      view therefore costs no tag query either. The library renders each row's tags as plain chips linking
      to `/?tag=x` and stays read-only: tags are edited where the clip is. An illegal `?tag=` on the
      library is a 303 to `/`, exactly as a garbage cursor is — there is nothing to render for a word no
      clip can carry, and a page is not an API.
    - **The anti-features, stated as absences.** There is no `/tags/{tag}` page, no tag listing, no count
      beside a tag, nothing trending, and no tag surface of any kind beyond the two filters above. Tags of
      a clip are reachable only through its DTO, its owner's page and the library — i.e. to logged-in users
      of the instance. `db.TestCleanTagGrammar` / `TestCleanTagsCap` / `TestListClipsTagCursor`,
      `httpapi.TestPatchTags` / `TestTagsAreNotOwnerPrivate` / `TestListClipsTagFilter` /
      `TestCaptureUploadTags`, `web.TestSharePageTagsAreOwnerOnly` / `TestIndexTagFilter` and E2E step 23
      cover it.
82. **A collection is an ordered list of links, its id is the whole access control, and "not yours" is 404**
    (`migrations/0004_tags_collections.sql`, `internal/db/collections.go`, `internal/httpapi/collections.go`,
    `internal/urls/urls.go` `Collection`, `internal/web/{pages,meta,server}.go`,
    `web/templates/collection.html`, `web/static/app.js`; Phase 4 feature #9, second half). §17 sketched
    `collections(id slug, owner_id, title, unlisted, created_at)` and an SSR `/c/{id}`. Five decisions turn
    that into the shipped shape, and four of them are departures worth their reasons.
    (a) **There is no `unlisted` column.** §17 offered one by analogy with clips, but a collection is never
    listed to anyone except its owner: `GET /api/collections` is the caller's own, there is no browse page,
    no other user's list and no route anywhere that enumerates collections. A flag distinguishing "listed"
    from "unlisted" would therefore have nothing to distinguish. What remains is the same access control a
    clip link has: an `ids.New()` slug — 12 crypto-random base62 characters, ≈71.4 bits (§7) — and the link
    is the auth. Adding the column later costs one `ALTER TABLE`; shipping it now would have cost a field
    in the DTO, a control on the page and a paragraph in DEPLOY explaining a distinction with no observable
    consequence.
    (b) **"Not there" and "not yours" are the same 404 on the mutating routes**, where clips answer 403.
    That is not an inconsistency, it is what the queries are: `PATCH`, `DELETE` and `PUT …/clips` scope by
    owner (`WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ?`), so the two cases are literally one result and one answer, from
    one statement. A clip route cannot do that — its `GET` is public and the row it reads IS the answer, so
    it knows the row exists before it checks who is asking, and 403 is the honest reading there. Nothing is
    leaked either way: both ids are public by construction.
    (c) **The public `GET` renders PUBLIC ClipDTOs, for every caller including the owner.** `views` is
    absent from a collection body entirely. *(Amended by the Phase 5 sweep: `clips` is a `*[]ClipDTO`, so
    the ONE route that renders members always emits the key — `"clips":[]` for an empty collection — while
    the shell routes leave it nil and omit it; as a plain `[]ClipDTO` with `omitempty` an empty collection
    was indistinguishable from a shell, which contradicted §8.1's "with clips" and the tags doctrine that
    `[]` is how empty is spelled. `httpapi.TestCollectionMembership` asserts the literal `"clips":[]`.)* The reason is the anti-feature rule read forwards: a collection
    exists to be pasted, so the bytes an owner sees while curating must be the bytes a stranger sees, and a
    list of links is not where a private count belongs. Members are every state except `deleting`, so a
    clip that is still encoding stays in the list its owner put it in — like the library, and unlike
    vanishing for two minutes.
    (d) **One PUT replaces the whole ordered membership**, in one transaction: ≤200 ids, duplicates collapse
    keeping the FIRST position, positions are assigned 0..n-1 so they are dense by construction and nothing
    ever renumbers, and every id must be a clip the SAME user owns and that is not a tombstone.
    *(Amended by the Phase 5 sweep: `clip_ids` is REQUIRED. `{"clip_ids":[]}` is the deliberate "empty this
    collection"; `{}` and `{"clip_ids":null}` are 400 `invalid_request` rather than a silent wipe. Pure PUT
    semantics would defend reading an absent key as "the resource is now empty", but PATCH on the sibling
    route reads an absent key as "unchanged", and one body meaning "leave it alone" on one route and
    "delete everything" on its neighbour is a footgun rather than a convention.)* An unknown
    id, a malformed one, a tombstoned one and another user's clip are ONE answer — 400 `not_your_clip`
    naming the first offender — so the route is not an existence oracle for the clip id space. There is no
    add-one or remove-one verb for the same reason `tags` has none: the control is a picker holding the
    whole list.
    (e) **Deletion is two cascades and no code.** `collection_clips` cascades from both `collections` and
    `clips`, so deleting a clip (owner `DELETE` or a TTL sweep, §12) removes it from every collection it was
    in, and deleting a collection removes its rows and **not one clip** — a list is not its links. The
    sweeper gained no step; `db.TestClipDeleteCascadesMembership` and E2E step 23 prove both directions on
    a real `PRAGMA foreign_keys(1)` connection. `clip_count` is a correlated subquery over the live members
    rather than a stored counter, because a clip can leave a collection with nothing asking it to and a
    counter nobody updates on that path lies.
    Caps are guards, not product: 500 collections per user (counted and inserted in one transaction on the
    single-connection writer pool, so two concurrent creates cannot both read 499 → 409
    `too_many_collections`) and 200 clips per collection. The page is §9.4. The membership picker is
    rendered server-side from `db.ListOwnerClips` rather than fetched from `GET /api/clips` in JS as the
    brief sketched: the API refuses any clip the caller does not own, so the library's visibility set is the
    wrong set to offer, and SSR removes a request, a filter and a failure mode from a control that is a
    `<select>`. Its options put the CURRENT members first in their current order, because a
    `<select multiple>` reports its selection in document order — that is what makes saving an unchanged
    selection a no-op rather than a reshuffle. Delete is a two-click button (`Delete` → `Really delete`,
    re-arming after 5 s) and never `confirm()`: these pages are CSP-clean and modal-free, and a browser
    dialog is neither styleable nor dismissable by the page.
83. **Backups are one command and a file copy, and `restore-check` is the only subcommand that needs
    nothing** (`internal/db/backup.go`, `cmd/clippet/admin.go` `backup`/`restoreCheck`,
    `cmd/clippet/main.go` dispatch; Phase 5 ops). `clippet admin backup <path>` is SQLite's
    `VACUUM INTO` on the rw pool's single connection: it runs inside a read transaction, so the
    output is the database as of one instant — WAL content included — taken while `serve` keeps
    writing from the other process, and it is ONE file with no `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars. The command
    writes to `<path>.part-<r12>` and renames, so an interrupted run leaves a `.part-…` file rather
    than a truncated file under the name an operator would restore from, and it refuses a
    destination that exists (checked before, and again immediately before the rename; `VACUUM INTO`
    refuses too, so the guard is belt-and-braces rather than the only one). It prints the size and
    `schema: applied=…`.
    `clippet admin restore-check <path>` is the dry run of a restore: `db.Inspect` opens the file
    with `mode=ro`, runs `PRAGMA integrity_check`, and reports the applied migrations and the
    users/clips/jobs counts. Everything that is not a sound Clippet database is an error and exit 1
    — a text file (`file is not a database (26)`), an empty file (valid SQLite, no
    `schema_migrations` → "this is not a Clippet database"), a truncated backup, a directory, a
    missing path. It is dispatched in `main.run` BEFORE `config.Load` and in `runAdminWith` before
    the database is opened, because its entire purpose is to validate a backup somewhere else: the
    documented invocation is a throwaway `docker run --rm -v <dir>:/backup:ro clippet-app:local
    admin restore-check /backup/<file>` in a container with no `.env`, no bucket and no database of
    its own. It expects a file with no live `-wal` sidecar (a backup, or a stopped app's database);
    pointed at a database a running app is writing to, SQLite may refuse the read-only open, which
    is the correct answer rather than something to work around.
    There is deliberately **no** `admin restore`: putting the file back is `rm` + `cp` into the
    volume while the app is stopped (DEPLOY.md §15.4), and the command that overwrites a live
    database should be one the operator typed. The ORDER of the two halves is documented there too,
    and it is derived, not asserted: an upload writes its objects before its row (§8.3) and a
    destroy deletes objects before the row (§12), so a hot pair should take the DATABASE first and
    the BUCKET second — then anything uploaded during the window is an orphan (harmless,
    `admin orphans --delete` reclaims it) instead of a row whose objects were never captured. On
    restore the order reverses: bucket first, so the app never sees a row it cannot serve.
    Tests: `db.TestBackupOfAQuietDatabaseIsExact` (row counts, schema, no sidecars, refuses to
    overwrite), `db.TestBackupWithAConcurrentWriter` (snapshot taken under a writer goroutine is
    internally consistent — `jobs == clips`, since `CreateClipWithJob` writes both in one
    transaction — and its count lands inside the window), `db.TestInspectRefusesWhatIsNotABackup`,
    `TestAdminBackupAndRestoreCheck` and `TestRestoreCheckNeedsNoConfiguration` (the config-free
    dispatch, proven through `run()` with every required variable unset).
84. **The tag filter is an uncorrelated IN-list, because that is the only shape that reaches the index
    migration 0004 built for it** (`internal/db/tags.go` `tagFilterSQL`, `internal/db/clips.go`
    `listClipsSQL`, `migrations/0004_tags_collections.sql`; amends erratum 81, whose "the `(tag, clip_id)`
    index is what the filter runs on" was true of the intent and false of the SQL). As first shipped the
    predicate was `AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM clip_tags t WHERE t.clip_id = clips.id AND t.tag = ?)`. That
    subquery is CORRELATED: it names `clips.id`, so SQLite evaluates it once per candidate `clips` row and
    the only index it can drive from is the PRIMARY KEY `(clip_id, tag)` — `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` reads
    `SCAN clips` / `SEARCH t EXISTS USING COVERING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_clip_tags_1 (clip_id=? AND
    tag=?)`. `clip_tags_tag` on `(tag, clip_id)`, added by migration 0004 for this one query, was never
    touched, and a filtered list cost a full scan of `clips` plus a probe per row (≈6.5 ms against ≈1.0 ms
    on a 20k-row library).
    The shipped predicate is `AND clips.id IN (SELECT clip_id FROM clip_tags WHERE tag = ?)`. It is
    semantically identical — `clip_tags.clip_id` is `NOT NULL`, so the `IN` has no three-valued-logic
    difference from the `EXISTS`, and it still cannot duplicate a row the way a join would — but it
    mentions no outer column, so it is evaluated ONCE: `LIST SUBQUERY` / `SEARCH clip_tags USING COVERING
    INDEX clip_tags_tag (tag=?)`, and the outer query becomes `SEARCH clips USING INDEX
    sqlite_autoindex_clips_1 (id=?)`. The visibility clause and the cursor clause are untouched and still
    apply to every row that survives, so the "narrows, never widens" rule of erratum 81 is unchanged, as is
    the cursor's filter binding.
    The statement is built by `listClipsSQL(filtered bool)` rather than being a literal inside `ListClips`
    so that a test can hand the EXACT query the list route runs to `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`:
    `db.TestListClipsTagFilterUsesTheTagIndex` asserts the plan names `clip_tags_tag` and does not say
    `CORRELATED`. Asserting on the returned rows would have passed under either predicate, which is why the
    original was wrong for two features without a failing test — a plan is not observable through the API,
    so it needs a test that looks at the plan.
85. **A 416 keeps the headers of the ERROR, not of the object** (`internal/httpapi/media.go`
    `writeRangeError`; amends §8.5 and §8.1's `/original` row, which describe the headers of a
    *representation* and were being applied to an error envelope). `serveObject` sets `Content-Type`,
    `ETag`, `Accept-Ranges`, the cache headers and — for `/original` — `Content-Disposition:
    attachment; filename="<sanitized>"` BEFORE the range gates run, because those are the headers of the
    200 that normally follows. When a range turns out to be unsatisfiable, `writeRangeError` replaced
    `Content-Type` and `Cache-Control` and set `Content-Range: bytes */size`, but left the rest standing:
    a 416 on `GET /api/clips/{id}/original` therefore arrived as a JSON error body wearing the clip's own
    `attachment; filename=`, and a download client saved that envelope to disk under the clip's filename.
    The user found a "video" that was a 90-byte JSON error.
    `writeRangeError` now deletes `Content-Disposition`, `ETag` and `Last-Modified` before writing.
    Content-Disposition is the one with observable teeth; the two validators go with it because they
    describe the OBJECT and a cache must never be able to revalidate the object against an error body —
    they were also asymmetric between the two 416 paths, which is its own bug. One call site covers both
    paths: the gates in `serveObject` (too many ranges, a zero-length suffix — answered before
    `http.ServeContent` is reached) and the stdlib 416 that `rangeErrorWriter` intercepts.
    `Content-Range`, `Cache-Control: no-store` and the JSON envelope are unchanged, as is "a 416 costs
    zero storage calls" (erratum 38). `httpapi.TestRangeErrorDropsTheObjectHeaders` asserts the 200 sets
    the three headers and that all four 416 shapes — both gates, both stdlib paths — drop them.
86. **`admin users` and `admin users prune`: the inventory, and the one command that deletes a user**
    (`internal/db/users.go` `ListUserSummaries`/`PruneUsers`, `internal/db/db.go` `ErrInvalidPattern`,
    `cmd/clippet/admin.go` `users`/`usersPrune`/`printUsers`; DEPLOY §8; Phase 5 ops). Automation leaves
    users behind: every `scripts/e2e.sh` run registers three throwaway accounts and deletes its clips but
    not its users, so a long-lived stack accumulates rows nothing can remove. There is deliberately **no
    HTTP route** for this and there never will be — deleting a user is not a product surface, it is
    housekeeping, and the account that does it is the operator's shell.
    `clippet admin users` prints one line per user: id, username, `created`, and the counts of clips
    (every state, tombstones included), collections and LIVE (unrevoked) API tokens. A revoked token is
    not a credential, so counting it would tell the operator the wrong thing about what can still upload.
    `clippet admin users prune <pattern> --older-than D --no-clips` deletes users who own NOTHING. All
    three arguments are required and none has a default, which is the whole design:
    - `<pattern>` is a SQL `LIKE` over `username` (`%`, `_`; case-insensitive, the column being
      `COLLATE NOCASE` — the same rule registration matches under). A blank pattern is `ErrInvalidPattern`
      and exit 2 rather than "everybody": an operator who means everybody types `%`, and a typo that
      expands to the whole table must not be spellable.
    - `--older-than D` must be positive, so whoever registered while the command was being typed is
      outside the set by construction.
    - `--no-clips` is required and has no alternative value. It is not a filter, it is the assertion the
      command makes, spelled where the operator types it: a user who owns a clip **or a collection** is
      never a candidate. That guard is load-bearing, not politeness — `clips.owner_id` and
      `collections.owner_id` CASCADE from `users`, so deleting an owner would drop the clip rows while
      their objects stayed in the bucket with nothing left to name them. `admin orphans` could find those
      prefixes afterwards, but the row that knew the clip's TTL, title and keys would already be gone.
    The listing predicate and the delete predicate are ONE string (`pruneWhere`) used by two statements
    inside ONE transaction on the single-connection writer pool, so the rows reported are exactly the rows
    removed — nothing can register into the candidate set between reading it and deleting it — and a
    mismatch between the reported count and `RowsAffected` is a hard error rather than a quieter lie.
    Matching nobody is exit 0 and an empty report, not a failure. Sessions and API tokens go with each
    user through their own cascade; the bucket is not touched, because a candidate owns nothing in it.
    Tests: `db.TestListUserSummariesCounts` (live vs revoked tokens, a tombstone still counting against
    its owner) and `db.TestPruneUsersOnlyRemovesOwnersOfNothing` (the empty pattern refused, the clip
    owner, the collection owner and the too-young user all spared, the session/token cascade taken);
    `TestAdminUsers` drives the same through the real dispatch including all six usage refusals.
87. **Six small corrections the Phase 5 sweep verified and fixed** (the cleanup list, Phase 2 rounds 6–7 and the
    Phase 4 verifiers). They share no theme except that each was a claim the code did not hold; they are
    recorded together because none is worth an erratum of its own and every one changes an observable.
    (a) **The tag cap counts RUNES** (`internal/db/tags.go` `CleanTag`). `MaxTagRunes` is named in runes
    and the message says "characters", but the guard compared `len(tag)` — bytes. A 20-character
    multi-byte tag was rejected with "is longer than 32 characters", a limit it was nowhere near. It is
    rejected either way by the `[a-z0-9-]` grammar; now with the message that names its actual problem.
    `db.TestCleanTagCountsRunesNotBytes`.
    (b) **A stale cursor keeps the tag** (`internal/web/pages.go` `index`). `ErrInvalidCursor` on
    `/?tag=x&cursor=…` bounced to `/`, dropping the filter the reader was looking at. It now lands on
    `/?tag=x` — the first page of the same list. An illegal TAG still bounces to `/`, because there is no
    filter left to keep. `web.TestIndexStaleCursorKeepsTheTag`.
    (c) **`PUT …/clips` requires `clip_ids`** (`internal/httpapi/collections.go`); see erratum 82(d) as
    amended. `{}` and `{"clip_ids":null}` are 400 `invalid_request`, `[]` still empties.
    (d) **`GET /api/collections/{cid}` carries the `view` limiter** (`internal/httpapi/router.go`).
    It is public, needs only the link, and renders up to 200 clip DTOs plus a tag query — roughly a
    hundred times the work and the bytes of `GET /api/clips/{id}`, which is the amplification that makes
    a leaked link worth pointing at something. 60/min/IP is far above what curating or reading a
    collection costs. The route is otherwise unchanged; its error column gains 429 `rate_limited`.
    (e) **A public `preview.gif` that loses the enqueue race reports the WINNER's state**
    (`internal/httpapi/gif.go` `enqueueGIF`). On `ErrConflict` the non-owner 202 always said
    `{"state":"running"}` although the job that won may still be queued — the common case when two
    viewers ask within the same second. It now reads the job. A job that finished between the failed
    insert and the read keeps `running` as the fallback: the caller is about to poll and will get the
    picture.
    (f) **The share page says whether there is a trim to REJOIN, and the GIF poll stops downloading the
    GIF** (`internal/web/{web,pages}.go`, `web/templates/clip.html`, `web/static/app.js`). The owner page
    fired `GET …/trim` on every single load, and "this clip has no trim" is a 404 — one 404 access-log
    line per view of a feature the owner had not used. The server now answers the question in the markup:
    `ClipView.TrimLive` (one indexed `LatestJobOfKind` on the owner path, beside the tag query already
    there) renders `data-trim-live`, and the browser rejoins only when it is present.
    In the same file, the GIF control downloaded the preview up to three times per click — the status
    `GET` (a ready preview answers with the whole GIF), the cache-busted `<img>` re-fetch, and once more
    on load when `data-gif-ready`. The poll now asks with **HEAD**, which carries the same status and no
    body, and re-asks with GET only for the three statuses that need a message (their bodies are JSON
    envelopes, never a GIF). The cache-buster is used ONLY where the bytes may have just changed — after
    a poll watched one being made — and never on a page load or on a click that found the preview already
    there, which is what its own comment always claimed. The client's poll interval is now the server's
    `Retry-After` (5 s, `gifRetryAfter`) instead of a faster one of its own.
88. **Five corrections to the E2E harness itself** (`scripts/e2e.sh`; §16.3 as amended). A test that fails
    for a reason other than the thing it tests is worse than no test, and four of these five were exactly
    that.
    (a) **`ENV_BASE` is what the APP is baked with, resolved the way compose resolves it** — the shell
    environment first (compose interpolates `${PUBLIC_BASE_URL:-…}` from it), then `.env`, then compose's
    own default — and BOTH sides of the `BASE`≠`PUBLIC_BASE_URL` comparison are trimmed of a trailing
    slash. Reading only `.env` meant a shell-environment value produced no warning at all and the run
    died at step 10 with a confusing diff (erratum 56's whole point); comparing an untrimmed `.env` value
    against a trimmed `BASE` produced a NOTE where nothing was wrong.
    (b) **Step 19's rescue has a one-shot retry, and U's expire moved off the critical path.** `admin
    expire` puts the clip two hours past its expiry and the rescue touch must beat the next sweep tick; a
    tick whose `SweepCandidates` + `MarkDeletingIfDue` landed in the window answered the touch 404 and
    failed the step as if the feature were broken (~0.5 % of runs). The control's `admin expire` — a
    whole `docker compose exec` round trip — used to sit INSIDE that window and now runs after the
    rescue, and a 404 buys one fresh clip and one more attempt. Twice is not luck, so a second 404 still
    fails, with a message naming both possible causes.
    (c) **`expect_prefix_count` retries the bucket once after 3 s.** Steps 19 and 22 exit their polls on a
    DATABASE observable (a key changed, a state changed) and then assert an object count, but a
    superseded object is deleted AFTER the row that stopped referencing it is committed — deliberately,
    since a delete that ran first and then failed to commit would have destroyed a live object. The
    assertion could therefore look inside that window. One retry closes it; a count still wrong after 3 s
    is a real failure.
    (d) **Step 20's `notify=0` failure names its own blind spot.** The count is global (`admin stats` has
    no per-clip notify count to scope it with), so on a shared stack a POSITIVE run that aborted leaves a
    row that fails the next NEGATIVE run. The message now says so and points at the log grep beside it,
    which IS run-scoped.
    (e) **Step 19 asserts all four owner-only lifetime attributes on the anonymous page**
    (`data-touch-url`, `data-keep-forever`, `data-expires`, `data-copy-note`), which is what erratum 62
    always claimed it did; it checked the first two.
    The run also ends by printing `clippet admin users`' total and then RUNNING
    `admin users prune 'e2e_%' --older-than 1h --no-clips` (erratum 86), best effort like the rest of
    step 17. It cannot prune its OWN three users — `--older-than` is required and positive by design —
    but every EARLIER run's are past an hour, so the shared stack stops growing three rows per run
    instead of merely being told that it does. An hour is short enough to keep the backlog small and
    long enough that no account an operator registered by hand is ever a candidate; `--no-clips` keeps
    a match that still owns something out of the set whatever the pattern says. **Superseded by erratum
    272**: that prune is now `e2e_sweep_own`, called at both ends of a run with `--older-than 1s`, so a
    run tidies up after itself as well as after its predecessors.
89. **The janitor asks the job table who owns a scratch dir, and the environment cap is not the crash
    cap** (`internal/sweeper/sweeper.go` `janitorWants`, `cmd/clippet/serve.go` `scratchJanitor`,
    `internal/db/jobs.go` `HasLiveJob`/`limitsFor`/`Cap`, `internal/worker/worker.go` `Busy`,
    `internal/httpapi/progress.go`). §12's janitor rule — "remove `$SCRATCH_DIR/{id}` whose clip row is
    missing or in `ready|failed|deleting`" — was written when `processing` was the only state in which
    the worker owned that dir. Phase 4 added two kinds that run against a clip which is `ready` for the
    whole run and use the SAME directory (`internal/worker/trim.go` `newTrimRun`,
