    `internal/worker/gif.go` `newGIFRun`, both `filepath.Join(cfg.ScratchDir, clip.ID)`), so from #5
    onwards the rule deleted the working directory of live work every tenth tick. What it cost was not
    theoretical: a removal after the cut made the upload fail as `store: upload rendition: open …: no
    such file or directory` and told the owner *"storage was unavailable while the trim ran"*, and a
    removal before `verify` made `ProbeOutput` run ffprobe on a missing file, which comes back as
    `bad_output:` → `FailPermanent` → the ERROR line §12 reserves for "a human is needed".
    (a) **The `ready|failed|deleting` branch is gated on two facts, not on the state.**
    `db.HasLiveJob(ctx, clipID)` (`SELECT 1 FROM jobs WHERE clip_id = ? AND state IN ('queued',
    'running') LIMIT 1`, covered by `jobs_clip`) answers "is there work outstanding for this clip",
    which is what the janitor actually wants to know and is the half that survives a crash — after a
    restart the row is the only record that a trim was in flight. `worker.Busy(clipID)`, over the run
    registry `withRun` already maintains, answers the same question for THIS process and this instant,
    which is the half that is true even before a job row exists in the state the DB can see. Both, not
    one: a `HasLiveJob` error keeps the dir (the existing `janitor: inspect` WARN, and the next pass
    retries). The sweeper reaches `Busy` through an optional `lifecycle.Deps.Busy func(string) bool` —
    nil means "nothing runs here", which is the right answer for every caller that has no worker. The
    boot janitor in `serve.go` gets the same clause for symmetry; it is harmless there, since
    `ReconcileOnStartup` has just requeued whatever the crash interrupted. **Unchanged**: the 24 h
    stale-mtime rule, the `.upload-*` spool rule (erratum 14), `janitorEvery`, and `lifecycle.Destroy`,
    which cancels the run synchronously before it removes anything.
    (b) **`limitsFor` splits the two counters for `trim` and `gif`.** It used to pin BOTH to the kind's
    own constant (2). The argument written above those constants is about the FILE and the owner — "a
    trim that fails leaves NOTHING broken … the owner can ask again" — and that is an argument about
    ATTEMPTS. §11 defines `FailTransient` as storage/scratch/DB/io: by construction not the file's
    fault, and not something asking again fixes any better than waiting does. The asymmetry was stark —
    the same MinIO restart cost a transcode nothing (`MaxTransient` 10 with a 1m·2ⁿ backoff, ≈2.5 h of
    outage absorbed) and permanently failed a trim on its second attempt, sixty seconds later; for a
    GIF it was worse than terminal, because `previewGIF` reports a `failed` gif job as 503 `gif_failed`
    to every anonymous visitor and never retries by design. So `KindTrim` now returns
    `{MaxAttempts: TrimMaxAttempts, MaxTransient: lim.MaxTransient}` and `KindGIF` the same shape with
    `GIFMaxAttempts`: the CRASH cap stays the kind's own constant (a crash-looping edit is exactly what
    "ask again" is the right answer to), the ENVIRONMENT cap is the instance's `TRANSCODE_MAX_TRANSIENT`.
    `KindTranscode` and the notify default are untouched, `limitsFor` fills the §4 defaults in first so a
    zero `Limits` still means 3/10, and `db.Cap(kind, FailKind, lim)` exists so the two "retry cap
    reached" log lines name the budget that was actually exhausted rather than the other one.
    (c) **`GET …/progress` reads the transcode job BY KIND.** Its DB fallback called `GetLatestJob`
    (`ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1`, no kind filter) and then published that row's `stage` as the CLIP's
    stage, its `updated_at` as the clip's, and its `checkpoint_json` as the 98 % marker — but since
    Phase 4 the newest job of a ready clip is routinely a notify, a trim or a gif. `db` enforces the §5
    partition in five other places; this route had opted out, and a ready clip's progress `updated_at`
    could jump to a running trim's timestamp. It now calls
    `LatestJobOfKind(ctx, c.ID, db.KindTranscode)` (same index, same shape). `GetLatestJob` stays: it is
    what `admin ls` prints, and "the newest job whatever its kind" is the right question there.
    **Wire format**: nothing changes — no route, no DTO, no status code; only which job the progress DTO
    can read. Tests: `sweeper.TestJanitorEveryTenthTick` (a ready clip with a queued trim, and one the
    registry claims, both SURVIVE; a ready clip with neither is still removed),
    `db.TestHasLiveJob`, `db.TestMediaKindsSplitTheirTwoCaps`,
    `db.TestTrimOutlastsTheEnvironmentButNotACrashLoop`, `worker.TestTrimSurvivesLosingItsScratchDir`
    (the dir is removed under two consecutive attempts and the edit still lands),
    `worker.TestGIFTransientFailureStopsAtTheConfiguredBudget`, `httpapi.TestProgress`, and E2E step 24.
90. **Ingest and the worker agree about scratch; a chunked body is gated; a full disk is not an outage;
    and a storage failure reaches the public as its class** (`internal/httpapi/upload.go`
    `beginUpload`/`declaredScratchNeed`/`chunkedScratchNeed`/`scratchHasRoom`,
    `internal/worker/pipeline.go` `acquireSource`/`AcquireScratchNeed`/`requireScratch`/`publicReason`/
    `redactPaths`/`noRoom`, `internal/worker/gif.go`, `internal/worker/trim.go`,
    `internal/db/jobs.go` `RequeueWithBackoff`, `internal/store/store.go` `StorageError`/`PublicClass`,
    `internal/store/minio.go` `mapErr`/`publicClass`/`transferErr`). Four defects of one family: what the
    two ends of an upload believe about the scratch disk, and what a failure is allowed to SAY about it.
    (a) **The source was counted twice.** §8.3 step 2 admitted an upload at `free ≥ 1.5×Content-Length +
    SCRATCH_MIN_FREE_BYTES` and then spooled `Content-Length` bytes, leaving `0.5×CL + M`; §10.2's
    `acquireSource` then ran AFTER confirming the source was on scratch and still demanded
    `2×source_size + M` — the source's own bytes, already on the disk being measured, reserved a second
    time. DEPLOY §1's "budget roughly `2 × (largest upload)`" therefore *guaranteed* the failure for that
    largest upload: admitted at `2S ≥ 1.5S + M`, refused at `S < 2S + M`. The guard is now split around
    the download: **before** one, `source_size + SCRATCH_MIN_FREE_BYTES` (the bytes about to land);
    **after** the source is local — the common transcode case, and after a successful download —
    `SCRATCH_MIN_FREE_BYTES` alone. `worker.AcquireScratchNeed` is exported so
    `httpapi.TestIngestAndWorkerAgreeAboutScratch` can drive BOTH formulas and fail if either drifts.
    `checkOutputRoom` (which reserves the plan-sized rendition before the encode and before a trim's cut)
    and `outputBudget`'s arithmetic are **unchanged**; `satAdd` and the `free ≥ 0` "unknown" convention
    are unchanged. Only `outputBudget`'s doc is corrected: its `2×source_size` term is a proportionality
    rule and one of three ceilings the clip has been GRANTED, not room acquire went and found.
    (b) **Both pre-flight gates were skipped for a chunked body.** They lived inside
    `if r.ContentLength > 0`, and net/http reports `ContentLength = −1` for `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`
    — so a client that omitted `Content-Length` bypassed the early 413 *and* the scratch precheck, and
    with it `SCRATCH_MIN_FREE_BYTES`, the operator's one lever over the transcode disk (proven live: a
    chunked multipart POST returned 201). A body with no declared length is now weighed against
    `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES/2 + SCRATCH_MIN_FREE_BYTES` — a deliberate compromise, since the true upper bound
    is the whole of `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` (4 GiB by default) and reserving that would refuse every capture
    upload on a scratch volume sized for real clips — and answers the same 507 `insufficient_scratch`.
    The **413 is deliberately unchanged**: `MaxBytesReader` is the real enforcement of `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`
    and stops the body at the limit whatever the framing, while a pre-emptive 413 on an undeclared body
    could only be a guess about a length nobody stated. `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` semantics, `uploadLimit`, the
    +1 MiB slack and the 1.5× factor are untouched.
    (c) **A scratch shortage no longer spends the outage budget.** It was `FailTransient`, so ten
    backoffs over ≈2.5 h ended as a `failed` clip whose PUBLIC `failure_reason` named the server's
    free-byte count, and `POST /retry` re-downloaded the source and hit the same guard. With a backlog on
    one loop it was self-sustaining: every queued clip kept its source on scratch across its failures, so
    nothing finished, nothing freed anything, and the whole batch failed together. `errNoScratchRoom` now
    routes to `db.RequeueWithBackoff` — job back to `queued` after `scratchRequeueDelay` (1 minute, the
    transient backoff's first step, which never grows because the counter it would grow with is the one
    this class does not touch), **both counters untouched**, one WARN naming the free bytes and what was
    being reserved. `ReleaseJob` could not serve: it schedules at `now`, which against a full disk is a
    spin. The stored reason is the bounded `insufficient scratch space` — no numbers — and all three run
    kinds take that ending, so a preview's anonymous 503 says the same bounded thing. A trim writes
    erratum 80's own sentence for this class instead (`msgDisk`, "the server had no room to make the
    cut; try again later"): its `last_error` is the owner's text, and that vocabulary is deliberate.
    (d) **Storage errors reached the public with only scratch paths redacted.** `redactPaths` (and its
    identical copy in `gifRun.reason`, and a third in `trimRun.reason`) substituted only `j.dir` and
    `SCRATCH_DIR`. `internal/store/minio.go` builds a transfer failure as `store: download <full object
    key>: %w` around minio-go, which for a transport failure is a `*url.Error` embedding
    `http://minio:9000/<bucket>/<S3_KEY_PREFIX>clips/<id>/original/source.mp4`; that text became
    `clips.failure_reason`, which the PUBLIC `GET /api/clips/{id}` (§8.2, deliberate) and the unlimited
    `GET …/progress` return and `clip.html` renders to every anonymous visitor, and which
    `gifFailureMessage` echoes by design. Errata 20 and 31 closed this class for scratch paths and for
    the health probes; this closes the storage half the same way erratum 31 did: `store.StorageError`
    carries a bounded `PublicClass()` from a CLOSED set — `storage unavailable`, `object missing`,
    `storage timeout` — set by `mapErr`/`transferErr` on every result, and `publicReason` renders a
    self-classifying error as `<stage>: <class>` and NOTHING else. Anything that does not classify itself
    keeps the redacted text: **the leak is closed by default, never by enumerating the shapes that would
    have leaked**. The full error goes to the WARN/ERROR line unchanged, which is why `jobRun.fail` and
    `gifRun.fail` now take the CAUSE rather than a rendered string. As a second belt the one remaining
    `redactPaths` (the three copies are now one) also strikes out `S3_ENDPOINT`, `S3_BUCKET` and
    `S3_KEY_PREFIX` when they are non-empty.
    **Wire format**: nothing changes — no route, no DTO, no status code; `failure_reason` and the gif
    503's message stay strings and only their CONTENT narrows, and the 507 `insufficient_scratch` code is
    the same. §8.2's decision to expose `failure_reason` to any clip-id holder stands. Tests:
    `httpapi.TestIngestAndWorkerAgreeAboutScratch` (the parity table),
    `httpapi.TestUploadAdmittedAtTheBoundaryLeavesTheWorkerRoom`,
    `httpapi.TestChunkedUploadIsGatedLikeAnyOther`,
    `worker.TestBacklogDrainsWithTheSourcesAlreadyOnScratch`,
    `worker.TestInsufficientScratchRequeuesWithoutSpendingTheOutageBudget`,
    `worker.TestPlannedOutputScratchGuard`, `worker.TestTrimScratchShortageSpendsNoBudget`,
    `worker.TestStorageFailuresNeverReachThePublicReason` (transcode and gif), and E2E step 25.
91. **ffmpeg is the second egress path, and a playlist is not a video** (`internal/transcode/exec.go`
    `protocolWhitelist`/`inputArgs`/`probeInputArgs`, `internal/transcode/probe.go`
    `allowedFormats`/`isAllowedContainer`, and the callers in `probe.go`, `encode.go`, `poster.go`,
    `gif.go`, `trim.go`). One defect with two halves, both closed by two additions and nothing else.
    (a) **No ffprobe or ffmpeg invocation stated a protocol whitelist.** `runFFprobe`, `Plan.EncodeArgs`,
    `PosterArgs`, `GIFPlan.PaletteArgs`/`EncodeArgs`, `TrimPlan.CopyArgs`, `KeyframeArgs` and `ProbeGIF`
    all handed the binary a path and nothing else, so what the demuxer was allowed to OPEN was whatever
    the vendored build defaults to. A demuxer opens what its input names: an HLS playlist, a DASH
    manifest, an ffconcat script and an SDP are text files listing further resources, and fetching them
    is the CVE-2016-1897/1898 SSRF class. Measured on ffmpeg 7.1.1 on the host and in the app container,
    the default (`file,crypto,data`) does refuse `http` — a listener recorded zero hits — so there was no
    live SSRF; but §15's "the only outbound HTTP besides S3 is the Discord webhook" was resting on a
    vendor default that an ffmpeg bump or a rebuild may change, and `check.sh`'s http.Client tripwire
    cannot see a subprocess. Every argv now carries **`-protocol_whitelist file`** immediately in front
    of the `-i` it governs (in front of the positional path, for ffprobe) — `file` alone, because the
    pipeline reads nothing but files. The flag is rendered by ONE helper pair (`inputArgs`,
    `probeInputArgs`) that every builder goes through, so a sixth call site cannot forget it, and it
    lives inside each builder's golden. A `check.sh` stage is the tripwire for the next hand-written
    argv: a non-test file under `internal/transcode` containing a literal `"-i"` must also name a
    `-protocol_whitelist` (self-tested over a planted temp dir, like its two neighbours).
    (b) **The `file` protocol IS permitted, and that half was live.** `ParseProbe` rejected only still
    images (`isStillImage`) and otherwise accepted any document with a video stream, while
    `store.SanitizeExt` lets the uploader choose the spool extension — so a 118-byte `evil.m3u8` was
    spooled as `source.m3u8`, demuxed as HLS, and its single `file:` segment made the ingest ffprobe read
    ANOTHER clip's scratch source; the upload was answered `201 {"state":"queued"}` and the playlist
    reached the bucket as a durable "original" of content type `video/mp4`, against §8.3 step 6's
    "garbage never reaches the bucket". (The cross-clip read is narrow and racy — the victim's scratch
    dir must exist — and `/api/clips/{id}/original` is owner-only, which is what made it worth closing.)
    `ParseProbe` now carries a container **ALLOWLIST** (`allowedFormats`), checked after `isStillImage`
    and before the stream scan: `format_name` is ffprobe's comma-separated alias list and one hit is
    enough, so `mov,mp4,m4a,3gp,3g2,mj2`, `matroska,webm`, `avi`, `mpegts`, `mpeg`, `mpegvideo`, `flv`,
    `asf`/`wmv`, `ogg`, `mxf` and `gif` pass. Everything else — `hls`/`applehttp`, `dash`, `concat`,
    `sdp`, `rtsp`, `ffmetadata`, a raw elementary stream, and an EMPTY `format_name` — is refused as
    `not_a_video: unsupported container (…)`. An allowlist, not a list of bad formats: unknown is not
    video. `store.SanitizeExt`, the spool extension policy and `isStillImage` are **unchanged** — the
    allowlist is what makes the extension harmless.
    **Wire format**: nothing changes. The refusal is the permanent verdict `probeGate` already turns into
    the existing **415 `not_a_video`** envelope; no new code, no new status, no DTO change. The only
    behaviour an operator can notice is that two inputs the pipeline used to accept are now refused with
    that 415: a raw H.264 elementary stream, and an audio-only file that used to be refused a step later
    as `no_video_stream`. An ORIGINAL already in the bucket that is one of those (only a raw elementary
    stream can be — an audio-only file never became a clip) would fail a `POST /retry` or a trim the same
    way, with the ordinary permanent verdict; nothing already `ready` is touched. Tests: `transcode.TestParseProbeContainerAllowlist` (hls/dash/concat/mp3/h264
    fixtures under `testdata/`, plus a format-name table including the empty one),
    `transcode.TestEveryFFmpegInputIsProtocolWhitelisted` and
    `transcode.TestEveryFFprobeInputIsProtocolWhitelisted` (the flag must sit immediately before the
    input it governs — an input option applies to the input that FOLLOWS it),
    `transcode.TestProbeRefusesACraftedPlaylist` (`-tags ffmpeg`: a real playlist reaching for
    `http://127.0.0.1:1` and one reaching for a sibling directory's `source.mp4`, both refused by the
    real ffprobe), `httpapi.TestUploadPlaylistIsNotAVideo` (415, nothing in the store, no clip row), the
    `check.sh` tripwire stage, and E2E step 26.
92. **The card image must not be a black frame** (`internal/transcode/poster.go` whole file,
    `internal/transcode/gif.go` `GIFPlan`/`PlanGIF`/`PaletteArgs`/`EncodeArgs`,
    `internal/transcode/verify.go` `OutputInfo.VideoEndSec`, `internal/worker/pipeline.go`,
    `internal/worker/trim.go`, `internal/worker/gif.go`). §10.3 step 6 and §17 #6 as amended above.
    One root defect, three symptoms. The poster is `og:image`, `twitter:image`, the `<video poster>` and
    the thumbnail in the library — for most people it is the only frame of the clip they ever see — and
    it was chosen by `t = 0.15·duration` and then trusted. `Poster`'s only retry fired when the
    extraction produced NO FILE, never when the frame it produced was black.
    (a) **The 15% seek is a guess, and on a game clip it is often a wrong one** (major). A 10 s clip of
    3 s black followed by 7 s of content was uploaded live: the served `/poster.jpg` measured
    `YMIN=0 YAVG=0 YMAX=0` — a completely black JPEG, unfurled as the card image on Discord and X. The
    spec's rule ("don't grab frame 1, it is often black — seek in") had been implemented by moving the
    same failure 15% along the timeline; a loading screen, a fade-in or a countdown is the normal shape
    of the clips this product exists for.
    (b) **A source whose picture stops before its audio seeks past the picture** (minor, same root). A
    capture whose device died mid-recording is 2 s of video in a 40 s container. `PosterSeek` asked for
    6 s, ffmpeg wrote nothing ("Nothing was written into output file"), and the ladder fell back to
    `-ss 0` — exactly the frame the rule exists to avoid. `extentOf` already measured a video stream
    that stops early (added for the trim path, erratum 78); the poster stage simply never consulted it.
    (c) **The GIF preview was always the first six seconds** (nit, same root, no fallback at all).
    `PlanGIF` took `min(6 s, duration)` from t=0, so on a black-intro clip half or all of the preview
    was a blank rectangle; `CheckGIF` asserts codec, dims and frame count ≥ 1, none of which a blank
    preview fails.
    **The fix.** The poster is now CHOSEN and MEASURED. Candidates in order: a **`thumbnail=n=100`** pass
    over a bounded window (`-ss {t} -t {min(20, remaining)}` in front of `-i`, so a two-hour rendition is
    still demuxed for twenty seconds), then the old single-frame seek at `{t}`, then `-ss 0`. Every
    candidate that produces a file is decoded (`jpegStats`, which replaces `jpegDims`: `image/jpeg` →
    mean and max luma over every 8th pixel, on the 0-255 scale `signalstats` prints) and REJECTED when
    near-black — `mean < 8` **and** `max < 24`. The AND is the whole of the judgement: a night scene has
    a mean near zero and highlights well past 24, a fade-in has neither. `{t}` is
    `clamp(0.15·duration, 0, duration − 0.5)` with `duration = min(container, video stream end)`, the
    stream end plumbed through as `OutputInfo.VideoEndSec` from the probe the verify stage already ran.
    And `GIFPlan` gains `StartSec = min(posterSeconds, max(0, duration − 6 s))`, emitted as `-ss`
    immediately before the existing `-t`, both still in front of `-i` — identical in BOTH passes,
    because a palette built from one set of frames and used on another is not the palette those frames
    need. The gif job has no stored poster timestamp (it writes five columns and holds none), so it
    re-derives the poster's own rule from the rendition it already has on disk.
    **Amended: "where the poster was" is the CHOSEN frame, not the seek it was looked for from.** As
    first shipped, `PosterResult.Seconds` was the window's START and the gif job re-derived
    `PosterSeek` — the blind 15% guess the thumbnail pass exists to overrule. On the very clip this
    entry was written for (3 s of black, then picture) the card image was right and the preview still
    opened on a black rectangle for a second and a half: (c) was half fixed. So the thumbnail pass now
    REPORTS its choice. Its `-vf` is `thumbnail=n={100},metadata=mode=add:key=clippet.poster:value=1,
    metadata=mode=print:file=pipe\\:1`; the `add` is load-bearing (measured on 7.1.1: `print` emits its
    `frame:N pts:… pts_time:…` header only for a frame that CARRIES metadata, and a decoded frame
    carries none), the sink is stdout because both poster passes leave it free and a constant needs no
    filter-path escaping, and the printed time is relative to the window (`-ss` in front of `-i` shifts
    the output timeline to zero), so `Seconds = start + pts_time`. A fallback candidate is a
    single-frame seek and reports its own seek, unchanged. `PosterFrameSeconds` is the same selection
    with `-f null -` instead of a JPEG — the answer without the picture — and the gif job runs it on
    the downloaded rendition, inside the ffmpeg slot it already holds, which moves `PlanGIF` from
    `recheckClip` to the render stage. It cannot fail the job: an unreadable print, a failed run or an
    expired auxiliary budget all yield the plain seek, which is what shipped before. PERSISTING the
    timestamp (a sixth poster column, so no second pass is needed) stays roadmap work.
    **A black clip still gets a poster.** If every candidate is near-black the LAST one is kept, the
    result carries `NearBlack`, and the worker logs one INFO line. A card with no image at all is worse
    than a dark one, and the poster stage must never be the reason a clip fails; only "no candidate
    produced a readable JPEG" is still a permanent `poster_failed`.
    **Wire format**: nothing changes. `poster_width/height` are still the MEASURED dims of the JPEG that
    was written (that is what `og:image:width/height` read), the gif dims and the 202/200 protocol are
    untouched, and so are the 6 s / 12 fps / 480 px / 8 MiB bounds, the two-pass palette chain, `-q:v 3`
    + the image2 muxer, the `poster_key`/`gif_key` naming and the superseded-delete behaviour. The trim
    re-renders its poster through the same rule. What an operator can notice: a poster may now come from
    a different frame than it did before (a re-transcode or a trim will produce one), and the extra
    thumbnail pass buffers 100 frames — ≈140 MB at 720p, for the moment one bounded auxiliary run takes,
    under the same ffmpeg semaphore the encodes hold.
    **Not in this cluster** (deliberately): the encode's `-t` and the clip's `duration_ms` still come
    from the container, so a 2 s-picture/40 s-audio clip is still described as 40 s long. That is a
    contract change (the DTO, the player, the trim's window arithmetic) and belongs to its own item.
    Tests: `transcode.TestPosterSeek` (the extent-clamp table), `transcode.TestPosterWindowIsBounded`,
    `transcode.TestNearBlackRejection` (a pure function over synthesised frames: all-black and a
    fade-in rejected; mean-30, bright, and black-with-one-lit-pixel kept),
    `transcode.TestPoster` (the candidate ladder, the kept near-black frame, no scratch left behind),
    `transcode.TestPosterSkipsABlackIntro` and `transcode.TestPosterOfAClipWhoseVideoStopsEarly`
    (`-tags ffmpeg`: the two fixtures above, the first proving its own premise — that the frame at the
    blind seek IS near-black — before proving the poster is not, and that the result NAMES the frame it
    chose rather than the window it opened, `PosterFrameSeconds` agreeing with it to the millisecond),
    `transcode.TestPosterSeek` (also the two argv goldens, thumbnail and pick),
    `transcode.TestPosterPickedSeconds` (start + `pts_time`, and every unreadable print falling back to
    the start), `transcode.TestPlanGIFBounds` +
    `TestPlanGIFStartsWhereThePosterDoes` + `TestGIFArgsAreTheTwoPassPaletteChain` (`-ss` before `-t`
    before `-i` in both passes, the identical pair, and still no watermark),
    `transcode.TestMakeGIFStartsAtThePosterFrame` (`-tags ffmpeg`, on the black-intro fixture: the
    premise measured on the SOURCE — the frame at the seek is near-black — then the preview planned at
    the poster's frame opening at `YAVG` 125 against the seek-planned one's 16, which is E2E step 9's
    `> 8` rule plus a 4× ratio, because a palettized black frame dithers to ~16 and would clear 8 on
    its own), and E2E step 9, which now
    measures EVERY matrix clip's `/poster.jpg` with the host ffmpeg's `signalstats` and dies naming the
    clip if `YAVG ≤ 8`.
93. **The rendition must not lie about its colour, and a variable-rate or many-track source must survive
    the plan** (`internal/transcode/probe.go`, `plan.go`, `encode.go`, `trim.go`; §10.3 steps 2–4 and
    §19 as amended above). Three defects that all live in the gap between what the plan MEASURES about a
    source and what the encode then CLAIMS about its output.
    (a) **An HDR source came out dark and still claimed to be PQ/BT.2020** (major, two separate faults).
    `ParseProbe` never read `color_primaries`/`color_transfer`/`color_space`; the video chain ended at
    `format=yuv420p`, which converts bit depth and chroma and does not touch the transfer function; and
    the encode set no output colour tags, so ffmpeg propagated the source's. Measured live on an HDR10
    upload: the SERVED rendition probed `pix_fmt=yuv420p color_space=bt2020nc color_transfer=smpte2084
    color_primaries=bt2020` — an 8-bit H.264 stream declaring HDR — at YAVG 79.4 against an SDR
    reference of the identical bars at 103.7, its poster JPEG (the `og:image`) at 73.8. Xbox, PS5, Game
    Bar, the NVIDIA App and recent iPhones capture HDR by default, so this was the ordinary path.
    **The mislabelling is the worse half and was never covered by anything**: a player that believes the
    tag applies a second HDR→SDR transform to a signal already truncated to 8 bits. **The tone map is the
    §19 deferral being LIFTED** ("accepted v1 limitation; `zscale`+`tonemap` is a Phase 2+ option") — the
    tools are in the shipped image, and the map costs under a second on a six-second clip.
    Fix: `ProbeResult` gains the three colour fields; `MakePlan` sets `Tonemap` when the transfer is
    `smpte2084` or `arib-std-b67` (trimmed, case-insensitive); the video chain gains the
    `zscale=t=linear:npl=100` → `tonemap` → `zscale=…bt709` prefix when it is set, and — **always,
    whatever the source said** — ends with `setparams=color_primaries=bt709:color_trc=bt709:colorspace=bt709`.
    **Amended: a source tagged only on the TRANSFER did not become dark, it stopped transcoding.** The
    fix above was specified and fixtured against a well-formed HDR10 file, and a great many real ones are
    not: several screen recorders — and any remux that dropped the container-level tags — write
    `color_transfer=smpte2084` with `color_primaries` and `color_space` unspecified. `zscale` converts
    between colorspaces it can NAME, so on such a file BOTH zscales in the chain answer `code 3074: no
    path between colorspaces`, ffmpeg exits non-zero and the clip fails PERMANENTLY — a file that
    transcoded fine (as SDR, untouched) before the tone map shipped, which makes this the one regression
    the map introduced. Measured on 7.1.1: zscale's own input overrides (`pin=`/`tin=`/`min=`) do NOT fix
    it; stating the fields on the FRAME does. So `MakePlan` also records `AssumePrimaries` /
    `AssumeMatrix` — set with `Tonemap` when the probe found that field empty or one of the enum's
    placeholders (`unknown`/`unspecified`/`reserved`, trimmed and case-insensitive: `isUnknownColour`) —
    and the chain is preceded by `setparams=color_primaries=bt2020` and/or `:colorspace=bt2020nc` for
    exactly those fields. BT.2100 defines both PQ and HLG over BT.2020 primaries with the
    non-constant-luminance matrix, so this is the container the signal is already in, not a preference;
    and because it is emitted per field, a fully tagged HDR10 source renders the graph it rendered before
    and its output is byte identical.
    **Two things were measured rather than assumed, and both contradicted the obvious answer.**
    *First*, `-color_primaries` and `-color_trc` as OUTPUT OPTIONS do not work on ffmpeg 7.1.1: the
    encoder takes those two from the frame the filter graph hands it, so with an untagged source the
    output probes `color_transfer=unknown color_primaries=unknown` and with an HDR source it probes the
    source's own tags. Only `-colorspace` lands (buffersink negotiation). The tag therefore has to be a
    FILTER — `setparams`, metadata-only, so an SDR encode is unchanged pixel for pixel — and the argv
    keeps the three options as well because they state what the file is and one of them is honoured.
    *Second*, the tone-map OPERATOR: `hable` (the first choice) makes the reference clip **darker than
    shipping nothing** — 74.0 against today's 79.7 and an SDR reference of 103.7 — because `zscale`
    drops the mastering-display and MaxCLL side data on the way to linear light, `ff_determine_signal_peak`
    then falls back to a fixed default, and Hable compresses a 100-nit signal as if it were twelve times
    brighter. `mobius` (100.9) is near-identity below its knee, rolls only the top off, and clips nothing
    at either a 100-nit or a 1000-nit grade; the full table is in §10.3 step 4. Residual, accepted: a
    genuinely non-709 SDR source (an SD `bt470bg`/`smpte170m` capture) is relabelled without a matrix
    conversion — a small hue shift on a shape this product does not see, against a converting `zscale`
    on every encode. `DecideTrim` also gains one disqualifier: a source declaring an HDR transfer is
    never stream-copied, because a copy would carry the PQ tag into a rendition that promises Rec.709
    (nearly all such sources are 10-bit and already refused; this catches the 8-bit one that claims PQ).
    (b) **A variable-rate source was decimated** (minor). `pickFPS` preferred `avg_frame_rate`. A VFR mp4
    whose action runs at 30 fps and whose still section runs at ~10 reports `r_frame_rate=30/1,
    avg_frame_rate=3600/293` (12.29, reproduced at 2100/149 on 7.1.1); the plan took 12.29 and
    `-fps_mode cfr` then threw away most of the action's frames while padding the stillness. Phone screen
    recorders, MediaRecorder captures and OBS replay buffers that dropped frames all produce this shape.
    Fix: the probe keeps BOTH rates (`FPS` = the average, `RFPS` = `r_frame_rate`) and `MakePlan` chooses
    with the pure `pickFPS(avg, r, MaxFPS)` of §10.3 step 3 — `r` when `r ≤ MaxFPS && r > 1.25·avg`, else
    `avg`, then the existing cap. The `≤ MaxFPS` guard is load-bearing: Matroska and WebM report the
    TIMEBASE as `r_frame_rate` (1000/1, 90000/1), and without it every mkv would become a 60 fps encode.
    (c) **A source with more than four audio tracks silently lost the extras** (minor). `maxAudioInputs`
    was 4; a five-track upload was measured live with tracks 1–4 at −24.1 dB and track 5 at the noise
    floor. An OBS scene with game + mic + Discord + music + browser audio is five. Fix: the cap is 8.
    Still a hard bound, still one `amix` and one `alimiter`, no DB column and no DTO field — the
    `audio_tracks_dropped` surfacing needs a migration and stays on the roadmap.
    **Wire format**: nothing changes — no DTO, no route, no status. Tests: `transcode.TestMakePlanTonemap`
    (PQ/HLG/case/padding against four SDR controls, the exact `FilterComplex` string for each, and the
    stamp closing the chain in every shape), `TestTonemapChainShape` (the five filters in order, and the
    map ahead of the rotate and the scale), `TestEncodeArgsGoldens` (the three colour flags in every case,
    a tone-mapped case, a tone-map-plus-rotate case and a five-input merge), `TestPickFPS` (VFR, both
    container timebases, CFR, the 25% boundary from both sides, the cap, and every missing-rate
    combination), `TestProbeRules`' `colour tags` and `audio track cap` subtests (1/4/5/8/9/16
    tracks → 1/4/5/8/8/8, in file order, through to the merge graph), `TestDecideTrim`'s PQ/HLG/bt709
    rows, and — with `-tags ffmpeg` — `TestFFmpegHDRIsTonemappedAndTaggedSDR` (a REAL PQ fixture built by
    taking SMPTE bars to linear light and re-encoding through the PQ transfer, not SDR values wearing an
    HDR label; asserts `yuv420p,bt709,bt709,bt709` on the output, that the untone-mapped control is
    darker than the SDR reference, that the map is brighter than the control, and that it lands within
    15% of the SDR reference), `TestMakePlanTonemapAssumesMissingColourTags` (the six probe shapes and
    the exact `setparams` prefix each renders, plus the SDR control that must assume nothing) and
    `TestFFmpegHDRTaggedOnlyOnTheTransferStillTranscodes` (`-tags ffmpeg`: an 8-bit yuv420p H.264 fixture
    tagged on the transfer alone, which first proves its own premise — the pre-amendment chain FAILS on
    it — and then asserts `yuv420p,bt709,bt709,bt709` and a valid mp4),
    `TestFFmpegVFRIsPlannedAtTheCaptureRate` (a real VFR mp4: `r_frame_rate`
    30/1, average below 24, planned and encoded at 30/1, ~300 frames out of ~10 s) and the colour
    assertion now in every `TestFFmpegMatrix` case. E2E: step 7 downloads A's served rendition and
    host-ffprobes `color_space,color_transfer,color_primaries` = `bt709,bt709,bt709`; no new step and no
    new matrix clip.
94. **The pages a stranger sees: a layout that survives a long title, honest copy, `noindex` for
    unlisted, and the three CSP directives `default-src` does not cover** (`web/static/app.css`,
    `web/templates/{index,clip,collection,login,notfound,unavailable}.html`, `web/static/app.js`,
    `internal/web/{pages,server}.go`, `internal/httpx/middleware.go`, `internal/httpapi/router.go`).
    Thirteen small defects on the SSR surface, found by one deep-dive pass over the pages themselves.
    They share an area rather than a cause, so they are recorded together; each changes something a
    visitor can see.
    (a) **A long unbroken title broke the whole watch page** (`app.css`). `h1, h2` carried no
    `overflow-wrap`, and a clip title is whatever the capture tool put in the file name — ShareX and
    RePlays both default it to one unbroken 100+ character run. Measured: a 120-character title gave
    `document.scrollWidth` 2515 in a 1265 px viewport, and at 390 px the header, the player, the
    controls and the whole page scrolled sideways with the video squashed into the left half. The wrap
    (`overflow-wrap: anywhere; word-break: break-word`) now covers `h1, h2`, the description, the fact
    values and the collection links. **No line clamp**: the title is the clip's name and the reader gets
    all of it. The only MAJOR of the thirteen, and it hit the anonymous watch page — the one surface the
    product exists to deliver.
    (b) **A portrait clip rendered as a strip in a letterbox** (`app.css`). `.clip video { width: 100% }`
    fixed the element to the column and let the browser `contain`-fit the picture inside it, so a
    720×1280 phone capture drew ~265 px of black on each side and used 41% of the width the block took.
    The element is now BOUNDED, not stretched — `max-width: 100%; width: auto; height: auto;
    max-height: 75vh; margin-inline: auto` — so the intrinsic ratio decides the box. `background: #000`
    stays for the pre-metadata frame.
    (c) **The trim boxes were unstyled** (`app.css`). `input[type="number"]` was in neither styled
    selector, so From/To were white 58 px UA defaults in Arial inside a dark UI. They join the shared
    rule and get `width: 7ch` (a value, not a sentence). `option` joins it too: the collection
    membership picker drew its selected rows from the UA palette.
    (d) **Tags sat after the submit button** (`index.html`). Tab order reached Upload before Tags, and
    Enter in the Title field — the natural thing after typing a title — uploaded the clip untagged,
    defeating the point of shipping tags with the upload. The label moves above the row that ends the
    form. No JS change: `setupUpload` reads the field by name.
    (e) **A tag filter that matched nothing said "No clips yet."** (`index.html`), directly
    contradicting the filter line above it. `{{if .Tag}}` picks `No clips tagged "…"` instead. Reachable
    from any stale chip or bookmarked filter URL; an ILLEGAL tag still bounces to `/` (erratum 87(b)).
    (f) **One clip-specific 404 served every unknown route, with no way out** (`notfound.html`,
    `unavailable.html`). "This clip no longer exists, or the link is wrong" was the wrong noun for a
    collection id, a typo'd `/settings/token` and every scanner path — and for an anonymous visitor
    `base.html` renders NO header (it is gated on `.Viewer`), so the body held not one link and not one
    wordmark. Both message pages now carry `<h1 class="brand-title">Clippet</h1>`, neutral copy and a
    home link, for every viewer. A brand and a way home on a 404 is not a watch-page CTA; `clip.html`
    is untouched and the §9 rule stands.
    (g) **The login page advertised a dead end** (`login.html`, `pages.go` `login`). It rendered "Create
    an account" unconditionally while only `register` ever read `RegistrationOpen`, so with
    `REGISTRATION=closed` the only destination that link had was `/register`'s own "registration is
    closed" notice. `login` now reads the flag and the paragraph says who to ask instead.
    (h) **The stage-prefixed ffmpeg error was on the anonymous page** (`clip.html`). `Processing failed:
    {{.FailureReason}}` sat OUTSIDE the `IsOwner` block, so a friend arriving from a Discord link got
    `encode: <ffmpeg stderr>` — text they can neither act on nor understand. What is split is the
    RENDERING, not the data: `failure_reason` stays on the DTO for any clip-id holder (§8.2 is
    deliberate), the owner keeps the technical line and the Retry button, and everyone else gets "This
    clip could not be processed." Retry also moves out of `.danger-zone` beside Delete, which is its
    opposite.
    (i) **Four copy and interaction consistencies.** `{{.Views}} views` / `{{.ClipCount}} clips` rendered
    "1 views" and "1 clips" (template and the `app.js` twin); the unlisted marker was a `<span
    class="tag">` styled identically to the real, clickable tag chips and is now a muted `.flag`; the
    ellipsised library title carried no `title=` tooltip in either the template or the JS-built row; and
    the GIF download link's bare `download` saved every clip's preview as `preview.gif`, so it is now
    `clippet-{id}.gif`. (The `confirm()`/`alert()` item from the same finding belongs to another
    cluster and is not touched here.)
    (j) **The tag editor's promise was not the one the wire keeps** (`clip.html`). It told the owner
    "they show in your library and filter it; nobody sees them on the watch page". The library is
    instance-wide (`db.ListClips` lists every listed clip of every user) and the PUBLIC clip DTO carries
    tags by design (erratum 81). The DTO is right and the sentence was wrong, so the sentence changed:
    tags appear in the library every account on this server sees, and to anyone holding the link, and
    never on the watch page. `ClipDTO.Tags` is NOT gated on `isOwner` — erratum 81 is deliberate and the
    E2E pins it.
    (k) **`noindex` for unlisted, always for a collection, and a `/robots.txt` that keeps the cards
    working** (`pages.go`, `server.go`). `unlisted` means "do not surface this" (§8.2) and the link is
    the only authentication, yet the page carried a self-referential canonical, the full `og:*` card and
    no robots directive — only the 404 and 503 pages ever set `NoIndex` — and `GET /robots.txt` was a
    404. Capability URLs reach crawlers routinely (toolbars, referrer chains, paste sites). Two
    mechanisms, neither a substitute for the other: an unlisted clip page and EVERY collection page
    (§9.4 lists a collection in one place, its owner's library) emit `<meta name="robots"
    content="noindex">`, and a static `GET /robots.txt` (`text/plain`, `public, max-age=3600`, HEAD
    allowed, 405 otherwise, no Resolver) `Disallow`s `/clips/`, `/c/` and `/embed/` for `*` while giving
    Discordbot, Twitterbot, facebookexternalhit and Slackbot-LinkExpanding a group each with an EMPTY
    `Disallow:` — "allow everything". That last part is load-bearing: a named group REPLACES the `*`
    group for the agent it names, so without it the unfurlers would obey the block and the product's
    whole point would stop working. `meta robots noindex` does not stop `og:` unfurling either (the tags
    are read, the page is simply not indexed), so the card is unaffected from both directions. Neither
    is a security control; the id is still 71 bits.
    (l) **CSP gains `object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'self'`** (`httpx/middleware.go`
    `cspBase`; §9.1, §9.2, §15). `base-uri` and `form-action` have NO fallback to `default-src` in CSP3,
    so they were unset: a single injected `<base href="//evil">` would have repointed every relative URL
    on the page — `app.js`'s own `src` included — and a rewritten form action would have posted the
    login credentials off-origin. `object-src` did fall back to `'self'`, which is the wrong answer for
    a site with no plugin content. No HTML-injection sink is known (`html/template` escaped every
    payload thrown at `og:title`, `<title>`, the collection `<h1>` and every attribute), so this is
    defence in depth — the cheap half of a CSP the project already takes seriously enough to forbid
    inline script and style outright. `frame-ancestors` stays per variant.
    (m) **HSTS on an https origin** (`httpx/middleware.go` `SecurityHeaders`). There was none anywhere,
    on a deployment whose cookies are `Secure`-only: a user who types the bare hostname makes a
    plaintext request first, and while the session cookie is not sent on it, the login page and the
    credentials typed into it are not protected on that hop, and nothing resists an SSL-stripping
    downgrade. `SecurityHeaders(embed, https bool)` now emits
    `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` when and only when the PUBLIC
    origin is https. The scheme is PASSED IN from `urls.Builder.IsHTTPS()` at both call sites
    (`web.handler`, `httpapi.routes`) rather than sniffed from the request — TLS is terminated upstream
    and the listener never sees a certificate, which is the same reason `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` decides the
    cookie `Secure` flag. A local http dev stack is unaffected; pinning https on `localhost` would lock
    a developer out of their own machine for a year. **No `preload`**: that is a hostname-wide,
    hard-to-undo commitment belonging to whoever owns the domain.
    **Wire format**: no route, DTO or status changes except the new `GET /robots.txt` (200 `text/plain`,
    HEAD allowed, anything else 405 with `Allow: GET, HEAD`). The §9.1 card tag inventory is unchanged —
    not one tag added or removed — and so are `frame-ancestors` per variant, the collection page's
    `<title>` and every owner-only control and `data-` attribute (erratum 62).
    Tests: `web.TestUnlistedPagesAreNoIndex` (unlisted yes, listed no, collection always, and the card
    tags still there), `TestRobotsTxt` (status, type, the three `Disallow`s, a bare `Disallow:` after
    each of the four unfurlers, HEAD, 405), `TestPageHeadersCarryTheNewDirectives` (the three CSP
    directives on the page AND embed variants; HSTS present for an https base and absent for an http
    one), `TestStylesheetWrapsUnbreakableText` (a 200-character no-space title renders whole; the served
    `app.css` carries the wrap — the same served-asset grep `TestStaticAssets` runs over `app.js`, since
    inventing a CSS parser would be worse than the rule it checked), `TestSharePageFailed` (the ffmpeg
    text absent for an anonymous AND a non-owner render, present for the owner, Retry above the danger
    zone), `TestIndexTagFilterEmptyStateSaysWhy`, the registration-closed half of
    `TestLoginAndRegisterPages`, and `httpx.TestSecurityHeaders` / `TestHSTSFollowsTheOrigin`.
    E2E: **step 27** "crawler policy and response headers" (before the step-16 log gate): `/robots.txt`
    200 `text/plain` with the three `Disallow`s and an allow-everything group for each unfurler; the
    run's unlisted clip E is `noindex` while the listed B is not; B is PATCHed unlisted → `noindex`
    appears with the card intact → PATCHed back → it is gone; and the share page's CSP carries all three
    directives, with HSTS asserted present over an https `BASE` and absent over http.
95. **The client stops losing the user's work: whole-membership Save, silent reloads over typed text, a
    stale GIF after a trim, and "authentication required"** (`web/static/app.js`,
    `web/templates/{collection,clip,tokens}.html`, `web/static/app.css`). Five client-side defects found by
    one deep dive over the pages as they are actually used. They share a cause, which is why they are one
    erratum: every one of them takes something the person in front of the browser had, and gives back
    nothing they can act on. No route, DTO or status changes — the wire is untouched.
    (a) **One stray click emptied a collection** (`collection.html`, `setupCollectionPage`). §9.4 specified
    the membership picker as a `<select multiple size="10">`, chosen because a multi-select reports its
    selection in DOCUMENT order and that is what makes the current-members-first rendering preserve the
    collection's order. The ordering reasoning was right; the CLICK semantics were never considered. An
    unmodified click on an option **replaces** the selection — ctrl/cmd-click adds, and nothing on the page
    says so — and Save PUTs exactly `selectedOptions`. On a ten-clip collection one click therefore sent a
    single id, dropped the other nine, and reloaded the page to show the damage as done: no diff, no
    confirmation, no undo, and the section's own hint ("anything you add lands after them") reads as an
    invitation to click. It is now a **checkbox list** in the same form — one
    `<label class="check"><input type="checkbox" name="clip_ids" value="…">` per choice, current members
    first exactly as `Choices` already orders them. Document order is still the PUT order, so the ordering
    contract is unchanged to the byte; a checkbox toggles only itself, takes a keyboard and a thumb, and
    needs no undocumented modifier. And because the PUT still replaces the WHOLE membership, a save that
    REMOVES members relabels Save to `Save clips (removes N)` and takes a second click (the two-click
    helper, never a dialog); a save that only adds goes straight through. §9.4's own text is amended.
    (b) **Two reloads threw away typed text** (`setupClipPage`, `setupCollectionNew`). The share page
    renders the complete owner block — title, description, TTL, unlisted, the tag editor — while a clip is
    still `processing`, deliberately: none of those fields describes the rendition, so a clip can be filed
    while it encodes. The progress poller then did `location.reload()` the instant the encode landed,
    unconditionally, and the product's own flow (upload → click through → start typing) walks you into that
    window, which is ten seconds to several minutes wide. The reload is still how a processing page becomes
    a watch page, so it stays — but only when there is nothing to lose: `dirtyOwnerFields` compares every
    `input`/`textarea`/`select` in the owner block against the value the SERVER rendered it with, which is
    precisely what a reload would restore. Dirty means no reload: the state line becomes "Processing
    finished — reload to watch" with a real link, and the poller stops. (The in-place `<video>` re-render
    is a different, larger change and is not this.)
    **The SELECT rule, amended.** This entry first specified the comparison as `defaultValue` /
    `defaultChecked` / `defaultSelected` throughout, and for a `<select>` that is WRONG — badly enough that
    it inverted the fix. `defaultSelected` mirrors the `selected` ATTRIBUTE, `clip.html`'s `ttl_days`
    options carry none (the first option is "Keep current", the no-op — marking it would be redundant), and
    a single-select must still have one option selected, so the browser selects index 0 with
    `defaultSelected === false`. `option.selected !== option.defaultSelected` was therefore TRUE on an
    UNTOUCHED page: every owner's processing page ended at "Processing finished — reload to watch" and the
    automatic reload this entry preserved never fired for the one audience that has an owner block.
    Reproduced in Chrome 151 and fixed in the deep-dive pass: a single-select is dirty when
    `selectedIndex` differs from the index of the option carrying the attribute (0 when none carries it),
    which is the option a reload would put back; a `multiple` select — none is rendered today, erratum
    95(a) having removed the last one — keeps the per-option comparison, where the absence of a forced
    pick makes it correct. Checkboxes, radios, text inputs and textareas are unchanged.
    There is still no JS test harness, so the rule is pinned from the other side, in the markup:
    `web.TestSharePageOwnerSelectHasNoDefault` asserts that the owner block's every `<select>` is the TTL
    one, is not `multiple`, and carries no `selected` attribute — the precondition the client's rule is
    written against, on both a `processing` and a `ready` page.
    Second reload: creating a collection reloaded the LIBRARY page, whose other half is the upload form —
    a chosen file, a typed title, typed tags, gone for the sake of re-rendering one `<li>`. The 201 now
    prepends that `<li>` into `[data-collection-list]` (newest first, which is `ListCollections`' own
    order), unhides nothing and hides `[data-collections-empty]`, and clears only the title field it spent.
    (c) **A trim left the GIF control describing a preview the server had deleted** (`applyTrimmed`,
    `resetGIF`). `db.FinalizeTrim` NULLs `gif_key/size/etag/width/height` and supersedes the object, so
    `HEAD …/preview.gif` answers 202 — while the page still showed the pre-trim `<img>` and a Download link
    whose click saved the 19-byte 202 JSON envelope under a `.gif` name. `applyTrimmed` now resets the
    control after `bustPlayer`: the `<img>` and the download link are hidden with their `src`/`href`
    removed, `data-gif-ready` comes off, and the row says "the preview was removed by the trim — make it
    again". The static hint below it says a trim replaces the GIF whether or not one just happened; this
    says it about the trim that did.
    (d) **An expired session read as "authentication required"** (`api()` callers, `authFailed`). `api()`
    had no 401 branch, so every caller printed the API's own message: beside Save on the Manage form, in an
    `alert()` for keep-forever and delete, and — after the entire file had been transferred — as "Upload
    failed: authentication required". Meanwhile the SSR header still said you were logged in. The trim
    watcher was the one place that knew this class existed. It is now `authFailed(el, r)`: true for a 401
    and for the 403 `token_not_allowed` (erratum 19), rendering "Your session ended — " plus a real
    `<a>` to `/login?next=<this page>` built as an element, never a markup string. Callers read
    `if (!authFailed(el, r)) show(el, …)`, so every existing message survives unchanged for every other
    failure. The login form itself is deliberately NOT converted: a 401 there means the password was wrong.
    For the upload only, one bodiless `GET /api/auth/me` runs before the XHR — a dead session now costs
    zero bytes instead of a whole file — and a probe that cannot be REACHED is not allowed to block the
    upload, because the XHR reports a network failure perfectly well itself.
    (e) **`confirm()` and `alert()` are gone** (`setupClipPage`, `setupTokens`). §9.4 justified the
    collection's two-click delete with "a browser dialog is neither styleable nor dismissable by the page",
    and then the clip delete and the token revoke used `confirm()` and four failures used `alert()`. The
    two-click pattern is now one helper (`confirmClick` + `disarm`, a `WeakMap` of armed buttons, re-arming
    after 5 s) used by all three destructive actions, and each failure renders into an inline element the
    section owns: `[data-owner-error]` (keep-forever, retry), `[data-delete-error]`, `[data-token-error]`,
    and the existing `[data-error]`/status elements elsewhere. `grep -n 'confirm(\|alert(' web/static/app.js`
    returns comments only.
    **Wire format**: unchanged. `PUT /api/collections/{id}/clips` still takes `{"clip_ids":[…]}`, still
    requires the key (errata 82(d), 87(c)), and still stores exactly the order it is sent; the checkbox
    list simply produces the same array. `app.css` gains `.picker` (the ten-row scrolling box the
    `size="10"` select used to be) and clip/collection/tokens gain only hidden hint and error elements.
    Tests: `web.TestCollectionPickerIsACheckboxList` (one checkbox per choice, in `Choices` order, members
    first and ticked, strangers' and `deleting` clips absent, no `<select` on the page),
    `TestCollectionPageOwner` (the rendered markup and `data-members-hint`), and
    `TestSharePageProcessingKeepsTheOwnerBlock` — which pins the shape (b) depends on, so the lost-typing
    bug can never be "fixed" by hiding the fields. There is no JS test harness in this repo and none was
    added; the client paths are covered by markup assertions and by the E2E.
    E2E: **step 23** gains the checkbox assertions (`type="checkbox" name="clip_ids"`, every current member
    `checked`, no `<select` on the page, the removal hint present) and a wire proof of the ordering
    contract — PUT back exactly the set the page renders, in the order it renders it, and the membership
    comes back identical.
96. **Operator truth: a loopback bind by default, a 0600 snapshot, bounded logs, and a backup job that
    survives one bad night** (`compose.yaml`, `cmd/clippet/serve.go`, `cmd/clippet/admin.go`,
    `scripts/check.sh`, `.env.example`, `DEPLOY.md` §1/§4/§7/§8/§9/§15/§16/§17.3/§18; §2's compose
    snippet and erratum 66's scope sentence amended). One deep dive over the operator surface — the
    parts of this product that are a document and a compose file rather than a handler — found five
    defects that share a shape: the safe thing was documented as a *remediation* while the unsafe
    thing shipped as the default.
    (a) **The published port is loopback by default; widening it is one `.env` line.** `ports:` was
    `8481:8080`, i.e. every interface, while `DEPLOY.md` §4 told the tunnel operator to set
    `TRUSTED_PROXIES=172.16.0.0/12` — which is correct behind a tunnel and catastrophic beside a
    published port. `clientip.Resolve` honours a caller-supplied `X-Real-IP` unconditionally once the
    TCP peer is inside a trusted prefix (§13, deliberate), and on Docker Desktop *every* client of a
    published port arrives as the same bridge gateway address cloudflared does. Proven on the live
    stack: four `POST /api/clips/{id}/view` with four different `X-Real-IP` values counted four views
    where three with one value counted one, and the same header resets the auth limiter's 10/min
    bucket, so brute-force protection is gone for anyone who can reach the port. The fix is the
    default, not a warning: `ports: ["${CLIPPET_PUBLISH:-127.0.0.1:8481}:8080"]`. Loopback costs
    nothing — `curl http://localhost:8481/readyz`, `scripts/e2e.sh` and cloudflared's
    `host.docker.internal` route are all unaffected — and `CLIPPET_PUBLISH=0.0.0.0:8481` in `.env`
    restores the old behaviour for the LAN case, documented with its consequence. `clientip.Resolve`
    is **unchanged**: `X-Real-IP` is still honoured from a trusted peer, and the Phase 3 gate's XFF
    walk still stands. What the binary gains is one `WARN` at boot whenever `TRUSTED_PROXIES` is
    non-empty (`serve.go`, immediately after the boot line), naming DEPLOY §4 — a container cannot see
    the host's port map, so the warning is on the *combination*, not on a detection, and a correctly
    bound stack logs it too. §4 is inverted to match: the loopback bind is why the recipe is safe, and
    widening it is the opt-in that must not be combined with a trusted prefix.
    (b) **`admin backup` writes 0600.** `VACUUM INTO` inherited the image's 0022 umask, so the snapshot
    — every bcrypt password hash, every session token hash, every API token hash — landed
    world-readable, and §15's own preamble said "there is no secret to escrow". `os.Chmod(tmp, 0o600)`
    runs between `db.Backup` and the rename, so the `.part-` window is covered too (the rename
    preserves the mode), and the command prints
    `warning: this file contains password and token hashes - keep it where you keep passwords`. §15 now
    says the snapshot IS the secret (the old sentence is true of key material, not of the database),
    and the copy-out step ends in `chmod 600`, because `docker compose cp` writes with the host's
    umask. Test: `TestAdminBackupAndRestoreCheck` asserts the mode and the warning line.
    (c) **Container logs are bounded.** No service declared `logging:`, and the daemon default is an
    uncapped `json-file`. The app writes one INFO access-log line per request (only `/healthz` and
    `/readyz` drop to DEBUG) and there is no global request limiter, so a scanner on a public origin
    writes on the order of a GiB a day — into the same filesystem as `app_data`, `app_scratch` and
    `minio_data`, which `SCRATCH_MIN_FREE_BYTES` does not guard because it is not the scratch path.
    `app` and `minio` now carry `json-file` with `max-size: 50m`, `max-file: 5` (~250 MB each);
    `docker compose logs --since` is unaffected, and `docker compose config -q` validates the key.
    DEPLOY §8 states the ceiling and names `LOG_LEVEL=warn` as the knob for a busy origin and
    `LOG_FORMAT=json` + shipping off-box as the alternative; §18 stops implying retention is covered,
    because a ceiling is not a retention policy.
    (d) **The outbound-client tripwire scans `web` too** (erratum 66's scope sentence amended to
    "`internal`, `cmd` and `web`"). Erratum 27's URL grep already covered `web`; the client grep did
    not, and `web/static/embed.go` and `web/templates/embed.go` are non-test Go files compiled into
    the binary. Reproduced with check.sh's own expressions against a planted `web/static/leak.go`:
    caught by the URL grep, missed by the client grep. Line 16 now scans `internal cmd web`; the
    planted-file self-test is untouched and still requires exactly 4 hits. README's "fails the build if
    a second outbound call site ever appears" is restated with erratum 66's own caveat — a tripwire over
    the common spellings, not a proof. Collateral fixed in the same commit: erratum 91's new comment in
    `internal/transcode/exec.go` spelled the client type in full and tripped the grep under the *old*
    scope already, which the grep cannot distinguish from code; the comment now says so instead.
    (e) **The documented backup crontab could stop backing up for good.** §15.5's line used a FIXED
    container path removed only by the last link of an `&&` chain, while `admin backup` refuses to
    overwrite by design: one failed `docker compose cp` left a complete `/tmp/db.db` behind and every
    later night exited 1, silently, until the operator needed the rollback §16 opens with (reproduced
    live). The path is dated, the cleanup is unconditional (`;`, and `rm -f /tmp/clippet-*.db
    /tmp/*.part-*`), and the whole line goes through `logger -t clippet-backup`.
    **Docs-only in the same pass**, each verified against the running stack: §15.5 says a restore is a
    *credential* rollback (revocation is a soft `revoked_at` on `api_tokens`, and `sessions` rows
    restored from a backup are live until `expires_at` with a 720h `SESSION_TTL` — re-revoke after
    restoring a snapshot older than an incident, and `/settings/tokens` is today's only remedy);
    §7's BYO-bucket block asks for an abort-incomplete-multipart-upload lifecycle rule, because 16 MiB
    parts stranded by a killed container are billed for and are invisible to both `admin stats` and
    `admin orphans`, which build their view from a `List` of completed objects only; §7's
    `S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE` default is written `true` *(compose)* / `false` *(binary)* and `.env.example`
    annotates the one commented line whose value is not the live one, since its preamble promises the
    opposite; §1 says named volumes are not isolation (all three plus the container log share one
    filesystem on a default Docker install, and `SCRATCH_MIN_FREE_BYTES` is all that stands between a
    4 GiB upload and the next WAL write); §16 upgrades with `docker compose build --pull && docker
    compose up -d`, because moving base tags never move without it, and distinguishes an ffmpeg PATCH
    bump from §17.1's full matrix; §9's upload-error table gains the proxy's HTML `502 Bad Gateway` on
    a large file with a refused token (the app answers 401 in microseconds and closes, the proxy is
    still streaming and reports the reset as its own), with "an HTML error page did not come from the
    app" as the tell; and §6 and §17.3 stop giving the E2E two different runtimes (both now
    ~10 minutes, 612 s on the reference stack — the suite has grown since this erratum was written;
    the two sections are reconciled to each other and to the measured figure by N078, roadmap run).
    E2E: **step 28**, physically before the step-16 log gate, asserts three controls that could be
    deleted outright and leave the suite green — a cross-site `Origin` and a `Sec-Fetch-Site:
    cross-site` `PATCH` are both 403 `csrf` and neither changes the title; an unlisted clip of user A
    is absent from user B's `GET /api/clips` and present in A's own; and a session that has just been
    logged out is refused by `GET /api/auth/me` when the jar still carries its cookie (the jar is NOT
    rewritten by the logout call, so this proves the ROW is gone rather than that a cookie was
    cleared). It reuses the second user of steps 19/21 and leaves it logged out, exactly as step 22
    did, so the step creates nothing and cleans up after itself.
97. **The link a capture tool pastes must already be a player: `POST /api/upload` waits for `ready`**
    (`internal/httpapi/upload_capture.go`, `internal/httpapi/upload.go`, `internal/httpapi/router.go`,
    `internal/httpapi/httpapi.go`, `internal/worker/registry.go`, `internal/worker/worker.go`,
    `internal/config/config.go`, `compose.yaml`, `.env.example`; §4 gains two rows, §8's TimeoutHandler
    bullet and §8.1's two upload rows are amended, §14's rate-limiting paragraph is amended;
    `DEPLOY.md` §7/§9, `README.md`). One deep dive over the capture path found the race the product's
    whole identity turns on, plus two defects on the same two routes.
    (a) **The 201 was answering before the clip was playable, and Discord caches what it saw.**
    `POST /api/upload` returned `{"state":"queued","url":…}` the instant the original was durable —
    that `url` being the string ShareX puts on the clipboard — while the standard 6 s 720p30 test clip
    measured 1.4 s from upload to `ready` on the live stack. Fetch that URL as Discordbot inside the
    gap and you get exactly the §9.1 LINK-OUT card (`og:type` `website`, `twitter:card`
    `summary_large_image`, `og:description` "Processing…", **no** `og:video*`, **no**
    `twitter:player*`), and Discord caches the embed it extracted **per URL**: the card stays a bare
    link long after the clip is playable. The operator notes already listed this as the first diagnosis
    for "a card with a thumbnail, but clicking opens a browser tab". The race was never necessary —
    the transcode almost always finishes before the human finishes pasting, and the capture tool is
    blocked on the HTTP response either way — so the route now HOLDS its 201 for
    `CAPTURE_READY_WAIT` (§4; default `8s`, `0` = off, hard ceiling `config.CaptureReadyWaitMax` =
    60s enforced at boot) and then answers with the clip's REAL state. A request may override the
    budget with a `wait` field: a whole number of SECONDS, clamped to [0, 60] (a tool asking for more
    means "as long as you will give me"), a malformed or negative one → 400 `invalid_request` naming
    the field, like every other capture field. `POST /api/clips` is deliberately **untouched**: its
    caller is a browser with a live progress bar, and blocking it would only stall the bar.
    Mechanism: `Worker.AwaitTerminal(clipID)` returns a channel closed when that clip's progress
    entry turns `ready`/`failed`, plus the deregister the caller must run — no DB polling. Two
    properties make it correct rather than merely fast. A clip that is ALREADY terminal comes back as
    a CLOSED channel, which closes the one race the handler cannot close itself (it enqueues the job,
    wakes the worker, and only then subscribes; a short clip can finish in that gap). And a run writes
    its terminal registry entry AFTER the commit that published it, so the handler's re-read of the
    row cannot see the state it was waiting past. The wait also ends immediately on client disconnect,
    and the route is already `long` — outside `http.TimeoutHandler` — so nothing else in the stack is
    counting; that is the ONE deliberate block in the API and §8's "no long-polling" bullet now says
    so. The 201 body is unchanged in shape (`toUploadDTO`'s five keys); only `state` can now read
    `ready` or `failed`, and **an expired wait is not an error** — still 201, still `queued`.
    (b) **The upload limiter bounded an account, and accounts are free.** `userKey` returns
    `"u:"+p.User.ID` and its IP fallback is unreachable (`RequireUser` runs first), so
    `RATE_UPLOAD_PER_HOUR` (60) was per account — while `POST /api/auth/register` is held only by the
    auth limiter at 10/min/IP, i.e. ~600 new accounts an hour from one address, each carrying its own
    60 uploads, each accepted upload queuing a transcode and parking an original in the bucket. A
    ~600× amplification of the exact spend limit the hook exists to impose, and "close registration"
    (DEPLOY §7) does not answer it: with registration closed a single leaked ShareX token still gets
    the full 60/h and the operator has no per-address lever at all. Both upload routes now require
    BOTH buckets — the existing user-keyed one and a new `ipKey`'d
    `ratelimit.Middleware(h.uploadIPLimit, h.ipKey)` on `RATE_UPLOAD_PER_HOUR_PER_IP` (120,
    deliberately the looser of the pair: it is there because accounts are free, not to punish a
    household behind one NAT). The user bucket is listed first, so a caller over their own budget is
    refused without spending an address token; the aggregate ceiling is the same either way. Same 429
    `rate_limited` envelope and `Retry-After`. The trim and gif routes keep the user-keyed limiter
    alone — they act on a clip that already exists and belongs to the caller. The IP bucket is keyed
    on `clientip.Resolve`, so it inherits §13's honesty condition: with `TRUSTED_PROXIES` unset behind
    a tunnel every request collapses onto the Docker gateway and all users share the one bucket, which
    is the second reason 120 is generous rather than tight (DEPLOY §7 says so where an operator will
    read it).
    (c) **The 413 stopped naming an environment variable.** All four `too_large` sites answered
    `"upload exceeds MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES"`, and `web/static/app.js` renders `message` verbatim: the
    person watching a 5 GiB clip bounce was shown the name of a variable they cannot read, cannot
    change, and which did not even tell them how far over the line they were. One helper
    (`writeTooLarge`) now renders `Cfg.MaxUploadBytes` through a small binary-unit formatter —
    "this file is larger than the server accepts (limit 4.0 GiB)". The error CODE `too_large` and the
    413 are unchanged, because clients key on those. (The client-side size precheck and rendering
    `Retry-After` in the browser remain roadmap items, not part of this.)
    E2E: **step 29**, physically before the step-16 log gate, is the assertion the whole feature
    exists for: `POST /api/upload` with `-F wait=20` must answer 201 **and** `state` `ready`, and the
    `url` it just handed back must then serve the PLAYER card (`og:video`, `twitter:player`,
    `og:type` `video.other`, `twitter:card` `player`) to a Discordbot fetch — step 5 already proves
    the link-out card is what a queued clip really serves. `wait=0` is checked too, because the old
    immediate 201 must stay reachable. There is deliberately **no** 429 assertion in it: the upload
    buckets are shared with every later step and a tripped one would poison the run, so both limiters
    are covered by unit tests instead. Both clips carry a one-day TTL and are deleted, and the token
    is revoked, so the step leaves nothing on the shared stack.

98. **A share page is for two things a viewer cannot otherwise get: the file, and the snippet.**
    Before this the only download affordances in the whole product were the owner's preview GIF and
    `clippet.sxcu`: the owner-only `GET /api/clips/{id}/original` route existed and was wired, and
    `urls.Builder` built `video.mp4`, `social.mp4` and the embed URL, but **no template linked to any of
    them**. An owner could not retrieve their own source file through the web UI at all, nobody could
    copy an `<iframe>` (DEPLOY §9's hand-written example was the only place the snippet existed, and
    only integrators read that), and `video.mp4` answered 200 with no `Content-Disposition`, so a
    visitor's only path to the file was the browser's native "Save video as" — which iOS Safari does
    not offer. The share row itself sat inside `{{if .IsOwner}}`, so an anonymous viewer had no
    control of any kind.
    (a) **`GET /api/clips/{id}/video.mp4?download=1`** serves the SAME object through the SAME
    `serveObject`, adding `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=<title-slug>.mp4` built by the
    renderer `/original` already uses (RFC 5987 plus the ASCII fallback, erratum 50 — reused, not
    reimplemented). The slug is the title lowercased and reduced to `[a-z0-9-]`, every run of anything
    else (a literal `-` included) collapsed to one `-`, never leading or trailing, capped at 60 runes,
    falling back to the clip id when nothing survives; the result is a bare RFC 2045 token, so the
    header needs neither quoting nor the extended form. Everything else about the response is
    byte-identical to the plain GET — ETag, `Last-Modified`, `Cache-Control`, Range handling, 304, 412,
    416 — so the query string, already part of the cache key, carries the whole difference and **no
    `Vary` is added**. Any other value of `download` is ignored rather than refused: the parameter is
    reached from a link, and a link must never be a way to make a route fail. This is therefore not a
    wire-format change to an existing route; it is recorded here anyway.
    (b) **The share row moved out of the owner block** and is rendered for every viewer of a `ready`
    clip: Copy link, Copy embed and Download, with Download original (and the source size) added for
    the owner in every state the page renders. The owner's copy-then-touch behaviour is unchanged, and
    a visitor's copy sends no touch at all — the keep-alive stays the owner's signal (erratum 62). A
    visitor's page still carries none of `data-touch-url`, `data-keep-forever`, `data-expires` or
    `data-copy-note`; that test contract was extended, never relaxed. The client-side change is three
    lines: two lookups that used to be scoped inside the owner section are now scoped to the page
    (the controls they find are the owner's, they simply live above it now), plus a clipboard
    handler for the embed snippet reusing the existing `copyText()`/`flash()` and the one
    `[data-copied]` element.
    (c) **A download link is not a CTA, and no share target is permitted.** §9's "no CTAs on watch
    pages" rules out anything that asks the viewer for something — an account, a follow, a repost. A
    Download button asks for nothing and hands over the clip the viewer came for, and the medal doc's
    anti-feature is "watermarks or download **paywalls** on users' own clips", so shipping downloads
    free is the differentiator rather than a violation. What stays forbidden, explicitly: share
    targets and social buttons of every kind (a "post to X" button IS the CTA class), and any
    third-party link. The row is anchors and clipboard writes over this origin's own URLs, and nothing
    else may be added to it.
    E2E: **step 30**, physically before the step-16 log gate, on the clip earlier steps already have.
    It proves `?download=1` answers 200 with an `attachment` disposition naming a `.mp4` and the SAME
    ETag, `Vary` and `Cache-Control` as the plain GET; that a ranged save is the same 206 with the same
    `Content-Range`; that a cookie-less fetch of the share page carries `data-copy-embed` and the
    download link but no `data-touch-url` and no link to the original; and that `/original` still
    refuses an anonymous caller and still serves the owner. It creates nothing and therefore cleans up
    nothing.

99. **`/healthz` and `/readyz` print a database CLASS, not the driver's message**
    Both endpoints answered a failed DB ping or `QueueStats` with `{"db":"error: "+err.Error()}` —
    verbatim, to an anonymous, unmetered caller — while the STORAGE half of the very same payload has
    rendered only a bounded class since erratum 31, on the argument that a ping failure carries the whole
    request URL and that §15 says `/healthz` exposes no configuration values. A modernc/SQLite error is
    the same shape of leak from the other side: it can name `DATA_DIR`'s file path or the failing
    statement. `db.HealthClass(err)` now renders a closed set — `timeout`, `locked`, `readonly`, `io`,
    `full`, `corrupt`, `unavailable` — chosen on the PRIMARY SQLite result code (the extended codes fan
    out into dozens of values that all mean the same thing to a prober), and the leak is closed by
    DEFAULT: anything unrecognised is `unavailable`, never the message. The full error still goes to the
    access log through the `SetLogField` call that was already there. **Wire-format change** to the two
    endpoints' failure bodies; the success bodies are untouched. (A "healthz DB error" finding was
    REFUTED in Phase 2 round 5 on the ground that the message is an operator's, not a secret; what
    settles it now is parity — the two halves of one JSON object cannot disagree about who is reading
    them.)

100. **The library list reaches its index, and a committed row survives a power cut**
    Two independent things the storage layer promised and did not deliver, fixed together because both
    are one line of SQL and neither is visible from outside.
    (a) **`clips_listed` was dead.** Migration 0001 creates `clips_listed ON clips(created_at DESC, id)
    WHERE unlisted = 0` for exactly one query, and `WHERE … AND (unlisted = 0 OR owner_id = ?)` is a
    predicate no partial index can drive: `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` over the statement `ListClips` really runs
    read `SCAN clips` + `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY` — a full table scan plus a sort of the whole table
    — on **every** anonymous library page, which is the hot one (every crawler, every unfurl fetch, every
    logged-out visit). `listClipsSQL` now takes the shape as well as the filter and emits
    `AND unlisted = 0` with no viewer placeholder when there is no viewer. The result set is identical
    (`owner_id` is a user id and is never `""`), and the plan is `SCAN clips USING INDEX clips_listed`
    with no sort. `TestListClipsAnonymousUsesTheListedIndex` pins it the way erratum 84 pinned the tag
    plan, and `TestListClipsAnonymousSeesTheSameRows` pins the equivalence. The signed-in shape is
    unchanged.
    (b) **`synchronous(NORMAL)` → `synchronous(FULL)`.** Under WAL, NORMAL survives an application crash
    but may roll back COMMITTED transactions after a host power loss, which is precisely the inverse of
    what §8.3 and §11 promise: the original object is fsynced into the bucket before the 201, so a
    lost clip row leaves an object with no row — findable only by `admin orphans`, and only after its 1 h
    min-age. FULL costs one fsync per commit, and this application commits tens of times a minute (an
    upload, a state flip, a session touch), so the durability is bought with a cost nothing here can
    measure. Recorded in §8.3 and in DEPLOY §15.3.

101. **Two orderings the worker and the sweeper had backwards**
    (a) **A failing sweep candidate was retried at the head of the queue, at full cost, forever.**
    `SweepCandidates` ordered by `expires_at` and SQLite sorts NULL first, so `deleting` tombstones with
    no TTL — a manual DELETE, the one candidate class that piles up — came back at position 0 on every
    tick. `RunOnce` walks the batch in order and synchronously, each `Destroy` costing up to
    `STORAGE_OP_TIMEOUT` (30 s) against a 55 s tick budget, and nothing recorded that a `Destroy` had
    failed: two blackholing prefixes consumed the whole tick and every expiring clip behind them starved,
    silently, while the rest of storage was healthy. TTL is one of the two headline promises. Two
    changes, no migration: the query orders `expires_at IS NULL` LAST (then `expires_at`, then `id`, so
    the batch is the same list every tick), and the sweeper keeps an in-memory `clipID → {failures,
    next attempt}` map — exponential backoff `2m·2^(n−1)` capped at 1 h, a WARN naming the clip and its
    failure count, and a per-tick budget of two attempts that a candidate is charged to only from its
    SECOND consecutive failure on. The free first retry is what lets a whole batch that failed because
    storage was down come back in ONE tick when storage returns, while a prefix that keeps failing is
    down to two attempts a tick by its third round. The map is bounded (1024 entries, the one due soonest
    evicted) and deliberately not persisted: a restart is the one event that plausibly fixes storage, so
    forgetting the schedule then is right, and a column for it would be a migration for a cache. `Stats`
    gains `Backoff`, logged as `backoff=` when non-zero.
