    &nbsp;&nbsp;**A Destroy the tick's own budget cut short is a DEFERRAL, never a failure** (added with
    this erratum's fix, after (a) and 100(b) between them made the miss reachable). `RunOnce` tested the
    error's chain — `cerr := ctx.Err(); cerr != nil && errors.Is(err, cerr)` — and a cancelled `Destroy`
    does not reliably surface a context error: `database/sql` answers a commit whose context died with
    `sql: transaction has already been committed or rolled back`, which wraps nothing. The guard missed,
    `recordFailure` ran, and a perfectly healthy clip was suppressed for 2 m → 1 h — the exact starvation
    (a) exists to prevent, now aimed at whatever candidate is in flight when a slow tick runs out, i.e.
    the tail of every batch. `synchronous(FULL)` (erratum 100(b)) put an fsync in each commit and made the
    cut common enough to fail `-race` runs of `TestStartBlocksAndTicks` outright. The test is now the
    CONTEXT and not the error: `if err != nil && ctx.Err() != nil` defers the rest and breaks. `err == nil`
    is deliberately excluded — a `Destroy` that finished counts as destroyed, and the loop head defers what
    is left on the next pass — and a storage failure while the tick is alive is still a sweep error.
    (b) **The transcode held the ffmpeg slot while waiting for a same-clip predecessor.** `runJob`
    acquired the semaphore BEFORE `runRegistered`, and `withRun` then blocks on `<-prev.done` for a run
    already registered under the same clip id — while `trim` and `gif` register first and take the slot
    inside the run. With `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY=1` that is a lock-ordering inversion: a wedge waiting for
    a clip that is simultaneously transcode-claimable and media-claimable. It is unreachable today only
    because `EnqueueTrim`/`EnqueueGIF` require `state='ready'` and nothing moves a clip from `ready` back
    to `queued` — load-bearing, and written down nowhere. The acquire moved inside `runRegistered`'s
    body, so all three kinds take the slot in the same order; an error there is `errStopping` or a
    cancelled run context, which are the same event seen twice (Stop cancels every registered run, and
    the run is registered by then), so `execute()` finds its context done and takes the release path,
    exactly as `trimRun` does. Behaviour is otherwise unchanged: the slot is still held for the whole
    run, because there are exactly as many slots as transcode loops.

102. **A commit that lands and reports an error is not a lost race**
    `finalize()` and `swap()` both retry on `err != nil` and then read `ok == false` as "the clip was
    tombstoned" — the state whose remedy is `lostRace()`, which DELETES this attempt's objects. But
    `ok == false` is also what the SECOND call returns when the FIRST one landed, which is exactly the
    state a retry loop reaches when a commit succeeds and is still reported as an error. The premise
    could not be provoked against modernc, so this is latent; the consequence is a `ready` row pointing
    at objects the run has just deleted, which is the worst outcome in §11's table. `FinalizeTranscode`
    and `SwapRendition` now return a third value, `alreadyApplied`, decided by re-reading the clip in the
    SAME transaction: a row that is `ready` and references exactly this attempt's rendition AND poster
    keys can only have been written by this attempt (the keys are attempt-scoped, §7). The check runs
    on both of the swap's refusal paths, because a landed swap moves the JOB to `done` too and the second
    call is turned away by the job guard before the clip guard is reached. The callers keep their outputs
    and log one WARN; `superseded` comes back empty on that path — the first call carried those keys off
    with the error — so the old objects are left to `admin orphans`, which is the safe direction. The
    tombstone still answers `(false, false)` and still deletes, which is the whole point of telling the
    two apart. **Signature change** to two `db` functions; no wire format moves.

103. **Four things a card, a media route and a counter each owed somebody**
    (a) **The 412 kept the object's headers.** Erratum 85 made the 416 drop `ETag`, `Last-Modified` and
    `Content-Disposition` and answer `Cache-Control: no-store`, because the body is an ERROR and not the
    object — a download client must not save the JSON envelope under the clip's own filename, and "a
    cache must never be able to revalidate the object against an error body". `rangeErrorWriter`
    intercepted 416 only, so the 412 that `net/http`'s `checkPreconditions` writes for a failing
    `If-Match` or `If-Unmodified-Since` escaped with every representation header `serveObject` had set,
    including `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600` — and an explicit max-age on an empty 412 makes it
    storable. The writer now intercepts both; `writePreconditionFailed` drops the same three headers,
    sets `no-store` and writes the standard envelope with code `precondition_failed`. No `Content-Range`:
    a 412 is a precondition failure, not a range one. **Wire-format change**: the 412 gains a JSON body
    and loses the object headers.
    (b) **Three additive card tags** (§9.1). `og:video:url` is the same OGP property as `og:video` (the
    bare name is the shorthand for its `:url` field), so emitting both is free and is the spelling
    Discord's self-hosting guidance names; `video:duration`, whole seconds rounded, is licensed by
    `og:type=video.other` and comes off a `duration_ms` the page body already renders; `og:image:alt` is
    the first alt text a Clippet card has ever had. The inventory is an EXACT set in three places, so the
    three were added together and the count moved with them: **23 → 26** tags on http, 24 → 27 on https,
    updated in §9.1, in the `BuildMeta` golden and in the E2E card check. `video:duration` is omitted
    for a row with no duration: a `0` would be a claim about the clip rather than a gap in the row. The
    LINK-OUT card gains nothing — there is no video to describe.
    (c) **A real favicon, a theme-color, and an icon on the embed.** `base.html` shipped
    `<link rel="icon" href="data:,">` — a valid EMPTY document, so every Clippet tab got the browser's
    generic glyph — and `embed.html` had no icon link at all, so a direct embed visit GETs `/favicon.ico`
    and receives `404 text/html`: the whole 404 page, for an icon. Both now carry the same inline SVG
    `data:` URI (a rounded square in the stylesheet's `--bg` with a play triangle in `--accent`) and a
    `<meta name="theme-color">` matching `--bg`. The URI is percent-encoded in full, including the `:` of
    the SVG namespace, so the value is a well-formed URL with no character the HTML parser or a
    mixed-content check has to think about. No new request, no outbound anything, and
    `img-src 'self' data:` already permitted it: the CSP is unchanged.
    (d) **The view-dedupe key drops the User-Agent** (§13). `Key = clipID + sha256(ip + "\x00" + ua)`
    and the handler fed `r.UserAgent()` verbatim, so three POSTs from one address with three invented
    User-Agents counted three views — proven live — and the only bound was the 60/min/IP view limiter;
    the churn also evicted live entries at `VIEW_DEDUPE_MAX` and so shortened the honest dedupe window for
    everybody else. The UA was there deliberately, to let two people behind one NAT each count, so this
    is a trade-off and not a correction: the count is bounded by ADDRESSES now, which a caller cannot
    mint, and a household is one view per window. That is the right side to be wrong on for a private
    number whose only job is to tell its owner roughly how a clip did. The address is still hashed. Also
    fixed here, with no behavioural consequence today: `app.js`'s "which option would a reload restore"
    rule is the HTML reset algorithm now — the LAST option carrying `selected` wins, not the first, and
    with none it is the first option that is not `disabled`, not index 0 — and
    `TestSharePageOwnerSelectHasNoDefault` pins the `disabled` precondition alongside the `selected` one.
    E2E: **step 31**.

104. **Configuration: every mistake at once, a ceiling on the one knob that had none, and a build that says which binary it is**
    (a) **All errors, not the first.** `loader.fail` kept only the first (`if l.err == nil`) while the
    loader deliberately kept running every later lookup — so with `restart: unless-stopped` an operator
    with three typos in `.env` learned about them one restart at a time. `Load` returns a
    `*config.Errors` (`Unwrap() []error`, so `errors.Is`/`As` still reach through) and `main` prints one
    `clippet: config:` line per entry. A single failure prints exactly what it always did.
    (b) **`TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY` is bounded 1 … 16** (`config.MaxTranscodeConcurrency`). It had a
    minimum and no maximum while DEPLOY §18 advised raising it, and every slot is a live ffmpeg inside
    the process that also serves HTTP and runs the sweeper: the failure mode of a trailing zero was the
    OOM killer taking the whole instance rather than one encode.
    (c) **Resource ceilings and a version.** `compose.yaml` gains `mem_limit: ${APP_MEM_LIMIT:-2g}` and
    `cpus: ${APP_CPUS:-1.0}` — compose's v2 single-host keys, because a `deploy.resources.limits` block
    is Swarm-only and `docker compose up` ignores it without a word — and
    `build.args.VERSION: ${CLIPPET_VERSION:-dev}`, which reaches the Dockerfile's existing `ARG VERSION`
    and is baked in as `-X main.version`. Without it every local build reported `dev` and §16's upgrade
    checklist had nothing that changes on a release without a migration. Measured on this stack for the
    sizing advice: the app container idles at ~20 MiB and peaks at ~520 MiB while one slot renders the
    heaviest clip in the test matrix (1080p60 → 720p), much of it reclaimable page cache — so ~0.5 GiB
    and one core per slot, and `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY <= min(cores, RAM_GiB)`. The two keys are NOT
    symmetric and the default is `1.0`, not the core-per-slot-plus-headroom `2.0` this first shipped
    with: the daemon accepts a `mem_limit` above physical RAM, but a `cpus` above the host's core count
    is a hard container-CREATE error (`range of CPUs is from 0.01 to N, as there are only N CPUs
    available`), so on a 1-vCPU VPS `docker compose up -d` would have finished with no app container at
    all and `restart: unless-stopped` could not help — nothing was ever created. `1.0` is the documented
    one core for the default `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY=1` and is safe on every host; DEPLOY §7 says
    `nproc` is the ceiling.
    (d) **One boot WARN on the published credentials.** `S3_ACCESS_KEY: ${S3_ACCESS_KEY:-${MINIO_ROOT_USER:-clippet}}`
    means a stock deployment runs on a credential printed in this repository, and the `:-` form treats an
    EMPTY value exactly like an unset one — a quiet way to land back on the dev pair after a
    half-finished switch to R2/B2. The exposure is bounded (MinIO publishes no port; `bucket-init` runs
    `mc anonymous set none`), so this is a warning and not a boot failure. It fires on the COMBINATION —
    shipped credentials AND a `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` whose host is not loopback — because a container cannot
    see its own port publish, which is the same reasoning and the same shape as erratum 96's
    `TRUSTED_PROXIES` warning. The values are never logged. `.env.example` and DEPLOY §7 say so too.
    E2E: **step 32**.

105. **A session may slide, but never past a ceiling** (`internal/db/migrations/0005_session_limits.sql`,
    `internal/db/users.go`, `internal/auth/auth.go` `slidTo`/`CreateSession`/`SetSessionCookie`;
    `SESSION_MAX_TTL`, default `2160h` = 90 days). §4 and §14 promised a *sliding* session and delivered
    exactly that: every request past the once-a-minute touch gate pushed `expires_at` another
    `SESSION_TTL` into the future. With the shipped `SESSION_TTL=720h` that made an actively used
    cookie **immortal** — a laptop stolen on Monday keeps working in March, because the thief's own
    traffic is what keeps renewing it — and the only revocation surface in the product was
    `POST /api/auth/logout`, which needs the very credential being stolen. `sessions` gains
    `max_expires_at`, written once at creation as `created_at + SESSION_MAX_TTL` and never moved by a
    touch: it is a fact about the SESSION and not about its traffic. `TouchSession` clamps in SQL
    (`CASE WHEN max_expires_at > 0 AND ? > max_expires_at THEN max_expires_at ELSE ? END`) rather than
    in Go, because the ceiling is a property of the row and the caller holds only the request's clock —
    computing it above would need a second read and would race a concurrent revocation between them.
    `GetSession` checks the ceiling **as well**, and that is not belt-and-braces: the touch gate is a
    minute wide, so a row whose ceiling passed inside the current minute would otherwise be accepted on
    every request until the gate next opened. The re-issued cookie's `Max-Age` is now the row's
    REMAINING life rather than a fresh `SESSION_TTL` (erratum 25 made the cookie slide with the row;
    this keeps it from outliving it), and `SESSION_MAX_TTL` below `SESSION_TTL` therefore clamps even a
    brand-new session. `0` in the column means "no ceiling recorded" and is read as UNBOUNDED, never as
    "already expired": the migration backfills every existing row with the 90-day default, and the
    defensive read means a row written by an older binary against a migrated file degrades to the
    behaviour that shipped before this — the safe direction, since a zero read as a deadline would log
    every user out at once. Migration 0005 also adds `sessions(user_id, created_at DESC)`, which the
    four new per-user statements all need. **Wire-format change**: none.

106. **`REGISTRATION` is `first` by default, not `open`** (`internal/config/config.go`
    `RegistrationMode`, `internal/httpapi/auth_handlers.go` `registrationOpen`, `internal/web/pages.go`,
    `compose.yaml`, `.env.example`, `cmd/clippet/serve.go`). The service is documented for the public
    internet — DEPLOY §3 brings a Cloudflare quick tunnel up in one `docker run` — and the default was
    `open`, so the instant that tunnel answered, anyone who found the hostname had an account that could
    read every listed clip's metadata and upload 4 GiB. DEPLOY §7 warned about it, *after* the quickstart
    that had already published the origin. The variable is now a three-state enum: `open` (anybody,
    forever), **`first`** (accepted only while the `users` table is EMPTY) and `closed` (nobody). `first`
    is the default because the two constants are each wrong for a fresh install in the opposite
    direction: `open` publishes a signup form to the internet, and `closed` ships a service with no way
    in at all. Under `first` the door is held by the INSERT itself: `db.CreateFirstUser` runs
    `INSERT INTO users … SELECT ?,?,?,? WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users) = 0` on the single-connection
    writer pool and answers `ErrConflict` — the same 403 `registration_closed` — when it wrote no row.
    That is not a refinement of a `COUNT(*)`-then-`INSERT` check but a replacement for it: `register`
    hashes with bcrypt (cost 12, a couple of hundred milliseconds) between the two, so a check-then-insert
    leaves a window hundreds of milliseconds wide in which a burst of concurrent registrations against an
    empty table ALL read zero and ALL succeed — the one guarantee `first` exists to make, lost to a race
    that needs no timing skill. Caching has nothing to do with it; the window is inherent to reading and
    writing in two statements. The separate `COUNT(*)` above the handler survives as a **fast refusal**
    only — a closed instance answers 403 without burning a bcrypt hash, and the two anonymous pages need
    the same question answered to decide whether to draw a form — and it is deliberately **not cached**,
    because the whole point is that it closes the instant an account exists and a cached "empty" would
    keep drawing a signup form after the bootstrap account walked through. A read failure is reported (503),
    never guessed at: "sure, go ahead" on an unreadable `users` table is the one answer this must not give. The
    two anonymous PAGES resolve the same question for the form and the "create an account" link, and
    there a DB failure reads as CLOSED rather than as a 503 page — the flag only decides whether a form
    is drawn, the route re-asks for real before creating anything, and drawing a signup form that cannot
    work is the worse of the two wrong answers. The effective mode is on the boot line
    (`registration=first`), and every successful registration now annotates its access-log line with
    `registered=<username> client_ip=<resolved address>` — on a public origin this is the only route that
    mints a credential out of nothing. `clippet admin users create` (erratum 109) is how accounts are
    added under `first` and `closed`. **Wire-format change**: none; `POST /api/auth/register` answers the
    same 403 `registration_closed` it always did, under a wider set of conditions.

107. **The active-session list, and "log out everywhere but here"**
    (`GET`/`DELETE /api/auth/sessions`, `internal/httpapi/auth_handlers.go`, `dto.go` `SessionDTO`,
    `internal/db/users.go` `ListSessions`/`DeleteOtherSessions`). Session-only, CSRF-guarded on the
    DELETE, `private, no-store` + `Vary: Cookie` on the GET. `SessionDTO` is
    `{created_at, last_seen_at, expires_at, current, user_agent}` and carries **no id and no handle of
    any kind**. That is the design, not an omission: a session's only identity is the hex sha256 of its
    cookie — that IS the security of the scheme — and a per-session revoke would need a name for it that
    a page, and therefore an attacker's page, could then send. The affordance an incident actually needs
    is "end every session but this one", which needs no id at all, so the list is a statement of fact and
    `current` is the only thing a reader has to match against the browser in front of them. The hash
    reaches `httpapi` (to mark `current`) and stops there. `user_agent` is the string that browser sent,
    capped at 256 bytes at insert and rendered as text; it is the caller's own data and reaches nobody
    else. The DELETE answers `{"sessions_revoked":n}` — a count is the only honest receipt, since the
    caller cannot see what it just ended — and a second call is a clean `0`, not an error.
    **The count is rows DELETED, which is an upper bound on what the list showed** (amended
    2026-09-07, nit sweep). `DeleteOtherSessions` carries no lifetime predicate while `ListSessions`
    carries two, and expired rows leave only on a sweeper tick, so the receipt also covers every
    session of that user that died since the last tick. The SQL is deliberately left that way —
    deleting a dead row is desirable, and repeating the predicates would strand it — so the number is
    "how many rows this call removed", not "how many of the sessions you were just looking at". The
    same is true of the sweep half of a password change (erratum 108).
    **Wire-format change**: two new routes and one new DTO.

108. **`PATCH /api/auth/password`: rotate the hash and sweep the other sessions in ONE transaction**
    (`internal/httpapi/auth_handlers.go` `changePassword`, `internal/db/users.go` `SetPassword`).
    Session-only, CSRF-guarded, `Content-Type: application/json` required, and held by the **auth**
    limiter rather than the upload one: this route takes a password and runs a bcrypt compare, so it
    belongs in the same per-IP bucket as login and register — a per-user budget bounds nothing against a
    thief who already holds the cookie. The current password is re-verified even though the caller holds
    a live session, because a session is "this browser was logged in once" and a password change is
    "this is still the account's owner": an unlocked laptop must not silently become a permanent
    takeover. The `UPDATE users` and the `DELETE FROM sessions WHERE user_id = ? AND token_hash <> ?`
    are one transaction, and that is load-bearing in both directions — a rotation that committed while
    the old sessions were still live would leave the thief logged in with the new password's blessing,
    and a sweep that committed first would log the owner out of a change that then failed. Rotating to
    the SAME password is a 400: not a security rule but a courtesy, since it would still sign every
    other browser out for a no-op the caller did not mean. The answer is `{"sessions_revoked":n}`, the
    same body the DELETE above returns, and no error or log line ever carries either password.
    This route also **amends erratum 95's premise in `app.js`**: `sessionEnded` treated every 401 as a
    dead credential, which was true while no page action could 401 for any other reason. A wrong
    `current_password` is the first 401 in the product that a LIVE session can provoke, so `sessionEnded`
    now excludes `error === "invalid_credentials"` — otherwise the single most likely mistake on this
    form reads as "your session ended — log in again", beside a link that bounces straight back to
    `/settings` because the caller is still signed in. The exclusion lives in `sessionEnded` and not in
    the form's handler so the rule stays in the one place erratum 95 put it.
    **Wire-format change**: one new route.

109. **Operator revocation: `clippet admin sessions`, `tokens` and `users create`**
    (`cmd/clippet/admin.go`, `internal/db/users.go` `DeleteAllSessions`/`RevokeUserTokens`). The whole
    incident response before this was editing SQLite by hand. Every verb is guarded the way
    `users prune` is (erratum 86): an **explicit selector, and no default that means "everything"**.
    `sessions list <username>` and `sessions revoke <username>` take an exact username (case-insensitive
    like registration — a LIKE pattern is for the command that reports what it will remove first, and
    these do not); `sessions revoke --all` is the instance-wide hammer and has to be typed, and a
    username *and* `--all` together is a usage error, because a command that can be read two ways is a
    command that will be. `tokens list <username>` and `tokens revoke <username> <tid> | --all`: a
    username alone is deliberately **not** a selector for a revoke, since "revoke alice's tokens" is a
    sentence an operator can type while meaning "show me alice's tokens". Unknown, already-revoked and
    somebody-else's token are one answer and exit 1, exactly as the owner's own DELETE gives one 404.
    Nothing prints a session hash, a token hash or a raw token — the lists show the same `prefix` the
    owner sees. (**Amended by erratum 308**: `tokens mint` prints a raw token, on **stdout**, once —
    that is the artefact it exists to produce, and it is the only exception. The sentence holds
    everywhere a PERSON is being written to: the mint's own confirmation, like every list here, carries
    the `prefix` and never the value.) `users create <username>` reads the password from **stdin**, never from argv: a command
    line is written into shell history, is visible to every `ps` on the host, and is echoed by
    `docker compose exec` in its own logs. It applies §14's username regexp and the 8–72 byte bcrypt
    guard verbatim, so the CLI and `POST /api/auth/register` cannot disagree about what an account is.
    **Wire-format change**: none (CLI only).

110. **`/settings` is the account page; `/settings/tokens` is a 303 to its anchor**
    (`internal/web/pages.go`, `internal/web/server.go`, `web/templates/settings.html` replacing
    `tokens.html`, `base.html`). Tokens stopped being a page of their own and became a section, because
    the password form, the session list and the token list are three answers to one question — "who can
    act as me right now" — and the incident that starts with "I pasted my token into the wrong channel"
    ends with revoking a session, or the other way round. The nav item is **Settings**. The password
    inputs carry `autocomplete="current-password"` / `"new-password"` so a password manager offers the
    right thing in each box. The Phase 1 URL keeps answering as a **303 to `/settings#tokens`** rather
    than a 404: it is documented in DEPLOY §9, printed in the ShareX instructions and bookmarked in
    browsers. It is a 303 and not a 301 because a permanent redirect would be cached by the browser
    forever for a compatibility shim, and it carries the private headers every principal-dependent
    bounce in that package carries. The session-list section degrades on its own: a failed
    `ListSessions` renders one inline message instead of taking the password form and the token list
    down with it. **Wire-format change**: `/settings/tokens` answers 303 instead of 200.

111. **A read-only token scope** (`internal/auth/auth.go` `ScopeRead`/`RequireSessionOrScope`,
    `internal/httpapi/token_handlers.go` `cleanScopes`, `router.go`). Erratum 19 made tokens
    upload-only, which is right for a capture-tool credential and also means no automation can *read*
    the library: no backup script listing your clips, no "sync my library to a NAS" cron. The closed
    scope set is now `upload | read`, and `read` opens exactly two routes — `GET /api/clips` and
    `GET /api/collections` — plus `GET /api/auth/me`, which every valid token has always reached.
    **Two routes is a statement about routes, not about rows**, and the operator docs must say so:
    `GET /api/clips` is the library listing and returns what a browser session gets — every `unlisted=0`
    clip on the instance, whoever owns it, plus the caller's own unlisted ones — so a `read` token can
    enumerate the share ids, and therefore the watch pages, of every listed clip on the instance. That is
    the existing, deliberate shape of the listing (§8.1) and a session has always had it; what is new is
    only that a token can be handed to somebody else, so DEPLOY §9/§19.5, README and the mint form say
    "the same library listing your browser sees" rather than "your own clips". `GET /api/collections`
    really is the caller's own rows, and the owner-private DTO fields still come back only on the
    caller's own clips (erratum 112).
    Everything else erratum 19 closed stays closed, `/original` and `GET …/trim` included: those are
    owner-only reads whose contents (the source bytes, a failure reason) are a different kind of thing
    from "list what I own". `RequireSessionOrScope` is `RequireSession` widened by exactly one scope,
    and its refusal keeps erratum 19's **`token_not_allowed`** code rather than gaining a more precise
    `insufficient_scope`: that answer is part of the contract clients were written against, and only
    the human-readable message names the way out. `POST /api/auth/tokens` takes an optional
    `scopes` array — absent or null is `["upload"]`, so every existing client is unchanged; an unknown
    scope or an **empty array** is a 400, because a token that can do nothing is a mistake rather than a
    request, and a row claiming a permission the binary does not implement is a lie a later release
    could accidentally make true. The stored order is canonical (`upload`, then `read`) whatever the
    client sent. `sxcu` is **null** for a token without the `upload` scope: handing a read-only token a
    ShareX destination would import cleanly and 403 on the first screenshot, with nothing on either side
    saying why. No migration: `api_tokens.scopes` has been a comma-separated column since 0001.
    **Wire-format change**: `scopes` on the mint request, and `sxcu` may now be null.

112. **`isOwner` is a session OR the owner's own `read`-scoped token** (`internal/httpapi/clip_handlers.go`
    `clipDTO`, `internal/auth/auth.go` `Principal.OwnerReader`). Erratum 19 defined the owner-private
    DTO fields (`views`, `source_duration_ms`, `trim`) as session-only, because the only token that
    existed was an upload credential and `GET /api/clips/{id}` — a PUBLIC route — was the one
    owner-relevant place it could reach. The `read` scope of erratum 111 exists precisely so the owner's
    automation can read the owner's own library, and those fields are that library, so the rule becomes
    "a session, or a token carrying `read`, whose user id equals `owner_id`". An upload-only token still
    sees the public DTO of its own clips, unchanged, and a `read` token belonging to somebody else sees
    the public DTO like every other caller: the scope widens WHO the owner may be, never WHOSE rows are
    readable. **Wire-format change**: `GET /api/clips/{id}` may now carry `views` for a read-scoped
    token of the owner. E2E: **steps 33–36**.

113. **`LIBRARY_SCOPE` narrows one query, and that is the whole feature** (`internal/config/config.go`
    `LibraryScope`/`LibraryScopeShared`/`LibraryScopeOwn`, `internal/db/clips.go` `ListQuery.ScopeOwn` +
    `listClipsSQL`, `internal/db/library.go` `ownerFilterSQL`, `internal/httpapi/clip_handlers.go`
    `listClips`, `internal/web/pages.go` `index`, `web/templates/index.html`, `.env.example`,
    `compose.yaml`; DESIGN §4, DEPLOY §20; ROADMAP #2). "I run Clippet for four friends and I do not
    want my job-hunting clip in their library" had no answer but "tick unlisted every time", because
    `listClipsSQL`'s visibility clause was a literal with no configuration behind it.
    `LIBRARY_SCOPE=own` appends `AND owner_id = ?` to that clause — the SAME predicate `?mine=1`
    appends (erratum 115), decided by the instance instead of by the request. `shared` is the default
    and is byte-for-byte the old behaviour: a configuration variable must never be the thing that
    silently hides clips a household could see yesterday, so the upgrade path is "nothing changes
    until you set it".
    **What it does NOT touch, deliberately.** `GET /api/clips/{id}`, the share page, `/embed/{id}`,
    `/c/{id}`, every media route and `POST /api/clips/{id}/view` are unchanged, because the
    unguessable 12-character id IS the authentication (§7) and always was: scoping the library is
    about what an account *browses*, not about who may follow a link somebody sent them. The Discord
    auto-post is unchanged too — one webhook is one channel, and "post only my own clips" is a routing
    feature (ROADMAP #26), not a consequence of this one. And it never widens: an owner check is still
    an owner check, so a stranger's PATCH is still 403 under either value.
    The scope is **not** part of the page cursor's filter binding (erratum 115), because a filter is a
    choice the reader can unmake with the next link while the scope is identical for every request
    that reader can make; refusing every outstanding page token because the operator edited `.env`
    would turn a settings change into a wall of `invalid_cursor`. Narrowing the set under a live
    cursor is safe on its own terms: the order is total over `(created_at DESC, id ASC)` and the
    cursor names a position in it, so removing rows can only shorten a page.
    `config.TestLibraryScope`, `db.TestListClipsMineAndScopeNarrowIdentically`,
    `httpapi.TestLibraryScopeOwn` / `TestLibraryScopeSharedIsTheDefault`,
    `web.TestIndexLibraryScopeOwn` and E2E **step 38** cover it. Step 38 is the shape worth copying:
    the lane's own app keeps its configured default for the whole run — recreating it would destroy
    the log history step 16 reads — and the scope is proven on a THROWAWAY `docker compose run`
    container over the same database, with its own port and its own `PUBLIC_BASE_URL`, removed before
    the log gate.

114. **Library search is a bounded substring over the same visibility set, and it has no index on
    purpose** (`internal/db/library.go` `CleanSearch`/`asciiLower`/`escapeLike`/`searchSQL`/
    `searchPattern`, `internal/db/clips.go` `ListQuery.Q`, `internal/httpapi/clip_handlers.go`,
    `internal/web/pages.go`, `web/templates/index.html`; ROADMAP #4). "That clutch from last month —
    what was it called" had no answer but scrolling *Older clips*.
    `?q=` is trimmed, ASCII-lower-cased, at most **64 runes**, and must be text: invalid UTF-8 or a
    control character is `invalid_request`, and so is a 10 KB paste. An EMPTY value is the absence of
    a filter rather than an error, because that is what an empty search box means. The lower-casing is
    ASCII-only for erratum 81's reason applied to a second field — a full Unicode fold maps U+212A
    KELVIN SIGN onto `k`, so a search for one word would silently match a different one — and because
    SQLite's own `lower()`, which the other half of the comparison uses, is ASCII-only too: folding
    more in Go would only make the two halves disagree.
    The predicate is `AND (lower(title) LIKE ? ESCAPE '\' OR lower(description) LIKE ? ESCAPE '\')`
    inside the existing visibility clause, so it NARROWS and cannot widen: a stranger's unlisted clip
    matching the needle is as invisible as it was. `ESCAPE` is not decoration — `%` and `_` are LIKE
    metacharacters, so a search for `50%` without it matches every row on the instance —
    and `escapeLike` quotes all three (including the escape character).
    **There is no index and no migration 0006.** A `%needle%` LIKE cannot use a B-tree in any
    database: the leading wildcard makes every row a candidate, so an index on `title` would be dead
    weight and an expression index on `lower(title)` would be dead weight with a migration attached.
    The documented bound is the scan itself: it runs inside the visibility clause, over `clips`
    ALONE (never over `clip_tags` or `jobs`), on a table a personal instance keeps in the low tens of
    thousands of rows, and it stops at `LIMIT+1` matches.
    `db.TestListClipsSearchPlanScansOnlyClips` pins that one-table shape, and
    `db.TestListClipsTagFilterKeepsItsIndexUnderTheNewFilters` re-pins erratum 84 with `?q=` and
    `?mine=1` applied beside `?tag=` — a filter that pushed the tag IN-list behind a scan would undo
    that erratum silently. `db.TestCleanSearchGrammar` / `TestEscapeLike` / `TestListClipsSearch`,
    `httpapi.TestListClipsSearchFilter`, `web.TestIndexSearchBox` and E2E **step 37** complete it;
    the E2E's two metacharacter probes (`<needle>_one`, `<needle>%one`) are anchored on a word the
    clip's title really holds, so an UNESCAPED `_` or `%` matches and the assertion fails in exactly
    the case the ESCAPE clause exists for.

115. **`?mine=1`, and a cursor that carries every filter it was minted under**
    (`internal/db/library.go` `listFilter`/`decodeFilter`, `internal/db/clips.go`
    `encodeCursor`/`decodeCursor`/`ListQuery.Mine`, `internal/httpapi/clip_handlers.go`,
    `internal/web/pages.go` `filterQuery`; amends erratum 81's cursor paragraph; ROADMAP #4).
    `?mine=1` adds `AND owner_id = ?` for the VIEWER and for nobody else: there is no `?owner=<id>`
    and there never will be, because a route that lists another account's clips is a user page, which
    is the social layer the anti-features rule out. Any other spelling — `mine=0`, `mine=true`,
    `mine=<someone>` — is `400 invalid_request` on the API and a 303 to the whole library on the page,
    for the reason an illegal `?tag=` is: a filter that silently did nothing would show a WIDER list
    than the caller asked for.
    The page token now carries the whole filter. Its three shapes, in the order they were introduced:

        <at>:<id>                     no filter          (Phase 1)
        <at>:<id>:<tag>               a tag alone        (§17 #9)
        <at>:<id>:mine=1&q=…&t=…      anything else      (this erratum)

    The first two are still MINTED, not merely decoded: erratum 81's "tokens minted before this
    feature still decode" is a standing promise, and a tag-only list is the common filtered case, so
    it keeps the short token it has always had. The two shapes cannot be confused — the tag grammar
    has no `=` in it — and the filter field is everything after the SECOND colon, so a value carrying
    one cannot truncate it (`url.Values.Encode` percent-escapes `:` anyway, which is the belt to that
    braces). Every field is re-validated on the way back in and must round-trip to what we would have
    minted: a cursor is our own token, so an un-normalised value, an unknown key, a repeated key or a
    `mine` that is not `1` is a forged or corrupted token and gets no benefit of the doubt.
    Spending a token under a different filter is `400 invalid_cursor`, exactly as before. What is NOT
    in the binding is `LIBRARY_SCOPE` (erratum 113).
    `db.TestCursorShapesAndBinding` / `TestListClipsCursorCarriesEveryFilter`,
    `httpapi.TestListClipsMineFilter` / `TestListClipsFiltersCombineAndBindTheCursor`,
    `web.TestIndexMineFilter` / `TestIndexFilterLinksCarryEveryFilter` and E2E **step 37**.

116. **One progress poll for the page, not one per row** (`internal/httpapi/progress_batch.go`,
    `internal/httpapi/progress.go` `baseProgress`/`registryProgress`, `internal/db/library.go`
    `ProgressRows`/`MaxProgressIDs`, `internal/httpapi/router.go`, `web/static/app.js`
    `watchLibrary`; §8.4 as amended; ROADMAP #15). `app.js` started an INDEPENDENT one-second poll
    per unfinished library row and `libraryPageSize` is 100, so a ShareX watch-folder drop of forty
    files — the exact workflow medal #1 exists to serve — made one open browser tab issue ~40
    requests a second at a box that was simultaneously running ffmpeg.
    `GET /api/clips/progress?ids=…` answers up to `MaxProgressIDs` (100, the library's page size)
    clips from ONE query: `clips` LEFT JOINed to each row's latest **transcode** job (never merely its
    newest job — since Phase 4 that is routinely a notify, a trim or a gif, erratum 89). An id that
    resolved to no live clip is **absent from the map**. That is this route's spelling of the single
    route's 404, it carries the same rule — a poller treats it as "gone", never as "done" — and
    spelling it as an absence rather than a per-id error object keeps the client's read one lookup and
    keeps the route from being a nicer existence oracle than the one it replaces. A MALFORMED id is a
    400 instead, because a silent omission there would report "this clip is gone" for what is a typo.
    It is **public**, like the single-clip route it replaces: same DTO, same facts, same three
    terminal signals, so it widens nothing. Unlike that route it carries the `view` limiter
    (60/min/IP), because one call can do a hundred times the work — erratum 87's reasoning for the
    collection GET, applied here.
    The two routes share `baseProgress` and `registryProgress` so they cannot drift, and the shared
    code preserves the single route's short-circuit exactly: a live registry entry answers on its own
    and the job row is not read at all. `httpapi.TestBatchProgressMatchesTheSingleRoute` compares the
    two answers as JSON for every state, with and without a registry entry.
    On the client, `watchLibrary` keeps `poll`'s rules because they are the same rules (1 s, then 2 s
    after a minute; a hidden tab waits for `visibilitychange`; `maxPollFailures` unreachable ticks end
    it) and adds one: there is no timer at all while no row is unfinished — rows leave the set as they
    finish and the last one to leave stops the loop. E2E **step 39**.

117. **`POST /api/clips/bulk`: one request, one action, a bounded set, and a PER-ID answer**
    (`internal/httpapi/bulk.go`, `internal/httpapi/router.go`; supersedes ROADMAP #16's sketch, which
    said "no new server route: a loop over the existing routes"). The loop was rejected once the
    partial-failure contract was written down: twenty rows is twenty round trips over one connection,
    each with its own CSRF check and session lookup, and a tab closed halfway through leaves the set
    half-applied with nothing that says which half. Here the half that applied is IN the answer.
    The route takes `action` ∈ {`delete`, `ttl`, `tag`, `collection`} and at most **100** ids (the
    library's page size: the action is "the rows I ticked on this page"), duplicates collapsed — a
    client that ticked one row twice meant one clip, and the results are one entry per clip. Each
    entry carries the status the equivalent single-clip request would have answered with, so a client
    that already knows this API needs no second vocabulary.
    **The request-level half of an action fails the request; the per-id half is reported per id.** An
    illegal tag, a `ttl_days` outside §8.2's five values, an unknown action and a `collection_id` that
    is missing or not the caller's are ONE mistake, not twenty, so they are 400/404 with nothing
    written. All four `collection_id` mistakes — absent, malformed, gone, somebody else's — answer the
    identical `404 not_found` **"no such collection"** (`writeCollectionNotFound`, the helper the
    `/api/collections/{cid}` routes already use): a 404 saying "no such clip" would be true of no clip
    in the request and would send the caller after the wrong parameter, which is erratum 30's rule
    applied to a route that carries two kinds of id. Everything about a clip — not yours (403), not
    there (404), the clip's own ten-tag cap
    (400 `invalid_tags`), a collection that is full (409 `too_many_clips`), a database error (503) —
    is that clip's own result, and the batch is still a **200**: no transport status can say
    "nineteen of twenty", and a 207-style body is the only honest shape.
    It is **not a transaction over the set**, and that is deliberate: each id is applied in its own
    database transaction (so no single clip is ever half-applied), and rolling back nineteen good
    deletes because the twentieth was a typo is a worse answer than the typo. An all-or-nothing delete
    could not be promised anyway — the bucket is not in the transaction.
    Posture is every other owner mutation's: **session only** (a capture token gets 403
    `token_not_allowed`, erratum 19), CSRF-guarded, `requireJSON`, and OUTSIDE the `TimeoutHandler`
    for `DELETE`'s reason (erratum 118). The path is a LITERAL segment, so the Go 1.22 mux prefers it
    over `/api/clips/{id}` without either pattern knowing about the other — and `bulk` could never
    have been a clip id anyway (`ids.Valid` wants twelve base62 characters).
    `httpapi.TestBulkDeleteReportsPerID` / `TestBulkTTL` / `TestBulkTag` / `TestBulkCollection` /
    `TestBulkRequestShape` / `TestBulkIsSessionOnly` and E2E **step 40**.

118. **A bulk delete has ONE budget, and an id it cannot reach is still gone** (`internal/httpapi/
    bulk.go` `bulkDeleteOne`). `DELETE /api/clips/{id}` runs `Destroy` inline under `DestroyBudget`
    (60 s) and answers 202 when the tombstone is set but the storage step did not finish (§12). A
    hundred of those in one request is not a request, it is an outage, so the whole batch shares ONE
    `DestroyBudget`: while it lasts each id gets the full inline destroy and its 204; once it is
    spent the remaining ids are TOMBSTONED instead and answer 202 — the outcome the single route
    already documents, and the one that makes them 404 to every reader immediately while the sweeper
    finishes their objects on its next tick.
    Two details are load-bearing. The destroy runs on a context detached from the client, exactly as
    the single route's does: once the tombstone is written the work must finish whatever the browser
    does. And a `Destroy` that failed for any reason falls through to `MarkDeleting` rather than
    reporting success — `MarkDeleting` is idempotent on an already-deleting row and `ErrNotFound`
    there means the row is already gone (the 204 outcome by another route), so a storage outage
    during a bulk delete produces 202s and a tombstoned row, never a 204 over a clip that is still
    live. `httpapi.TestBulkDeleteTombstonesWhenTheBudgetIsSpent` and
    `TestBulkDeleteStorageFailureIsStillATombstone`.

119. **The two add-one verbs bulk actions need, and why erratum 81's "no add-one verb" bends here**
    (`internal/db/bulk.go` `AddClipTag`/`AddClipToCollection`). Erratum 81 says there is no add-one
    tag verb, and gives the reason: the editor driving `PATCH {"tags":[…]}` is a text field holding
    the whole list, so a partial verb there would need a merge rule nobody can see in the box they
    are typing into. A bulk action is the opposite shape — one word, twenty clips, each with a
    different existing set — and REPLACING those sets is exactly the accident erratum 95 was written
    about. So `AddClipTag` adds one tag and leaves the rest of the set alone; a tag already present
    is a success that writes nothing and does not stamp `updated_at` (an action that says "these
    twenty carry `clutch`" is done when they do); a clip that already carries ten OTHER tags is
    `ErrLimitReached` → that clip's own 400, because the cap is the clip's (erratum 81) and not the
    request's.
    `AddClipToCollection` is the same shape for membership. `SetCollectionClips` replaces the whole
    ordered list, which is right for the picker that sends the whole list and wrong for "file these
    five as well": a client that had to read-modify-write the membership to add a clip would race
    every other tab doing the same. The append takes `MAX(position)+1` inside its own transaction —
    the rw pool is a single connection under `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, so two concurrent appends cannot
    collide and the sequence stays dense — leaves the members already there exactly where they were,
    and is idempotent. A collection that is missing or not the caller's is `ErrNotFound` (erratum
    82's rule: the mutating routes scope by owner, so the two cases are one query and one answer),
    and a clip that is missing, tombstoned or somebody else's is one `NotYourClipError`, so neither
    verb is an existence oracle. `db.TestAddClipTag` and `db.TestAddClipToCollection`.

120. **The library page: a search that works without JavaScript, controls that do not appear without
    it, and two badges that were already in the row** (`web/templates/index.html`,
    `web/static/app.css`, `web/static/app.js` `setupLibrary`/`setupBulk`/`applyRowFacts`,
    `internal/web/pages.go` `indexPage`/`clipRow`/`resolutionText`; ROADMAP #30). Three rules the
    page follows, all of them §9's.
    **The search is a plain `<form method="get" action="/">`.** It produces the same URL the tag chips
    already link to, so it works with scripting off, it is bookmarkable, and the back button means
    what it says. The box is re-filled with the NORMALISED needle, because the server is the authority
    on what was searched for and a box showing something else is a page lying about its own results.
    The box's `maxlength` **is** `db.MaxSearchRunes` (64), not the 200 the title field uses: the page
    must not hand the user a value its own server discards, or a 65-character paste lands back on the
    unfiltered library with an empty box and nothing that says why. `web.TestIndexSearchBox` asserts
    the attribute against the constant so the two cannot drift apart again.
    **The bulk controls are server-rendered and inert.** The bar carries `hidden` and the per-row
    checkbox is `display:none` until `app.js` sets `data-bulk-ready` on the library section; without a
    client neither appears, and every action they offer is still available one clip at a time on that
    clip's own page. The bar is a `<div role="group">` and NOT a `<form>`: `POST /api/clips/bulk`
    takes JSON, so a form that could be submitted without JavaScript could only ever be a 415. A
    checkbox is rendered only on a row the caller owns (`IsOwn` already existed), because the API
    answers 403 for somebody else's clip and offering the box would be offering an error. Delete is
    the one action that asks twice, through the same `confirmClick` the clip and token pages use —
    never `confirm()` — and changing the selection disarms it, so the second click always means the
    set the first one was about.
    **The badges are facts the row already carried.** `duration_ms`, `width` and `height` are in the
    DTO and on the share page; the row now renders the duration over the thumbnail and the resolution
    beside the date, which is how a four-second clip is told from a four-minute one in a list of
    pictures. They are rendered only for a `ready` clip: a queued row has no duration, and a `0:00`
    that later becomes `4:12` is a wrong fact rather than a missing one. When a row goes ready under
    the poll, `app.js` fetches that ONE clip once and fills them in, because a progress poll carries a
    job's progress and never a clip's dimensions — one request per clip, at the transition, against
    the ~40 a second erratum 116 removed. Styling stays in `app.css` and every value the client writes
    goes through `element.style.<prop>` or `classList` (CSP `style-src 'self'`);
    `web.TestIndexRowBadges` / `TestIndexBulkBarIsHiddenWithoutJS` / `TestIndexSearchBox` assert the
    markup and `assertNoInline` re-asserts the CSP rule on every page this bundle touched.

121. **The card gets its own file, and the rule for when is measured** (`internal/worker/social.go`,
    `internal/db/social.go`, `internal/transcode/social.go`; §17 #3, ROADMAP #3). `/social.mp4` is what
    `og:video`, `og:video:secure_url` and `twitter:player:stream` point at, and it has always served the
    main rendition byte for byte. That rendition is sized for a player somebody chose to open: up to
    60 fps, CRF 23, no bitrate ceiling at all. A card is the opposite case — Discord fetches the file
    itself and stops playing it inline somewhere past ~100 MB (community-reported; no official figure
    was fetchable) — so the long high-motion clip this product exists to share is exactly the one that
    degrades to a link.
    **Measured first, on ffmpeg 7.1.1, before anything was built** (60-second sources, so the figures
    are per minute):

    | source | main rendition | social rendition |
    |---|---|---|
    | the matrix `hd-1080p60` clip (testsrc2, moderate motion) → 1280×720 | 1.64 Mbps = **11.7 MB/min** | 0.89 Mbps = **6.4 MB/min** (54 %) |
    | worst case (`mandelbrot` 1080p60, fine detail in constant motion) → 1280×720 | 14.3 Mbps = **107 MB/min** | 2.35 Mbps = **17.7 MB/min** |
    | the real capture ROADMAP #3 measured | 3.64 Mbps = **27.3 MB/min** → 4 min ≈ 109 MB | ≤2.5 Mbps ≈ 18.8 MB/min → 4 min ≈ **75 MB** |

    The middle row is the argument: CRF alone has no ceiling, so a four-minute clip of that content is
    428 MB, and the same four minutes with the ceiling is 71 MB. (Step 0 of the roadmap sketch —
    pasting a real capture into Discord and watching — cannot be done by an agent; it is
    the owner's live Discord paste. The feature is built behind the skip rule so that nothing an operator has
    today changes until a clip is genuinely in the shape the numbers above describe.)
    - **The job.** `social` is a MEDIA kind (`db.MediaKinds`), so its ffmpeg takes a slot from the same
      `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY` semaphore every other encode does (erratum 79) and a default install
      still runs ONE ffmpeg whatever is queued. It is enqueued INSIDE the transaction that publishes a
      rendition — `FinalizeTranscode` after the ready flip, and `SwapRendition` after a trim — through
      one bool on `db.ReadyFields` (`QueueSocial`), which is the payload both commit points already
      carry; at most one social job per clip is ever live.
    - **The skip rule.** A social file is encoded when the rendition is at or above `SOCIAL_MAX_BYTES`
      (default 25 MiB) **OR** runs above 30 fps; a rendition that is both small and calm is already the
      file a card wants, and a second copy of it would spend an ffmpeg slot to produce something
      indistinguishable. The two halves are independent on purpose: a six-second 60 fps clip is far
      under any byte threshold, and 60 fps is precisely what makes a longer one of the same footage too
      big — the rule catches the SHAPE, not only the instance. `SOCIAL_MAX_BYTES=0` turns the feature
      off entirely.
    - **It is encoded from the RENDITION, not the original** (a decision the roadmap sketch left open).
      The rendition IS the clip as everyone sees it — trim window, rotation, tone map and all — so
      re-deriving from the upload would mean re-deciding every one of those in a second place, and a
      card that showed something the player does not is the one failure this feature must not have. The
      cost argument agrees (a rendition is bounded; an original is whatever somebody uploaded) but it is
      the second reason. This is the same choice §17 #6 made for the GIF, for the same reason.
    - **The encode.** `MakePlan` over a probe of the rendition with `SocialPlanOptions` — the instance's
      own frame box with `MaxFPS = min(TRANSCODE_MAX_FPS, 30)` — so nothing is rescaled (the input
      already fits) and only the frame rate moves; then CRF 26, `-maxrate 2500000 -bufsize 5000000`,
      `-b:a 96k`, faststart, a fresh `{r8}` key. Measured 54 % of the rendition's bytes on the matrix
      clip.
    - **Failure doctrine, unchanged (§11).** The clip is `ready` before, during and after; `db.SetSocial`
      writes the five `social_*` columns and nothing else and refuses a `transcode` job outright; the
      commit is guarded by the rendition's ETag, so a trim landing mid-run makes the attempt delete its
      own object and resolve `done`/`skipped` rather than publish a card file of frames nobody can see;
      the crash cap is `db.SocialMaxAttempts` (2) and the environment cap the instance's
      `TRANSCODE_MAX_TRANSIENT` (erratum 89). A social rendition that never arrives is invisible: the
      route falls back to the main rendition, which is what it served before this shipped.
    - **The window between the ready flip and the commit serves a real card, and Discord keeps it.**
      The job is enqueued AFTER the ready flip precisely so nobody waits for it, which means a share
      pasted in that window unfurls from the MAIN rendition — the one file this feature exists to keep
      out of a card. The later swap is not retroactive. `max-age=3600` bounds only a crawler that comes
      back on its own; Discord decides an unfurl from its FIRST fetch of the URL and caches it (the same
      fact `CAPTURE_READY_WAIT` exists for, erratum 97), so a link-out card survives the good file
      landing. The window is a few seconds idle — ~11 s for a 4-minute 1080p60 source, measured on the
      lane stack — and as long as the queue when it is not, because the social encode waits for the one
      ffmpeg slot (erratum 79) behind everything already on the media loop. `clippet admin ls <id>` is
      the operator-visible check: `social: (none: /social.mp4 serves the rendition)` until it lands.
      No code changes here. Covering the social job with `CAPTURE_READY_WAIT` would make the capture
      endpoint block on a job this design deliberately put after the reply, and is a ROADMAP question,
      not a defect. It is, however, a precondition on the owner's live Discord paste: a Discord paste made before
      that `social:` key exists measures the RENDITION, so a card that does not play would be blamed on
      the 2.5 Mbps ceiling instead of on the race. DEPLOY §21 states all of this for the operator.
    - **Operator surface.** `admin ls` already printed `social:`; it now prints the measured dims with
      it, and `admin stats` counts the kind. `admin ls --stat`, `admin orphans` and the clip delete
      needed no change at all: the key is under the clip prefix and `db.KeysOf(clip).Keys()` has always
      listed `social_key`.
    E2E: **step 41**, physically before the step-16 log gate. A 60 fps upload's `/social.mp4` ETag stops
    equalling `/video.mp4`'s, its `Content-Length` is smaller than the rendition's and under the cap, the
    file probes h264 at ≤30 fps with `moov` before `mdat`, a Discordbot-UA ranged GET answers 206, and
    the card's `og:video:width/height` equal what ffprobe says about THAT file. The small 30 fps clip of
    the matrix is the control: no job, and `/social.mp4` still serves the rendition byte for byte.
    **Measured 2026-09-08 (the owner's measurement):** a 150 s 720p60 capture at 12 Mbps produced a 203.3 MiB
    60 fps rendition and a 46.8 MiB social rendition at the shipped 2.5 Mbps ceiling; Discord played the card
    inline. The ceiling stays.


122. **Migration 0007 adds `social_width` and `social_height`**, and `SwapRendition` NULLs all five
    `social_*` columns. The first three have existed since 0001 and have been NULL on every row ever
    written; the producer needs the dimensions too, because a card must state the dimensions of the file
    a crawler is about to fetch (erratum 123). Two nullable columns, no index, no CHECK, no rewrite —
    an installation running on 0001–0004 upgrades by applying the file and nothing more.
    `SwapRendition` was already the place erratum 70 reserved for this ("when #3 ships, `social_key`
    must be invalidated here too"): the trim's one UPDATE now clears the social columns alongside the
    GIF's, returns the old social key among the superseded ones, and — when the caller's skip rule says
    so — queues the replacement encode in the same statement. So a clip is never a trimmed rendition
    beside an untrimmed card file, not even for the width of a commit.

123. **`og:video:width/height` and the `twitter:player` dims describe the SOCIAL file** (`internal/web/
    meta.go`, `socialDims`). This is a wire-format change to the card, and the only one: the §9.1 tag
    INVENTORY is untouched, two of its values move. `og:video` has always pointed at `/social.mp4`, so
    stating the main rendition's dimensions beside it was already a claim about a different file — true
    only because the route's COALESCE served the rendition. A clip with a social rendition now states
    its measured dims; a clip without one states the main rendition's, which is exactly what that route
    then serves. The pair is never mixed: both come from one file or neither is emitted (a row with
    only one of the two falls back). Today the social encode keeps the rendition's geometry and only
    halves its frame rate, so the two agree in practice — they agree by CONSTRUCTION, not by
    definition, and an operator who narrows `TRANSCODE_MAX_WIDTH/HEIGHT` after a clip was encoded makes
    a regenerated social file genuinely smaller than the rendition beside it. `poster_width/height`
    already worked this way for the same reason (erratum 92).
    The `twitter:player:width`/`height` pair also takes `socialDims()`'s numbers, even though
    `twitter:player` itself is `/embed/{id}` (an iframe that plays `/video.mp4`, the main rendition,
    not `/social.mp4`) — deliberately, not by oversight. The player box only needs the ASPECT RATIO,
    and the social encode preserves the rendition's aspect ratio by construction (it only rescales the
    frame rate), so the two files' dimensions describe the same box shape even when their pixel counts
    diverge. Splitting the pair — main rendition dims on `twitter:player:*`, social dims on `og:video:*`
    — was considered and rejected: it buys nothing a crawler acts on and is itself a wire-format change
    for no gain.

124. **`TRANSCODE_MAX_BITRATE` — a ceiling on the main rendition** (media-3; the cheap half of #3).
    `EncodeOptions` gains `MaxRateBits`/`BufSizeBits`, rendered as `-maxrate`/`-bufsize` between the
    colour options and `-g`; zero renders NEITHER option, so every argv this package emitted before this
    erratum is byte-identical. The social encode uses the same mechanism with its own numbers and
    OVERWRITES the operator's rather than combining them — two ceilings would mean the lower one
    silently wins. The variable is in bits per second and is bounded to \[100000, 2^34\] when set,
    because `2500` from an operator thinking in kilobits would otherwise encode every clip at 2.5 kbps
    and nothing would say why. `EncodeOptions.AudioBitrate` is the same shape: empty renders §10.3's
    128k, and only the social encode sets it (96k).

125. **Interlaced sources are deinterlaced, not relabelled** (`internal/transcode/plan.go`,
    `encode.go`, `probe.go`, `trim.go`; ROADMAP #28). The probe reads `field_order`; a value naming
    FIELDS (`tt`, `bb`, `tb`, `bt`) sets `Plan.Deinterlace`, which puts `yadif=deint=interlaced,` at the
    HEAD of the video chain — in front of the tone map, the rotate and the scale, because yadif is the
    only filter in the chain that reads the source's field structure and every later filter would have
    averaged two moments of time together first. `progressive`, `unknown` and an absent field are left
    alone: inferring interlace from silence would run every untagged upload through a deinterlacer.
    The bug is that the metadata DENIES what the picture is: a 720×480 TFF source encoded as-is comes
    out probing `field_order=progressive` with the comb still in the pixels, so no player can correct
    it. Measured on 7.1.1 with `idet` over 100 frames of the new `interlaced-576i` fixture: the source
    is 100/100 interlaced, the as-is encode is 100/100 interlaced (while declaring `progressive`), and
    the deinterlaced encode is 96/100 progressive. `deint=interlaced` processes only FLAGGED frames, so
    a progressive source renders identically with the filter forced on (SSIM 1.0000) — which is why
    every existing golden is unchanged.
    One consequence beyond the encode: `DecideTrim` refuses a stream COPY of an interlaced source
    (`ReasonInterlaced`). A copy keeps the coded fields, and the trim's whole premise is "already the
    shape the pipeline would have produced"; after this erratum that shape has no fields in it.
    E2E: **step 42**, before the log gate — an interlaced upload's rendition measures ≤10/100 combed
    frames under `idet` while the fixture it came from measures ≥90/100, and the step asserts the
    fixture's own combing FIRST so a broken fixture fails loudly instead of passing vacuously.

127. **The card image is a decision somebody can make, and it is recorded on the timeline that does
    not move** (`internal/db/migrations/0008_poster_seconds.sql`, `internal/db/types.go`
    `Clip.PosterSeconds`/`clipCols`/`scanClip`; ROADMAP #5). Erratum 92 made the AUTOMATIC choice
    much better — a thumbnail pass, a near-black test, a candidate ladder — and left the owner with
    no say at all. `posterSeekFrac = 0.15` plus "pick the most representative frame of the next
    twenty seconds" is a good guess, and the clip whose card matters most to a person is exactly the
    one where a guess is not what they want.
    **One nullable column: `clips.poster_seconds REAL`.** It means "the frame the OWNER chose", in
    seconds, and NULL means "wherever the automatic rule put it" — which is what every clip that
    exists today carries and what a clip goes back to when a cut removes the chosen moment. There is
    deliberately **no backfill**: the automatic choice is not a decision anybody made, and writing it
    into this column would make an accident look like one.
    **It is on the ORIGINAL's timeline**, which is the whole of the design. Erratum 68 established
    that coordinate system for the trim and gave the reason: the upload is retained for the life of
    the clip, so its timeline is the one that does not move under the owner. A choice recorded on the
    RENDITION's timeline would mean a different frame after every cut — silently, and with no way for
    anything downstream to notice. Recorded on the original's, a cut that still contains the moment
    KEEPS it (erratum 130) and one that does not clears it, and both are one comparison.
    Everything that needs the moment on the rendition subtracts `trim_start_ms/1000`
    (`worker.trimStartSeconds`), which is the only conversion this feature has.
    *(Erratum 92 closed with "PERSISTING the timestamp (a sixth poster column, so no second pass is
    needed) stays roadmap work". This is that column, and it does remove the second pass — but only
    where a frame was CHOSEN. An automatic poster still holds no time, so the gif job still
    re-derives one for it; see erratum 131.)*
    `db.TestMigrate0008UpgradesAnOlderDatabase` rehearses the upgrade with a row in the file, proving
    the column is new (`GetClip` cannot scan the row before the migration) and that the feature works
    on the upgraded row afterwards.

128. **`POST` / `GET /api/clips/{id}/poster`: the trim's conventions, one artefact along**
    (`internal/httpapi/poster.go`, `router.go`; the §8.1 rows above). Two owner routes over one job,
    and every decision in them is erratum 68's or 76's, taken again for the same reason.
    - **The POST takes `{"seconds":n}` on the ORIGINAL's timeline** and answers **202
      `{"job_id","state","seconds"}`**. It never touches the clip: the answer says a job exists,
      nothing more, and the poster's URL, its dimensions, its ETag and its cache headers are all
      still true when it lands. `seconds` in the reply is **rounded to the millisecond** the server
      will actually seek to (the argv carries three decimals), so the number the caller is told is
      the number the clip will store.
    - **One 400, `invalid_poster`**, for a moment this clip does not show. The reachable range is
      built from `duration_ms` — what the rendition HOLDS — rather than from `trim_end_ms`, which is
      what was asked of the original: a stream copy ends on a packet boundary, so the two differ, and
      taking the shorter, measured one means the API never accepts a moment the worker then cannot
      find. The last **100 ms** (`posterEdgeGuardMS`) is not choosable, because a seek at or past the
      last picture makes ffmpeg write no file at all — erratum 78's lesson, and the same answer:
      refuse it in the handler rather than let a request the API had every reason to accept come back
      as a failed job. **The button clamps into that bound rather than walking into it.** "Use this
      frame" reads the player's clock, and a player left to run to its end reports exactly the
      forbidden moment — with the frame in question on screen — so `setupPoster` takes the smaller of
      the playhead and `cut start + (duration_ms − 100 ms)`, built from the `data-duration-ms` the
      facts list already carries (a trim rewrites it there, so the bound is never the pre-trim one)
      with the same operations in the same order as `posterChoiceRange`, which makes the two numbers
      the same `float64` and the clamped moment an accept rather than a rounding hair short of one.
      It is `minTrimMS`'s rule one control along: a page must not compose a request the server is
      bound to refuse, least of all one that would have it argue with its own picture.
      `TestPosterEdgeGuardIsMirroredInTheClient` reads both files and fails if the two copies of the
      guard ever differ, and `TestStartPosterBoundsFollowTheCut` asserts the exact clamped double is
      a 202. *(`applyTrimmed` also rewrites the control's `data-cut-start-ms` when a trim lands in
      the page, for the same reason it rewrites the facts list: the conversion from the player's
      clock to the original's timeline IS that number, and a stale one names the wrong frame.)*
    - **409s are the database's.** `db.EnqueuePoster` checks `state='ready'`, counts the clip's
      queued-or-running poster jobs and INSERTs in ONE transaction on the single-writer `rw` pool, so
      two clicks produce exactly one job and the loser gets **409 `poster_in_progress`**; a clip that
      is not ready gets **409 `not_ready`**. `db.TestEnqueuePosterIsSerialisedUnderConcurrency` fires
      eight simultaneous enqueues and asserts one winner.
    - **The GET reports the LATEST poster job**, `no-store`, and **404 `not_found`** when nobody has
      chosen a frame — a poller must not read "no job" as "finished". `seconds` is what was ASKED
      for; `applied_seconds` is read from the CLIP once the job is `done`, which is what makes it
      honest: a swap that lost its race resolves `done` too and wrote nothing, so echoing the request
      there would report a choice the clip does not carry. The share page compares the two — a `done`
      whose `applied_seconds` is not the moment that was asked for is reported as "the clip was
      edited while the frame was being taken", never as a success, because the job's STATE says only
      that the attempt is over.
    - **A `done` job with `applied_seconds: null` is not always a lost race** (N110, roadmap-run nit
      sweep): the SAME null is what a `done` job reports once `poster_seconds` has gone back to NULL
      by any of three routes — a swap that lost its race (above), a later trim whose applied window
      dropped the chosen moment (erratum 130), or a later replacement, which retires `poster_seconds`
      exactly as it retires the trim window (`db.SwapSource`). All three read as "the clip's card
      image is automatic now"; `seconds` keeps naming the moment that was asked for, which by then may
      be a moment on a retired original the clip no longer has. This is deliberately NOT a 404: the
      job genuinely finished, `web/static/app.js`'s `watch()` treats 404 as "the clip or its poster
      job is gone" and silently hides the status, and turning a stale-but-honest `done` into a 404
      would swallow the "the clip was edited while the frame was being taken" message this erratum
      requires on the lost-race path specifically. A direct API poller can see the stale answer; the
      share page never does, because it renders the "chosen frame" note only when `PosterSeconds !=
      nil` (`internal/web/pages.go`), so a clip back to automatic simply shows no note at all. The
      identical shape exists on `GET …/trim` after a replacement, for the identical reason
      (`SwapSource` also NULLs `trim_start_ms`/`trim_end_ms`): a `done` trim job can report
      `applied_start_ms`/`applied_end_ms: null` once the clip that trim cut is no longer the clip's
      original.
    - **Auth, CSRF and limits are the owner-route conventions**, identical to the trim's:
      `RequireSession` + the CSRF rule + `requireJSON` on the POST + the 15s `TimeoutHandler`;
      anonymous 401, a stranger 403 `forbidden`, a capture token 403 `token_not_allowed` (erratum
      19). The **GET is session-only too** — its `error` is the operator-facing reason a job failed.
      The POST carries the **`upload` limiter**, because it queues an ffmpeg run that takes a slot
      from the very semaphore `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY` sizes (erratum 79).
    - **`/poster.jpg` is untouched.** The path here is a LITERAL segment beside it; the media route
      stays public, stays on `serveObject`, and keeps every header it had. Its ETag changes when the
      job commits, and `Last-Modified` moves with it because `SetPoster` stamps `updated_at` — a
      cache revalidating with `If-Modified-Since` alone must not be told 304 about bytes that were
      replaced (erratum 70's rule for the trim, and erratum 76's for the preview).
    - **Nothing in the ClipDTO changes.** `poster_seconds` is deliberately NOT a DTO field: the
      clip's `poster` block carries the measured dimensions `og:image:width/height` read, the share
      page renders the choice from the row, and a client that wants the moment asks the route whose
      subject it is. `BuildMeta` is untouched, and crawlers catch up within the 1 h `max-age`.

129. **A `poster` job is the third media kind, and it cannot cost a clip anything**
    (`internal/worker/poster.go`, `internal/transcode/posterat.go`, `internal/db/poster.go`,
    `internal/db/jobs.go` `MediaKinds`/`limitsFor`, `internal/worker/worker.go` `runJob`/`Runner`).
    It is deliberately built out of the gif job's parts, because it has the gif job's shape: read the
    RENDITION, write a small object, commit with one guarded UPDATE, and leave the clip `ready`
    before, during and after.
    - **`db.KindPoster` joins `MediaKinds()`**, so it runs on the media loop beside `trim` and `gif`
      and its one ffmpeg pass takes a slot from the `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY` semaphore (erratum 79).
      One seek is cheap; "cheap" is not the promise DEPLOY §7 makes. The promise is that a default
      install runs ONE ffmpeg, and a third media kind that ignored the semaphore would falsify it the
      way a trim once did.
    - **It is REGISTERED in the run registry** (erratum 71's rule, for the third time): it runs
      ffmpeg, writes scratch and uploads an object, which is exactly the set §10.1's `Cancel`
      promises to have finished when it returns. `worker.TestPosterIsCancelledSynchronously` pins
      that `Cancel` blocks on an extraction that ignores its context.
    - **`transcode.PosterAt` is `Poster` with the search taken out**, and the absence is the design.
      No thumbnail pass, no seek ladder, no near-black rejection: somebody said which frame they
      wanted, so a fallback would publish a DIFFERENT frame under the answer "your frame was used",
      and "this frame is too dark to be a card image" is a judgement that is not this program's to
      make about a decision a person took while looking at the picture. The result still REPORTS
      `NearBlack`, and the run logs one INFO line so an operator asked "why is the card black" can
      answer it. What it keeps from `Poster` is the measurement: the JPEG is decoded, and the
      dimensions `og:image:width/height` read come from the same pass that proves there is a picture
      in it. `transcode.TestPosterAtTakesTheFrameThatWasAskedFor` (`-tags ffmpeg`) pins it on a
      fixture that is a different flat colour every second, so the picture says which second it came
      from and nothing else could.
    - **A moment with no picture is the CLIENT's**, not ours: `transcode.ErrNoFrameAt`, wrapped as
      `ErrPermanent`, so the attempt fails at INFO with the plain sentence *"there is no picture at
      that moment in the clip"* (`worker.msgNoFrame`), no retry, no ERROR, and the clip still on the
      card image it had. It is erratum 78's `ErrWindowEmpty` one artefact along and it exists for the
      same reason: a request and a file that disagree must never put an ERROR line in an operator's
      log. Around it are four more fixed sentences (`msgFrameMedia`, `msgFrameDisk`,
      `msgFrameStorage`, `msgFrameInternal`) — erratum 80's rule applied again, and deliberately a
      vocabulary of its OWN rather than the trim's reused: every one of the trim's seven sentences
      says the word "trim", and telling an owner whose chosen frame could not be taken that "the
      trim failed" would send them after the wrong thing. A `bad_output` — a JPEG we wrote and then
      could not read — is ours, not the request's, so the owner gets the generic sentence and the
      operator gets the ERROR line with the detail.
    - **Its caps are `db.PosterMaxAttempts = 2`** on the crash counter, for the reason
      `TrimMaxAttempts` and `GIFMaxAttempts` are constants: `TRANSCODE_MAX_ATTEMPTS` is a knob about
      the encode a clip cannot exist without. The environment counter stays the instance's (erratum
      89). `db.FailAttempt` moves no clip for this kind, so at every ending — permanent, transient
      cap, panic, cancellation, a lost race — the clip is still `ready`, still playable, still on the
      card image it had. `worker.TestPosterOfAMomentWithNoPictureCostsTheClipNothing` and
      `TestPosterFailurePreservesTheClip` assert it from both sides.
    - **It keeps no progress registry at all** — not §8.4's, whose subject is the clip (`ready`
      throughout), and not the trim's second one. One seek has no meaningful percentage, and a number
      nobody can ask for is a registry nobody can evict. Stages are persisted, so `admin ls` still
      says where a failure happened.

130. **`SetPoster` is `SetGIF`'s statement, and a cut carries the choice through `SwapRendition`**
    (`internal/db/poster.go` `SetPoster`, `internal/db/trim.go` `SwapRendition`,
    `internal/worker/trim.go` `poster`/`chosenPosterSeek`). Two commits, one rule.
    - **`SetPoster` writes the poster columns AND the choice of a clip that is still `ready` and
      still on the rendition the job read at its start**, in one UPDATE whose predicate carries that
      ETag — `SetGIF`'s exact shape, for `SetGIF`'s exact reason. A trim landing mid-run replaces the
      frames the picture was taken from, so the output is a perfectly valid JPEG of a frame the clip
      no longer contains and **nothing downstream could ever tell**. The refusal is not a failure:
      the attempt deletes its own object and resolves the job `done`/`skipped` with the reason,
      because there is nothing to retry and the owner can choose again on the clip that exists. The
      superseded poster key comes back and is deleted after the commit, best effort, exactly as
      erratum 70 describes for the rendition.
    - **The preview is deliberately NOT invalidated.** A trim NULLs `gif_*` because the frames the
      preview was cut from are gone; choosing a card image removes nothing — the preview is still
      frames of the rendition people are watching. It simply no longer opens where the poster does,
      and the owner regenerates it if they care. The share page's hint says so.
    - **`SwapRendition` gained `poster_seconds` in its SET list**, written from
      `ReadyFields.PosterSeconds`, which is the ONE poster column a trim can also clear. The trim run
      decides: if the applied window contains the chosen moment (and the measured output is long
      enough to hold it — a copy ends on a packet boundary, so both bounds are checked), the frame is
      re-taken from the new rendition at `chosen − applied_start` and the choice is carried; if it
      does not, the automatic search runs and the column goes back to NULL. `FinalizeTranscode` does
      **not** write the column: a transcode renders the whole upload of a clip that has never been
      ready, so it has no choice to carry.
    - **A chosen frame can never fail a trim.** If the single-frame extraction says anything but yes
      — the moment is a hair past the last picture of a cut that came out a frame short, say — the
      run falls back to the automatic search and drops the choice, at INFO. The alternative is
      failing an edit of a playable clip over a picture, and §17 #5's whole doctrine is that a trim
      costs the ATTEMPT and never the clip. `worker.TestTrimKeepsOrDropsTheChosenFrame` and
      `TestATrimSurvivesAChosenFrameThatCannotBeTaken` pin both halves.

131. **The preview opens where the card does** (`internal/worker/gif.go` `planGIF`/`posterSeconds`,
    `internal/worker/poster.go` `renditionPosterSeconds`). Erratum 92(c) made the GIF start at the
    poster's frame and had to RE-DERIVE that frame every time, because nothing stored it: a second
    ffmpeg pass (`PosterFrameSeconds`) on every preview, on a file the job already had on disk.
    With a chosen frame the answer is a column, so the pass is not run at all — the subtraction
    `poster_seconds − trim_start_ms/1000` is the whole of it, and the preview opens on the very frame
