    the card shows, which is most of the reason for having chosen one. With no choice, nothing
    changes: the derivation runs exactly as it did. `renditionPosterSeconds` refuses a choice that
    does not lie inside the rendition, so a row whose cut moved under a choice a trim should already
    have cleared falls back to the derivation rather than planning a window past the end.
    `worker.TestGIFStartsAtTheChosenFrame` asserts both halves — the pass is absent with a choice and
    present without one — and E2E step 43 measures the preview's first frame against the fixture's
    own luma bands.

132. **The trim scrubber previews with the PLAYER, and adds no route** (`web/templates/clip.html`,
    `web/static/app.css`, `web/static/app.js` `setupTrim`'s scrubber block; ROADMAP #6). What shipped
    for the trim was two `<input type=number step=0.1>` over a timeline the owner had to read off the
    player's clock by hand. The control above them is a track whose full width is the ORIGINAL's
    timeline with a draggable handle at each end.
    **No `frame.jpg?t=` endpoint was added, and that is a decision.** ROADMAP #6 offered a bounded
    owner route for handle thumbnails or the player, "whichever is cheaper", and the player is
    cheaper by an enormous margin: it is already on the page, it is already the frames in question,
    and it costs no ffmpeg, no cache story, no rate limit and no new authenticated surface. Dragging
    a handle SEEKS the player to `value − trim_start_ms/1000` while the moment is inside the current
    cut, and greys the picture (`video.out-of-cut`) when it is not — the rendition holds only the
    cut, so a handle past its edge is naming footage this player cannot show, and saying so is better
    than leaving the wrong frame on screen as if it were the right one. A filmstrip along the track
    stays a later step, as the roadmap already said.
    **The number boxes stay, and they are the truth.** They are what the API takes, what a reader
    with no JavaScript gets, and what the handles write into — the scrubber has no state of its own.
    The markup is server-rendered `hidden` and revealed by `app.js` (erratum 120's rule for the bulk
    bar), and it is not rendered at all for a clip whose ORIGINAL was never measured: a track with no
    scale cannot be a scrubber, and the boxes already carry no maximum for such a clip. A drag can
    never compose a window shorter than the API's own 500 ms floor.
    **CSP:** every pixel goes through `element.style.left` / `.width` and every state through
    `classList` — never a style-attribute string (`style-src 'self'`). **Keyboard:** the handles are
    real `<button>`s with `role="slider"` and live `aria-valuenow`/`aria-valuetext`; arrows move a
    tenth of a second, PageUp/PageDown a second, Home/End the ends. Two "= now" buttons set either
    end from the player's current time, and they are `hidden` in the markup for the same reason the
    track is. `web.TestSharePageScrubberIsOwnerOnlyAndInert` pins the markup, its `hidden` state and
    its absence from a stranger's page; E2E step 46 asserts the same on the live stack.

133. **Every timestamp is an instant a browser can read, and the UTC sentence is still what renders**
    (`internal/web/pages.go` `fillDates`/`rfc3339`, `web/templates/clip.html`, `web/static/app.js`
    `decorateTimes`/`renderLifetime`; ROADMAP #8). "How long have I got" is the one number a per-clip-TTL
    product exists to communicate, and the watch page answered it with a fixed UTC string to
    everybody the link was ever shared with.
    **The server output is unchanged.** `formatDate` and `expiryText` still produce exactly what they
    produced; the page now wraps the DATE in `<time datetime="{RFC3339}">` and leaves the English
    outside it — `expires <time …>2026-09-07 17:29 UTC</time>`, so the element carries an instant and
    the sentence carries the meaning. A reader with no JavaScript, and every crawler, sees precisely
    what they saw before. A clip kept forever names no instant and gets no `<time>` at all, which is
    also what stops a countdown appearing on one.
    **The client re-renders it.** `decorateTimes` rewrites each `<time data-local>` into the viewer's
    own locale (`toLocaleString`), and one marked `data-countdown` gains a relative phrase — but only
    **under a day**: above that the date is the useful answer and "in 27 days" is noise. It refreshes
    once a minute and only while the tab is visible, and a `datetime` the browser cannot parse is
    LEFT ALONE, so a bad value degrades to the server's string rather than to an empty line.
    `applyLifetime` rebuilds the same shape after a keep-alive or a keep-forever
    (`renderLifetime`, `createElement` and `textContent` throughout — no markup strings), so one
    formatter serves the rendered page and the updated one.

134. **The share page's player answers the keyboard, and remembers two things in the browser**
    (`web/static/app.js` `setupPlayer`/`typingInto`/`toggleFullscreen`, `web/templates/clip.html`;
    ROADMAP #29). A native `<video controls>` reacts to keys only while the player itself has focus,
    so the page ignored Space and the arrows until somebody clicked the picture.
    The map is on the DOCUMENT — Space/K play-pause, J/L ±10 s, ←/→ ±5 s, ↑/↓ volume, M mute, F
    fullscreen, 0–9 seek to a tenth (the roadmap wrote J/L ±5 s; ±10 s is the convention viewers
    already have, and a sketch that lists J/L and the arrows separately only makes sense if the two
    differ) — which is exactly why it refuses to fire inside a control:
    `typingInto` excludes inputs, textareas, selects, contenteditable **and buttons**, where Space is
    "press me" and the arrows belong to the scrubber's own handles. A modifier held, or a key some
    other handler already consumed, is not ours either. *(The roadmap suggested focusing the video on
    load; a document-level handler makes that unnecessary, and auto-focusing moves the viewport and
    disturbs the tab order for a page whose first control is a link.)*
    **Two preferences live in `localStorage` and nowhere else**: `clippet.muted` and `clippet.loop`,
    each read and written inside a try/catch, because a private window, blocked site data or a full
    quota must not stop the player working. Nothing is sent anywhere — a taste is not telemetry, and
    this file has no route to tell. The Loop toggle is server-rendered `hidden` beside a one-line
    keyboard legend and revealed by `app.js`, so a button that cannot be wired never appears; both
    belong to every viewer of a ready clip, because player chrome is not owner data and a loop
    control is not a call to action.
    **SHARE PAGE ONLY.** `setupPlayer` runs after `setupClipPage`'s `isEmbed` return, so an embed
    gets none of it: its `autoplay`/`muted`/`loop` are the EMBEDDER's choice expressed in the URL
    (erratum 77), and a viewer preference that overrode them would silently change a contract other
    people's pages depend on. `web.TestSharePagePlayerExtras` and E2E step 45 assert the markup on
    the share page and its absence from the embed.

135. **Clip replacement: the same link, a different file** (`internal/db/replace.go`, `internal/worker/
    replace.go`, `internal/httpapi/replace.go`, `internal/store/keys.go` `ReplacementKey`,
    `internal/db/types.go` `KindReplace`, `internal/db/jobs.go` `limitsFor`/`MediaKinds`,
    `internal/web/pages.go`, `web/templates/clip.html`, `web/static/app.js`, `cmd/clippet/admin.go`;
    ROADMAP #31). "I uploaded the wrong file" had exactly one answer — delete it and upload again,
    which costs the link, the tags, the lifetime, the view count and every paste of that link that
    already exists. The two §8.1 rows above are that answer instead, and their shape is binding:
    - **The clip never leaves `ready`.** This is the difference from the ROADMAP sketch, which
      proposed flipping the clip back to `processing` and accepting a minute of link-out cards. It is
      not necessary and it is not free: `processing` makes the share page a link-out card for every
      viewer *and* makes Discord CACHE that card (erratum 97's whole argument), so a replacement would
      degrade a posted link that was working. A replacement is therefore a MEDIA-loop kind like the
      trim, the gif and the social encode: it runs against a ready clip, leaves it ready however it
      ends, and commits with ONE guarded UPDATE. `clips.state`, `failure_reason` and both failure
      counters are never written — `db.FailAttempt` moves a clip only for `transcode` — so a failed
      replacement leaves a playable clip and a `failed` job row saying why.
    - **The upload is sacred, so the ordering is the feature.** The handler stores the new original
      under a per-attempt key (`ReplacementKey`: `…/original/source-{r8}.{ext}`) BESIDE the live one,
      never over it: writing to `OriginalKey` would destroy the file the clip still is — the file
      `/original` is serving and the file the worker re-downloads — before the replacement had proved
      it can be transcoded at all. `db.SwapSource` then points the row at the new original, the
      rendition and the poster in one statement and RETURNS the previous original among the superseded
      keys, and the run deletes them AFTER that commit, best effort. So at every instant the clip has
      exactly one original and it is reachable; the only window is the one where it has two.
    - **What survives and what resets.** Surviving: the id and therefore the share URL, the title,
      description, `unlisted`, tags, collection membership, TTL and `expires_at`, the view count,
      `created_at` and `ready_at` (the clip has been ready the whole time; `updated_at` moves, which is
      what the media routes date from — §8.5). Resetting: `trim_start_ms`/`trim_end_ms` to NULL (the
      new original is its own timeline), the preview GIF and the social rendition to NULL with their
      objects superseded (both described a rendition that no longer exists), and `source_duration_ms`
      to what THIS run measured — assigned, not COALESCEd as the trim's is, because a probe that
      measured nothing on a NEW file must not leave the old file's length behind for the next trim to
      be validated against.
    - **The request grammar is the capture endpoint's, minus the fields.** Text parts before the file
      are bounded exactly as `readCaptureForm` bounds them and then ignored, every one of them: a
      replacement changes the FILE, and title, tags, TTL and `unlisted` are the clip's — `PATCH` is
      where those change. Silently applying them here would make "I uploaded the wrong file" also mean
      "and lost my tags". The file part is `file` or `video`, the two names both upload routes take.
      A field that breaks the 16 KiB bound is refused with the capture form's own message under a
      FIXED label — "the form field is larger than 16 KiB". `readCaptureForm` may name the field
      because it only ever names one of its own six literals; this route reads NO field, so the name
      would be whatever the caller invented, and `mime/multipart` carries megabytes of part headers
      happily. An owner-facing error never reflects unbounded caller text — erratum 26's rule for
      filenames, applied to field names.
    - **Auth is the owner-route convention, and deliberately narrower than an upload's.** Session only:
      a capture token gets 403 `token_not_allowed` (erratum 19), because a leaked ShareX credential
      must not be able to overwrite the clips it once created — the blast radius of that leak is
      "somebody uploaded junk to your account", not "somebody replaced the clip you posted last week".
      CSRF as every owner mutation, BOTH upload limiters (a replacement spends an upload's bytes,
      scratch and ffmpeg slot), and no `TimeoutHandler`, because it carries a body.
    - **`replace_in_progress` is the database's answer**, decided by the same one-transaction guard
      `EnqueueTrim` uses: clip `ready`, no queued-or-running replacement, then the INSERT. A live TRIM
      or GIF is deliberately NOT refused — two runs of one clip never overlap (the worker registry
      serialises them) and each commit carries its own predicate, so the worst case is a trim whose
      window a replacement then supersedes, which is what the owner asked for by uploading a different
      file.
    - **`ReplaceMaxAttempts = 2`**, split from the environment counter exactly as erratum 89 split the
      other media kinds': the crash cap is the kind's own constant (a replacement that keeps crashing
      is what "upload it again" is the right answer to), the transient cap is the instance's
      `TRANSCODE_MAX_TRANSIENT` (a MinIO restart is not an argument about this file).
    - **No migration.** The job row carries the attempt — `ReplaceParams` in `params_json` — exactly as
      the trim's window does, so an installation upgrades by pulling the image.
    - **The operator surface** is one word: `admin stats` counts the kind (`replace=n`). `admin ls`,
      `admin ls --stat`, `admin orphans` and the clip delete needed no change at all — every key is
      under the clip prefix and `db.KeysOf(clip).Keys()` already lists the source.
    - **The UI** is one form in the owner block of a ready clip's share page: pick a file, watch the
      upload percentage, then the transcode percentage from `GET …/replace`, then the page reloads
      (or offers to, when the owner has unsaved text — erratum 95's rule). Nothing about it is
      rendered for a visitor.
    E2E: **step 49**, before the log gate. A tagged, viewed, trimmed clip with a GIF is replaced by a
    file of a different SHAPE (landscape over vertical), and the step asserts the id and URL are
    unchanged, the rendition ETag is new, the dimensions are the new file's, the tags, TTL and views
    survived, the trim window and the GIF are gone, `/original` served the OLD file during the run and
    the NEW one after it, the previous original is gone from the BUCKET (not merely unreferenced), the
    card still unfurls as a player, and a token and an anonymous caller are both refused.

136. **A replacement runs in its own scratch directory, and one delete path may touch an original**
    (`internal/scratch/scratch.go` `ReplaceTmpDir`/`ReplaceTmpName`/`ValidTmpName`,
    `internal/worker/pipeline.go` `deleteReplacedKeys`, `internal/worker/replace.go`). Two interlocks
    the feature above could not have without them.
    (a) **The working directory is `$SCRATCH_DIR/.upload-{id}-{r8}`, never `$SCRATCH_DIR/{id}`.** The
    clip's own directory belongs to whatever run is registered for it, and a TRIM keeps the CURRENT
    original in it under the very name a replacement would spool to (`source.{ext}`): one file over
    the other, mid-encode. The `.upload-` prefix is erratum 14's, so the janitor already knows the
    shape — a row-less spool is kept unless nothing in it has been written for 24 h — and the attempt's
    `{r8}` is what keeps two replacements of one clip apart, which matters because the at-most-one
    guard is the database's and is only reached once the body is already on disk. A queued replacement
    that waits out the stale bound simply loses its spool and re-downloads the object the handler
    stored, which is `acquireSource`'s ordinary path.
    (b) **`deleteKeys` refuses every key under `original/`, and that refusal is right.** It is the
    interlock that says the upload is sacred, and no attempt-scoped exception to it would stay
    scoped. So the replacement uses a SECOND function with interlocks of its own:
    `deleteReplacedKeys` never deletes the key the row names RIGHT NOW (after the swap that is the new
    original; before it, the old one) and never deletes a key outside this clip's own prefix, and logs
    an ERROR if it is ever asked to. What is sacred is the CURRENT upload; a replacement is how the
    current one changes, and these two conditions are what make that sentence checkable rather than a
    comment. `db.ParseReplaceParams` and `scratch.ValidTmpName` are the same idea one layer down: a
    job row names a directory and an object key, and a row is not a place to take either on trust.

137. **The phone share sheet: a manifest, a share target, and the CSRF story that makes it safe**
    (`internal/web/server.go` `webManifest`/`manifest`, `internal/httpapi/share.go`,
    `internal/httpapi/router.go`, `web/templates/base.html`, `web/static/icon-192.png`,
    `web/static/icon-512.png`, `scripts/lib/mkicons.py`; ROADMAP #27). "I saved a clip on my console,
    opened it on my phone, hit Share — Clippet is not in the list." Now it is, on Android.
    - **`GET /manifest.webmanifest`** is a static document served like `/robots.txt`: no principal, no
      row, `public, max-age=3600`, the registered `application/manifest+json` media type. Every URL in
      it is ROOT-RELATIVE, like every in-page resource this package renders (§9): the manifest is
      fetched from whatever host the browser is on, and baking `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` into it would make an
      install under a second name point its share target at the other one. It declares the two icons
      Android requires before it will install anything (192 and 512, generated by `mkicons.py` so the
      mark is reproducible and needs no rasteriser on a host that has neither Go nor Node), and
      `share_target`: `POST`, `multipart/form-data`, `action: /api/share`, file part named `file` —
      the same name `clippet.sxcu` uses, so the share sheet and ShareX speak one grammar.
    - **`POST /api/share`** is `captureUpload`'s core with a browser's conventions: the same
      `beginUpload` gates, the same `readCaptureForm` (Android sends `title`, `text` and `url` beside
      the file; `title` is taken, the other two are ignored like any unknown field, and erratum 60's
      "a title that is the filename is not a title" applies because Android fills it from the filename
      constantly), the same ingest, the same ready wait (erratum 97) — and then a **303 to the clip's
      share page** instead of a JSON body, because its caller is a browser being navigated rather than
      a tool reading an answer. The 303 is also what stops a reload of that page from re-posting the
      file.
    - **The CSRF story, in full.** A share-sheet launch is a top-level navigation the BROWSER starts,
      so it carries no `Origin` (there is no initiating document) and `Sec-Fetch-Site: none` rather
      than `cross-site`. The binding is therefore the session cookie plus the ordinary §15 rule this
      route runs under, unchanged: `auth.CSRF` refuses a cookie-authenticated mutation whose `Origin`
      is another origin, or whose `Sec-Fetch-Site` is `cross-site`. A hostile page's cross-origin form
      POST carries both marks and is refused; a share-sheet launch carries neither and is admitted,
      exactly as a same-origin form POST is. There is no token to add, because there is no page of
      ours to put one on — the browser composes this request from the manifest, and any secret a
      manifest could carry would be a secret every reader of the manifest has. The route is
      **session-only**: a Bearer token gets 403 `token_not_allowed`, because this one answers with a
      redirect and a capture credential has no business steering a browser.
    - **A logged-out share is an interstitial, not a redirect.** The browser does not re-POST after a
      login, so sending the user to `/login` would silently drop the file they picked. The answer is
      **401 with a page that says so** and links to the login form — for a client that accepts HTML;
      everything else gets the JSON envelope. The file is never read on that path (erratum 138), which
      is also why the honest text is "nothing was uploaded" rather than "we saved it, sign in".
    - **No service worker.** Nothing here caches and nothing here is offline; the one thing a service
      worker would add is an install prompt on some Chrome versions, and that is not worth a script
      that outlives the page, can serve stale HTML and would need its own answer to §15's "what does
      this binary call". DEPLOY §23 says so where an operator will read it, together with the honest
      limits: Android Chrome only (iOS has no share target) and https only (an install needs it).
    - **This is the INBOUND direction, and erratum 98(c) still stands.** That erratum forbids share
      TARGETS on the watch page, meaning controls that hand a viewer's clip to a third party — the CTA
      class. This hands the phone's own file to Clippet. Nothing leaves, no third-party origin is
      contacted, and the watch page is untouched.

138. **An upload nobody is allowed to make is refused before its body is read** (`internal/httpapi/
    bodyguard.go`, `internal/httpapi/router.go`, `internal/httpapi/upload.go` `beginUpload`; ROADMAP
    #32). Every upload route already answered 401/403/429/413/415/507 from middleware or from
    `beginUpload`, before a byte of the body had been read — nothing in the credential chain touches
    `r.Body` — and that property is now asserted rather than assumed. What was missing is what happens
    to the CONNECTION afterwards: the client is still sending, and net/http drains what is left so the
    connection can be reused. On a body that declares a gibibyte — or declares nothing at all, the
    case with no upper bound — that drain is exactly the transfer the refusal exists to avoid.
    `closeUnlessRead`, the outermost middleware on `POST /api/clips`, `/api/upload`, `/api/share` and
    `…/replace`, pre-sets `Connection: close` for a request whose declared length is past 256 KiB
    (net/http's own `maxPostHandlerReadBytes`, so a small body still drains and a capture tool about
    to retry with a good credential keeps its connection), and `beginUpload` takes the header off
    again at the one point where the body IS about to be read. Pre-setting rather than deciding on the
    way out is deliberate: a ResponseWriter wrapper would have to be threaded through
    `http.MaxBytesReader`, whose too-large handling recognises only net/http's own writer.
    **Wire format**: nothing changes — no route, no DTO, no status code; one response header appears
    on refusals that were already refusals. The ROADMAP entry's other half — draining up to 16 MiB so
    a proxy cannot turn the 401 into an HTML 502 — is deliberately NOT implemented: reading a body to
    be polite about it is the behaviour this erratum exists to remove, and net/http's own half-close
    delay already gives the client time to read the answer. E2E **step 50** measures it from a raw
    socket: a declared 1 GiB body is answered 401 with `Connection: close` after ZERO body bytes were
    accepted, on both upload routes.

139. **The upload form takes several files, a drop, a cancel and a retry — and works without
    JavaScript** (`web/static/app.js` `setupUpload`, `web/templates/index.html`, `web/static/app.css`;
    ROADMAP #7). Six clips from one evening were six page round-trips with the tags and the TTL
    retyped each time, and a wrong 4 GB file could only be stopped by closing the tab —
    `xhr.onabort` was wired to a handler with no call site.
    - **The batch is SEQUENTIAL and bounded.** One request at a time keeps `RATE_UPLOAD_PER_HOUR`, the
      scratch precheck and the single ffmpeg slot honest, and six parallel POSTs would only make each
      of them slower. `maxBatch` is 20: past that, "I dropped a folder in by accident" is the likelier
      explanation, and the status line says which files were taken. One metadata document is shared by
      the whole batch — the tags and the lifetime are typed once — and the title, when one is typed,
      is suffixed `(2/5)`, trimmed so the result can never exceed the API's 200-rune cap and come back
      a 400. A single file keeps the title exactly as typed, which is the contract `POST /api/clips`
      has always had.
    - **Cancel and retry.** While a batch is in flight the submit button is replaced by Cancel, which
      calls `xhr.abort()` and drops the rest of the queue — the server's own disconnect handling
      removes the partial spool and the partial object, so nothing of a cancelled TRANSFER survives
      (§8.3, and E2E step 47 measures the row, the object and the scratch directory). After the last
      byte is sent the client stops claiming that: `sentAll` makes the abort message say the file may
      still land, because from that instant the outcome is the server's — it may already have
      committed the row, and it answers whether or not anybody is listening. A failure or an abort
      reveals Try again, which re-sends the SAME `File` from the queue it is still holding (a cancel
      keeps exactly that one and drops the rest): the file is in hand, so the answer to a failure is
      one button and not "pick it again".
    - **Drop and paste.** `dragover`/`drop` on the upload CARD (a file dragged from a folder lands
      near the form, never on a 20-pixel control) and a document-level `paste` that ignores text
      fields, so pasting a title never steals the paste. The only feedback is a `.dropping` CLASS —
      never an inline style, which the CSP forbids.
    - **The no-JS form actually works now, and that is a wire-visible change.** The form posted to
      `POST /api/clips` with the file field FIRST, so a browser without JavaScript sent `video` as
      part 1 and got 400 `metadata_first`: the plain form had never worked at all. It now posts to
      **`/api/upload`**, whose grammar a plain browser form fits exactly — text fields in any order,
      then the file part — with the file field LAST in the markup and first on screen (a CSS `order`
      on a flex column, so nothing moves visually). "Last" means last of the NAMED controls, and the
      list is exhaustive: `title`, `description`, `tags`, `ttl_days` and `unlisted` all precede the
      file input, and only the buttons, the progress bar and the status line follow it, because those
      submit nothing. This is a property no half-measure satisfies — `readCaptureForm` RETURNS at the
      file part, so a field left after it is not read late, it is never read at all, and the two that
      would land there are the lifetime and the per-clip Discord opt-out (§8: `unlisted` hides the
      clip from the shared library AND suppresses the webhook post, so dropping it silently publishes
      a clip its owner marked private). Both guards therefore name every field rather than a
      neighbouring one: `TestIndexLibrary`'s `assertFileFieldLast` and E2E step 47, whose part 2 now
      sends the served order as the POSITIVE and the same fields after the file part as the NEGATIVE.
      `data-upload-api` carries `/api/clips` for `setupUpload`, which still posts the §8.3
      metadata-first document because that route answers with the whole ClipDTO the new library row is
      built from. The served markup carries **no `multiple`**: app.js adds it, because without app.js
      a second file part would be sent and never read (erratum 58 — parts after the file part are not
      read, and E2E step 47 pins that a two-file body makes exactly one clip).

143. **`clippet admin doctor` — one preflight, before the stack goes down** (`cmd/clippet/doctor.go`,
    `cmd/clippet/main.go` dispatch, `internal/db/backup.go` `IntegrityCheck`). Every ingredient existed and
    none was reachable as a check: configuration was validated only by BOOTING (and, before erratum 104,
    only the first error survived), ffmpeg and ffprobe were resolved only inside `serve`, storage
    reachability was only `/readyz` — which needs a running app — free disk was only inside the upload
    path, and the resolved configuration could only be inspected as `docker compose config`, which prints
    `S3_SECRET_KEY` in the clear. `restore-check` already proved the pattern: a read-only subcommand that
    runs BEFORE `config.Load` in a throwaway container and prints a verdict.
    `doctor` runs nine checks and prints one line per fact as `<check> <verdict> <detail>` —
    `config`, `baseurl`, `paths`, `db`, `ffmpeg`, `creds`, `bucket`, `proxies`, `webhook` — with verdicts
    `ok`, `warn`, `FAIL` and `skip`, a summary line, and exit 0 unless something FAILED (a warning never
    fails). The preflight invocation is `docker compose run --rm --no-deps app admin doctor`, which
    answers *before* `up -d` and is the form DEPLOY §24.1 recommends: compose resolves every `${VAR:-…}`
    default the running container would get and the throwaway container joins the compose network, so a
    service-name `S3_ENDPOINT` resolves. `docker compose exec app clippet admin doctor` answers for the
    stack as it runs, and `docker run --rm --env-file .env.new <image> admin doctor` checks a
    configuration that stands on its own — with neither compose's defaults nor its network.
    Three properties are load-bearing. (a) **It is dispatched before `config.Load`**, exactly as
    `restore-check` is, and calls the loader itself: a broken `.env` is the thing it exists to DESCRIBE, and
    every invalid variable is reported (erratum 104's `config.Errors`), after which every downstream check
    prints `skip` rather than a guess. (b) **It is read-only** apart from one probe object under
    `{S3_KEY_PREFIX}doctor/` — never under `clips/`, so nothing that walks clip prefixes can see it — which
    it removes again, and one temp file in each of `DATA_DIR` and `SCRATCH_DIR`, because `os.Stat` says
    nothing about whether uid 10001 may WRITE there. It never creates the database and never migrates.
    (c) **It prints no secret**: credentials are never formatted, the webhook is rendered by
    `config.DiscordWebhook.String()` (host + numeric id), and every line is passed through a redaction that
    replaces any configured secret — the backstop for a storage library that quotes the credential it
    signed with inside an error. Two footguns get their own verdicts: the published MinIO credentials
    resolved against a NON-bundled `S3_ENDPOINT` is a FAIL (an empty `S3_ACCESS_KEY=` counts as unset to
    compose's `:-` form), and a non-empty `TRUSTED_PROXIES` beside a `CLIPPET_PUBLISH` that is not loopback
    is a FAIL (DEPLOY §4) — a warning when `CLIPPET_PUBLISH` is not in the environment to check.
    The bucket check is a PING **and a write**: `/readyz`'s `BucketExists` succeeds for a read-only key
    that then fails the first upload. **Wire-format change**: none (CLI only). E2E: **step 51**.

144. **`admin jobs`, `admin ls --state/--owner`, `admin retry`** (`cmd/clippet/admin_ops.go`,
    `cmd/clippet/admin.go`, `internal/db/ops.go` `ListJobs`/`JobKindStateCounts`). "MinIO was down for three
    hours overnight. Which clips ended `failed`, which trims and previews died with them, and can I put
    them all back on the queue?" `admin stats` said `failed=1` and not WHICH, `admin ls` had no filter, and
    the only retry was `POST /api/clips/{id}/retry` — session-only, CSRF-guarded, one human click per clip.
    `admin jobs [--kind k] [--state s] [--clip id] [--since D] [--limit N]` prints the job table newest
    first (id, clip, kind, state, stage, attempts, transient, the age that matters for that state,
    `run_after`, `started`, `finished`, whether a checkpoint exists, and the truncated `last_error` **as a
    `%q` token**, so a value carrying a newline cannot forge a second line in something an operator greps),
    followed by a per-kind/state totals block. `--limit` defaults to 100 and is clamped, because a busy
    instance keeps every job it ever ran. An unrecognised `--state`/`--kind`/`--clip` is a **usage error**,
    never an empty listing: "no clips in state redy" is the wrong answer to a typo.
    `admin ls` gains `--state` and `--owner`, filtered in Go over the listing it already reads rather than
    in a second SQL definition of what a clip listing is; the count line names the filter, so a short
    listing is never mistaken for an empty instance, and `--state`/`--owner` may not be combined with a
    single `<id>`.
    `admin retry <id>… | --all-failed` needs an explicit selector and applies two guards: `db.RetryClip`'s
    UPDATE is predicated on `state = 'failed'` (§5 — a ready, queued or processing clip is never re-queued,
    and a second process must not be able to break that), and the ORIGINAL must still be in the bucket
    (§11 — a retry re-derives everything from the upload, so a clip whose original is gone would be
    re-queued only to fail again). A partial batch exits 1. The retry is picked up by the worker's next
    5 s poll: the CLI is a separate process and does not reach into the running worker.
    **Wire-format change**: none (CLI only). E2E: **steps 52–53**.

145. **`/healthz` reports the queue, not just its depth** (`internal/httpapi/health.go` `queueDTO`,
    `internal/db/ops.go` `QueueHealth`). `QueueStats` counted only `queued` and `running`, so every worker
    failure mode was invisible: a backlog of `failed` jobs did not appear at all, and `queued:3` could not
    distinguish "three uploads just arrived" from "nothing has been claimed for an hour". The block gains
    three fields, computed in one statement:
    `failed_24h` (jobs that reached `failed` in the last 24 h), `oldest_queued_age_s` and
    `longest_running_age_s`. `oldest_queued_age_s` measures only jobs that are **claimable**
    (`run_after <= now`): a job waiting out a backoff is not claimable yet, so counting it would report a
    stuck queue every time a storage blip requeued something. Both ages are 0 when no such row exists, and
    an age is never negative — the container clock steps backwards (DEPLOY §8). The alerts are defined in
    DEPLOY §24: `longest_running_age_s` past `TRANSCODE_HARD_TIMEOUT` means a stuck row (erratum 146
    repairs it); `oldest_queued_age_s` climbing with `running:0` means nothing is claiming.
    Every field is a COUNT or an AGE. `/healthz` is anonymous and unauthenticated (§15), so nothing here
    names a clip, a user, a key or a configured value, and the block stays a CLOSED set of five numbers —
    the per-kind/state matrix an operator wants lives in `admin jobs`, on the box. `/readyz` is unchanged,
    and nothing is sent anywhere: this is a local endpoint an operator polls, not telemetry.
    **Wire-format change**: three additive fields inside `healthz.queue`. E2E: **step 52**.

146. **`admin jobs unstick` — repairing a job stuck `running` without a restart** (`internal/db/ops.go`
    `UnstickJob`/`UnstickStaleJobs`/`repairRunningJobTx`, `internal/db/jobs.go` `ReconcileOnStartup`,
    `cmd/clippet/admin_ops.go`). `jobRun.fail()`'s `case err != nil:` branch logs ERROR, cleans up its keys
    and **returns** — leaving the job `running` and, for a transcode, the clip `processing`; `gifRun.fail`
    and `trimRun.fail` have the same shape. The only thing that ever repaired such a row was
    `ReconcileOnStartup`, i.e. a process restart, so §11's "always claimable or retryable, never stuck" held
    only at boot.
    `admin jobs unstick <job-id> | --older-than D` applies **the boot repair's own per-job rule**: a
    running job WITH a checkpoint is released (no counter spent, the retry is finalize-only), a job WITHOUT
    one takes a `FailCrash` attempt. That rule is now one function, `repairRunningJobTx`, called by both
    `ReconcileOnStartup` and the CLI, so the §5 coupling cannot be written two different ways — only a
    `transcode` job moves its clip, through the same `failAttemptTx`/`releaseJobTx` every other caller uses,
    and a `trim`, `gif` or `notify` job leaves a `ready` clip exactly as ready as it was.
    **The age floor is a conservative heuristic, not a proof, and the command says so.** The boot repair can
    be certain nobody is running a job because nothing is running at all; the CLI is a SECOND PROCESS and
    cannot consult `Worker.Busy`, so age is the only evidence it has, and `TRANSCODE_HARD_TIMEOUT` is the
    largest bound it can name. That timeout bounds **one encode**
    (`transcode.EncodeOptions.HardTimeout` → `context.WithTimeoutCause`), NOT a job's lifetime: a run is
    acquire + probe + encode + verify + poster + store + checkpoint, acquiring a large original is bounded by
    `STORAGE_TRANSFER_MAX` (6 h by default) instead, and a `trim`, `gif` or `notify` job is bounded by
    neither — `GIFHardTimeout` is 60 s. So a job older than the floor is very probably abandoned and is not
    provably so, most visibly on an instance that lowered `TRANSCODE_HARD_TIMEOUT` while a multi-gigabyte
    original is still downloading. A shorter `--older-than` is therefore **raised to the floor and the raise
    is printed**, never silently obeyed; a threshold below `STORAGE_TRANSFER_MAX` prints a second `note:`
    naming the bound the floor is not, and both point at `admin jobs --state running` (the `running_for=`
    column), which is the number to read first. What the floor does rule out is the common shape of the
    mistake: repairing a job an ffmpeg is still writing lets a second worker claim it, and the older run then
    reaches `lostRace()` → `CancelJob` on the row underneath it. The guard lives INSIDE the transaction
    (`db.ErrNotStale`), not in the caller, so a job claimed a moment ago cannot be repaired through the
    window between a check and a write. A `NULL started_at` on a running row counts as stale: `ClaimJob`
    always sets it, so such a row is already inconsistent and repairing it is the point.
    The reason written into `last_error` — and, for a transcode that has now exhausted its attempts, into
    `clips.failure_reason`, which the share page renders to ANY viewer — is the fixed sentence
    `interrupted: the job was found running with no worker`: no path, no host, no job id, no operator.
    **No migration**: a lease or heartbeat column was considered and rejected; `jobs.started_at` already
    carries the only fact the repair needs. **Wire-format change**: none (CLI only). E2E: **step 53**.

147. **`admin stats` reports free disk** (`cmd/clippet/admin.go` `printDisk`,
    `cmd/clippet/freebytes_unix.go` `diskUsage`/`sameDevice`). `admin stats` reported bucket bytes and never
    free disk, though `507 insufficient_scratch` is a documented error whose whole cause is free space and
    `freeBytes` already existed. Two lines: a parseable one
    (`data_free= data_size= scratch_free= scratch_size= min_free= same_device=`) and a human one, plus a
    WARNING line when the scratch filesystem is already below `SCRATCH_MIN_FREE_BYTES` — the state in which
    every upload answers 507. `same_device` is reported because with the shipped compose file `DATA_DIR`
    and `SCRATCH_DIR` are two named volumes on ONE filesystem, so "the scratch disk is full" and "the
    database has nowhere to write" are the same sentence. Off unix, and for a directory that does not
    exist, the line degrades to `disk:    unavailable: …` rather than failing the command. The same
    `queue:` observables erratum 145 added to `/healthz` are printed here too, so the operator on the box
    and the operator polling the endpoint read the same numbers. **Wire-format change**: none (CLI only).

148. **`admin orphans` gains its third report: objects under a LIVE clip** (`cmd/clippet/admin.go`
    `reportExtras`). Every trim replaces the rendition, poster and preview and deletes the superseded keys
    *after* the commit, best-effort and never retried; a crash in that window leaves objects under a **live**
    clip prefix that no column names, and the two existing reports could not see them — one looks for
    prefixes with no row, the other for referenced keys with no object. `db.KeysOf(clip).Keys()` is already
    the single definition of what a row references and `meta/probe.json` is the only key that legitimately
    has none, so the allowlist is exactly one entry. Each finding prints
    `extra <clip> state=… key=… bytes=…` with a per-clip subtotal, and the three counters are **appended**
    to the summary line (`… foreign=N extra=N extra_bytes=N extra_deleted=N`) rather than inserted where
    they read best, because the first five fields are what operator notes and this repository's tests
    already grep for. It honours the existing `--min-age` — sharper here than for the orphan report,
    because an in-flight transcode or trim uploads its outputs BEFORE the commit that starts referencing
    them, so a young unreferenced object under a live clip is usually a job that is still running — and the
    existing `--delete`, which removes one object at a time (a key is its own prefix, §20.6, which is how
    the worker already removes a superseded output). **`--delete` never touches anything under
    `original/`**: the upload is sacred (§11) and the one code path allowed to remove it is
    `lifecycle.Destroy` deleting the whole clip; such an object is reported and left alone. A clip with a
    **live job** is excluded from the report's findings entirely — see erratum 150, which is the guard
    `--min-age` cannot stand in for.
    **Wire-format change**: none (CLI only). E2E: **step 54**.

149. **`admin backup <dir> --rotate N`** (`cmd/clippet/admin_backup_dir.go`). `admin backup` is deliberately
    non-destructive and DEPLOY §15.5 accepted the consequences: keep a month of snapshots, and hunt for
    stranded `.part-` files by hand. When the argument is a **directory** the command now mints the
    filename itself — `clippet-<RFC3339 basic UTC>.db`, which sorts lexicographically in time order — and
    that derived name is the whole safety argument: rotation considers exactly the files matching that
    shape plus the `clippet-…​.db.part-…` files this command's own interrupted runs leave, and **every other
    file in the directory is invisible to it**, which the summary line states as `untouched=N`. It keeps
    the newest N, never removes the snapshot it has just written whatever the sort says, removes `.part-`
    files older than an hour (a younger one may still be being written by a run in flight), prints one line
    per file kept or removed, and exits 1 if any removal failed. Two snapshots in the same second are
    refused by the existing never-overwrite rule, which is not weakened just because the name is derived.
    The single-file form (`admin backup <path>`) is unchanged in every respect, `--rotate` without a
    directory is a usage error, and the snapshot is still written to a `.part-` file beside the destination,
    chmod 0600 before the rename (erratum 96). **Wire-format change**: none (CLI only). E2E: **step 54**.

150. **`admin orphans` never touches a clip that has a live job** (`internal/db/ops.go`
    `ClipIDsWithLiveJobs`, `cmd/clippet/admin.go` `orphans`/`reportExtras`). Erratum 148's third report
    called every object a column does not name garbage, subject only to `--min-age`. A column is not the
    only thing that references an object: §10.3 step 8 uploads the rendition and poster and **checkpoints
    their keys on the job** BEFORE `FinalizeTranscode` writes `rendition_key`/`poster_key`,
    `failAttemptTx`/`releaseJobTx` never clear that checkpoint, and the retry of a checkpointed job is
    finalize-only (`pipeline()` → `finalize()`) with no re-check that the objects are still there. Between
    those two writes the outputs are referenced by `jobs.checkpoint_json` alone — and `--min-age` cannot
    bound that window, because the population it happens to is jobs that have been stuck for hours, which is
    precisely what DEPLOY §24.3's `unstick` exists for. `orphans --delete` would eat them, `unstick` would
    then release the job, and the finalize-only retry would flip the clip to `ready` on keys that no longer
    exist: `video.mp4` and `poster.jpg` 404 for ever, `admin retry` refuses a `ready` clip, and the only
    remaining repair is deleting the clip. So the report now asks the database **which clips have a job in a
    non-terminal state that could still write an object** (`queued` or `running` — a trim writes objects
    under a `ready` clip too)
    and prints such an object as `extra … (skipped: the clip has a live job, which can reference this object
    through its checkpoint)`, never counting it and never deleting it.
    **`notify` is excluded, and it is the only exclusion** (amended 2026-09-07, nit sweep). The interlock
    is about objects, and a notify job posts to a webhook and writes nothing to the bucket — while a queued
    announcement is the longest-lived non-terminal row this system produces, because `NOTIFY_MAX_ATTEMPTS`
    backoffs against a Discord that is down can hold one for hours. A clip whose only live job is an
    announcement was therefore shielded from the sweep by a job that cannot reference a single one of the
    objects in question, which is precisely the case an operator hunting for leftovers is looking at. It is
    written into the query as the EXCLUSION `AND kind <> 'notify'` rather than as an allowlist of the kinds
    that do write objects: a kind added later starts out protected, so the day this system learns a new
    media job the interlock covers it without anybody remembering to say so. The set is read BEFORE the column
    snapshot, so a job that finalizes between the two reads is caught by the first: read the other way round,
    its brand-new rendition would look like garbage of arbitrary age. A `failed` clip is NOT excluded —
    `RetryClip` sets `checkpoint_json = NULL`, so a retry re-derives everything from the original. The other
    two reports are unchanged: an `orphan` prefix has no row and therefore no job, and `missing` deletes
    nothing by construction. **Wire-format change**: none — the summary line keeps the shape erratum 148
    fixed, because a skipped object is not a finding, exactly as a `--min-age` skip is not.
    E2E: **step 54** (clip C is `ready` with a done job, so the sweep it proves is unaffected); the
    interlock itself is proven by `TestAdminOrphansNeverDeletesTheOutputsOfALiveJob`, which checkpoints a
    running job, sweeps, and then finalizes onto the objects that survived, and its one exclusion by
    `TestAdminOrphansSweepsAClipWhoseOnlyLiveJobIsANotify` (which then re-arms the interlock with a live
    gif job on the same clip) and by `TestClipIDsWithLiveJobs`, which also pins that an UNKNOWN kind is
    protected.

151. **One clip at a time, beside the whole-list PUT** (`internal/db/collections.go`
    `RemoveClipFromCollection`/`collectionOfOwnerTx`/`ownedClipTx`/`CollectionsOfClip`,
    `internal/db/bulk.go` `AddClipToCollection`, `internal/httpapi/collections.go`
    `addCollectionClip`/`removeCollectionClip`/`collectionClipEdit`, `web/templates/clip.html`,
    `web/templates/collection.html`, `web/static/app.js` `setupClipCollections`/`setupCollectionRows`;
    ROADMAP #17). Curation worked in one direction only: `PUT …/clips` owns the whole membership, and
    `clip.html` had no collection control at all — "file this clip I am looking at" meant remembering
    its title, finding the collection and picking rows out of a list.
    **`POST`/`DELETE /api/collections/{cid}/clips/{id}` are that edit expressed server-side.** The
    roadmap's sketch was a read-modify-write PUT from the clip page; two of those racing lose one of
    the two edits with no error anywhere, and a client would have to hold the whole 200-clip list to
    add one row. The single-clip routes take no body — the two ids in the path are the request — and
    answer with exactly the shapes their neighbours already answer with: 404 for a collection that is
    missing OR not the caller's (erratum 82's one query, one answer), 400 `not_your_clip` for a clip
    that is unknown, malformed, tombstoned or somebody else's (erratum 82's non-oracle), and the
    CollectionDTO the PUT answers with.
    **Both verbs are idempotent in the CLIP and neither is in the COLLECTION.** Adding a clip that is
    already a member is 200 and does not move it (the caller asked for a state, and the state holds;
    moving it because they ticked a box twice would be a surprise, not an edit); removing one that is
    not a member is 204. A collection that is not the caller's is still 404 either way, so the route
    can no more be used to probe somebody else's id space than any other collection route can.
    **The ADD is `db.AddClipToCollection`, which erratum 119's bulk action already needed**: one
    statement, one meaning of "add", and a position of `MAX(position)+1` so a hole left by a removal
    is never reused by a row that still holds it.
    **The UI.** The clip page gains an owner-only "Collections" checkbox list, ticked from
    `CollectionsOfClip` in one query rather than from a request the client makes; a failed toggle puts
    the box BACK, because a checkbox that stayed ticked after the server refused it is the page lying
    about what is stored. The collection page gains a per-row Remove and two reorder arrows,
    server-rendered `hidden` and revealed by `app.js` (erratum 120's rule for the bulk bar) — Remove
    uses the single-clip DELETE, and a MOVE PUTs the whole list, because order is a property of the
    list and has no single-clip spelling. *(The roadmap also asked for a separate "add clips" picker
    on the collection page; the picker that is already there is that, so only the per-row half was
    added.)*

152. **oEmbed: additive reach, and one host check** (`internal/httpapi/oembed.go`,
    `internal/urls/urls.go` `EmbedCode`, `internal/web/pages.go` `oembedLink`,
    `web/templates/base.html`, `cmd/clippet/serve.go`; ROADMAP #18). Slack's documented unfurl order
    is oEmbed first and the OG/Twitter tags second, discovered through a
    `<link rel="alternate" type="application/json+oembed">`. Discord and X read the tags and are
    **completely unaffected** — §9.1's inventory is untouched — so the whole feature is reach: a
    consumer that shows a title-and-thumbnail card today shows the player.
    **The route lives at `/oembed`, not under `/api/`**, because that is where a consumer's discovery
    link points; `serve.go` mounts that one path on the API handler, so it gets the JSON envelope, the
    TimeoutHandler, the security headers and the `view` limiter (erratum 87's reasoning: anonymous,
    reachable by anyone holding a link, one row read per call). §9.1's discipline is otherwise
    unchanged — `ids.Valid` before any database access, 404 for a missing clip or a tombstone, 503
    and never a 404 for a backend failure, and an UNLISTED clip answered exactly as a listed one is,
    because the share page does and the link is the auth.
    **The host check is the security property.** An oEmbed endpoint takes a URL from the caller and
    describes it; without a check it is a small open proxy for metadata and a place to point a
    consumer at somebody else's site under this instance's name. A URL is ours when, after dropping a
    default port, its scheme and its lower-cased host are byte-equal to `PUBLIC_BASE_URL`'s, its path
    is exactly `/clips/{id}` or `/embed/{id}` with a valid id, and it carries no userinfo —
    `https://our.host@evil.example/clips/x` has `evil.example` as its host and reads, to a person
    skimming, as ours. Nothing else is normalised, so `example.com.`, a punycode lookalike and a
    different port are all simply NOT this origin. Every failure is the SAME 404 a missing clip gets,
    with no message about the URL: telling those cases apart would make the route an oracle about
    both. A query string and a fragment ARE ignored — consumers routinely carry tracking parameters,
    and they name the same clip.
    **`EmbedCode` moved to `internal/urls`** so the document's `html` and the share page's "Copy
    embed" are one function: an oEmbed consumer and a person pasting into a forum must not end up
    with two different players. `maxwidth`/`maxheight` scale DOWN only — a ceiling is what the
    consumer can accommodate, not a size it is asking for — and `format=xml` is 501, which is the
    spec's own answer for a format a provider does not implement.

153. *(unused)*

154. *(unused)*

155. **Per-account upload defaults, resolved in ONE place** (`internal/db/migrations/0011_user_defaults.sql`,
    `internal/db/defaults.go`, `internal/httpapi/settings.go`, `internal/httpapi/upload.go`
    `applyDefaults`, `internal/httpapi/upload_capture.go` `resolveCaptureTTL`,
    `web/templates/tokens.html`; ROADMAP #22). One friend wants everything unlisted and 7-day,
    another wants keep-forever, and the only default was instance-wide.
    **The resolution order is `field sent > account default > DEFAULT_CLIP_TTL`**, and the first
    clause is what makes this safe to add to a shipped API: a capture tool that sends `ttl_days` and
    `unlisted` — which the `.sxcu` this app mints does — behaves exactly as it did before accounts had
    preferences. Only silence is filled in. It is implemented in `applyDefaults`, which BOTH upload
    routes run, because the two grammars (a JSON metadata part and a form field) are the only
    difference between them and a default that applied to one and not the other would be a difference
    the user could feel.
    **The column stores WIRE DAYS, not seconds**, because the field has three states and seconds have
    two: `NULL` is "no preference, follow the instance", `0` is "this account CHOSE keep-forever", and
    1|7|30|90 are days. Storing seconds would have collapsed the first two into one `NULL` and made
    "keep everything forever" unexpressible on an instance whose `DEFAULT_CLIP_TTL` is 7d. The wire
    keeps the same three states, which is why `PATCH` distinguishes an ABSENT key (leave it alone)
    from an explicit `null` (clear it) — a distinction `dto.go`'s `ttlDays` deliberately does not
    make, because on an UPLOAD those two are the same request.
    **Merge note.** The settings section is rendered on `/settings/tokens`, which is the only settings
    surface this build has. Nothing about the section depends on the URL: it is one `<section>` in
    `tokens.html` plus one `defaultsForm` on the page model, so it moves whole if that page is ever
    renamed to `/settings`.

156. **The owner's own tally, and one clip's stored size** (`internal/db/stats.go`,
    `internal/httpapi/settings.go` `getAccountStats`, `internal/web/pages.go`
    `libraryStats`/`storedBytes`, `web/templates/index.html`, `web/templates/clip.html`; ROADMAP #23).
    "Private view counts are the ceiling" is the anti-feature line, and an aggregate of your OWN clips
    is inside it — it never leaves the session that owns the rows. `GET /api/auth/me/stats` is session
    only, has no `{user}` form, and the library renders one line from the same numbers.
    Every value is DERIVED at read time from columns that already exist, for the reason every derived
    number in this codebase is derived: a clip leaves by a TTL sweep or an owner delete without
    anything asking a counter to move, and a counter nobody updates on that path lies. The tally is
    deliberately dull — no rank, no comparison, no "top clip", no history, nobody else's number
    anywhere. Those would be the social layer this product does not have.
    **Deviation from the bundle brief.** The brief described #23 as a per-clip strip on the owner's
    share page (views, size, duration, rendition, expiry). Four of those five were already there —
    the view count, the duration, the expiry and the source size beside "Download original" — so what
    shipped is the ROADMAP entry's own sketch (the account aggregate, which was not built at all)
    plus the one fact the brief named that was genuinely missing: a `Stored` line on the owner's share
    page carrying `source + rendition + poster + gif` for that clip, from the same arithmetic
    `StorageUsed` does for the instance. It is owner-only, like every other number on that list, and
    is absent from an anonymous page and from every card.

157. **`STORAGE_BUDGET_BYTES` is a WARNING** — and "can never become a cap", as this erratum's title
    read until 2026-09-13, is AMENDED by erratum 277: it can, on one opt-in variable
    (`STORAGE_BUDGET_HARD=1`), whose refusal is decided at the upload from a live database read and
    never from the holder below. Everything this erratum says about the holder, the WARN and the
    surfaces is unchanged and still binding; what changed is that an operator who WANTS a line that
    holds now has one, and every sentence that promised otherwise names the variable that lifts it.
    (`internal/config/config.go`,
    `internal/db/stats.go` `StorageUsed`, `internal/httpx/budget.go`, `internal/sweeper/sweeper.go`
    `checkBudget`, `internal/httpapi/health.go`, `cmd/clippet/admin.go` `stats`,
    `web/templates/index.html`; ROADMAP #24). README's "no tiers, no storage quotas" is deliberate,
    but an operator paying for R2 or B2 had no signal that the bucket passed 200 GB except running
    `admin stats` by hand.
    **Nothing reads the verdict to refuse work.** There is no path from the holder to an upload, a
    transcode or a route, and there is deliberately no configuration that would create one. `over`
    being true changes nothing the app does — the library's warning, `/healthz`'s object and the CLI's
    line all say so in the sentence itself, because an operator who sees a red line and cannot tell
    whether their friends' uploads have stopped is worse off than one who saw nothing.
    **The number is what the DATABASE says is in the bucket**, not a bucket listing: one indexed
    aggregate over `clips` (`source + rendition + poster + gif`, tombstones excluded) instead of a
    paginated `LIST`, available to a process that cannot reach the bucket at all. It therefore does
    NOT count an object no row references any more — `admin orphans` is the report for those, and
    DEPLOY §25 says so rather than letting the number be read as a bill.
    **The WARN is edge-triggered**: once on the crossing, once on the way back under (at INFO), and
    silence in between. A line that fired every tick would be a line an operator filters out, which is
    the same as not having it. The sweeper measures it — the liveness probe compose calls every ten
    seconds must not grow a scan of `clips` — and publishes it to an `httpx.StorageBudget` holder that
    `/healthz` and the library page read. The reading is taken IMMEDIATELY at `Start`, before the boot
    delay, so an operator who has just set the variable and reloaded `/healthz` sees an answer rather
    than a gap. A read error never fails a tick: the previous reading stands, because destroying
    expired clips is the sweeper's job and a number for a dashboard must not be able to interrupt it.
    *(The roadmap said "once every N ticks"; every tick is one aggregate on the smallest table in the
    schema, and it makes the number as fresh as the sweep that changed it.)*
    **The library line is shown to every logged-in viewer**, not to an "operator" the app has no
    concept of: §14 has users and nothing else, the number is the same one `admin stats` and
    `/healthz` print, and on a household instance the person who would clear space is as likely to be
    the friend uploading as the person who owns the bucket. It is never on a public page — the library
    is session-only — and it names no clip and no account.

158. **`DISCORD_WEBHOOK_ROUTES`, and why it is one variable** (`internal/config/config.go`
    `discordRoutes`/`parseDiscordURL`/`cleanRouteTag`, `internal/notify/notify.go`,
    `cmd/clippet/serve.go`; ROADMAP #26). The unshipped half of §17 #4: DEPLOY §11 recorded "one
    webhook per instance, one channel".
    **Deviation from the bundle brief.** The brief asked for `DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL_<TAG>` — one
    environment variable per tag. The code refuses it twice over: `config.Load` is handed a
    `getenv(string) string` and cannot ENUMERATE the environment (changing that signature is a
    non-mechanical edit to the file every other package reads its rules from), and erratum 57 requires
    `compose.yaml` to interpolate every §4 variable with its documented default, which is impossible
    for an open-ended family of names. The ROADMAP entry's own spelling — `<tag>=<url>;<tag>=<url>` in
    ONE variable, plus `DISCORD_WEBHOOK_UNMATCHED=default|skip` — is a fixed name, interpolates, and
    is what shipped. A semicolon separates the rules because a comma is already `TRUSTED_PROXIES`'
    separator and a webhook URL's charset contains neither; `=` assigns because a tag's grammar cannot
    contain one, so the FIRST `=` is unambiguously the split point whatever the URL holds.
    **Every routed URL is held to `DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL`'s exact rule** — https, the closed host
    allowlist, `/api/webhooks/<numeric id>/<token>`, no userinfo, no query or fragment — from the same
    function, so the §15 claim ("outbound traffic goes to `S3_ENDPOINT` and to Discord, and nowhere
    else") is unchanged by this feature. Every TAG goes through the tag grammar, because a rule whose
    tag no clip could ever carry is a rule that silently never fires, which is exactly the class of
    misconfiguration §4 says must fail at boot rather than at 3am. A duplicate tag is refused: "first
    match wins" is only a rule an operator can reason about if the list they wrote is the list that is
    walked and a tag appears once. No rejection ever echoes the value — a routes variable is a list of
    secrets — and each one locates the offending rule by its **1-based position** instead. A tag is
    named in a message only once it has PASSED the grammar, when it is at most 32 characters of
    `a-z0-9-` and therefore cannot be a URL. *(Corrected by erratum 160: the first version echoed the
    RAW tag half.)*
    **One client, still.** `notify.New` takes a map of named endpoints and builds exactly one
    `http.Client`: the §15 tripwire is about how many ways this binary can reach the network, and a
    per-route client would have been three. The scrub list covers EVERY endpoint's spellings, so a
    rejection body echoing a routed webhook's token comes back with the token gone. An unknown route
    NEVER falls back to the default — posting to a channel nobody chose for the clip is the one thing
    routing exists to prevent — so a job whose route the operator has since removed is SKIPPED, the
    same shape as every other "the configuration moved" outcome.

159. **The route is chosen inside the ready transaction, and stored as a TAG** (`internal/db/jobs.go`
    `FinalizeTranscode`/`enqueueNotifyTx`/`matchNotifyRouteTx`/`NotifyRouteOf`,
    `internal/worker/notify.go`; ROADMAP #26). WHICH webhook a clip is announced to is decided in the
    same commit that flips it `ready`, from the tags it has at that instant, and the answer goes into
    the job's `params_json`. A later tag edit therefore never re-routes a post that is already queued,
    and the worker never has to guess.
    **What is stored is a NAME — a tag, or nothing.** `{}` means the default webhook, which is what
    every job written before routing existed carries and what an unrouted clip still gets, so the
    feature needed no migration and no backfill. A webhook URL has no path into the database at all:
    `db` is handed rules made of tags and a bool, and it writes a tag. Every notify log line carries
    `webhook=<name>` for the same reason — an operator running several channels can see which one a
    post went to, and the line still names no secret.
    **Rules are walked in the operator's configured ORDER, not the alphabet's**: the first rule whose
    tag the clip carries wins, so priority is something they can read off the line they wrote.
    **An unmatched clip with nowhere to go queues NOTHING.** With `DISCORD_WEBHOOK_UNMATCHED=skip`, or
    with routes configured and no `DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL`, a clip no rule matched writes no job at all —
    which is what keeps "no webhook, no outbound request" true per clip and not merely per instance.
    Routing changes WHERE a post goes and nothing about WHETHER an unlisted clip is announced: the
    per-upload opt-out is checked exactly where it was.
    **`FinalizeTranscode`'s routing argument is VARIADIC**, and that is a merge decision as much as an
    API one: every existing caller and every existing test keeps compiling unchanged, and a caller
    that passes nothing gets the single-webhook behaviour byte for byte.

160. **Three ways routing could fail in silence, all three now loud at boot** (`internal/config/config.go`
    `discordRoutes`/`Load`, `internal/notify/notify.go` `New`; ROADMAP #26). Corrections to errata 158
    and 159, from the bundle's own adversarial review.
    **A rejection quotes no part of `DISCORD_WEBHOOK_ROUTES`.** `strings.Cut` splits a rule on the
    FIRST `=`, so an operator who types it backwards (`<url>=<tag>`) hands the entire webhook — token
    and all — to the tag half. The first version echoed that half with `%q`, which put a live
    credential in the boot error, on stderr and into `docker compose logs app`, where it persists and
    is shipped wherever logs are shipped. Rules are now located by their **1-based position** in the
    variable, and a tag is named only after it has passed the grammar (≤32 characters of `a-z0-9-`,
    which no URL can be). Bounding the echo was considered and rejected: 32 characters of a webhook on
    a SHORT host is still most of a token, and the value that failed is by definition not one the
    parser understands.
    **`default` is a reserved route tag.** It satisfies the tag grammar, but it is also the name
    `internal/notify` gives `DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL`'s own channel in a boot line, in a delivery line and
    in a queued job's `params_json`. `notify.New` adds the default webhook FIRST and keeps the first
    endpoint registered under a name, so a rule tagged `default` was accepted by config, LOGGED as
    configured, then silently dropped — and every clip carrying the tag was announced in the default
    channel, which is exactly what routing exists to prevent. Config now refuses it by name. The
    first-writer-wins rule in `notify.New` stays as the last line of defence.
    **`DISCORD_WEBHOOK_UNMATCHED=skip` with no rules is refused.** `skip` means "announce only the
    clips a rule matched"; with no rules nothing can ever match, so the pair announces NOTHING while
    the boot log still reports `discord webhook configured` — one typo in `DISCORD_WEBHOOK_ROUTES`
    stops every post, invisibly. It fails at boot instead, naming the variable to fix. With no
    `DISCORD_WEBHOOK_URL` either, Discord is simply off and the variable is inert, so a leftover line
    in a `.env` still boots. The alternative — logging the routing line whenever `unmatched` is not the
    default — was rejected because it makes the state visible without making it any less wrong, and
    once the boot refuses it that branch is unreachable code.
    **`internal/config` still imports nothing but the standard library** (§18.1): the reserved word is
    restated as `reservedRouteTag` beside the restated tag grammar, and `TestReservedRouteTagIsNotifys`
    pins it against `notify.DefaultRoute` from a TEST file, whose imports are not the package's.

161. **`API.md` documents this branch's routes; it does not add a `check.sh` route-coverage
    tripwire** (ROADMAP #20, deviation from the sketch). The sketch's "~300 lines" also asked for a
    `check.sh` stage that greps every `route("…")` path in `router.go` and fails the build if `API.md`
    does not mention it — deliberately not built here. Two reasons, not one: `check.sh` is the
    merge gate's own script, run once against the merged tree (this bundle's
    brief forbids running it from a lane at all, so a new stage in it could not be proven green before
    committing), and lanes 1 and 2 are landing their own routes into `router.go` at the same time this
    document was written — a tripwire added now would grep a `router.go` that is a moving target and
    would very likely fail on the very next merge for reasons that have nothing to do with `API.md`
    going stale. `API.md`'s own header says so and asks for a reconciliation after the
    three lanes land; a `check.sh` stage that keeps it honest going forward is left as a cleanup-list
    candidate for whoever next touches `router.go` and this file together, once the tree is no longer
    three lanes wide.

162. **The reverse-proxy recipes (DEPLOY.md §26, ROADMAP #19) are proven by reading and by the app's
    own request handling, not by a live run of `scripts/e2e.sh` through a real Caddy or nginx** —
    deviation from the sketch's "verify once by running the E2E over the proxy". Both recipes forward
    to `127.0.0.1:${CLIPPET_PUBLISH port}` with nothing rewritten before the app's own request handling
    (§8) takes over, so §6's existing instruction — `BASE=https://<your domain> bash scripts/e2e.sh` —
    already IS that proof once a real domain sits in front of either recipe; DEPLOY.md §26 says so
    rather than inventing a second E2E path for the same assertions. What a live run needs and this
    build environment does not have is a publicly resolvable domain with ports 80/443 reachable from
    the internet, so Let's Encrypt can issue a certificate — neither exists inside a lane's private dev
    stack, and none of ROADMAP #19's own headline items (`TRUSTED_PROXIES`, `client_max_body_size`,
    `proxy_request_buffering`) are new application behavior a unit test could exercise either; they are
    proxy-side configuration the app never sees as distinct from a direct connection. Left for whoever
    next stands up a real domain behind one of these recipes to confirm; DEPLOY.md §26 is explicit that
    reading a Caddyfile or an nginx block is not a substitute for that run.

165. **A failed media job speaks its own kind's vocabulary, whatever wrote the row**
    (`internal/worker/registry.go` `OwnerError`/`ownerVocabulary`/`ownerFallback`,
    `internal/httpapi/owner_error.go` `ownerJobError`, `internal/httpapi/{poster,trim,replace,gif}.go`,
    `internal/db/types.go` `MsgInterruptedByRestart`, `internal/db/ops.go` `IsOperatorReason`).
    Erratum 80 fixed the owner's vocabulary at the point the WORKER writes it, and `internal/worker`
    has honoured that ever since: the trim, the poster and the replacement each map every ending onto
    one of their own sentences. `internal/db`
    writes that column too, in the two places that repair a job nobody is running —
    `ReconcileOnStartup` (`interrupted by restart`) and `admin jobs unstick` (`UnstickReason`) — and
    those sentences are an operator's, written for every kind alike. Three owner routes
    plus one ANONYMOUS route hand the column straight to their reader (`GET …/poster`,
    `GET …/trim`, `GET …/replace`, and `preview.gif`'s 503, which is public). `PosterMaxAttempts` is 2,
    so two crash-class restarts of a running poster job with no checkpoint are all it takes to reach
    `failed` carrying an operator's sentence. **Wire-format change** to the `error` field of those
    three DTOs and to the 503's `message`: a text that is not one of that kind's own sentences is now
    rendered as the kind's generic sentence (`the card image could not be changed`, `the trim failed`,
    `the replacement failed`), and the gif — whose `last_error` is `publicReason`'s redacted
    "stage: message", an OPEN set by design and the right one for a route an operator also reads —
    drops any sentence `db` itself wrote (`db.IsOperatorReason`, which lives beside those constants so
    a third one is covered without anybody remembering the other end) and says only "the preview could
    not be made". The job row is never rewritten: the operator still reads the truth in the log and in
    `admin jobs`, and DEPLOY §24.3 says so where an operator will meet it.
    Two choices worth recording. The mapping is a VOCABULARY test, not a test for that one string, so
    the next operator sentence somebody puts in a job row is covered before it is written; and it
    lives in `internal/worker` (which owns the sentences) rather than in `internal/db` (which would
    otherwise have to know six sentences it never writes), with `httpapi` holding a four-line adapter
    so the four routes share one spelling. Option (a) from the nit — a per-kind sentence inside
    `repairRunningJobTx` — was rejected for exactly that coupling.

166. **`{"seconds":-0}` is stored and echoed as plain `0`** (`internal/httpapi/poster.go`
    `startPoster`, `internal/httpapi/poster_test.go`). `-0` is a legal moment: IEEE says `-0 == 0`,
    so it passes `secs < first` for a clip whose reachable range starts at 0, and
    `math.Round(-0*1000)/1000` preserves the sign bit — so the negative zero survived into the 202's
    `seconds`, into `params_json` and into the ffmpeg argv as `-0.000`. Nothing misbehaved (the frame
    taken is frame 0 and the clip normalises `applied_seconds` back to `0`), but the route's whole
    promise is that the echoed number, the stored number and the seek are ONE number, and `-0` broke
    that promise in the only place a client can see it. One line after the rounding normalises the
    zero. **Wire-format change**, narrowly: the 202's `seconds` for a `-0` request now reads `0`; no
    other input's answer changes and no field is added or removed. A nullable `seconds` was NOT
    adopted for the related corrupt-row case (a `params_json` no parser can read still leaves
    `seconds` at 0, indistinguishable from a genuine first-frame choice): that row is unreachable
    from the write path — `startPoster` refuses NaN and Infinity, and `MarshalPosterParams` writes a
    self-describing string rather than `{}` when it cannot marshal — so `posterStatus` now logs it at
    WARN for the operator instead of changing a public shape for a hand-corrupted row.

167. **`SQLITE_CANTOPEN` reports `io`, not `unavailable`** (`internal/db/db.go` `HealthClass`,
    `internal/db/health_test.go`). Erratum 99 pinned the closed set `/healthz` and `/readyz` may print
    for a database failure and closed the leak by DEFAULT, which is right; but result code 14 —
    "unable to open database file" — fell through that default, so the single most likely production
    misconfiguration of `DATA_DIR` (a volume that is not mounted, a directory the container user
    cannot write) answered with the one class that names no cause at all. It is now folded into the
    existing `sqliteIOErr` arm: `io` tells an operator to look at the mount and the permissions,
    which is exactly what happened. **No wire-format change** — `io` was already in erratum 99's set,
    and the set is unchanged; what changes is which failures land in it. `TestHealthClass`'s
    closed-set assertion still holds, and `TestHealthClassOnRealDriverErrors` now drives the arm with
    a real driver error (a database under a directory that does not exist), which is the half a
    hand-built `*sqlite.Error` cannot prove.

168. **The session pruner covers both ways a row stops authenticating** (`internal/db/users.go`
    `DeleteExpiredSessions`, `internal/db/sessions_test.go`). Erratum 105 gave every session an
    absolute ceiling and taught `GetSession`, `ListSessions` and `TouchSession` to honour it, but the
    one pruner the sweeper calls still asked only `expires_at <= ?`. A row whose ceiling has passed is
    invisible to every read and usable by nobody, and nothing pulls its `expires_at` down — the only
    writer that clamps is `TouchSession`, which is reached only for rows that still resolve — so such
    a row sat in `sessions` until its OWN expiry arrived: up to `SESSION_TTL` (720 h by default) after
    it stopped working. Migration 0005's backfill (`max_expires_at = created_at + 7776000`) creates
    exactly that population on any instance upgraded with sessions older than 90 days, so the dead
    rows are not hypothetical. The predicate is now
    `expires_at <= ? OR (max_expires_at > 0 AND max_expires_at <= ?)`; `max_expires_at = 0` still
    means "no ceiling recorded" and is never pruned on that account, which is the safe direction for a
    row an older binary wrote. **No wire-format change** and no security change — the rows removed
    could not authenticate before or after; what changes is that the table now shrinks when it should.
    (The migration-side clamp the nit offered as an alternative was rejected: it helps only rows that
    existed at migration time.)

169. **A social job re-applies the skip rule to the rendition it actually found**
    (`internal/worker/social.go` `recheckClip`, `internal/worker/social_test.go`). Erratum 121's rule
    is decided at COMMIT time by whoever publishes a rendition — `FinalizeTranscode`, `SwapRendition`,
    `SwapSource` — and carried as `ReadyFields.QueueSocial`; `enqueueSocialTx` then leaves an
    already-live job alone rather than re-deciding, on the argument that the ETag predicate throws
    away work done against a rendition that is no longer current. That predicate only catches a job
    that had already STARTED and read the old ETag. A job still `queued` when a trim commits reads the
    NEW rendition in `recheckClip` and encodes it — so a clip that qualified by SIZE alone (30 fps,
    large) and was then trimmed small got exactly one social encode the rule would have refused: an
    ffmpeg slot and an object spent on a file `/social.mp4` would not have served anyway (the route
    falls back to the rendition through its COALESCE). `recheckClip` now rebuilds the rule's inputs
    from the row it just re-read and answers `skip("social", "the rendition no longer qualifies")`
    when `socialWanted` is false, which is the same function the commit used and the same skip path a
    deleted or no-longer-ready clip takes — the job resolves done/skipped, nothing is deleted and the
    card keeps working. **No wire-format change**; the card is correct either way, and what changes is
    that the work is not done. The `CancelJob` alternative was rejected: it would put a job-lifecycle
    mutation inside `SwapRendition`'s single commit.

177. **`twitter:image:alt` joins the ready card: the §9.1 inventory is now 27 tags on an http origin
    and 28 on https.** *(Its "emitted by `readyMeta` only" is narrowed by erratum 294, which carried
    the same pair to the LINK-OUT card with a sentence about the placeholder rather than about a frame;
    the collection card is still outside both.)* Erratum 103 added `og:image:alt` — the one accessibility affordance a card has —
    and stopped there, so Discord got a sentence describing the poster and X got none. The two tags
    describe the same picture, so they carry the same sentence from the same helper (`imageAlt`), and
    a test pins them equal rather than letting the two goldens drift apart. Nothing else moves: the
    tag is emitted by `readyMeta` only (a processing or failed card has no real frame to describe, and
    the collection card is a link-out whose picture belongs to a member clip, not to the list), it is
    `name=` like every other `twitter:*`, and it carries no URL, so the https "every URL-valued tag is
    on the public origin" sweep is unaffected. The count moved in the same commit everywhere it is
    pinned — §9.1's checklist and count sentence, the `BuildMeta` golden, and
    `TestReadyInventoryIsTwentySevenTags` (renamed from `…TwentySix…`) — because the inventory is an
