    EXACT set and a tag added without moving it is how the set stops being exact.

178. **The auth and mint forms stay JSON-only, and say so in a `<noscript>`.** `/login`, `/register`,
    `/settings`'s password and token-mint forms and the library's "New collection" form all carry
    `method="post"` to routes that accept only JSON — `byMethod.handler()` filters the method outside
    every middleware, so a form POST to the PATCH-only password route is a 405 envelope, and
    `requireJSON` answers 415 on the other four. Without JavaScript each was a raw JSON dead end with
    no way back to the page. The fix is a `<noscript>` line inside each form saying so; the other
    half of the suggestion — accepting `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` on those routes and
    redirecting — is REFUSED. `requireJSON` is documented as a §14 CSRF measure ("forms cannot send
    it cross-origin without a preflight") and erratum 120 already settled this exact question the
    other way for the bulk bar, which is a `<div role="group">` and not a `<form>` for precisely this
    reason. Dropping it from the password and token-mint routes would remove that layer from the two
    most sensitive owner routes an account has. If a real no-JS path is ever wanted the precedent is
    `internal/httpapi/share.go` — multipart plus a 303 for a browser navigation, session and CSRF
    kept — and it is its own piece of work, not a relaxation of this one. Recorded here so the next
    reader does not re-open it.

189. **`check.sh` re-draws the app icons, and its URL tripwire says out loud that it reads comments**
    (`scripts/check.sh`, `scripts/lib/mkicons.py`; §16.1; nit sweep N095 and N008). Two changes to the
    merge gate, neither of which relaxes anything. (a) `web/static/icon-192.png` and `icon-512.png` are
    drawn by `scripts/lib/mkicons.py` and committed as binaries, and nothing checked that the committed
    bytes still came from the generator: a hand-edited or stale icon shipped silently. The script grows
    two modes — an optional output directory, and `--check`, which decodes each committed PNG and
    compares its PIXEL ROWS against a fresh draw — and `check.sh` runs `--check` beside the `jget.py`
    self-test, skipping itself the same way on a host with no python. The comparison is over decoded
    rows and never over the compressed bytes on purpose: those depend on the zlib the interpreter
    ships, so a version bump would otherwise fail the gate without the mark having moved at all.
    (b) The no-outbound-URL grep is line-based and does NOT skip comments, so a URL written in PROSE
    fails exactly as a real egress would — which has happened, at the cost of a fix commit. That
    behaviour is kept (a reviewer cannot tell a commented-out client from a sentence) and is now
    stated in the stage's own description and pinned by its self-test, which plants a prose comment in
    each of the four scanned languages and requires every one of them to be flagged. The
    documentation half of the nit — a line in the contributors' rules — is made outside this document;
    this file and the failure message now carry the same warning.

200. **The ORIGINAL tier: a web-playable upload is streamed, not re-encoded.** Every upload used to be
    re-encoded exactly once, into a rendition fitted to `TRANSCODE_MAX_WIDTH`×`TRANSCODE_MAX_HEIGHT`
    (1280×720 by default) and capped at `TRANSCODE_MAX_FPS`. So a 1440p60 capture — the shape this
    product exists to share — came back WORSE than it went in, silently, and the owner's only copy of
    the good frames was the download link. The owner asked on 2026-09-08 whether the full quality has to be
    encoded at all rather than played directly. It does not, for most of what people upload.

    A source is **web-playable** when every row of this table says so
    (`transcode.OriginalPlayability`, and deliberately the same predicates
    `transcode.DecideTrim` uses to choose a stream copy — two answers to "does this file already have
    the shape the pipeline would have produced" is how they drift apart):

    | property        | playable                     | refused → a FULL tier instead    |
    |-----------------|------------------------------|----------------------------------|
    | container       | mp4 / mov / m4v (ISO-BMFF)   | matroska, webm, avi, mpegts, …   |
    | video codec     | h264, av1                    | hevc, vp9, prores, mpeg4, …      |
    | pixel format    | yuv420p, yuvj420p            | 10-bit, 4:2:2, 4:4:4, rgb        |
    | colour transfer | SDR                          | PQ / HLG (needs a tone map)      |
    | field order     | progressive / unknown        | tt, bb, tb, bt (needs yadif)     |
    | audio           | none, or ONE aac track       | two or more (the merge is ours)  |
    | rotation        | Display Matrix, or none      | a legacy `rotate` tag            |
    | pixel aspect    | square                       | anamorphic (needs `setsar=1`)    |
    | duration        | declared and positive        | absent (a broken index)          |
    | picture         | ≤ 7680×4320                  | larger (erratum 202)             |

    Four rows are judgements rather than facts and are recorded as such. **Matroska and WebM are
    refused although browsers play them**: `/video.mp4`, `/light.mp4` and `?download=1` are one object
    behind three promises of an mp4, and remuxing VP9 into mp4 is not a copy anybody should rely on.
    **HEVC is refused although Safari plays it**: desktop Chrome and Firefox do not, so "playable"
    would mean "playable for some viewers", which is worse than a Full everyone can watch. **AV1 is
    accepted**: Chrome 70+, Firefox 67+, Edge and Safari 17+ decode it from an mp4, and a source
    already in it is exactly the source nobody wants re-encoded. **Two audio tracks are refused**
    because merging them is a feature (§10.3 step 2): a browser plays the first track only, so direct
    play would silently drop the microphone.

    A playable upload whose CONTAINER is not servable as it stands is **REMUXED**: `-c copy
    -movflags +faststart` into a fresh `renditions/main-{r8}.mp4`, mapping the one video and at most
    one audio stream, `-sn -dn -map_metadata -1 -map_chapters -1` (so a phone's creation time, device
    name and GPS tags do not travel into a public object). Not one coded byte changes, so **a remux is
    the Original tier and not a Full**. Two CONTAINER properties trigger it, and between them they cover
    almost every real upload: `moov` after `mdat` — which is what ffmpeg writes unless told otherwise —
    and a stored media type that is not `video/mp4` (a `.mov` Firefox declines). A third trigger, the
    file's own METADATA, is the amendment below. `original_remuxed` records that one happened.

    **MEASURED**, on this lane's stack with compose's default `cpus: 1.0`, ffmpeg 7.1.1, `veryfast`.
    The subject is a 150 s 720p60 12.2 Mbps H.264 + AAC mp4 with `moov` last (227.9 MB — the file
    the owner's measurement used), timed inside the app container:

    | | before (one 720p60 CRF 23 rendition) | after (remux + the card's copy) |
    |---|---|---|
    | the encode(s) | 181 s → 213.2 MB | **remux < 1 s** → 227.9 MB, then the LIGHT copy 99 s → 49.1 MB |
    | time to `ready` | 181 s (no card file yet) | **~100 s, and the card's file exists AT `ready`** |
    | time to a card Discord inlines | ~280 s (the social encode ran after it) | **~100 s** |
    | stored, beyond the upload | 213.2 MB rendition + 49.1 MB card copy | **49.1 MB card copy** |
    | what a viewer streams | a re-encoded 213 MB copy | **the 12.2 Mbps upload** |

    So the fast path is worth −45 % on time-to-ready, −64 % on time-to-a-working-card, −213 MB of
    stored bytes per clip of this shape, and the picture the owner uploaded instead of a copy of it.
    On the E2E's own six-second matrix the seconds are too small to be the point (A/B/C ready in 0–1 s,
    D in 3 s, where every one of them used to need a full encode): what the matrix shows is D, the
    1080p60 clip, coming back **1920×1080 at 60 fps** instead of 1280×720.

    The remuxed original is stored BESIDE the upload, so a clip on this path costs its bytes twice.
    That is the price of a container a crawler will fetch, it is why the DIRECT branch exists at all,
    and DEPLOY §27 prices it per tier.

    **Amended (M1 fix pass, 2026-09-08).** There is a THIRD remux trigger, and it is a privacy rule
    rather than a container one: **metadata beyond the structural keys**. The direct branch is the one
    place this pipeline publishes bytes it did not render, so an upload's own `location` /
    `com.apple.quicktime.location.ISO6709` / `make` / `model` / `artist` / `comment` /
    `creation_time` travelled unchanged onto `/original`, onto `/video.mp4` and into the file a crawler
    fetches — which is exactly what `-map_metadata -1 -map_chapters -1` is in every other argv of this
    package to prevent (§10.3, "strips GPS/device tags (privacy)"). Such a file now takes the `-c copy`
    branch, which strips all of it: measured on ffmpeg 7.1.1, a faststart mp4 tagged with a location, an
    artist, a comment and a creation time comes back carrying nothing but the brand boxes and the
    muxer's own name.

    The test is an ALLOWLIST — `major_brand`, `minor_version`, `compatible_brands`, `encoder`,
    `language`, `handler_name`, `vendor_id`, on the container and on every stream — for two reasons.
    The direction that has to be safe is the UNKNOWN one: a vendor key nobody here has heard of is
    exactly the kind that turns out to hold a serial number or a place. And that list is precisely what
    this pipeline's own remux output carries, which makes the rule a fixed point — nothing is ever
    remuxed twice for its metadata. The cost is the sub-second copy the common (moov-last) case already
    pays, on the subset of faststart uploads that carry a tag; the tier is still **Original**, because
    not one coded byte is rewritten; and a capture tool that writes clean faststart mp4 (OBS, ShareX, an
    `ffmpeg -movflags +faststart` step) stays on the zero-copy path the measurement above was taken on.
    A phone's camera roll — DEPLOY §27's own example of the fast path — is the case that changes: it
    keeps the fast path's speed and stops publishing where it was filmed.

201. **`rendition_key` IS the Full tier's object, and `/video.mp4` is "the best playable tier".** The
    tiers deliberately add NO second key column. `clips.rendition_key` has always meant "the main
    playable web file", and after erratum 200 that file is either the Full re-encode, or the `-c copy`
    remux of a playable original, or a trim's cut. Giving the Full its own trio would have created a
    second name for one object — and `db.KeysOf`, `admin ls --stat`, `admin orphans`, the sweeper, the
    trim's supersede list, `lifecycle.Destroy` and `StorageUsed` would each have had to learn it.
    Every one of them already covers `rendition_key`, which is why migration 0012 is twelve `ALTER
    TABLE`s and no invalidation work at all.

    The price is that `rendition_key` can now be NULL on a `ready` clip, in two legitimate states: the
    remux fast path took the direct branch (there is no second object — the upload IS the playable
    file), and card-first ordering has published the LIGHT copy while the Full encodes. So the ONE
    definition of "which bytes does this clip play" is `db.PlayObject`, in tier order: the rendition
    when there is one, else the upload when `original_playable AND NOT original_remuxed`, else the
    Light copy. `/video.mp4` resolves it, and so does every job that derives something from a clip —
    the preview GIF, the chosen card frame and the Light copy itself — whose commit predicates are
    correspondingly generalised from `rendition_etag` to `db.playETagSQL` (the same order, in SQL).
    `ok=false` from `PlayObject` on a `ready` row remains the §12 invariant violation the media routes
    answer 503 for.

    For the same reason there are no `light_*` key columns: the LIGHT tier is the file that shipped as
    the "social rendition" in erratum 121, and it keeps its `social_*` columns and its
    `renditions/social-{r8}.mp4` key. The rename is in the API, the UI and the documentation, where a
    person reads it (erratum 210).

    **Amended (M1 fix pass, 2026-09-08).** Two readers of `rendition_key` were still testing the column
    instead of asking `db.PlayObject`, and both were bugs of exactly the shape this erratum's "price"
    paragraph predicted.

    (a) `POST /api/clips/{id}/replace` answered 409 `not_ready` on every clip on the remux fast path and
    every clip inside the card-first window — a plainly `ready` clip, and the very shape DEPLOY §27
    calls the ideal case — while the watch page went on rendering the Replace form for it, because that
    form is gated on "the route would answer". ROADMAP #31 was therefore unreachable for exactly the
    uploads this bundle exists to serve. The precondition is now `state = ready` **plus**
    `db.PlayObject`; `ok=false` there is the §12 invariant violation, answered **503 `unavailable`** as
    the media routes answer it, because a row with no playable bytes needs a human and not a retry.

    (b) `db.attemptAlreadyApplied` — erratum 102's "this attempt already committed" classifier —
    required `rendition_key` to be non-NULL and equal, so a finalize RETRY of a fast-path or card-first
    commit was classified as a genuine lost race: the caller then deleted the poster (and, on a
    card-first clip, the LIGHT copy) that the just-committed `ready` row was pointing at. That is erratum
    102's own defect, restored on a clip that is live and shareable. The classifier now turns on the
    **poster** key, which is attempt-scoped and written by every commit that flips `ready`, so a `ready`
    row carrying it can only be this attempt's own work; the rendition and light keys are compared only
    when this attempt HAS them, because an absent one is not evidence in either direction —
    `db.SetFull` writes that same column later, on a clip that is already ready, so demanding NULL would
    have been a second way to get the same answer wrong.

    One consequence for OPERATORS belongs here too, because it is the same "PlayObject returns the
    SOURCE" fact: on a clip with no rendition object every derived-artefact job — the preview GIF, a
    chosen card frame, the Light copy — downloads the UPLOAD rather than a ≤720p rendition, and its
    scratch reservation scales with the upload. `SCRATCH_DIR` must therefore hold the largest accepted
    upload plus `SCRATCH_MIN_FREE_BYTES` for those jobs and not only for a transcode; on an install where
    it cannot, such a job requeues without counting an attempt for ever (`errNoScratchRoom` →
    `requeueNoCount`). DEPLOY §27, §13 and §21 say so out loud.

202. **The FULL tier: a faithful re-encode at the SOURCE's own resolution and frame rate.** It exists
    only when the original is not web-playable, and it is the one stored copy of such a source, so it
    is never downscaled and never slowed — the owner's definition of 2026-09-08: Full means the quality
    and fidelity are kept, with no cap.

    `transcode.FullPlanOptions` hands `MakePlan` the source's own long and short sides, so the scale
    factor is exactly 1. The frame-rate ceiling is the one number that is not simply removed, and the
    reason is `pickFPS` (erratum 93): `r_frame_rate` is where containers put nonsense — Matroska
    routinely reports 1000/1 or 90000/1, the timebase rather than a rate — and `pickFPS` uses the
    ceiling to tell a genuine high rate from that. So the ceiling is RAISED to the source's own average
    rate whenever that is higher than the operator's: it can no longer bind below what the source
    actually ran at (a 240 fps phone capture is encoded at 240) while a container claiming 1000 fps
    still falls through to the average it measured.

    A picture past **7680×4320** is refused rather than downscaled: the clip fails `permanent` with
    `source_too_large: the picture is larger than this server encodes (WxH)`. That is the failure
    doctrine of §11 applied to the one case where obeying the tier's promise is impossible, and it is
    stated in the plan so both the transcode run and the `full` job reach it.

    `TRANSCODE_CRF` does NOT apply: the Full's floor is a constant (CRF 18 for libx264, 32 for
    libsvtav1), because "Full" is a promise about fidelity and a knob that could set it to 30 would be
    shipping a tier whose name lies. `TRANSCODE_PRESET` still chooses how much CPU an H.264 Full
    spends, and `TRANSCODE_MAX_BITRATE` is still available — and is now the one operator setting that
    can make a Full less than faithful, which DEPLOY §27 says out loud.

    Since these tiers `TRANSCODE_MAX_WIDTH`/`HEIGHT`/`FPS`/`CRF` bound the **LIGHT copy alone**. They
    are not deprecated: an operator who wants smaller cards still lowers them, and the Light box takes
    the MINIMUM of theirs and its own.

203. **The LIGHT tier: the card's own copy, and the skip rule restated.** Erratum 121's numbers are
    unchanged — ≤30 fps, CRF 26, a 2.5 Mbps VBV ceiling, 96k audio, H.264 **always** — and its
    measured fact stands: a crawler fetches the file itself and stops inlining somewhere past ~100 MB.
    H.264 is pinned in `SocialEncodeOptions` rather than merely left alone, because `FULL_CODEC` may
    say `av1` and the card must not follow it.

    Two things change. The BOX is now the tier's own **1280×720**, narrowed but never widened by the
    instance's: erratum 121 used the instance box alone, which was right while the input was always a
    rendition that already fitted it and is wrong now that the input can be a 4K upload. And the SKIP
    RULE is restated as a function of the tier that will serve the card
    (`transcode.LightWanted`): a Light copy is made when that file is **larger than 1280×720**, OR
    **above 30 fps**, OR **at or above `SOCIAL_MAX_BYTES`**. The first term is new and is why a 4K
    upload gets one even when it is small; the size term applies only when the size is KNOWN, which it
    is for a playable original (it is the upload) and not for a Full that has yet to be encoded — a
    Full at ≤720p and ≤30 fps already has the card's shape, and whether it also came out small enough
    is a question its own commit re-asks. `SOCIAL_MAX_BYTES = 0` turns the tier off whatever the shape.

    `SOCIAL_MAX_BYTES` keeps its name. Renaming a configuration variable breaks every `.env` in
    existence for a word, and the variable is documented under both names in DEPLOY §21 and §27.

    One consequence worth recording, because it is the only thing in this bundle that a Light copy was
    quietly protecting. **The card image is taken from the LIGHT copy whenever there is one** — the
    poster is cut from the last file the run produced, and Light is ≤1280×720 by construction — so with
    the tier ON a poster is never larger than that. With `SOCIAL_MAX_BYTES=0` the poster comes from the
    Full (or the upload) instead, so a 4K clip gets a 4K JPEG: ~8.3 MP and a megabyte or two, inside
    Discord's 8 MB / 20 MP limits but past X's 5 MB on a busy frame. That is the operator's trade for
    turning the tier off and is stated in DEPLOY §27; nothing else in the pipeline changes.

204. **`FULL_CODEC`.** `h264` (the default) or `av1`; anything else is fatal at boot. H.264 is the
    default because it is the only codec every browser, every Discord client and every embedded player
    decodes, and it encodes fast. AV1 (`libsvtav1 -preset 8 -crf 32 -svtav1-params tune=0`) roughly
    halves the one stored copy of an unplayable source for the same picture, encodes considerably
    slower, and wants decoder hardware from about 2019. It bounds nothing else: a playable original is
    never re-encoded, a trim's cut is H.264 (its copy path only ever copies H.264), and the card's
    Light copy is H.264 whatever this says.

    `libsvtav1` takes an INTEGER preset (0 slowest … 13 fastest), so `TRANSCODE_PRESET` — an x264 word
    — cannot be passed through and `transcode.FullAV1Preset` is used instead. The argv is otherwise the
    graph this package has always rendered, colour stamp included; `-profile:v high` is emitted for
    libx264 only (there is no profile worth stating for an 8-bit 4:2:0 AV1 stream).

205. **The tier states, and how they are reported.** `clips.full_state` and `clips.light_state` are
    one of `''` (unknown), `skipped`, `encoding`, `ready`, `failed`. They are COLUMNS and not a job
    lookup because `ClipDTO` is rendered from a clip row alone on six routes, and a per-tier job query
    on each would be six new queries for two words. `db.ReconcileTierState` settles a stored word
    against the OBJECT — the object wins when it exists, which is how a row migrated from before 0012
    reads correctly — and an unknown state reads as `skipped`, the honest answer to "is a better copy
    coming".

    `ClipDTO` gains `tiers: [{tier, url, width, height, fps, bytes, codec, playable, state}]` (ALWAYS
    present, never null, best first: original, full, light) and `card_tier`. `url` is null for a tier
    with no file, so a client is never handed an address that 404s. `playable` is true for every Full
    and Light by construction and is the probe's verdict for the Original, narrowed by
    `db.OriginalIsTheClip` — so a TRIMMED clip reports its Original present and not playable, which is
    the truth: the file is there, the owner can download it, and it is not what this clip plays.
    `urls` gains `light` and `original`; `urls.social` stays an alias of `light` (erratum 210). **This
    closes cleanup nit N079** ("no DTO says whether a clip has a social file"): the answer is a `light`
    entry whose state is `ready`.

    (`db.SetTierState` is no longer the only writer: since erratum 236 `failAttemptTx` writes the same
    column in the same transaction as a `social` or `full` job's own `failed`, so an ending with no
    worker to run an exit path — the automatic repair, the boot reconcile, `admin jobs unstick` — settles
    the tier as well; and since erratum 237 the workers' own settling writes go through the GUARDED
    `db.SettleTierEncoding` instead, which is also what closes the two endings that resolve a job as
    `done` without producing its file.)

    `GET /api/clips/{id}/progress` and `GET /api/clips/progress` both gain `tiers: [{tier, state}]`,
    built from `db.TierStatesOf` so erratum 116's promise — a batched poll and a single poll cannot
    answer differently — holds for the tiers too. `db.SetTierState` is the one write that records a
    terminal tier state for a job that ended without producing its tier (since erratum 237 the workers
    take its guarded sibling `db.SettleTierEncoding` for exactly that, and this one stays as the
    unguarded primitive); it refuses any tier or state it does not know and is a no-op on a tombstone,
    because it is a footnote on a job's ending and never a reason to fail one.

    `transcode.CheckTierOutput` replaces `CheckOutput` for the tiers: the same assertions minus the
    frame box (which since these tiers bounds the Light copy alone) plus EXACT expected dimensions,
    which is strictly stronger — a tier that came out at the wrong size is caught whether that size is
    inside the old box or not. `AllowOdd` is set by exactly one caller, the remux, because a `-c copy`
    inherits the frame it was handed and H.264 permits an odd cropped size.

    **Amended (M1 fix pass, 2026-09-08).** The state vocabulary gains a fifth word, **`pending`**, and
    the DTO's promise is "ALWAYS the same three entries" (the Go doc comment also claimed `[]` on a clip
    that is not ready yet; `ToDTO` never produced that, and API.md's table was the accurate half — the
    sentence is gone). A queued or processing clip has `''` in both columns — migration 0012's own
    header calls it "not decided yet" — and reporting that as `skipped` told a client that a Full the
    clip may be about to get was never coming, in the one state a client is most likely to be polling.
    `db.ReconcileClipTier` reports `pending` for exactly that case: no object, an unknown column, and a
    clip that is `queued` or `processing`. It is DERIVED and never stored (`db.SetTierState` still
    refuses it), a FAILED clip stays `skipped` because nothing is coming for it either, and both
    progress routes get it from the same function — erratum 116's promise, applied to the tiers.

206. **Card-first ordering: `ready` now means CARD-READY, and the Full is a job of its own.** The
    §5 state machine gains one rule and one kind.

    The transcode run produces the **card tier** and flips `ready` on it. Which tier that is comes
    straight out of the plan: the Light copy when one is planned, otherwise the Full (a ≤720p30
    unplayable source, where the Full IS the card's file), otherwise the playable Original. So a
    1440p60 upload no browser can play becomes ready in the time a 720p30 encode takes, with a card
    Discord will inline, instead of in the time a 1440p60 encode takes — and the faithful copy is
    queued by the very commit that flipped `ready` (`kind = 'full'`, `db.enqueueFullTx`), exactly as
    the notify and social jobs are. A clip cannot become ready without the work its better tier needs
    being durably queued.

    `db.SetFull` is the guarded commit: one UPDATE on a clip that is STILL `ready`, STILL on the same
    original (`source_etag`) and STILL untrimmed. The trim guard is not a refinement of the etag one —
    a trim re-derives from the SAME original, so the etag still matches, and the window it wrote is the
    only trace that the clip is no longer the whole of that file; publishing a whole-file Full over a
    trimmed clip would silently un-cut it. It writes `rendition_*`, the five measurements and
    `full_state`/`full_codec`, and NOTHING about the original: a Full landing later must not be able to
    overwrite the measurements of the file it was made from. A failure costs the clip nothing but
    quality — the Light copy goes on playing, `full_state` becomes `failed`, and the watch page says
    so. `db.FullMaxAttempts` is 3 (two more than a social job's) because this file is the only faithful
    copy of a source the browser cannot play.

    **Invariants that are unchanged, and were checked.** A `full` job runs on the MEDIA loop and takes
    a slot from the same `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY` semaphore, so a default install still runs one ffmpeg;
    it is REGISTERED in the run registry (ffmpeg, scratch, one PutFile — erratum 71's rule); it never
    writes `clips.state`, `clips.failure_reason` or either failure counter (§5); and a failed Light
    still costs a clip nothing, because the card route falls back to the playable tier.

    **DEVIATION from the brief.** The brief asked for Light and Full to run in PARALLEL at
    `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY ≥ 2`. They cannot, and must not: `worker.withRun` admits at most ONE
    registered run per clip id (erratum 32), because everything a run's exit path touches — its
    objects, `$SCRATCH_DIR/{id}`, the progress entry — is keyed by the CLIP and not by the attempt.
    Two runs of one clip is the wedge that invariant exists to prevent. What ships is strict ordering
    for one clip (the card's file first, always) and real parallelism ACROSS clips at concurrency ≥ 2,
    which is where a busy instance's throughput actually comes from.

    The `checkpoint` blob carries the tier decision and the Light copy's fields, because a
    finalize-only retry has no probe to re-derive them from. Recomputing them from a nil probe was a
    panic in the one code path the checkpoint exists for, found by `TestCheckpointFinalizeOnly`.

207. **`/api/clips/{id}/original` is anonymous-readable exactly when the upload IS the clip.** It is
    the URL the watch page streams for a directly playable upload, so it has to be, and the gate is
    `db.OriginalIsTheClip`: `original_playable` **AND NOT** `original_remuxed` **AND** no trim window
    **AND** `state = ready`. Each conjunct is a way for the upload to stop being the clip. REMUXED: the
    bytes a viewer plays are the faststart rewrite, which `/video.mp4` already serves anonymously, so
    nothing is gained by opening a second door onto the raw upload. TRIMMED: a cut clip is a WINDOW of
    the upload, and serving the whole file to a link-holder would hand out the footage the owner
    removed — the one thing a trim is for. NOT READY: a queued, processing or failed clip has published
    nothing, and its upload stays the owner's rescue copy exactly as before.

    The brief said "anonymous-readable ONLY when `original_playable`"; the three extra conjuncts are a
    deliberate narrowing, recorded here because the verifier will attack this gate.

    The route no longer carries `auth.RequireSession` — the answer depends on the ROW, which a
    middleware cannot see — so `serveMedia` writes all three refusals itself, in the same order and
    with the same codes that middleware wrote them: **401** for anonymous, **403 `token_not_allowed`**
    for a Bearer token (erratum 19: a capture credential never downloads), **403 `forbidden`** for
    another account's session. One behaviour does change: because the row is now read first, an
    anonymous request for an UNKNOWN id gets 404 where it used to get 401. That is the same
    information `GET /api/clips/{id}` already gives anonymously, and every other public route answers
    the same way.

    Presentation follows erratum 98: a public original is served INLINE (no `Content-Disposition`,
    `public, max-age=3600`, no `Vary`) because it is a player URL, and `?download=1` is what asks for
    the attachment — which is what the owner's "Download original" link now sends. An owner-only
    original keeps `private, max-age=3600`, the credential `Vary` and the attachment, unchanged.

    **Amended (M1 fix pass, 2026-09-08).** A publicly cacheable answer must never carry a CREDENTIAL.
    This route is a public player URL that still runs the credential resolver, and that resolver's
    once-a-minute sliding touch re-issues the session cookie on whatever response it happens to land on
    (`auth.Resolver.Middleware`) — so a `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600` answer with the credential
    `Vary` deliberately deleted could carry a `Set-Cookie`: one account's session, offered to a shared
    cache to hand to the next caller of the same URL, which is precisely what RFC 9111 §3.5 makes
    `public` the opt-in for. Most shared caches special-case `Set-Cookie` and would not store it;
    nothing in the RFC obliges them to, and this codebase's own rule — a response a cache must not
    reuse is `private` with the credential `Vary` — is not a thing to leave to a CDN's defaults.

    `serveObject` therefore answers `private, max-age=3600` + `Vary: Cookie, Authorization` for ANY
    response that is carrying a `Set-Cookie`, whatever the object and whichever route. The ANONYMOUS
    request — the one a CDN is there for, and the one this erratum was written about — carries no
    cookie and keeps `public, max-age=3600` with no `Vary`, so nothing it bought is given back.

208. **A trim is planned in the Full tier's box.** An owner shaving two seconds off a 1440p60 capture
    used to get a 720p60 clip back, because the trim planned in the instance box like every other
    encode. That is the silent downscale these tiers exist to remove, arriving through a different
    door. The cut is now planned with `transcode.FullPlanOptions` and verified against the plan with
    `CheckTierOutput` rather than against the box (a box check would fail every cut of a clip above
    1280×720 — exactly the clip this feature is for). A cut is the FULL tier whatever the upload was:
    `db.TrimTierFields` writes `full_state = ready`, `full_codec = h264` (the copy path only ever
    copies H.264), carries the ORIGINAL's own measurements through from the trim's re-probe, and sets
    `original_remuxed` back to false because the remux the cut replaces is one of the objects the same
    statement supersedes. Nothing blanks `original_playable`: it is still true of a file the trim did
    not touch, and a later trim back out to the whole original needs it again. The Original TIER stops
    being offered by the WINDOW, through `db.OriginalIsTheClip`.

    A trim's cut also becomes a stream-copy candidate far more often, for free: the copy rule requires
    `plan.W == p.CodedW && plan.FPS == p.FPS`, which the old 720p box refused for every clip above it.

209. **`StorageUsed` and the owner's "Stored" line count the card file.** `social_size` was missing
    from both sums, which was an understatement rather than a policy: that object has been real, under
    the clip's own prefix, since erratum 121, `admin orphans` has always counted it, and an operator
    comparing `STORAGE_BUDGET_BYTES` against a bucket total was short by every card file on the
    instance. Both sums now read source + rendition + poster + gif + social. The tiers make the
    correction matter more, because a remuxed original stores the upload twice (DEPLOY §27 prices each
    tier).

210. **`/light.mp4` is the LIGHT tier's canonical route; `/social.mp4` is kept and is what the cards
    point at.** Two paths, one handler, one object. The canonical name is what `tiers[]`, `urls.light`,
    the quality selector and the documentation use, because "social" named a destination and the tier
    is a QUALITY. `/social.mp4` keeps working and keeps being the URL in every card tag — every Discord
    message already posted and every crawler cache keys on it, and a tag that moved would re-fetch
    nothing while the old URL kept working anyway. The **§9.1 tag inventory is unchanged** (27 tags
    http / 28 https), by construction: not one tag was added, removed or repointed.

211. **The quality selector.** The owner's ask of 2026-09-08: an option to stream the Original, which
    means a quality selector — at least the source, the tier considered Full, and the shareable
    low-quality one.

    It is a server-rendered `<label>` + `<select>` in the watch page's PLAYER region, one `<option>`
    per tier that really has a FILE, best first and with the best one `selected` — so a browser with no
    JavaScript shows which tier it is playing and the `<video src>` is that tier's own URL (`/original`
    for a direct upload, `/video.mp4` for a remux or a Full, `/light.mp4` for the card copy).
    `app.js` turns the change event into a src swap that restores the position and the play state.
    Labels carry REAL NUMBERS — "Original 2560×1440 60fps · 38.0 MiB" — because "high/medium/low" tells
    a viewer nothing about a clip whose dimensions are printed on the same page; a fractional rate
    stays fractional ("29.97fps"). The viewer's choice is a tier NAME in `localStorage` and nowhere
    else: it is not a fact about the clip and never reaches the server.

    It is EVERY viewer's control and not the owner's — choosing what to stream is a viewer's decision —
    and it renders for a clip with more than one tier. A clip with one tier gets no control at all,
    because one tier is not a choice. A tier that is still coming gets ONE short line instead
    ("Full quality still encoding.", "Full quality could not be encoded."; since the light pass of
    2026-09-10 a FAILED Light copy gets "Card copy could not be made." for the OWNER alone — a viewer
    is told nothing, because `db.CardObject` falls back and nothing a viewer can see is missing), and a clip whose better
    tier is `encoding` is the ONE case where a READY clip carries a `data-progress-url`: `app.js`
    polls `…/progress` slowly (5 s, bounded at 20 minutes), and when no tier is `encoding` any more it
    re-reads the clip's DTO and rebuilds the `<select>` — without touching what the viewer is
    watching. The label formatter exists twice, in `internal/web/tiers.go` and in `app.js`, which is
    the one duplication this feature carries; the E2E pins the server's rendering, which is what a
    scriptless reader and a crawler see. Since errata 217 and 235 both tiers come out of ONE ffmpeg and
    publish at the ready flip, so the `full=encoding` this line reports is reached only off the ordinary
    upload path — a replacement, or the `FullNeeded` arm that fires when the flip produced no main file
    — and the `data-progress-url` poll is near-dormant with it. Both stay: both are still correct when
    reached.

    The EMBED page plays the best playable tier and carries no selector: an embedder chose the player
    (erratum 77), not the bitrate.

    **Amended (M1 fix pass, 2026-09-08).** The tier watch is bounded on both sides now.

    `GET /api/clips/{id}/progress` carries a rate limiter — `pollsPerMinute`, **120/min/IP**. It was the
    one progress route with none, which was defensible while only a QUEUED or PROCESSING clip polled it
    (such a clip is nobody's share link, so the traffic was the owner's own tab) and is not defensible
    now that a READY clip whose better tier is encoding is polled by every viewer holding the link:
    erratum 87's rule for an anonymous per-clip read applies to it exactly as it applies to
    `preview.gif` and to the batched sibling. It is its OWN bucket and not the `view` one that sibling
    shares, which is a product decision rather than a numeric one: the view bucket also counts VIEWS and
    serves preview GIFs, and a NAT'd household or office of viewers must not spend their view counts on
    polling. 120 is twice what one tab can issue at the fastest interval below.

    And the poll eases off: **5 s for the first minute, then 15 s**, with the ceiling unchanged at 20
    minutes (wall clock now, rather than a tick count). The first minute is when a viewer is still
    looking at the page; after it, a long Full costs a viewer a fifth of the requests.

212. **The capture link is handed over only when the CARD works, and a client can no longer switch
    that off.** The owner's decision of 2026-09-08: a link is given only when it is ready, and ready
    means ready for sharing, which means the Discord card is ready; and a user is not allowed to set
    up a breaking behaviour at all.

    `POST /api/upload` held its 201 until the clip reached a TERMINAL state (erratum 97). It now holds
    it until **`db.CardReady`**: `state = ready` **AND** a poster **AND** the object the card's
    `og:video` points at (`db.CardObject` — the LIGHT copy when there is one, else `db.PlayObject`,
    which is the `/social.mp4` route's own resolution asked as a predicate). Since erratum 206 `ready`
    already means card-ready, so the two extra conjuncts are the belt: a `ready` row with no poster or
    no playable bytes is the §12 invariant violation the media routes answer 503 for, and "the card is
    ready" is the one answer that must not be given for it.

    ONE predicate, THREE readers, deliberately — the capture reply, the crawler hold (erratum 213) and
    the watch page's line. Three answers to "is the card ready" is how they drift apart.

    **Amended by erratum 235**: the predicate gains a third conjunct, `light_state <> 'encoding'`. As
    written here it answered TRUE for a clip whose card copy was still being encoded, because
    `CardObject` falls back to `PlayObject` — the exact window erratum 235 closes.

    **`CAPTURE_READY_WAIT` rises from `8s` to `30s`**, because what it waits for changed: 8 s was sized
    for "the clip is playable" and the card's own file is a second encode behind that. The 60 s ceiling
    (`config.CaptureReadyWaitMax`) is unchanged, and at the ceiling the link is STILL RETURNED — a
    capture tool cannot be held for minutes — with `card_ready: false`.

    **The `wait` field is REMOVED**, and removed as a **400** rather than as a silently ignored field.
    `wait=0` bought a faster answer and a permanently link-out card for everybody who read that link,
    which is not a trade a client makes on an operator's behalf; and this route's grammar IGNORES
    unknown text fields, so dropping `wait` from the known set would have let a `.sxcu` carrying
    `wait=0` go on uploading while quietly getting the opposite of what it asked for. It stays in
    `captureField`'s list precisely so that it can be refused with a sentence naming
    `CAPTURE_READY_WAIT`. An EMPTY `wait=` is still "not sent", like every other capture field. The
    shipped `clippet.sxcu` never sent it, so nothing this project ships is affected.

    **Wire change.** `UploadDTO` gains `card_ready` (bool) and `tiers` (erratum 205's list, always
    three entries, best first). `state` is unchanged and is documented as the CLIP's state: a client
    that wants to know about the card reads `card_ready`, and a client that wants to know about the
    clip reads `state`. There is **no estimate** of the remaining time in the body, in a header or on
    the page — the owner's call: no estimated time, because an estimate is so often wrong.

    `POST /api/share` takes the same wait, for the same reason and one more: the browser is about to
    LAND on the share page.

213. **A link-preview crawler is HELD rather than told the wrong thing.** The owner's decision above has a
    twin: the reason the reply waits at all is that **Discord caches what it extracted, per URL,** and
    a link fetched a second too early stays a bare link for as long as that cache lives. The wait
    closes that window for the link the capture tool hands over. It does nothing for the link somebody
    pastes from the browser, or for a second fetch of a clip still encoding.

    So while `db.CardPending(clip)` — not card-ready, and not `failed` — a `GET /clips/{id}` whose
    `User-Agent` names a known link-preview crawler is answered **503 with `Retry-After: 30`,
    `Cache-Control: no-store`, and the outage page**, which carries not one `og:` tag. That is
    §9.1's own doctrine for a backend failure, applied for the identical reason it was written down:
    *"a backend failure must never render as 404 — Discord caches 'no embed' per URL"*. A crawler that
    honours `Retry-After` comes back to a real card; one that does not has cached nothing.

    The table is `web.linkPreviewCrawlers`: `discordbot`, `twitterbot`, `facebookexternalhit`,
    `slackbot`, `telegrambot`, matched as lower-cased SUBSTRINGS of the agent (every one of them
    appends a version and a URL, and two change that suffix between releases). It is a table and not a
    regexp so that the list is greppable and obviously the whole of the rule, and the DEFAULT is
    "human": a crawler missing from it gets today's behaviour, and a person never gets a 503.

    **Two clips are deliberately never held.** A READY one has its card. A **FAILED** one has the
    link-out card it will have for ever (§9.1), so holding it would withhold the only card it is ever
    going to get — that case is a regression guard, not a detail.

    The HUMAN gets the processing page unchanged, plus **one short line** in the player region:
    *"Encoding on the server — the Discord card is not ready yet."* The owner asked for exactly two things
    of it — say where the processing happens, and say it briefly (the existing tooltips were too verbose
    for what they were) — so it names
    the machine, names the consequence, and stops. No countdown, no percentage of its own, no estimate.
    It renders whenever `db.CardPending` holds and is empty for a failed clip, which has its own line.

214. **The LIGHT tag: the one amendment to "no watermarks".** The owner's decision of 2026-09-08: the
    low-quality copy carries a tag, so it is not taken for the product's best — clear yet unobtrusive.

    > **Amended by §20 erratum 287(b) (2026-09-15).** This erratum's card description — the owner's
    > words first, then the quality clause — keeps that ORDER, and gains two things in front of and
    > around it: the clip's length now leads the description, and the owner's half is clamped to a
    > 200-rune budget so the clause can no longer be the first thing Discord cuts off a wordy clip.
    > The burned-in tag itself, and everything this erratum says about which artefact carries it, is
    > unchanged — the poster's new duration label (287(e)) is not a watermark and is not it.

    The hard constraint (medal-feature-research.md: no watermarks on anything the site plays or the
    user downloads) STANDS, and this is the single artefact it is amended for: the **Light copy**, which
    is the file a crawler fetches and — once a better tier exists — the file nobody watches on the site.
    Not the Original, not the Full, not a poster, not a preview GIF, and not anything a viewer
    downloads or the player plays. The reason is what a card IS: a reader watching a 720p30 copy of a
    1440p60 capture inside Discord with no way to know the difference, concluding that this is a 720p
    product.

    One `drawtext` link at the END of the Light copy's video chain: bottom-right, `fontsize` =
    round(2.2 % of the frame height) with a 12 px floor, `white@0.55` over a one-pixel `black@0.45`
    shadow, inset 1.5 % of the height. Bottom-RIGHT because bottom-left is where a phone's recording
    indicator and most games' killfeeds live.

    `LIGHT_TAG_TEXT` (§4) is the template: `{light}` is the card copy's own quality and `{best}` the
    quality the link leads to, both from `transcode.QualityShort` — the SHORT side of the picture, a
    `p`, and the rate ("720p30", "1440p60", "1080p29.97"; a fractional rate stays fractional, because
    rounding 29.97 to 30 would be the card lying about the very number it exists to state). A template
    that asks for a quality nobody measured renders **nothing at all** rather than a sentence with a
    hole in it: the line is burned into the picture, so a gap is permanent.

    **How the tag is turned OFF, spelled once here**, because there are two plausible spellings and
    only one of them works: `LIGHT_TAG_TEXT=off`. An **EMPTY** value is the DEFAULT template and not
    "off" — `config.Load` reads the environment through one `getenv` and cannot tell a variable nobody
    set from one set to nothing, and compose's `${LIGHT_TAG_TEXT:-…}` collapses the two before the
    process ever sees them, so reading empty as "off" would leave the shipped `compose.yaml` unable to
    express the default at all. §4's table, `.env.example` and DEPLOY §21/§24/§27 all say `off`; this is
    the sentence they say it from.

    Three implementation facts, each of which cost something to learn:

    (a) The text reaches ffmpeg through a **file** (`textfile=`), never the argv. It is
    operator-supplied, and `drawtext`'s `text=` value passes through two levels of filtergraph
    escaping in which a colon, a comma, a bracket, a backslash and a `%` each mean something to a
    different level. `expansion=none` is set for the same reason: a `%{…}` in an operator's line is
    text.

    (b) A filter option VALUE is **quoted**, not escaped. Measured on ffmpeg 7.1: a `fontfile` carrying
    a colon fails to parse when the colon is backslash-escaped ("No option name near '/Windows/…'")
    and parses and draws when the whole value is single-quoted. **Amended by erratum 312 (2026-10-04):** wrong
    for a Windows path — the quotes are stripped before the option level splits on `:`, so a drive letter
    needs its colon escaped INSIDE the quotes too; the value is now escaped for both levels.

    (c) A missing font or a build without `drawtext` is a **WARNING** and the tag goes off (erratum
    216's boot check). The line is cosmetic; an encode is not, and a font nobody shipped must not fail
    every clip that wants a card copy. The image installs `font-dejavu` / `fonts-dejavu-core` and the
    font is **DejaVu Sans** under the DejaVu Fonts License (a Bitstream Vera derivative: free to use,
    redistribute and modify, no attribution in the rendered output). No font file is vendored — there
    is still no `LICENSE` in this repository and nothing here needs one; DEPLOY §27 records it.

    **PROVEN by pixels**, not by argv: `TestLightTagIsBurnedIntoTheCorner` encodes one black 1280×720
    source twice, with and without the tag, and measures each corner's mean luminance through ffmpeg's
    own `signalstats`. Bottom-right +6.60 YAVG; the other three corners +0.000. The "not a poster" half
    of the paragraph above needed a fix of its own — the card image used to be cut from this very file;
    erratum **219** says how it is cut now.

    **The card's DESCRIPTION states both qualities too.** When a Light copy serves the card,
    `og:description` / `twitter:description` / `description` carry `Preview 720p30 · Original 1440p60
    at this link`, after the clip's own description when it has one and in place of the §9.1 default
    when it does not (the numbers say more than "Shared with Clippet"). The second word is the TIER the
    link leads to, in the quality selector's own vocabulary — "Original" for an upload this clip
    streams, "Full" otherwise. Nothing is said when the card plays the clip's own file, when the card
    copy has the same shape as the clip (it got one for its SIZE alone), or when the row was never
    measured. **The §9.1 tag inventory is unchanged** (27 http / 28 https): these are values.

215. **`-threads` is pinned to the container's CPU quota, and the ffmpeg thread count is no longer
    ffmpeg's guess.** `nproc` inside a container reports every core the HOST has, whatever `cpus:`
    says, because a CFS quota is a share of time and not a cpuset — and nothing in `/proc` changes when
    the quota does. So on the shipped `cpus: 1.0` on a sixteen-core host, x264 sized its frame-thread
    pool for sixteen cores and was then throttled to one.

    **MEASURED** (2026-09-08 investigation, this host, the app's own ffmpeg and argv, three samples —
    150 s 720p60 12.2 Mbps, 60 s 1080p60 20.2 Mbps, 30 s 1440p60 30.3 Mbps): pinning `-threads` to the
    quota is **−25 %** on the first sample at 1 cpu (main 173.3 s → 128.6, Light 98.6 → 74.2), −13/−16 %
    on the other two, −5 to −11 % at 4–8 cpus, and the output is 2–5 % **smaller**. One regression: a
    source already at the output size, at 8 cpus, is 18–20 % SLOWER pinned, because frame threading is
    the only parallelism a no-op scale leaves x264. That is why the quota is used as the number and
    `TRANSCODE_THREADS` exists to override it.

    `transcode.ResolveThreads` reads cgroup v2's `cpu.max` first (Docker Desktop's WSL2 kernel and
    every current distro), then v1's `cpu.cfs_quota_us`/`cpu.cfs_period_us` under `cpu/` and at the
    root, rounds UP (half a core is one thread), and is bounded by `runtime.NumCPU()`. "max"/-1 mean no
    quota, which is not a failure to read but the honest answer that the core count is the bound. The
    boot line prints the resolved number. `-filter_threads` and `-filter_complex_threads` carry it too.

    Two settings the same investigation says NOT to change, recorded so nobody re-measures them.
    **`APP_CPUS` stays `1.0`** in `compose.yaml`: a `cpus` above the host's core count is a hard CREATE
    error, so raising the shipped default would refuse to start on every 1- and 2-vCPU VPS. What DEPLOY
    §27 gains instead is the curve — 4 cpus is 3.9–4.0×, 8 is another 1.9×, 12 buys 10–20 %, 16 nothing
    — and the sentence telling a home-server operator to set it. **`TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY` stays `1`**:
    past about `APP_CPUS/8` it trades latency for throughput, which is the wrong trade for a share link.
    Peak RSS measured 0.61 GiB worst case, set by the SOURCE's resolution rather than the output's, so
    DEPLOY §7's "~520 MiB, budget ~0.5 GiB/slot" is right in shape and 0.61 is the honest number.

    And **`TRANSCODE_PRESET` stays `veryfast`** for the Light copy: `superfast` is 13–21 % faster and
    `ultrafast` 24–44 %, at +81 % bytes on the worst-case sample *at the same VBV ceiling*, and on clean
    content `ultrafast` needs 2.5× the bytes for +3.5 VMAF and lands at 2.68 Mbps — over the card's own
    ceiling, which is the failure erratum 121's ceiling exists to prevent.

216. **The GPU flavour: `TRANSCODE_HWACCEL=cuda`, opt-in, a second image, and a fast path with a CPU
    fallback rather than a replacement.**

    **MEASURED**: a full CUDA path — `-hwaccel cuda -hwaccel_output_format cuda`, `scale_cuda`,
    `h264_nvenc` — is **9–11× libx264 at ONE cpu** and nearly core-count independent, so a 1-vCPU box
    with a card beats a sixteen-core box without one. Swapping only the ENCODER (CPU decode, CPU scale,
    NVENC) is 1.4–3.6× and is not worth an image: the decode and the lanczos are ~82 % of that
    pipeline.

    Two facts make it a config value the PLAN reads rather than a build flag. The app's own static
    ffmpeg (`mwader/static-ffmpeg:7.1.1`) lists **zero** nvenc encoders, so the ordinary image cannot
    use it however it is asked. And a CUDA graph cannot render most of this pipeline's filter chain:
    `yadif`, `zscale`/`tonemap`, `transpose` and `setsar` are CPU filters (and `setparams` too), so the
    interlaced, HDR, tag-rotated and anamorphic sources errata 93/125/200 exist for MUST fall back.
    `transcode.HWAccelFor` is that decision, it returns the REASON when it refuses, and the worker logs
    the pair on its per-clip `planned` line so an operator can see which argv ran and why. `Plan`
    gains one field for it, `Anamorphic`, which changes no CPU argv (`setsar=1` was always emitted).

    `FULL_CODEC=av1` also stays on the CPU: `av1_nvenc` is the fastest encoder on the card and no card
    platform plays AV1, so the investigation's verdict was "do not build" and it is not built. A
    two-output encode (erratum 217) whose tiers disagree about the accelerator renders the CPU argv for
    BOTH, because one decode cannot be on the card for one output and off it for the other.

    **The trap that cost the investigation an afternoon, recorded so it cannot be re-introduced:
    `-colorspace bt709` on the output cannot survive a CUDA graph.** It is the one of the three colour
    options ffmpeg 7 honours, so it forces buffersink colorspace negotiation, ffmpeg inserts a CPU
    `auto_scale` the CUDA frames cannot reach, and the run dies with exit 218 and a zero-byte file. The
    CUDA argv therefore writes the Rec.709 stamp with the **`h264_metadata` bitstream filter**
    (`colour_primaries=1:transfer_characteristics=1:matrix_coefficients=1` — BT.709's own code points),
    which touches no pixel; the output probes `bt709` exactly as the CPU one does. VERIFIED on this
    host's ffmpeg.

    **The tag on the CUDA path.** `drawtext` is CPU-only too, so a tagged Light branch adds
    `hwdownload,format=yuv420p` after the scale and the encoder uploads again — the hardware decode and
    scale, which is where the 9–11× came from, are still what they were. VERIFIED end to end on this
    host: 1280×720@30, 11.37 MB, `bt709` on all three colour fields.

    **`cq` calibration, per tier, MEASURED on this host's ffmpeg against the 60 s 1080p60 sample.**
    NVENC's quantizer is not x264's — at the same number it writes 1.8–4× the bytes — and the offset is
    not one number either:

    | tier | x264 | bytes | NVENC | bytes | Δ |
    |---|---|---|---|---|---|
    | **Full** | CRF 18 | 238.7 MB | `-cq 18` | 299.9 MB | +25.6 % |
    | | | | `-cq 20` | 294.3 MB | +23.3 % |
    | | | | **`-cq 22`** | 232.9 MB | **−2.4 %** ✓ |
    | | | | `-cq 24` | 183.0 MB | −23.3 % |
    | | | | `-cq 26` | 141.8 MB | −40.6 % |
    | **Light** | CRF 26 | 10.06 MB | `-cq 26` | 18.84 MB | +87.4 % |
    | | | | `-cq 30` | 18.29 MB | +81.8 % |
    | | | | `-cq 32` | 14.64 MB | +45.6 % |
    | | | | **`-cq 34`** | 11.38 MB | **+13.2 %** ✓ |

    So `NVENCCQOffsetFull = 4` and `NVENCCQOffsetLight = 8`, each the value landing inside the ±15 % the
    brief asked for; an encode that names no tier (a trim at `TRANSCODE_CRF`) gets `6`.

    The image is the Dockerfile's **`gpu` target**, and it is placed BEFORE the ordinary stage so a
    build with no `--target` never resolves the CUDA bases. One correction to the investigation's own
    recipe, and it fails loudly: that ffmpeg is **dynamically linked** against `/usr/local/lib`, so
    copying the two executables alone produced an image whose ffmpeg exits 127 on every invocation
    ("error while loading shared libraries: libavdevice.so.61"). The stage copies `/usr/local/lib` and
    runs `ldconfig`. `compose.yaml`'s `app-gpu` is the `app` service under `extends` with three changes
    — the `gpu` build target, `gpus: all`, its own tag — in the **`gpu` profile**, so an operator
    without a card resolves nothing and pulls nothing. It is `gpus: all` and **not**
    `deploy.resources.reservations.devices`, which is Swarm-only and `docker compose up` ignores
    silently.

    **Three settings now have a BOOT CHECK** (`cmd/clippet/ffcaps.go`), against `ffmpeg -encoders` and
    `-filters` read once: `FULL_CODEC=av1` without `libsvtav1` and `TRANSCODE_HWACCEL=cuda` without
    `h264_nvenc`+`scale_cuda` are **fatal**, because otherwise every encode of an unplayable source
    fails one clip at a time with a reason nobody reads; `LIGHT_TAG_TEXT` without `drawtext` or without
    a font is a **WARN** that switches the tag off. A listing that cannot be read at all is a WARN and
    the checks are skipped: refusing to boot over an unreadable `-encoders` would be worse than the
    failure it guards.

    **VERIFIED here**: the `gpu` image builds, lists `h264_nvenc`/`hevc_nvenc`/`av1_nvenc`,
    `scale_cuda`, `hwdownload` and `drawtext`, ships DejaVu, and boots with `hwaccel=cuda
    light_tag=true`; the ordinary image refuses `cuda` at boot with the sentence above; the CPU
    fallback renders byte-for-byte the argv this package always rendered. **NOT verified live**: an
    actual NVENC run inside a container. `nvidia-smi` works there (RTX 5090, driver 616.64) and
    `libnvcuvid.so.1` does not load — the stale WSL driver-library state after a Windows driver update,
    cured by a Docker Desktop restart, which could not be done with three lane stacks running. The
    numbers above are therefore HOST-ffmpeg numbers with the app's own argv, and the live container
    proof is pending that restart. **Superseded on this point by erratum 247 (2026-09-10): the proof
    ran; the cause was the missing `video` driver capability, not the driver update; and the `app-gpu`
    profile service became the `compose.gpu.yaml` override.**

217. **The FULL tier and the LIGHT copy come out of ONE ffmpeg, which supersedes erratum 206's
    ordering for the case where both are wanted.**

    **MEASURED**, and every alternative is worse. Two processes at once — the obvious "publish the card
    copy first" implementation — is worse than serial: both decode the same source, and the first file
    appears **2.2× later** than it would encoded alone (720p60 at 8 cpus: Light alone 12.3 s, in
    parallel 26.9 s; the pair finishes no sooner than back to back). One process with `split`/`asplit`
    into two encoders costs **1.05–1.42× the Full alone** instead of 1.6–1.9×, and the two files are
    byte-identical to the separate runs. Chunked parallel x264 is −9 % at four chunks, +12 % at eight,
    and a fresh rate-control ramp at every seam: not built.

    So `produce()`'s `FullNeeded && LightNeeded` branch runs `EncodeTiers`: one decode, the CPU-only
    head (deinterlace, tone map, pre-rotate) once, a `split`, each tier's own scale — the Full's scale
    factor is exactly 1, so the expensive lanczos is paid once for real — and each tier's own encoder
    settings, rendered by the same `outputArgs` a single-output encode uses. `TestSingleEncodeArgvUnchanged`
    pins that the ordinary encode's argv is byte-for-byte what it was.

    **What this changes, stated plainly, because two of the three are costs.**

    (a) The clip becomes `ready` with BOTH files in the bucket. `ready` now means card-ready AND
    best-quality: nothing ever serves the 720p30 card copy as a clip's own playable bytes, which closed
    a window the owner's own complaint is about (a 720p clip places the product in exactly the market it
    is trying not to be in) — during erratum 206's card-first window `db.PlayObject` fell back to the
    Light copy for every viewer who opened the link early.

    (a′) **Amended by erratum 235**: this promise holds only for clips the PLAN routes into this branch,
    and until 235 the plan had no size for the Full, so a card-shaped source whose Full turned out to be
    over `SOCIAL_MAX_BYTES` took the single-encode branch instead and became `ready` with the card copy
    merely QUEUED. 235 gives the plan `transcode.PlannedOutputBytes(t.Full)`, so those clips come here
    too and "both files at the flip" is the whole of the rule rather than most of it.

    (b) The ready flip waits for the FAITHFUL encode rather than the quick one. On the report's samples
    at 1 cpu the card's file therefore arrives later for an unplayable source — 1440p60: ~37 s → ~51 s;
    1080p60: ~57 s → ~98 s — while the TOTAL falls (~79 s → ~51 s and ~126 s → ~98 s). The COMMON
    capture path is untouched: a playable mp4 needs no Full, so a remux plus the card copy is exactly
    what it always was, and that is the path `CAPTURE_READY_WAIT` is sized for.

    (c) A permanent encoder failure now fails the CLIP rather than costing it only its better tier. One
    process writes both files, so there is no "the Light survived" outcome to keep — erratum 206's *"a
    failure costs the clip nothing but quality"* was what paying for the decode twice was buying. The
    recovery is every other upload's: `TRANSCODE_MAX_ATTEMPTS`, then the owner's retry.

    `replace.go` takes the same branch, for the same reason: a replacement of an unplayable file is the
    same encode with somebody else's clip id on it, and card-first ordering there would downgrade a
    clip people already hold the link to. The **`full` job KIND is retained** (`db.EnqueueFull`,
    `worker/full.go`, `db.SetFull` and their tests) and is no longer enqueued by either producer — the
    same shape erratum 121's `social` job kind has for the trim/replace paths. Nothing was deleted:
    this is a parallel run, and removing a sibling bundle's just-verified code would be a merge hazard
    for no gain.

    **MEASURED time-to-shareable on THIS lane's stack**, at compose's default `cpus: 1.0`, with two
    other lanes encoding at the same time — so these are loaded-host numbers, not best cases. Every one
    is a line the E2E prints on a green run (steps 62–64 and 67–69):

    | upload | what runs | time to a link whose card works |
    |---|---|---|
    | 6 s 720p30 mp4, `moov` first (2.2 MB) | probe + poster, no encoder | **1–2 s** |
    | 6 s playable mp4 carrying phone metadata | a `-c copy` remux | **2 s** |
    | 6 s 720p30 HEVC (card-shaped, unplayable) | ONE Full encode, which IS the card file | **4 s** |
    | 6 s 1080p60 mp4 via `POST /api/upload` | remux + the card's copy | **4 s**, `card_ready: true` |
    | 5 s 1080p60 (the tag fixture) | remux + the card's copy | **2 s** |
    | 24 s 1080p60 matroska (BOTH tiers, one decode) | one ffmpeg, Full + card copy | **14–30 s**, both files at the flip |

    The last row is the one this erratum changed, and the only honest "before" for it is a ratio rather
    than a number: the report measured the card's copy alone at 0.57–0.86× the main encode and the
    two-output pass at 1.05–1.42× it, so on that fixture the card previously arrived at roughly
    two-thirds of these seconds and the faithful copy roughly one and a half times later again. What the
    E2E can state as a FACT is the other half — the ready flip now carries both files, and no `full` job
    is queued behind it at all.

    The report's own projection for real captures at 1 cpu is what an operator should plan against: a
    150 s 720p60 in-box upload is ~1 s to a shareable link (the remux fast path, erratum 200); a 60 s
    1080p60 or a 30 s 1440p60 that no browser plays is the Full encode — ~70 s and ~43 s with `-threads`
    pinned, ~18 s and ~11 s at `APP_CPUS=4`, and ~10 s and ~7 s on the GPU image.

218. **What this bundle CHECKED and deliberately did not change.** Three of the perf investigation's
    recommendations were re-examined against what is already here and are recorded as decisions rather
    than as code, so nobody re-opens them from the report alone.

    (a) **The playability verdict is NOT `DecideTrim`'s condition set verbatim, and must not be.** The
    report's remux-first recommendation said to reuse it "verbatim — it is already this project's answer
    to 'is a copy indistinguishable from the encode'", and erratum 200 says the verdict uses
    "deliberately the same predicates". Both are true of the SHARED predicates —
    `isMP4Container`, `isHDRTransfer`, `IsInterlacedFieldOrder`, the audio shape, the square-pixel test,
    the declared duration — and `OriginalPlayability` is deliberately WIDER on exactly three rows,
    because it answers a different question ("can every browser play these bytes") from the one
    `DecideTrim` answers ("would a stream copy of a cut be the file this pipeline would have rendered"):

    | row | `DecideTrim` | `OriginalPlayability` | why the difference is right |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | video codec | `h264` only | `h264` **or `av1`** | every current browser decodes AV1 from an mp4, and a source already in AV1 is the one nobody wants re-encoded (erratum 200). A trim cannot copy it because this pipeline's own cut is H.264. |
    | pixel format | `yuv420p` | + `yuvj420p` | the same samples with a full-range flag, which capture hardware really writes. A trim's copy would carry that flag into a file the pipeline promises is limited-range. |
    | rotation | ANY non-zero | only a legacy `rotate` TAG | ffmpeg and every browser autorotate from the Display Matrix, so such a file plays right side up as it stands; a `-c copy` CUT keeps the matrix but the pipeline's rendition has the turn baked in, so the two would disagree. |

    Narrowing the verdict to `DecideTrim`'s would re-encode every AV1 upload and every phone capture with
    a rotation matrix — precisely the clips erratum 200 exists to stop re-encoding — so the divergence
    stays and this is the record of it.

    (b) **A 854×480 "preview" tier as the card gate is NOT built.** The report measured it 2.0–3.5×
    faster than the main encode and sitting exactly on the decode floor, which is real; it is refused on
    brand grounds. The owner's objection of 2026-09-08 — people would see a 720p clip and place the product
    in exactly the market it is trying not to be in — was said about 720p, so 480p is further the wrong way. The card tier stays Light
    (720p30, 2.5 Mbps), and time-to-shareable for a source that needs an encode is that encode.

    (c) **The original's `PutFile` stays on the request path.** The report measured it free on the
    bundled MinIO (0.28–0.35 s for 228 MB) and **18 s at 100 Mbps / 90 s at 20 Mbps of dead time in
    front of every encode** on a remote bucket, and suggested overlapping it with the encode. It is not
    a contained change: `ingest()` currently answers 201 only after the upload is DURABLE, and every
    failure path from there — the 503 with cleanup, the spool the worker then reads, `source_etag` as
    the predicate half of every derived-artefact commit — is written around that ordering. Overlapping
    it means a clip that exists before its bytes do, and a new failure mode (the PUT fails after the 201)
    with no owner-facing answer. Deferred deliberately, with the measurement recorded here so the next
    pass starts from the number rather than from the idea.

219. **The card IMAGE is cut from an UNTAGGED frame, and only borrows the card copy's size.** Erratum
    214 says the tag goes on the Light copy and on nothing else — *"not the Original, not the Full, not a
    poster, not a preview GIF, and not anything a viewer downloads or the player plays"*. As this bundle
    first shipped, that sentence was false about the poster, and this erratum is the fix and the record.

    **What was wrong.** Erratum 206 had moved the poster's SOURCE onto the Light copy, for a good reason
    that survives: a still cut from a 1440p or 4K frame is a card image no crawler inlines, and the card
    copy was the one file already at the card's size. Then erratum 214 burned a line into that same file,
    and the poster — cut from it by the very next stage of the same run — inherited the line. Measured on
    lane 4's stack: a black 1080p60 upload's `poster.jpg`, YAVG of the bottom-right 420×40 corner
    **8.29** against **0.00** bottom-left; brightened, that corner reads `720p30 preview · 1080p60 on
    Clippet`. A poster is exactly what the amendment does not cover — it is `og:image`, it is
    `poster="…"` on the watch page's and the embed's own `<video>`, it is the frame Discord's inline
    player shows before play, and it is an anonymous JPEG anybody can download.

    **The fix.** `posterSrc` stays on the untagged file the run had already chosen — the Full, the
    remuxed original, or the upload itself — and what the Light copy lends the poster is its SIZE, as
    `transcode.PosterBox`: one `scale=W:H:flags=lanczos` link at the end of both candidate passes
    (`PosterArgs`, and last in `PosterThumbArgs`' chain, so frames are still SCORED at the size they
    were decoded at and only the chosen one is resized). W and H are the Light plan's own, so the card
    image is geometrically the card copy's frame.

    A plain `scale`, not a fit-inside expression: W and H were computed from this source's DISPLAY
    dimensions by the same `MakePlan` call, so they already carry its aspect ratio, and the frame this
    pass reads can never arrive with a non-square pixel aspect (`NotPlayableAnamorphic` sends such an
    upload down the Full path, whose output is `setsar=1`). The zero box is "no scaling", which is what
    every other caller passes: a trim writes the file `/video.mp4` serves, and an owner's chosen frame
    (`PosterAt`) is taken from that same file — neither carries a tag, so neither needs a box.

    Two producers are affected, the two that can make a card copy and a poster in one run: the transcode
    pipeline and a replacement. The GIF job and the post-hoc poster job read `db.PlayObject` and never
    the card copy, so neither was ever tagged.

    **Proven three ways**, because a poster with a line burned into it is otherwise perfectly correct —
    right frame, right dimensions — and nothing else would notice:
    `transcode.TestThePosterIsCutFromAnUntaggedFrame` cuts a poster both ways from one black 1080p
    source and measures the corner (untagged source: bottom-right **1.000** = bottom-left **1.000**;
    the tagged copy, as a control: **8.060**) and asserts the box held at 1280×720;
    `worker.TestTheCardImageIsNeverCutFromTheTaggedCopy` asserts WHICH file and WHICH box per source
    shape (both tiers → the Full at the card's box; a playable upload with a card copy → the upload at
    the card's box; no card copy → the Full at no box); and E2E step 69 downloads the live `poster.jpg`,
    measures the same two corners and checks its dimensions against the card copy's.

    The cost is one decode of a bigger file: the poster's three-candidate ladder now reads the Full or
    the original rather than the 720p copy. It is the pre-erratum-206 cost, seconds at most, and it buys
    a card image the constraint's amendment actually covers.

220. **The trim scrubber's FILMSTRIP: a new `filmstrip` media job kind, migration 0014, and one
    public route** (`internal/transcode/filmstrip.go`, `internal/worker/filmstrip.go`,
    `internal/db/filmstrip.go`, `internal/httpapi/filmstrip.go`; ROADMAP #6's open half; the owner's
    first look, 2026-09-08: the trim scrubber should sit closer to or inside the video player, and a
    thumbnail scrubber might be enough on its own; the build was approved).
    A filmstrip is ONE JPEG holding ~24 thumbnails of the clip's CURRENT rendition, evenly spaced
    across the whole of it, laid out in a **single row**. The scrubber draws it along the track and
    puts the tile of a handle's own moment above that handle, so dragging shows the frame instead of
    a number.
    **Why one sprite sheet and not N objects.** A scrubber wants every tile at once — a handle can be
    anywhere on the track a millisecond after the page loads — and 24 requests for 24 eight-kilobyte
    images is 24 round trips, 24 cache entries and 24 access-log lines against one object a browser
    fetches once and positions with an offset. One object is also one KEY, which is what lets the
    clip delete, `admin orphans` and the trim's supersede list cover it without learning a new place
    to look. A single row rather than a grid costs the client one coordinate instead of two, and the
    widest sheet this produces (24 × 160 px) is an ordinary 3840-pixel JPEG.
    **It is the preview GIF's twin in every structural respect** (§17 #6, erratum 73+), deliberately:
    same kind of artefact, same three rules. It reads the RENDITION and never the original (the tiles
    a scrubber shows must be frames the player can seek to, and after a cut the original holds
    footage the rendition does not); it writes its own seven columns and nothing else, with the clip
    `ready` before, during and after; and its commit is guarded by the rendition's ETag, so a trim
    that lands mid-run makes the swap a no-op and the attempt deletes its own object — a stale
    filmstrip is worse than none, because its tiles would sit under handles naming moments it does
    not show and nothing downstream could tell. It is REGISTERED in the run registry (erratum 71) and
    holds one of the `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY` ffmpeg slots (erratum 79): its pass DECODES a whole
    rendition, which is exactly the work that limit exists to bound.
    **The pass.** One ffmpeg run: `fps=1000/{interval_ms},scale={tileW}:-2:flags=lanczos,tile={N}x1`
    with `-frames:v 1 -update 1 -q:v 5 -f image2`. The sampling rate is written as a RATIONAL
    (tiles per interval) rather than as a decimal, so the times ffmpeg picks are exactly
    i × interval with no rounding of ours in front of it. `tile` pads an incomplete last sheet with
    its default colour, which is why a rendition whose picture stops before its container does still
    yields a sheet of the planned width rather than nothing at all. There is deliberately no
    `-skip_frame nokey`: a keyframe-only decode puts the same picture in several tiles of a short
    clip, which is a worse filmstrip than a slower one. The bound is `FilmstripHardTimeout` (180 s)
    and there is no stall watchdog and no progress, for `CopyTrim`'s and the poster's reason — the
    pass emits ONE output frame, so there is nothing to watch tick. A clip so long that the decode
    exceeds the timeout fails the job permanently and the scrubber keeps its plain track (DEPLOY §22).
    **The plan** (`PlanFilmstrip`, pure and table-tested): 24 tiles of 160 px, spaced
    `duration/tiles` apart, with two rules — the LAST tile always lies inside the clip, and no two
    tiles are closer than 100 ms (a clip too short for 24 of them gets proportionally fewer rather
    than the same picture repeated). A rendition narrower than 160 px keeps its own width; a filmstrip
    is never upscaled.
    **Every number is MEASURED from the produced JPEG**, never copied from the plan — poster_width /
    poster_height's reason (erratum 92) one artefact along: the client positions tiles from these
    numbers, and a sheet placed by a plan the encoder did not follow would show the wrong frame under
    the handle. The verify step is therefore part of the same call, and a width that is not exactly
    `tiles × tileW` is a permanent `bad_output` — our own output, which cannot be wrong by design
    (§12).
    **Migration 0014** adds seven additive nullable columns to `clips`: `filmstrip_key`,
    `filmstrip_size`, `filmstrip_etag`, `filmstrip_tiles`, `filmstrip_tile_w`, `filmstrip_tile_h`,
    `filmstrip_interval_ms`. All seven are NULL together (one UPDATE writes them), and NULL means
    "nobody has asked for a sheet since the last cut". The key layout gains
    `{P}clips/{id}/filmstrip/strip-{r8}.jpg` (§6) — its own directory rather than `renditions/` or
    `poster/`, because it is neither a rendition nor the picture a card shows, and a name that says so
    is what stops the next reader of `admin ls` from mistaking a 3840-pixel JPEG for the card image.
    `db.KeysOf`/`ListAllClipIDsAndKeys` list it (so `admin orphans` never reports a live sheet as
    unreferenced — the trap social_key fell into), `StorageUsed` and `AccountStats` count its bytes,
    `admin ls --stat` prints its geometry, `admin jobs`/`admin stats` know the eighth kind, and
    `SwapRendition`/`SwapSource` NULL the columns and list the key as superseded exactly as they
    already do for `gif_*`.
    **The route** is `GET`/`HEAD /api/clips/{id}/filmstrip.jpg`, and it is `preview.gif` with the
    owner POST removed — **amended by erratum 227**, which keeps every word of this paragraph for the
    SERVING of a sheet and makes the MAKING of one the owner's: **public** like `poster.jpg` (the link
    is the auth, and thumbnails of a clip
    the caller may already watch frame by frame leak nothing), 200 through the same `serveObject` as
    every other media route, **202** `{"state":"queued"|"running"}` + `Retry-After: 5` when the clip
    is `ready` and has no sheet (and a `filmstrip` job is enqueued iff none is live), 409 `not_ready`,
    503 `filmstrip_failed` when the latest job failed (reported, never retried: the route would
    otherwise re-run a doomed pass for every visitor), 404 for an unknown or `deleting` clip, 416,
    429. It carries the `view` limiter for `preview.gif`'s reason exactly — anyone holding the link
    may ask for a sheet, and nobody may walk the id space queueing them — and the one-live-job guard
    in `db.EnqueueFilmstrip` is what makes "it may start work" safe at all.
    **There is no owner POST beside it**, and that is the one place this route is smaller than the
    GIF's pair. A GIF is an artefact a person asks for, keeps and downloads, so "make it again" is a
    decision somebody takes; a filmstrip is a tool the trim control needs whenever it is on screen,
    and it is invalidated by exactly the events that invalidate the rendition — with one DEAD
    exception, recorded here rather than fixed: `db.SetFull` swaps `rendition_key` without touching
    any `filmstrip_*` column, which is harmless (the Full tier is the same footage at a higher
    fidelity, so the tiles still name the moments they show) and sits on a path erratum 217 leaves
    with no producer at all. Clearing the columns there would be a live-object delete on a path with
    no reaper behind it, which is the larger of the two wrongs. The GET's own
    202-and-enqueue therefore covers every case a POST could: after a cut the next owner to open the
    control asks for a sheet, does not find one, and one is made.
    **The DTO** gains `filmstrip: {url, tiles, tile_width, tile_height, interval_ms} | null`. It is an
    OBJECT and not a URL for the reason `gif_url` is a URL and not an entry in `urls`, one step
