    further on: the address alone is useless to a client, which cannot place a single tile without
    knowing how many there are, how wide one is and how much clip time it covers. So the fact and the
    geometry travel together, and null is how "no sheet for this rendition — ask the route and it will
    make one" is spelled (for the OWNER's client, since erratum 227). It is NOT owner-private: a sheet
    that exists is served to anybody, and the geometry says nothing the video does not.
    **The client** (`app.js`, inside `setupTrim`) reads the geometry the PAGE shipped and paints
    immediately when a sheet already exists — no request, no poll, which is every visit after the
    first. Only a clip with no sheet asks the route (a HEAD, which both enqueues and polls), and one
    GET of the clip DTO then settles the layout. The strip is a plain `<img>` in a box inset to the
    applied cut (`left`/`width` as percentages of the ORIGINAL's timeline, written through
    `element.style`, never a style attribute — `style-src 'self'`), and both handle tiles reuse the
    same object out of the browser's cache. `object-fit: fill` stretches the sheet to the strip's box,
    which trades a horizontal squash for exact time alignment: the strip's job is to be readable AS A
    TIMELINE, and the handle tiles show the same frames at the sheet's own scale. A handle outside the
    applied cut gets no tile, which is the fact the greyed player and the dashed handle already state.
    A trim that lands takes the strip down and asks for a new one. A missing or failed sheet is never
    an error on screen: the scrubber worked before this existed and works identically without it.
    **AMENDED by bundle W2's fix pass (2026-09-08): the client BUSTS the sheet's address when a trim
    lands.** This paragraph's own two facts collide. The address is stable for the life of the clip
    (`urls.Filmstrip`, deliberately, like every other media URL) while the bytes behind it are per
    RENDITION, and a served sheet is `public, max-age=3600` — so `resetFilm` taking the `<img>` down
    does not empty the HTTP cache behind it, and the next sheet's fetch of the same address was served
    the SUPERSEDED sheet out of the owner's own browser cache for up to an hour: the retired
    rendition's frames stretched into the new cut's box, and a handle tile showing a frame the clip no
    longer has — precisely what `resetFilm` exists to prevent. `setupTrim` therefore keeps one nonce
    (`filmBust`), `resetFilm` mints a fresh one (`"?t=" + Date.now()`, the same thing `bustPlayer` does
    to the video and the poster and `bustPoster` does after a card-image swap) and `readFilm` returns
    it on the url, so the strip and both handle tiles ask for ONE address and share one cache entry.
    It is EMPTY until a trim lands, on purpose: an ordinary page load of a clip that already has a
    sheet must still come straight out of the cache, which is the whole point of the public directive
    (erratum 227 justified that directive for "an artefact fetched once per rendition" — true of the
    artefact, and this is the client half that makes it true of the address too). The query reaches no
    key: the route reads its id from the path, so the busted address is the same object with the same
    ETag, asserted on the live stack in step 70(c). The server-side alternative — a rendition-scoped
    address — was considered and refused: it would put a changing URL inside pages and cards that
    caches and chat clients keep, which is the property `urls.Filmstrip` was written to avoid.
    `db.TestEnqueueFilmstripAdmitsOneLiveJob` / `TestSetFilmstripIsGuardedByTheRendition` /
    `TestTrimDropsTheFilmstrip` / `TestReplaceDropsTheFilmstrip` /
    `TestFilmstripKeyIsAccountedEverywhere` / `TestMigrate0014UpgradesAPopulatedDatabase`,
    `httpapi.TestTheClientBustsTheSheetAfterATrim` (the directive on the wire and the bust in the
    shipped client, in one test, because the hazard is the pair and not either one),
    `transcode.TestPlanFilmstrip` / `TestFilmstripArgs` /
    `TestMakeFilmstripProducesTheSheetThePlanDescribes` (`-tags ffmpeg`, and it measures that tile
    i+1 is a LATER frame than tile i — a geometry check cannot see a sheet of one frame repeated),
    `worker.TestFilmstripIsSampledFromTheRenditionAndCommittedOnce` /
    `TestFilmstripSkippedWhenTheRenditionChanged`, `httpapi.TestFilmstripEnqueuesThenServes` /
    `TestFilmstripFailureIsReportedNotRetried` / `TestClipDTOCarriesTheFilmstripGeometry`,
    `web.TestSharePageFilmstripAttributes` and E2E **step 70**.
    ***Amended at the lane-4 merge (2026-09-09).*** "It reads the RENDITION" and "its commit is
    guarded by the rendition's ETag" were written when `rendition_key` was never NULL on a ready
    clip. Erratum 201 ended that: on the remux fast path the UPLOAD is the playable file and there is
    no rendition object at all, which is now the commonest shape of all. Both sentences therefore read
    **`db.PlayObject`** — the one definition of "which bytes" — exactly as the GIF, the poster and the
    Light copy do: `worker.filmstripRun` samples `PlayObject`'s key and size, and `db.SetFilmstrip`
    guards on `playETagSQL` rather than on `rendition_etag`. Left as written, the sheet would have been
    skipped ("clip has no rendition to sample") for every clip whose upload the browser can play, and a
    sheet made from a Light copy could never have committed.

221. **The trim control moves out of Manage and sits with the PLAYER** (`web/templates/clip.html`,
    `web/static/app.css`, `app.js` `setupTrim`; the owner's first look: the trim scrubber should sit
    closer to, or inside, the video player). It is the one owner control whose subject is the picture
    on screen — its handles seek that player and its filmstrip is made of that player's frames — and
    it was a section heading and a scroll away from both. It is now a `<section class="trim">`
    rendered directly under `.player-extras`, gated on `IsOwner AND CanTrim` (the template gate is
    what keeps it off a visitor's page; nothing about the route's auth changed). `setupTrim` searches
    the PAGE rather than `[data-owner-controls]` for that reason and takes no owner block. Nothing
    about the control's behaviour moved with it: the number boxes are still the API's truth and the
    only half that works with scripting off, `data-trim-*` and `data-scrub-*` are still app.js's
    selectors, and the keyboard behaviour (arrows a tenth, PageUp/Down a second, Home/End the ends) is
    untouched. **`dirtyOwnerFields` — corrected, see erratum 226(c).** The sentence this paragraph
    first carried ("it runs only on the queued/processing → ready transition, where `CanTrim` is
    false and this block does not exist") is true of ONE of its two call sites and not of the other.
    The ready-transition reload is as described. The REPLACE flow's post-success reload calls it too,
    on a ready owner page where this block does exist — so moving the trim inputs out of
    `[data-owner-controls]` does change one thing: typed or dragged trim values no longer count as
    unsaved work there, so a successful replace reloads unless something ELSE in the owner block is
    unsaved, where before a touched From/To box alone was enough to hold the reload back and offer it
    as a link instead. That is the right answer and is kept deliberately: a replacement RETIRES the
    trim window — `internal/db`'s `SwapSource` NULLs `trim_start_ms` and `trim_end_ms` and rewrites
    `source_duration_ms` in the same UPDATE that swaps the source — so the numbers left in those
    boxes describe a clip that no longer exists, and carrying them across the reload would preserve
    stale work rather than the owner's. Every other control in the owner block is compared exactly as
    before.
    Two of the owner's other watch-page notes are the same edit's other half, and both are behaviour and
    not restyling. (a) The handles' words are their own `<span class="handle-label">` positioned
    BELOW the disc: "From" at 0.6 rem inside a 1.6 rem circle in `--muted` was four letters wide and
    unread, and out here it is at the page's own size and colour. (b) The `From (s)`/`To (s)` number
    inputs lose their spinner arrows (`appearance: textfield` plus the WebKit pseudo-elements, scoped
    to `.clip .trim`), which sat on top of the digits in a field that narrow. The values are still
    typed and still bounded by `min`/`max`/`step`.
    The owner's wider note — too many buttons in too many places on one page; the Manage section wants
    one visual grammar — is the design pass's and is deliberately NOT attempted here.
    `web.TestSharePageTrimSitsWithThePlayer`, `TestSharePageScrubberIsOwnerOnlyAndInert` and E2E
    **step 70**.

222. **The bulk bar appears with the FIRST selection and goes away with the last** (`app.js`
    `setupBulk`; amends erratum 117's "the bar carries `hidden` … until `app.js` sets
    `data-bulk-ready`"; the owner's first look: the bulk bar was visible before anything was selected,
    where it was expected to appear on the first tick). What erratum 117 was protecting is unchanged and
    still asserted: the per-row CHECKBOXES are what may not appear without a client, and `app.js`
    still reveals them by setting `data-bulk-ready`. What changed is that a bar of buttons about "the
    selected clips" is no longer on screen while none is selected — `refresh()` owns the bar's
    `hidden` from the first tick on, and the server still renders it hidden, so a page with no client
    is exactly as it was.
    One exception is load-bearing: a bar that still has something to SAY stays. A bulk delete removes
    the very rows whose checkboxes were the selection, so the moment it succeeds nothing is selected —
    and hiding the bar there would take "deleted 3 clips" off the screen with it. The bar therefore
    stays while its status or error line stands, and the next change of selection clears both (a
    summary of the last set is not true of this one, which is also why a selection change already
    disarmed a primed Delete). `select all` is reached by ticking one box first, which is the
    consequence of the change and is accepted: it lives in the bar about a selection, and there is no
    selection before the first tick. E2E **step 71** (the server-rendered `hidden`).

223. **"Mine only" submits the search form by itself** (`app.js` `setupLibrarySearch`; the owner's first
    look: having to press Search after ticking Mine only was not intuitive). Progressive
    enhancement and nothing more: the library search is a plain `<form method="get" action="/">`
    (erratum 114) whose Search button works with no client at all, and this only saves the second
    click for a browser that has one. `requestSubmit()` is preferred over `submit()` so the browser
    runs the form's own validation and fires the submit event exactly as the button does; `submit()`
    is the fallback. The checkbox, its `name=mine value=1` and the URL it produces are unchanged, so
    `?mine=1` is still bookmarkable and the back button still means what it says. E2E **step 71**
    (the form without a client).

224. **A library row says WHAT is happening, in two or three words** (`internal/web/pages.go`
    `stageNote`, `web/templates/index.html`, `app.js` `stageNotes`; the owner's first look: a row saying
    only processing left open what was happening and where). The striped bar says that something is
    happening and could not say what. Each unfinished row now carries one short phrase after its
    label — `Processing… · encoding on the server` — derived from the clip's own state and the stage
    of its latest TRANSCODE job: `reading the upload`, `inspecting the video`, `encoding on the
    server`, `checking the result`, `making the thumbnail`, `uploading to storage`, `finishing up`.
    It is **server-rendered**, from ONE `db.ProgressRows` read for the whole page (the same query the
    batched progress route makes, so the phrase the page ships and the phrase the first poll writes
    over it come from the same source), and only when something on the page is still working. A
    failure of that read is a WARN and not a 503 page: the phrase is a courtesy on a row that already
    says it is processing, and a library that refused to render because one aggregate failed would be
    the worse answer.
    Three details. A clip whose state is `queued` reads **`Queued…`** in the label with no phrase
    after it — app.js's own first word for that state, so the two renderers of one line cannot
    disagree; the clip page, the embed and every card keep the undifferentiated "Processing…" for
    `queued`, where the line is one clip's whole status and the distinction earns nothing. An
    unrecognised stage yields NO phrase rather than the raw word, because a stage name is this
    server's vocabulary and printing one would be showing a reader an internal identifier — which is
    exactly what the old ` (encode)` parenthetical did. And the two lists are pinned against each
    other by `web.TestLibraryStageNotesMatchTheClient`, which reads the SHIPPED `app.js`: if they ever
    drift, a row changes its words a second after it loads for no reason a reader could guess.
    `web.TestLibraryRowCarriesTheStagePhrase` and E2E **step 72**.
    ***Amended at the lane-4 merge (2026-09-09).*** The §8.4 vocabulary grew two stages the same day
    (erratum 200's `remux`, erratum 203's `light`), and they are the two a modern upload spends its
    wait in — so both lists gained them, in the same words on both sides: `remux` is **"repacking the
    upload"** (no frame is re-encoded, and "encoding" would be a lie about the one path that is fast
    because it does not encode) and `light` is **"encoding the card copy"**. `filmstrip` and `gif` are
    deliberately absent: those stages only ever run on a clip that is already `ready`, where
    `stageNote` says nothing at all. The vocabulary lives in THREE places, not two — `internal/web`'s
    `stageNote`, `app.js`'s `stageNotes`, and E2E **step 72**'s `W1_PHRASES`, which fails on any phrase
    the server did not mean to say — so a new §8.4 stage moves all three together. (The Go/JS pair is
    pinned by a test; the E2E's list is not, and it is what caught this one.)

225. **The collection clip picker carries each clip's card image** (`internal/web/pages.go`
    `collectionChoice`/`choicePoster`, `web/templates/collection.html`; the owner's first look: picking
    clips for a collection by title alone was hard). Each entry of the membership picker renders the
    clip's `poster.jpg` at a fixed 80 × 45 beside its title. The thumbnail is DECORATIVE (`alt=""`)
    and the label still reads as the title, so the control says the same thing to a screen reader and
    works the same with images off; it is `loading="lazy"` and carries explicit `width`/`height`, so a
    hundred-clip picker neither fetches everything at once nor reflows as it fills. A clip that is not
    ready has no poster and keeps the state word `choiceLabel` appends — `poster.jpg` answers 409 for
    one, and a broken image would be the worse answer. The picker's mechanism is untouched: still a
    checkbox list (erratum 95), still the owner's own clips only, still current members first in
    position order, which is the order the PUT sends. The hover/inline PLAYER the owner also asked for is
    the design pass's and is deliberately not attempted here. `web.TestCollectionPageOwner`,
    `TestCollectionPickerIsACheckboxList` and E2E **step 72**.

226. **Bundle W1's verification pass: four corrections, one test made patient, and one cost trade-off
    recorded rather than changed** (`app.js`, `web/templates/index.html`, this file,
    `internal/worker/worker_test.go`, `DEPLOY.md` §22.2). Nothing here changes a wire format, a route
    or an auth class; (a) and (d) are the only things a reader of the library can see.
    **(a) The bulk bar's own `select all` / `clear` are selection changes** (`setupBulk`'s `setAll`).
    Erratum 222 says the bar "goes away with the last" tick and that "the next change of selection
    clears both" the status and the error line — and only the `change` LISTENER did that clearing.
    Setting `c.checked` from script fires no change event, so `clear` left the last action's summary
    standing, which held the bar on screen over "0 selected" (exactly what the owner asked to stop) and
    left "Tagged 1 of 1." above a two-clip selection after `select all`. `setAll` now does the
    listener's whole job — disarm, clear the summary, hide the error, refresh — so erratum 222's rule
    holds for every way a selection can change. The delete exception is untouched: it is the ACTION
    handlers that leave a summary standing on an emptied selection, not `setAll`.
    **(b) The filmstrip poll tests for 200, not for `ok`** (`setupTrim`'s `pollFilm`). `Response.ok`
    is true of every 2xx, and this route's normal first answer is the **202** of erratum 220 — so the
    branch commented "the sheet exists" was entered on the tick that says the sheet does NOT exist,
    and spent a `GET /api/clips/{id}` (a route with no limiter) whose `filmstrip` was null. The poll
    now enters it on 200 exactly; a 202 falls through to the sleep, which is all it ever meant. A
    clip whose sheet takes the whole window cost 24 HEADs plus up to 24 pointless DTO reads and now
    costs 24 HEADs plus one. The 409/503 terminal check below it is unchanged.
    **(c) Erratum 221's claim about `dirtyOwnerFields` was wrong, and the delta it hid is kept**:
    the function has two call sites, not one — the ready-transition reload AND the replace flow's
    post-success reload, which runs on a ready owner page where the trim block does exist. Erratum
    221 above now states this and states the consequence: with the trim inputs outside
    `[data-owner-controls]`, a touched From/To box no longer holds back the post-replace reload, so
    those values are discarded — which is right, because `SwapSource` retires the trim window in the
    same UPDATE that swaps the source. Every other owner field still holds the reload back exactly as
    it did.
    **(d) The bulk bar's TEMPLATE comment was left describing erratum 117's behaviour** after
    erratum 222 replaced it ("app.js unhides it together with the per-row checkboxes"). It now says
    what the code does — the server renders the bar hidden, `app.js` reveals the CHECKBOXES by
    setting `data-bulk-ready`, and the bar itself follows the selection. Comment truth is load-bearing
    here: `scripts/check.sh` reads comments as if they were code (erratum 189(b)), and this one had
    started to contradict the comment beside the reveal.
    **(e) `worker.TestStorageFailuresNeverReachThePublicReason` is no longer racy** (test-only, and
    a PRE-EXISTING race this bundle did not introduce — it touches neither `jobRun.fail` nor the
    harness). `h.waitJob(...)` returns the moment `FailAttempt` commits the attempt, which is the
    FIRST statement of `jobRun.fail`, while the WARN line carrying the store's whole error is the
    LAST — behind the key deletes, the scratch removal and the progress write. The test read
    `h.logs` inside that window and failed once under `-race -count=1`, which is precisely what the
    merge gate runs. The new harness helper `waitLog` polls the same locked buffer to the harness's
    own 10 s deadline, so the assertion waits for the line instead of racing it.
    **(f) `GET …/filmstrip.jpg` keeps its public 202-and-enqueue — the decision, and its price.**
    Anyone holding a clip's id can make a ready clip with no sheet queue one `filmstrip` job, and
    that job DECODES the whole rendition (erratum 220's `fps=…,tile=Nx1` pass, no `-ss`, no
    `-skip_frame nokey`), holds one of the `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY` ffmpeg slots and is bounded only
    by the 180 s kill — one to two orders of magnitude more work per triggered job than the cited
    precedent, `preview.gif`, whose pass is six seconds at 480 px. Nothing anonymous CONSUMES a
    sheet: its only reader is the owner's own trim control. The obvious tightening — resolve the
    session and enqueue only for `c.OwnerID` — is deliberately NOT taken, because it costs more than
    it buys: the route is mounted on the media chain, which carries no credential resolution at all,
    and adding it would put the sliding-session `Set-Cookie` of §4/erratum 25 on a response
    `serveObject` marks `public, max-age=3600` with no `Vary` — trading a bounded, id-gated cost
    lever for the chance of a shared cache storing one owner's session cookie against a URL every
    visitor fetches. Making the sheet `private` to avoid that would then take shared caching away
    from an artefact whose whole point is to be fetched once and cached. What bounds the cost stands
    where erratum 220 put it: an id nobody can guess, the `view` limiter (60/min/IP), the
    one-live-job guard in `db.EnqueueFilmstrip`, one job per clip per rendition for ever after, and
    `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY` over the whole media loop. DEPLOY §22.2 now names the per-job cost in the
    operator's own words. If a future pass wants the owner gate anyway, it is a bundle of its own:
    the media chain's credential resolution, the cache directive and the E2E's anonymous enqueue all
    move together. **That bundle is erratum 227**, taken on the owner's decision the same day: the cache
    objection above turned out to be answerable by resolving the credential on the NO-SHEET arm alone,
    which leaves the served sheet's `public, max-age=3600` untouched, so (f) records the reasoning of
    the day and 227 is what the route does.

227. **`GET …/filmstrip.jpg`: serving a sheet stays public, MAKING one is the owner's**
    (`internal/httpapi/filmstrip.go`, `router.go`, `web/static/app.js`, `API.md`, `DEPLOY.md` §22.2, §8.1's
    row; the owner's decision of 2026-09-08 on erratum 226(f), which recorded the opposite and named the
    price). The route now has two arms with two different rules:
    - **A sheet that EXISTS is served to anybody**, exactly as before and for erratum 220's reasons: the
      link is the auth, thumbnails of a clip the caller may already watch frame by frame leak nothing,
      and the URL travels inside pages that caches and chat clients keep. 200/206/304 through the same
      `serveObject`, `public, max-age=3600`, no `Vary`, no `Set-Cookie` — byte for byte the answer it
      was.
    - **A request that finds NO sheet is answered by who is asking.** The clip's owner, through a
      browser session, gets the whole table unchanged (202 + `Retry-After` while one is made, 409
      `not_ready`, 503 `filmstrip_failed`) and that request is what enqueues the pass. Every other
      caller gets **404 `not_found`**, and nothing happens: no job is queued, the worker is not woken,
      and no job row is even read.
    **The cost this closes** is the one erratum 226(f) measured: the pass decodes the WHOLE current
    rendition (`fps=…,tile=Nx1`, no `-ss`, no `-skip_frame nokey`), holds one of the
    `TRANSCODE_CONCURRENCY` ffmpeg slots and is bounded only by the 180 s kill — one to two orders of
    magnitude more work per triggered job than `preview.gif`'s six seconds at 480 px — while nothing
    anonymous CONSUMES a sheet: its only reader is the owner's own trim control.
    **The cache hazard 226(f) refused the gate over is answered by WHERE the credential is resolved,
    not by a new cache directive.** The handler resolves nothing until the serving arm has declined, so
    a request that gets the sheet has already returned before any cookie is looked at: no
    sliding-session `Set-Cookie` can land on a response marked `public, max-age=3600`, and the sheet
    stays shared-cacheable, which is the whole point of an artefact fetched once per rendition. The
    no-sheet arm mounts the Resolver itself (`h.auth.Middleware(authGate(privateNoStore(…)))`, composed
    per request over the clip already in hand) and every answer it writes is `private, no-store` +
    `Vary: Cookie, Authorization` — including the 404, because that answer depends on a credential too.
    Nothing else on the media chain changed; `/original` remains the other credentialed media route and
    keeps its own shape.
    **Session only, not session-or-`read`-scope.** Erratum 19's rule is that a Bearer token is an
    UPLOAD credential, and errata 111/112 widened it by exactly two READS of rows the owner already has
    (`GET /api/clips`, `GET /api/collections`). Enqueueing is not a read — it is the one verb on this
    route that costs the operator something — so a `read` token, which cannot upload a byte, must not be
    able to spend a transcode slot per clip across a library it can list. Nothing needs it: a sheet is
    useless to anything but the owner's own trim control, in a browser, with a session. A token of
    either scope is therefore treated exactly like a stranger, and if a future pass wants it in, it is
    one predicate in `filmstripMaker`.
    **404 and not 403**, for every refused caller alike — anonymous, another account's session, a token,
    a dead credential. It is the truth this URL has to tell (there is no sheet at it), it is what the
    same caller would get for a clip that legitimately has none, and a distinct refusal would turn the
    route into an oracle for "is this id mine".
    **The 409 and the 503 moved behind the gate with the 202**, which is the one wire change a non-owner
    can observe: a not-ready clip's sheet used to answer 409 `not_ready` to anybody and now answers 404
    unless the owner asks. That is deliberate — this route is about a SHEET, the clip's state is already
    public on `GET /api/clips/{id}`, and a stranger can act on neither answer — and it means the state
    check, the job read and the enqueue all sit inside the gate rather than in front of it.
    **No CSRF token, and that is not an omission.** The session cookie is `SameSite=Lax` (§4), so the
    cross-site subresource an attacker's page would use (`<img src=…>`) carries no credential at all and
    lands on the 404; what Lax does let through is a top-level GET navigation, and the most that can buy
    is the one sheet the owner's own control would have made on their next visit — once per rendition,
    under the `view` limiter, which the route keeps and which now bounds the served bytes and the
    strangers' 404s as well as the owner's asking.
    **The client** needed one line: `setupTrim`'s `pollFilm` treats 404 as terminal beside 409 and 503,
    because a session that ends under an open page now turns the poll's answer from 202 into 404, and
    silently stopping is what the other two already do. The `fetch` was already
    `credentials: "same-origin"`, which is now load-bearing rather than tidy.
    `httpapi.TestFilmstripIsMadeForTheOwnerAlone` (the matrix: anonymous, another account's session,
    upload / read / both-scope tokens, a stranger's token, a made-up token, listed and unlisted, before
    and after the sheet exists, with the job count asserted at every step),
    `TestFilmstripEnqueuesThenServes`, `TestFilmstripNotFoundAndNotReady`,
    `TestFilmstripFailureIsReportedNotRetried`, `TestFilmstripIsPublicAndTakesNoOtherMethod` and E2E
    **step 70**.

228. **Two corrections to the owner's client: the card-image note after a trim, and how "not changed"
    is decided** (`web/static/app.js`, the nit sweep's S12 and S13). Neither changes a wire format or an
    auth class; both replace a guess with the answer the server already had.
    **(a) The trim-done path now ASKS what card image the clip carries** (`setupTrim`'s `applyTrimmed`,
    new `refreshChosen`). Erratum 130's fix cleared the note only when the chosen moment fell OUTSIDE
    the new cut, and left the inside case for the next page load. But a single-frame extraction that
    FAILS inside the window also makes the server fall back to the automatic frame and drop the choice
    (`internal/worker/trim.go`), so the page kept reading "the frame at 0:06" for a clip that no longer
    had one. The page cannot work that out from what it holds, and the clip DTO deliberately carries no
    `poster_seconds` (erratum 128) — so the note is re-rendered from the owner-only status route the
    control already knows the address of: 404 or `done` with a null `applied_seconds` → "chosen
    automatically"; `done` with a number → the note at that moment; a job still queued or running, a
    failure, or an unreadable answer → say nothing, because a wrong note is worse than a stale one and
    the next page load renders the truth. It costs ONE extra owner request per completed trim, and it is
    issued last, after everything on screen has settled.
    **AMENDED by bundle W2's fix pass (2026-09-08): the "say nothing" clause has one exception, and the
    window test is kept as the fallback rather than replaced.** Dropping erratum 130's outside-the-cut
    clear made the note WORSE in one reachable case, because "say nothing" assumed the silent branches
    are all inconclusive and one of them is not. `posterStatus` fills `applied_seconds` only for a `done`
    job, and a FAILED poster job never touches the clip (`internal/worker/poster.go`'s `finish`: the clip
    is untouched whatever happened) — so an owner who chooses a frame, then chooses another one whose job
    fails, then trims the first moment out of the clip gets: the server drops the choice
    (`internal/worker/trim.go` falls back to the automatic frame and writes `poster_seconds = NULL`), the
    status route answers `state:"failed"` with no `applied_seconds`, the client says nothing, and the page
    keeps asserting a card image the clip no longer has until a reload. The in-flight variant self-heals
    (the poster watcher finishes and calls `applyChosen`); this one does not heal at all. So
    `refreshChosen` now takes the applied window and, on every branch that says nothing from the status —
    not `done`, unreadable, no status URL — clears the note when the chosen moment (both numbers on the
    ORIGINAL's timeline, which is why the choice is stored that way) falls outside `[start_ms, end_ms)`.
    The union of the two tests is strictly better than either: the route sees extractions that failed
    INSIDE the window, which the window cannot; the window settles the outside case with certainty and no
    request, which the route cannot when the latest job is `failed`. A window this page cannot read
    (`end_ms` not after `start_ms`) proves nothing and clears nothing — the one deviation from the
    reported fix sketch, which would have treated an unreadable window as "everything is outside".
    `httpapi.TestTheClientCorrectsTheNoteFromTheWindowToo` pins the client in both languages and asserts
    the wire state that makes the fallback load-bearing (a failed latest job carries no `applied_seconds`
    while the clip still carries the choice).
    **(b) `applyChosen` reads the not-changed case off the job row** (`setupPoster`). It inferred it from
    the seconds — "applied is still what the page was rendered with" — which was the only discriminator
    the REJOIN path had and which reported a job that re-took the SAME moment as "The card image was not
    changed", although it had published a fresh object. The wire already carries the right field: a lost
    race resolves `state=done, stage=skipped` (`internal/worker/poster.go`'s `skipped`) and a real swap
    resolves `state=done, stage=done`, and `stage` has been in `PosterStatusDTO` and in `API.md` since
    erratum 127. So `stage === "skipped"` is now the test, the `before` parameter and the rejoin special
    case are gone, and the asked-vs-applied comparison stays where it belongs — the click path, where a
    job that published a different moment from the one this click sent is not this click's success.
    `httpapi.TestTheClientReadsTheSkippedStage` pins the string in both languages and asserts the field
    is on the wire.

229. **Two one-line honesties: the owner block says it needs a client, and `regCache` says it is per
    mount** (`web/templates/clip.html`, `internal/web/server.go`; the nit sweep's S16 and S15).
    **(a)** The N109 `<noscript>` treatment covered `/login`, `/register`, `/settings`' two forms and the
    library's collection form, and the share page's owner controls — which send JSON to routes that take
    no form submission, so with scripting off they look live and do nothing — carried none. There is now
    ONE line at the top of **Manage**: "Editing this clip needs JavaScript; replacing the video still
    works." One sentence, because the owner's first look found the page's copy too verbose already, and it
    names the exception rather than over-claiming: Replace IS a real multipart form with an action and a
    method, CSRF is Origin/`Sec-Fetch-Site` based, and without a client it really does post and land on
    the JSON 202. The library's bulk bar is NOT given one here: it is a `<div role="group">` (erratum
    120) whose buttons the client reveals, so a scriptless page shows nothing to explain.
    **(b)** `regCache` (erratum 106's nit) lives on `*server`, so a process that mounted this package
    twice would have two independent one-second caches. That is correct in every respect — each still
    re-counts within the second, and `POST /api/auth/register` asks uncached before it creates anything —
    just not shared, and the doc block now says so. `serve.go` mounts the package once. Documentation
    only; no behaviour, no configuration.

230. **`JOBS_UNSTICK_AFTER`: the app repairs its own stuck jobs, and one function says what it will do**
    (`internal/config/config.go`, `internal/config/unstick_test.go`; §4; ROADMAP #12's automatic half,
    which the owner asked for by name on 2026-09-08). §11 promises a job is "always claimable or retryable,
    never stuck", and until now that promise held at BOOT (`ReconcileOnStartup`) and BY HAND
    (`clippet admin jobs unstick`, erratum 146) and nowhere in between: a row left `running` by a crash
    inside a job's own exit path sat there until somebody restarted the container, and for a transcode it
    sat there with its clip `processing` — a clip that never becomes playable and, with the shipped
    `DEFAULT_CLIP_TTL=never`, is never swept either. The variable is how long a job may be `running`
    before the app repairs it itself. It has three states, which is one more than any other §4 duration:
    **unset** means `TRANSCODE_HARD_TIMEOUT + config.UnstickMargin` (15 m), a default that cannot be
    spelled in `compose.yaml` because it is computed from another variable — so compose interpolates it
    EMPTY and `config.Load` owns the coupling (erratum 57's "the default in compose equals config.go's
    default" is satisfied by there being no literal on either side); **0** switches the repair off, which
    is the state every version before this one was in; **a duration** is obeyed, floored only at a
    30-second sanity bound (`MinUnstickAfter`). That floor is deliberately NOT
    `TRANSCODE_HARD_TIMEOUT`, which is where the CLI floors `--older-than` (erratum 146): the CLI floors
    there because age is its only evidence, and this loop has another — it never repairs a job it has
    claimed, at any age (erratum 231). What a value under the hard timeout does cost is the
    SECOND-process case, so it is obeyed and WARNED about, at boot and in `admin doctor`, in the shape
    erratum 96 gave the `TRUSTED_PROXIES` warning: one line, on the combination, naming what would have
    to be true for it to matter. That is what makes the feature usable — six hours is a long time for a
    clip to sit unplayable, and an operator running one container can now say five minutes.
    `Config.UnstickPlan()` resolves all of it in one place — the effective age, the floor, whether the
    value was raised, whether it is under the hard timeout, and the tick (a quarter of the age, clamped
    to [5 s, 5 min]) — so the boot log line, `admin doctor` and the loop itself cannot disagree. The
    worker logs ONE line at startup either way, naming the variable: an operator reading a boot log must
    not have to work out whether the instance heals its own queue.

231. **The automatic repair lives in the WORKER, and its evidence is the set of jobs this process has
    claimed** (`internal/worker/repair.go`, `internal/worker/worker.go`, `internal/db/ops.go`
    `StaleRunningJobs`, `internal/httpapi/health.go`, `cmd/clippet/doctor.go`, `cmd/clippet/serve.go`;
    E2E steps 73-74). ROADMAP #12 sketched this as a branch of the sweeper's tick, filtered by
    `Worker.Busy`. It is neither, and the difference is the whole safety argument.
    &nbsp;&nbsp;**Where.** A loop of its own in the worker, started by `Start` when the plan is on. The
    sweeper cannot host it: the evidence the repair needs is the worker's, and a tick bounded by
    `SWEEP_INTERVAL` would let an operator lengthening the sweep silently lengthen the repair.
    &nbsp;&nbsp;**What "nobody is on this job" means.** Two kinds of evidence, both required. (a) THIS
    process's claims: `runJob` records every claimed job id in `worker.live` for exactly as long as it
    runs it, and a job in that set is never repaired, however old — for EVERY kind, because `runJob` is
    the one door all of them go through (no kind list anywhere: `admin jobs` knowing four of seven kinds
    was a merge bug, and a `filmstrip` kind added tomorrow is covered by construction). This is precisely
    the evidence the CLI cannot have. `Worker.Busy` is NOT that evidence and using it would be wrong
    twice: it answers about a CLIP, not a job, so it would refuse to repair a genuinely stuck old row of
    a clip that has a healthy new run, and it is only true for the kinds that register a run, so it says
    nothing at all about a live `notify` job. (b) AGE, for the process that is not this one — the one
    that died, and the second instance somebody pointed at the same database — floored as erratum 230
    describes.
    &nbsp;&nbsp;**What it does.** `db.StaleRunningJobs` lists the candidates (state only, `staleEnough`
    itself as the filter rather than a second copy of it in SQL, capped at 100 a pass), the live set is
    subtracted, and each survivor goes through `db.UnstickJob` — the same transaction the CLI's
    single-job form uses, whose age test is INSIDE the transaction, so a job claimed a moment ago cannot
    be repaired out from under the ffmpeg running it. Same `repairRunningJobTx`, so the same
    `db.UnstickReason` in `last_error`, the same §5 clip coupling and the same §11 accounting: a
    checkpointed job is released with no attempt spent, a job without one spends one crash attempt and
    fails for good at the cap. Row-at-a-time rather than `UnstickStaleJobs`' single transaction because
    the live filter is per job and an all-or-nothing sweep cannot skip a row. A pass that repaired
    anything calls `Wake`.
    &nbsp;&nbsp;**What it reports.** `/healthz` grows an optional `"repair"` object —
    `{repaired, released, requeued, failed, errors}`, five lifetime counts published through a holder the
    worker writes and the route reads (`worker.Repairs`, the shape of the sweeper's storage budget). It
    carries NO configured value: the route is anonymous (§15), so the SETTING is reported by
    `admin doctor`'s tenth check (`repair`), to somebody who is already inside the container. **Wire
    format**: additive and omitted when nothing is wired, like `sweep` and `storage_budget`.

232. **The sweeper's destroy-failure backoff survives a restart** (migration **0013**
    `sweep_failures`, `internal/db/sweepfail.go`, `internal/sweeper/sweeper.go`; N004, the owner's call: build;
    E2E step 75). **This amends erratum 101(a)**, which introduced the per-clip
    `{failures, next attempt}` map and said it was "deliberately not persisted: a restart is the one
    event that plausibly fixes storage, so forgetting the schedule then is right, and a column for it
    would be a migration for a cache". That is true of a restart an operator performs. It is exactly
    wrong for the restart nobody performed: `restart: unless-stopped` plus a process that dies every few
    minutes (an OOM kill during an encode, a host reboot loop) resets the schedule on every boot, and the
    sweeper then re-attempts the same black-holing prefix at up to `STORAGE_OP_TIMEOUT` a call for as
    long as the loop lasts — the starvation 101(a) exists to prevent, reached from the other side. The
    map is now a WRITE-THROUGH cache of one row per failing clip: `failures`, `last_attempt_at` and
    `next_attempt_at`, written on each failed Destroy, deleted when one finally goes through, and read
    ONCE per process at the first tick (bounded by the same `failingMax` = 1024, taking the rows whose
    next attempt is furthest away — the ones the in-memory eviction policy keeps). The POLICY is
    unchanged: same `2m·2^(n−1)` capped at an hour, same free first retry, same two-per-tick budget from
    the second consecutive failure on, same `Stats.Backoff`. Three properties keep it from being able to
    cost anything: the row is keyed by a foreign key onto `clips`, so a schedule cannot outlive the clip
    it describes (and a clip destroyed under a failing sweep takes it along); every write is on a context
    DETACHED from the tick's, because the tick's budget running out is when remembering a backoff matters
    most; and a read or write that fails is logged and ignored, leaving the process exactly as forgetful
    as it was before this table existed. **No wire-format change**; nothing outside `internal/sweeper`
    reads it.

233. **The poster job photographs a ranged PREFIX of the rendition** (`internal/worker/poster.go`;
    N051, the owner's call: build, without widening the ffmpeg protocol whitelist). A card image is one frame
    near a known moment, and §10.3 step 5 asserts that every rendition this system writes is a faststart
    MP4 — `moov` before `mdat`, i.e. the index of every frame in the file is at the FRONT. So the poster
    job no longer downloads the whole rendition to take one frame out of it: it fetches
    `index + media-up-to-the-moment` through `store.GetRange` into the same scratch file it always used,
    where `index = max(512 KiB, size/32)` (≈3%, comfortably above the ~1% a 720p h264 rendition
    measures) and `media = size · (seek + 3 s) / duration`, floored at 256 KiB. Measured on the lane
    stack (E2E step 76's own fixture, a 20 s 720p30 clip): a **6,729,432-byte** rendition was
    photographed from a **1,870,174-byte** prefix for a frame at 1 s — **72% fewer bytes off the
    bucket** — and the frame decoded on the first attempt. The arithmetic on the owner's 150 s 720p60
    Task 2 clip is 203 MiB → ~17 MiB for a frame at 5 s. Four cases fetch the whole file instead, because a prefix cannot be trusted or cannot
    pay: a rendition at or under 1 MiB, a row with no duration, a seek at or past the end (that refusal
    is about the FILE and must be reached with all of it), and any answer that is not at least an eighth
    smaller than the file. **Nothing about ffmpeg's inputs changes** — the prefix is a local file written
    by the same store, so the erratum-91 protocol whitelist is untouched and no new URL is ever opened.
    The FALLBACK is the safety: a prefix that does not decode (an index bigger than the allowance, a
    fragmented MP4, a duration the row is wrong about, a file some older version wrote without
    faststart) is logged at INFO and retried against the complete file INSIDE THE SAME ATTEMPT, so it
    costs one wasted range request and never an attempt, a failure or a different frame. Two conditions
    skip that retry because repeating the work cannot help: a context that is done, and a scratch
    refusal. The owner-facing vocabulary, the ETag predicate on the commit and `PosterAt`'s no-fallback
    rule (erratum 129) are all unchanged; the scratch reservation is now the PREFIX plus the poster,
    which is also the point on a small disk.
    ***Amended at the lane-4 merge (2026-09-09).*** "the rendition" throughout this erratum now means
    **`db.PlayObject`** — the rendition when there is one and the UPLOAD ITSELF on the remux fast path
    (erratum 201), which is the commonest shape there is. `acquireAndRender`, `acquirePrefix` and
    `acquireWhole` read `p.renditionKey`/`p.renditionSize`, the triple `recheckClip` resolves, instead of
    dereferencing `*p.clip.RenditionKey`: on a playable upload that pointer is NIL and the old expression
    was a panic in the poster job, not a wrong number. The prefix arithmetic, the fallback and both log
    messages are untouched, and E2E step 76's fixture is now a direct-path clip — it ranges 4,330,176
    bytes of an 18,725,088-byte UPLOAD, measured on the merge stack. That step also had to stop reading
    `rendition_bytes=` out of the whole log: `clip ready` truthfully prints `rendition_bytes=0` for a clip
    with no rendition object, so the number is read from the one line that reports the fetch.

234. **Five more merge-gate tripwires, and the E2E's own sharp edges** (`scripts/check.sh`,
    `scripts/e2e.sh`, `scripts/e2e.d/*`, `.gitignore`; the verified half of the "[nit sweep, …]"
    entries). Nothing here changes the product; all of it closes a CLASS where the previous pass closed
    an instance. **DEPLOY §17.2's stage table is the register** of what `check.sh` proves — one row per
    stage, each naming the erratum behind it — and it is the place a new stage is written down; this
    entry says why these five exist.

    (a) `check.sh` gains five stages in the house style, in this order, each with its own
    planted-file self-test: the product display name is spelled once in `internal/httpapi/oembed.go` and
    once in `internal/web/meta.go` and §3 forbids an import either way, so a stage asserts the two
    literals are equal (an empty match fails, so renaming either const trips it); `jobs.last_error` may
    only be written by `internal/worker` and `internal/db` — the invariant `worker.OwnerError` and
    `db.IsOperatorReason` depend on (erratum 165) — so a stage greps the four reason-carrying writers and
    fails a call from anywhere else; no `scripts/e2e.d/*.sh` drop-in may ASSIGN one of the harness's own
    globals, because those files are *sourced* into `scripts/e2e.sh` and a bare `X=` would clobber a
    shared clip id (the expression names only what the harness owns, so the short names drop-ins already
    use stay free); any file under `scripts/` that boots `clippet serve` on a private `DATA_DIR` must
    redirect `SCRATCH_DIR` too, because compose still mounts the service's volumes and the probe's boot
    janitor would otherwise empty the LIVE scratch directory under an in-flight transcode (a MAJOR finding of the audit;
    a probe that does not run `serve` has no janitor and is exempt, which is why the rule is
    per FILE and keyed on both spellings); and `DEPLOY.md`'s numbered headings and its Contents entries
    must match, which three lanes adding a section at once is exactly the way to break.

    (b) The two E2E steps whose timing lost to four-lane load are now polls rather than sleeps, and
    the one that races the `TRANSCODE_HARD_TIMEOUT` floor reads the age the CLI itself prints and SKIPS rather than fails when
    the floor has already passed — no threshold is loosened anywhere.

    (c) `card_check` is now the complete §9.1 inventory: the four tags it never asserted
    (`og:image:type`, `twitter:image`, `twitter:description`, `description`) plus a COUNT, so a card that silently lost a tag fails the
    suite and not only the Go golden.

    (d) `.gitignore` covers `__pycache__/` and `*.pyc`, and `scripts/e2e.sh` takes an opt-in `E2E_CLEAN=1` for the scratch directory nothing has ever swept
    (default off: after a failed run those bodies are the post-mortem).

    (e) *Amended by this bundle's fix pass:* two assertions of its own were wrong about CONFIGURATION
    rather than about behaviour, and both would have failed a stack that is perfectly healthy. Step 51 asserted doctor's `repair` verdict was
    `ok`; a `JOBS_UNSTICK_AFTER` under `TRANSCODE_HARD_TIMEOUT` — the `5m` `.env.example` suggests and
    DEPLOY §24.6 tells a single-instance operator it "probably should" use — adds a second `repair` line
    at `warn`, so the step now accepts either verdict and fails only on `skip`, `FAIL` or absence (it is
    the one check in that loop that differs by `.env` and not by origin). Step 75's host-side `mc` paths
    prepended the stack's `S3_KEY_PREFIX` to a probe prefix that had REPLACED it (a `compose run -e`
    overrides, it does not nest), which agreed with the objects the probe wrote only while the shipped
    default leaves that variable unset; the probe's own prefix is the whole prefix.

    (f) *Amended at the lane-4 merge (2026-09-09).* (b)'s poll for step 54 waited for the fact at the very threshold the two
    runs after it use, and the app's clock stepped BACKWARDS in between — the poll saw
    `extra <id> subtotal objects=2`, and the next command reported the planted original at `age=4s
    (skipped: younger than --min-age 5s)`, so the `--delete` run never reached the upload-is-sacred
    interlock the step asserts. The poll now asks a STRICTER question than the runs it precedes
    (`ORPH_MARGIN` 25 s against their `ORPH_MIN` 5 s) and re-takes the report at `ORPH_MIN` once the
    margin is there: no threshold under test moved, and the next backwards step has 20 s to eat before it
    can hide a fact that is true. The general lesson for any step that polls this app's clock: waiting
    for exactly the threshold you are about to assert is not waiting, because that clock is not monotone.

235. **The tier plan is given a SIZE for the Full it has not encoded yet, and `CardReady` waits for a
    card copy that is still `encoding`** (`internal/transcode/tiers.go` `MakeTierPlan`,
    `internal/transcode/plan.go` `PlannedOutputBytes`, `internal/db/full.go` `CardReady`; amends errata
    212 and 217).

    **What was wrong.** Erratum 203's skip rule applied its SIZE term only when the size was known, and
    it was known for a playable original (it is the upload) and not for a Full — `MakeTierPlan` passed
    `sizeKnown = play.Playable`, which is FALSE for every clip that needs one. For a source that is not
    web-playable but is already card-SHAPED — ≤1280×720 and ≤30 fps, so neither the picture term nor the
    frame-rate term fires — the plan therefore said `LightNeeded=false`, `CardTier=full`, and the run
    encoded ONE Full at CRF 18 and flipped `ready` on it. Only in `finalize` did the commit-time rule
    (`worker.lightWanted`) weigh the Full's now-known bytes, find them past `SOCIAL_MAX_BYTES` (25 MiB
    shipped, which is about 70 s of 720p30 at CRF 18) and queue a `social` job.

    In that window the clip was `ready` with a poster and playable bytes, so `db.CardObject` fell back to
    `db.PlayObject` — the Full — and `db.CardReady` was TRUE. All three of its readers therefore said
    the card worked: `POST /api/upload` returned `card_ready: true` and handed the link over, the crawler
    hold let a Discordbot through (erratum 213), and the human got no note — while `og:video` pointed at
    a file ABOVE the very threshold the Light tier exists to stay under, which is the one thing erratum
    213 exists to stop Discord remembering per URL. The shapes that hit it are ordinary: a WebM from a
    browser MediaRecorder, an MKV from OBS, a 720p30 HEVC phone clip — long enough, and nothing else
    about them unusual.

    **The braces: the plan gets a size.** `plannedOutputBytes` — the 0.2 bits-per-pixel estimator the
    worker has used for the §10.2 scratch guard since erratum 42 — moves into `internal/transcode` as
    `PlannedOutputBytes` (the worker keeps its own name as a one-line delegate, so two packages ask ONE
    estimator and cannot come to disagree), and `MakeTierPlan` asks it about `t.Full`. So a card-shaped
    Full whose estimate crosses the cap carries its clip into erratum 217's `FullNeeded && LightNeeded`
    branch: one ffmpeg, both files, both in the bucket at the flip. `replace.go` is covered by the same
    change — it reaches the same verdict through the same `tierPlanFor`.

    The estimator's direction is what makes this safe rather than merely different. `OutputBitsPerPixel`
    is the measured CEILING (libx264 runs 0.02–0.15 bits per encoded pixel; 0.2 is that with headroom),
    so the plan OVER-estimates, so it over-plans. That is the cheap error: over-planning spends one
    encode of a 720p30 file nobody watches, and the two-output pass costs 1.05–1.42× the Full alone
    rather than 1.6–1.9× (erratum 217), while under-planning hands a crawler the thing the tier exists to
    prevent. A plan nobody can size — a matroska muxed to a pipe declares no duration — estimates 0,
    which is "unknown", and the shape alone decides exactly as before; the commit-time rule is what
    covers that clip.

    **The belt: `CardReady` is false while `light_state = encoding`.** The commit-time rule still runs,
    and it still has a case to catch — an unsizeable plan, and a high-motion encode that beat the
    ceiling — so the state it leaves behind must not read as "the card works". A clip whose card copy is
    `encoding` has a card file COMING that is NOT the one `CardObject` resolves to: the fallback is the
    Full, or the cut a trim just made, and the reason the tier was planned at all is that such a file is
    too big, too smooth or too large a picture for a crawler. So all three readers wait, which is
    erratum 213's doctrine applied to the one state it had not been: the capture reply reports
    `card_ready: false` at its ceiling, a crawler is held with `Retry-After: 30`, and the human gets the
    one short line. An encoding FULL is deliberately NOT a reason to wait — the card already has its own
    copy — and a FAILED clip is never held, unchanged.

    **This is why errata 236 and 237 had to ship with it.** Waiting on `light_state = encoding` is only
    safe if that word cannot stick, and it could, twice over: until 236 a REPAIRED `social` job left it
    there for ever, and until 237 so did one that SKIPPED — the ending an operator reaches by raising
    `SOCIAL_MAX_BYTES`, or turning it off, under a job that was queued while it was on. Both are closed,
    and erratum 237's table of every ending is what makes "cannot stick" a claim rather than a hope. What
    the wait is bounded BY, in the worst case, is that job's own budget: a `social` job backing off
    through `TRANSCODE_MAX_TRANSIENT` against a storage blip keeps the column at `encoding` for as long as
    the backoffs last, and a crawler is answered `503 Retry-After: 30` for that whole time — except a
    `noRoom` requeue, which spends none of that budget (erratum 90) and is bounded instead by scratch
    freeing, which is the condition an operator fixes and the only thing that ends it. That is the same
    answer the media routes give during such a blip, it ends at the cap (which now writes `failed`, and
    the card falls back), and it is the direction to be wrong in: a bare link that becomes a card is
    recoverable, a cached wrong card is not.

    **What a TRIM now does, stated because it is a behaviour change.** A trim NULLs the card columns and
    queues a fresh card copy (erratum 70), writing `light_state = encoding`; for the seconds that encode
    takes, a crawler re-fetching that clip is held rather than shown the cut itself. That is the correct
    answer for the same reason as above — the cut is planned in the Full tier's box (erratum 208), so it
    can be 1440p60 — and the E2E's own trim steps already wait for the new card file before asserting
    anything about the card (`wait_social`).

    **Proven by**: `TestMakeTierPlan/not playable, card-shaped, but too long to fit the cap`, its
    `unsizeable` sibling and `TestPlannedOutputBytes` (internal/transcode);
    `TestUnplayableCardShapedSourceOverTheCapGetsBothTiersAtTheFlip` (internal/worker), which asserts
    both objects AND `db.CardReady` at the flip and that no `social` job was queued behind it;
    `TestCardReadyWaitsForAnEncodingLightCopy` (internal/db); and E2E step 63's second subject — a 48 s
    720p30 HEVC upload (T2's own six seconds stream-copied eight times, so the host pays nothing) whose
    `POST /api/upload` reply is only `card_ready: true` when `/light.mp4` answers, and whose `card_tier`
    is `light` with both tiers `ready` at the flip. Measured on the fix lane's stack: the plan estimated
    33.3 MB, the Full came out at 23.2 MB and the card copy at 8.8 MB, and the reply came back
    `card_ready: true` in 23 s — which is the estimator over-estimating by 43 %, i.e. exactly the
    direction this erratum relies on. The E2E pins the PLAN half; the race half — `ready` with the card
    copy merely queued — is pinned by the two Go tests, because a 720p30 fixture whose real Full crosses
    the cap cannot also finish inside `CAPTURE_READY_WAIT`.

    One test fixture moved with the change and the move is worth recording, because it says what is left
    of the commit-time rule. `worker.socialHarness` used `SOCIAL_MAX_BYTES = 1` so that the 31 bytes its
    fake encoder writes would qualify; a cap of one byte is now crossed by every estimate, so the
    transcode plans the card copy itself and no `social` job is queued at all. The harness is now the
    only shape that still reaches that job from a transcode — the estimate UNDER the cap (3.95 MiB) and
    the file OVER it (6 MiB) — with `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` raised alongside, because the plan's estimate is
    otherwise the only bound `outputBudget` grants a 1 KiB source (erratum 46) and the run would be
    killed for writing the file instead of committing it.

236. **A `social` or `full` job that is REPAIRED to its cap settles its tier column, in the same
    transaction** (`internal/db/jobs.go` `failAttemptTx`, `internal/db/full.go` `tierOfKind` /
    `tierStateColumn`; amends errata 205, 230 and 231).

    **What was wrong.** `db.SetTierState` was the only writer of `light_state` / `full_state` for a job
    that ended without producing its tier, and its only callers were the workers' own exit paths
    (`worker/social.go`, `worker/full.go`). There are three endings that run no exit path at all,
    because there is no worker on the job: the automatic repair (`JOBS_UNSTICK_AFTER`, erratum 230/231),
    the boot reconcile, and `clippet admin jobs unstick`. Each of them ends the row through
    `repairRunningJobTx` → `failAttemptTx`, so a `social` job repaired to its cap of 2 — or a `full` job
    to its cap of 3 — was `failed` with `light_state`/`full_state` still reading `encoding`, and nothing
    would ever write them again.

    Every reporter of a tier state then repeated it for ever: `db.ReconcileClipTier` (the object is
    absent and the column says `encoding`), the clip DTO's `tiers`, both progress routes, the quality
    selector's "still encoding" line — and `web.tiersLive`, which put a `data-progress-url` on a page
    for a clip that is `ready`, so `app.js` polled `GET …/progress` for its full twenty minutes on every
    single view of that clip, for as long as the clip existed. The cost is one poll loop per viewer per
    view, for ever, for a job that stopped.

    **The fix.** `failAttemptTx`'s `final` branch writes the tier column beside the job's own `failed`,
    for the kinds that own one. The mapping is `tierOfKind` — `social` → light, `full` → full, and ""
    for everything else — deliberately a mapping FROM the kind rather than a list of kinds to treat
    specially, because "the kinds this function knows about" is exactly what goes stale when a kind is
    added (`admin jobs` knowing four of seven kinds was a merge bug of this run). It is one transaction
    with the job row on purpose: a crash between two statements is the stuck state this closes.

    The workers' own `SetTierState` calls are left in place and become redundant, idempotent
    restatements. Removing them would make a worker that really did run its exit path depend on the DB
    having got there first, which is a coupling worth nothing.

    A `transcode` job is untouched: it owns no tier column (its tiers are settled by `TierFields` when it
    succeeds) and its `final` branch already fails the CLIP, which is the §5 coupling rule and stays
    exactly where it was. The write carries `state <> 'deleting'`, `SetTierState`'s own guard: this is a
    footnote on a job's ending and never a reason to fail one.

    **Proven by** `TestRepairedTierJobSettlesItsTierState` (both kinds, one repair per attempt in the
    budget — a REQUEUED job's tier is still `encoding`, and only the last repair writes `failed`) and
    `TestRepairedNonTierJobTouchesNoTierColumn` (six kinds through their whole budget, both columns
    untouched).

237. **EVERY ending of a tier job settles its tier column, and every write of that column is guarded by
    the promise it replaces** (`internal/worker/social.go` `markSkipped`, `internal/worker/full.go`
    `markSkipped` / `settleTier`, `internal/db/full.go` `SettleTierEncoding` / `settleTierSQL`,
    `internal/db/jobs.go` `failAttemptTx`; amends errata 205, 235 and 236).

    **What was wrong.** Erratum 236 closed the endings that FAIL a job without a worker on it. It did not
    close the endings that resolve a job as **done without producing its file**, and a `social` job has
    two: `finish`'s `errSkipped` case (`recheckClip` decided the job must not run) and `skipped` (the
    guarded commit found the rendition changed). Both resolve the row through `CompleteJob` — `done`,
    stage `skipped` — and wrote no tier state at all, so `light_state` stayed exactly as the commit that
    queued the job had left it: `encoding`, for the life of the clip.

    The trigger is an ordinary operator action. A card copy is queued, or in a transient backoff, with the
    column at `encoding` — after a trim, after a replacement, or after the commit that found its Full past
    the cap — and the operator restarts with `SOCIAL_MAX_BYTES=0`, or raised above what the rendition
    weighs. `recheckClip` re-applies the rule (erratum 169), skips "the playable file no longer
    qualifies", and the job is done. Since erratum 235 that stuck word is not a cosmetic one:
    `db.CardReady` is FALSE while it stands, so a crawler is answered `503 Retry-After: 30` for ever,
    `GET /api/clips/{id}` says `card_ready: false`, the watch page carries the "card still being prepared"
    note, and `web.tiersLive` polls `…/progress` on every single view. `ReconcileTierState` reports
    `encoding` to everything else. No operator command clears it: `admin jobs retry` acts on a FAILED job,
    and this one is `done`.

    `full.go` already had `markSkipped` for its own `errSkipped` case — which is where the shape of this
    fix comes from — and it covered neither the lost race nor its own guard's second half.

    **Every ending of a `social` or `full` job, and the column it leaves.** This table is the erratum: it
    is what makes erratum 235's belt safe to wait on, and a new ending that does not appear here is a bug
    of exactly the kind this closes.

    | Ending | What resolves the job | The tier column after it |
    |---|---|---|
    | the file was published | `SetSocial` / `SetFull`, in the commit that writes the object's keys | `ready` (with `full_codec`, for a Full) |
    | failed at its cap, worker present | `FailAttempt` → `failAttemptTx`, one transaction | `failed` (and `settleTier` restates it) |
    | failed at its cap, no worker — automatic unstick, boot reconcile, `admin jobs unstick` (erratum 236) | `repairRunningJobTx` → `failAttemptTx` | `failed` |
    | skipped: the job must not run (`recheckClip`'s reasons — the clip is gone, deleting, not ready, has no playable file, is its own Light copy, or no longer qualifies) | `CompleteJob` + `markSkipped` | `skipped` |
    | skipped: the commit lost its race (`swap.OK == false`) | `CompleteJob` + `markSkipped` | `skipped`, or `encoding` kept when the winning commit queued a replacement |
    | requeued inside its budget (transient or crash) | `FailAttempt` → `queued` | `encoding` — a job really is coming |
    | requeued with no budget spent (a scratch shortage, erratum 90) | `RequeueWithBackoff` | `encoding`, until scratch frees |
    | released (Cancel, Stop, shutdown) | `ReleaseJob` → `queued` | `encoding` |
    | the row is gone — the clip is being deleted, or was | `MarkDeleting` cancels the clip's live jobs | nothing: a clip being destroyed has no tiers to describe |

    **The guard, and why a read is not one.** Every settling write now goes through
    `db.SettleTierEncoding`, whose statement (`settleTierSQL`, shared with `failAttemptTx`) writes only
    while the column still says `encoding` AND no job of that kind is live for the clip. The two terms are
    one sentence: `encoding` is a PROMISE that a job of this kind is coming, so the only write entitled to
    replace it is the ending that makes the promise false — and an ending is only that ending when nothing
    of the kind is left to keep it.

    Without the second term the same write is a race with every commit that publishes or re-queues a tier.
    A trim publishes a Full (`full_state = ready`, `rendition_key` set to the cut) while a stale whole-file
    `full` job is still queued; a replacement or a trim queues a fresh card copy (`light_state =
    encoding`) — and a late footnote from a job that had already stopped would bury a file the bucket
    holds, or tell every reader that a queued encode is not coming, which for the card's own copy releases
    erratum 235's belt while the file really is still being encoded. `full.markSkipped` used to read the
    clip and compare, which is the first term and cannot be the second: a read followed by a write is not
    a guard, and this one now lives in the statement.

    The `NOT EXISTS` term is only correct because the job in hand is resolved FIRST — `CompleteJob` writes
    `done` above every `markSkipped` call, and `failAttemptTx` writes `failed` above its own settle — so a
    job never reads itself as the reason not to settle. A job whose row could not be resolved (it was
    cancelled underneath the worker) settles nothing, which is the same rule pointing the same way.

    This amends erratum 236's last-but-one paragraph. The workers' own writes are still redundant
    restatements of what `failAttemptTx` wrote in the failing transaction — kept for the reason 236 gave —
    but they are no longer UNGUARDED restatements, which is what made them able to undo the guard the
    repair's write now carries. `db.SetTierState` keeps its old, unguarded shape and no longer has a
    caller in the worker: it is the primitive that STATES a tier (the four words, both tier names), which
    is what the tests that plant one need.

    **One ending stays open, and it is not this one.** When a trim or a replacement commits while a tier
    job is RUNNING, `enqueueSocialTx`/`enqueueFullTx` leave "an already-live job alone" — and that job
    then loses its ETag race, so no replacement is ever queued and the new rendition keeps no card copy of
    its own. This erratum makes the STATE of that clip honest (`skipped`, so the card falls back and the
    readers stop waiting) and deliberately does not change the queueing rule, which is a separate
    behaviour with its own trade: it is recorded as a cleanup nit rather than fixed inside a fix
    pass for erratum 235's belt.

    **Proven by** `TestSkippedTierJobSettlesItsTierState` (internal/worker: the operator's own trigger
    through the loop — `SOCIAL_MAX_BYTES=0` under a queued job, `light_state` `encoding` → `skipped` and
    `db.CardReady` true; and the lost race, driven by hand, with no replacement behind it),
    `TestSettleTierEncodingOnlyOverwritesAPromise` (internal/db: eleven rows — a promise settled, a
    published tier and an already-settled one left alone, a queued or running job of the same kind holding
    the promise, another kind's job not holding it — plus the refused kinds and words and the tombstone)
    and `TestRepairedTierJobLeavesAPublishedTierAlone` (internal/db: a stale `full` job repaired to its cap
    over a `full_state = ready` written by a trim).

    **(a) 2026-10-27 (run 23, lane `v1-cardhole`, D13): the open ending above, CLOSED.** A trim or a
    replacement that commits while a tier job of the kind it queues is RUNNING now ends that job's row and
    queues a fresh one, in the same commit (`internal/db/social.go` `supersedeRunningTx`, called by
    `SwapRendition` before `enqueueSocialTx` and by `SwapSource` before `enqueueSocialTx` and
    `enqueueFullTx`, each only when the commit queues that kind). The at-most-one guard read the running job
    as the one that would serve the new file; it cannot — it read the OLD rendition (or original) when it
    started and its guarded commit can only lose — so the guard now meets only a QUEUED job, which has read
    nothing yet and is still kept as before (an owner trimming twice in a minute queues one job, not two).
    The row goes to `cancelled` with `last_error = superseded: a newer file was published while this job
    ran`, the hand `MarkDeleting` already uses. The worker holding it is not signalled: it finishes its
    encode, and every ending it then reaches meets the row as erratum 293's "not this attempt's" — its
    commit is refused (the job is no longer running), `CompleteJob`/`FailAttempt`/`ReleaseJob` answer
    `ErrStateMismatch` and it discards its own object; its tier footnote finds the fresh job live and
    writes nothing, so the column keeps the commit's `encoding`. The queue is the only scheduler: the
    fresh job is claimed like any other, its `SetSocial` publishes the copy of the cut and erratum 330's
    card-ready hook fires for it. What it costs is one wasted encode, which the lost race already cost; a
    job claimed in the instant before the commit whose `recheckClip` then reads the NEW rendition is also
    superseded, and its encode is thrown away for the same price. The table above changes in one row:
    "skipped: the commit lost its race" now reads `skipped` only for a race no commit queued a job behind
    (an owner's trim that asked for no card copy); when the commit did queue one, the stale job never
    resolves its own row and the column stays `encoding` until the fresh job settles it. No E2E step pins
    the race: putting a job in `running` across a trim's commit on a live stack needs a timed hold, which
    the harness's sleep lint refuses; **proven by** `TestSwapSupersedesARunningTierJob` (internal/db: a trim
    over a running card copy, a replacement over a running card copy AND a running Full — each stale row
    `cancelled`, ONE fresh queued job, the stale attempt's `CompleteJob`/`FailAttempt` refused and both
    settle words leaving `encoding`; a trim that queues no card copy leaves the running job alone; a queued
    job is kept, not doubled) and `TestTrimDuringARunningCardCopyQueuesAFreshOne` (internal/worker: the
    stale run driven to its commit across a real `SwapRendition`, then the loop — the fresh job publishes,
    `light_state = ready`, `db.CardReady` true, the card-ready hook called, no ERROR line). Both fail with
    the change reverted (`light_state` reads `skipped` and no job is queued).

    Two behaviours changed on the way, both in the direction of 87: the owner page renders

    **Proven by** the container loop (every `internal/web` pin re-shaped to the new markup), E2E steps

    (`internal/web/meta.go` `siteName`,
