    setting and walks every literal route). The card tag INVENTORY is unchanged at 27 http / 28 https —
    asserted by `card_check`, not believed. `internal/db`'s 0014 upgrade test stopped assuming its
    migration was last (the correction `sweepfail_test` had already made for 0013), and 0015 has its
    own; `NewHandler` was split so a test can read the patterns `routes()` registered. Docs: DESIGN §7
    (rewritten), §8.1 and §9's route tables, API.md, DEPLOY §29, README, `web/STYLE.md` and
    `scripts/e2e.d/README.md`. **Deliberately unchanged:** `/embed/{id}` and `/c/{id}` (ROADMAP #35
    says so), every `/api/…` path including `/api/clips/{id}` and the `/api/collections/{cid}/clips/{id}`
    membership route, the storage key layout (`{prefix}clips/{id}/…` is a bucket path, not a URL), the
    §9.1 tag inventory, the oEmbed document's contents, and the rate limits — the owner's rule that compact needs no
    rate limit at all applies to both grammars, and four words is the answer for the case that would
    have wanted one. **Numbering:** 248–252 were pre-allocated to this lane (247 = the GPU erratum,
    253–257 = the Discord-bot lane running beside it).


253. **The Discord bot is an INTERACTIONS ENDPOINT, not a gateway connection** (ROADMAP #33, the owner's
    decision of 2026-09-10: launch with one feature, and decide what the bot is for after using it;
    `internal/httpapi/discord.go`, `internal/notify/bot.go`, both new).
    ROADMAP #33 sketched "a gateway connection to Discord (opt-in, `DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN`)". The skeleton
    ships the other transport Discord supports, and the choice is the erratum.
    - **What it is.** Discord POSTs every slash-command interaction to a URL we host, signed with the
      application's Ed25519 key; we verify with the standard library's `crypto/ed25519`, answer within
      Discord's **3-second** deadline, and finish the work through the interaction's own follow-up
      webhook. Nothing is held open, nothing reconnects, and the app has no notion of being "online".
    - **Why, in the order the reasons weigh.** (a) **The binary stays stdlib-only.** The Go standard
      library has no WebSocket client, so a gateway would have meant a dependency plus the protocol
      around it — heartbeats, sequence numbers, RESUME, IDENTIFY, intents, reconnect backoff — none of
      which §1's "one static binary, stdlib + three modules" was going to absorb for one command.
      (b) **The endpoint needs what we already have**: a public HTTPS origin. `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` is that
      origin, it is already the thing every card tag is built from, and an operator who can receive a
      Discord card can receive a Discord interaction. (c) **It needs no privileged intent** and no bot
      permission in the server beyond `applications.commands`: Discord's own message-content intent is
      gated behind a review once an app is in ~100 servers, and an endpoint that never reads messages
      never asks. (d) **The follow-up is the SAME shape** as the webhook `internal/notify` already
      posts to — `POST/PATCH /webhooks/{application_id}/{interaction_token}/…` — so it reuses the one
      client, the one host allowlist, `newPayload`'s empty `allowed_mentions`, and the scrubbing
      discipline of erratum 63 verbatim.
    - **What it costs, stated rather than discovered later.** The endpoint can only answer what
      Discord SENDS it, which is interactions. **"Attachment rescue"** — noticing a video attachment
      posted in a channel with no command, re-posting it as a card and optionally deleting the
      original — needs the gateway *and* the MESSAGE_CONTENT privileged intent, and is therefore
      DEFERRED with the rest of the owner's opinions (ROADMAP #33's status says so too, so nobody builds a
      gateway by accident). So are: reacting to messages, per-guild collections, `/clip` on a URL, and
      any command that needs to know who is in a channel.
    - **Scope, deliberately one feature.** `/clip <file>` and nothing else. The endpoint answers a
      PING, a `/clip`, and refuses everything else in one line; the CLI binds a server to an account
      and publishes the command. The owner's framing is the reason and it is worth keeping in front of
      whoever extends this: the opinions come from using the tool.

254. **The bot's configuration: three variables, all or none, one of them a secret — and two new hosts**
    (`internal/config/discordbot.go` (new), `config.go` (`Config.DiscordBot`, `Load`), `compose.yaml`,
    `cmd/clippet/doctor.go` (`checkBot`, the `bot` check), `cmd/clippet/serve.go`).
    - **The three.** `DISCORD_APP_ID` (the application snowflake — 15–25 digits; in every interaction
      and in the follow-up URL, **not** secret), `DISCORD_PUBLIC_KEY` (64 hex characters; it VERIFIES
      signatures and cannot make them, so it is not secret either), `DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN` (**secret**,
      20–200 characters of `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]` — Discord's own charset, required for the reason erratum
      63 requires the webhook token's: it keeps the configured spelling and the spelling `net/url`
      puts on the wire byte-identical, which is what lets a plain `strings.ReplaceAll` scrub it out of
      an echoed error).
    - **All three or none.** All unset is the OFF state: `POST /api/discord/interactions` is not
      registered at all (the path is the router's own 404), no client is built, no command is ever
      registered, `/healthz` says nothing, and `admin doctor` prints `discord bot: off`. Any ONE of
      them set without the others is a **boot error naming all three**. The webhook's precedent is the
      argument: a half-configured integration that boots is a silently dead one — a bot with no token
      registers no command, a bot with no public key refuses every interaction as unsigned, and both
      look like Discord's fault from the outside — and by then the operator has already pasted an
      endpoint URL into the portal. Fail at boot (§4), not at 3am.
    - **The token is a secret and is treated like one** (erratum 84's discipline, applied to a second
      value). It lives behind `DiscordBot.Token()`; `String()`/`LogValue()` render
      `app <id>, public key <8 hex>… , token (redacted)`, so a `Config` printed with `%v` or handed to
      slog cannot leak it; no validation error echoes it; `admin doctor` registers it as a redaction
      needle from the RAW environment (before `config.Load` can fail) and from the loaded value;
      `internal/notify` scrubs every spelling of it out of every string it returns. It is sent on
      exactly ONE route — the guild command registration — and never on the follow-up, which the
      interaction token authenticates.
    - **The egress, and the one thing that is new about it.** The API host is `discord.com`, which the
      webhook allowlist already names (a test pins the pair), so the §15 destination LIST gains no
      name there. What is new is the attachment fetch: `cdn.discordapp.com` and
      `media.discordapp.net`, the closed set `discordCDNHosts`, checked by `config.ValidAttachmentURL`
      (absolute `https`, no userinfo, host matched exactly — no port, no subdomain, no lookalike).
      That check exists because this URL is the first outbound destination in the program's history
      that arrives in a REQUEST rather than in `.env`: "fetch what the interaction names" is precisely
      the server-side request forger ROADMAP's "upload via URL" was refused for, and this binary sits
      inside the compose network where `minio:9000` and `host.docker.internal` resolve. The refusal is
      also why the client does not follow redirects: a 3xx off an allowlisted host is how you would
      launder one.

255. **The guild binding: one Discord server, one account, named by the operator** (migration
    `0016_discord_guilds.sql`, `internal/db/discord.go`, `cmd/clippet/admin_bot.go`, all new;
    `cmd/clippet/admin.go` dispatch + usage).
    - **The table.** `discord_guilds(guild_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, user_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES
      users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, created_at INTEGER NOT NULL)`. The guild id is TEXT because a
      snowflake is a 64-bit unsigned integer that JSON and JavaScript cannot hold, and it is a string
      everywhere it travels. No index beyond the primary key: the read path is one lookup per
      interaction and the listing is the whole table, which is one row per server the operator runs.
    - **CASCADE, matching `clips.owner_id`.** The alternative — refusing to delete a bound account —
      would make `admin users prune` fail on a row the operator cannot see from the users listing, and
      a binding costs one command to restore. The consequence is stated in DEPLOY §30 and is the safe
      direction: deleting an account silently unbinds its guilds, and the next `/clip` there is
      REFUSED rather than uploading into somewhere unexpected.
    - **The CLI.** `clippet admin bot bind <guild-id> <username> [--no-register]`, `bot unbind
      <guild-id>`, `bot ls`, `bot register [<guild-id>]`. `bind` publishes `/clip` in that server as
      part of the same command, because "this server uploads into that account" is not TRUE until the
      command exists in the server, and a bind that left it unpublished would look like a broken bot;
      `--no-register` stores the binding alone (an air-gapped restore, a test harness — the E2E uses
      it), says so, and names the command that finishes the job. Registration is per GUILD and never
      global: a guild command is live the moment the call returns, where a global one takes up to an
      hour to propagate. `PUT` (which REPLACES that guild's command set) is deliberate — `/clip` is
      the only command this build defines, so an operator re-running `register` after an upgrade gets
      exactly what this build says. Re-binding an already-bound guild REBINDS it and says which of the
      two happened; `created_at` survives, because it records when the server was first connected.
      A failed registration exits 1 with the binding still stored, and says both facts.

256. **The interaction flow: verify, answer in three seconds, finish in a goroutine** (`internal/httpapi/
    discord.go`, `internal/httpapi/ingest.go` (new), `internal/notify/bot.go`, `internal/httpapi/
    upload.go`/`upload_capture.go` (the two cores split out), `cmd/clippet/serve.go`).
    - **The order, and why each step is where it is.** (1) Read at most 64 KiB (`maxJSONBody`).
      (2) **Verify** `ed25519.Verify(pubkey, timestamp‖body, sig)` over the RAW bytes — not over a
      re-serialisation of the parsed object, which would verify a different message than the one that
      was signed — before the body is parsed, logged or acted on. A failure is **401 with an empty
      body** and an access-log `reject=bad_signature` that never includes the body (an unverified body
      is attacker-chosen text; since erratum 279 (g)'s 2026-10-27 amendment the timestamp must also be within
      ±300 s of the box's clock, else 401 and `reject=stale_timestamp`): Discord's endpoint validation sends a deliberately bad signature when
      the URL is saved and refuses an endpoint that answers 200. `ed25519.Verify` is constant-time by
      construction. (3) `type: 1` (PING) → `{"type":1}` — the whole of "is this URL ours".
      (4) `type: 2` with `data.name == "clip"` → the guild lookup, then the attachment. (5) Anything
      else — an unknown command, components, autocomplete, an unparsable body — is a type-4 ephemeral
      "Clippet does not know that command", never a 5xx: Discord renders every 5xx as "The application
      did not respond", which tells the person who ran the command nothing and the operator nothing.
    - **What is refused before any work.** An unbound guild ("This server is not connected to a Clippet
      account."), a DM ("Run /clip in a server, not in a DM."), no attachment ("Attach a video to
      /clip."), a non-video (`store.ContentTypeFor` over Discord's content type and the filename's
      extension — the same pair the ingest would store; ffprobe is still the real gate), and one past
      `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` by Discord's own `size`. All type-4 with `flags: 64` (ephemeral: a channel
      does not need to see that somebody's file was too big), one terse line each, no CTA and no link
      (§15 anti-features, the owner's copy rule).
    - **The deferred answer.** A bound `/clip` is answered **`{"type":5}`** — public, "thinking…" —
      IMMEDIATELY, and the rest runs in a goroutine owned by `notify.Bot`: fetch the attachment from
      an allowlisted CDN host, stream it into the ingest, wait for the card, `PATCH
      /webhooks/{app_id}/{interaction token}/messages/@original` with **the share link as the whole
      content**. Bounded three ways: a 12-minute job budget, a 5-minute fetch, a 10-second API call.
      `Bot.Shutdown` cancels every running job and is joined to the WORKER's 20-second `Stop` budget in
      `serve.go`, so a `/clip` in flight at SIGTERM edits its reply to "Clippet was restarting — run
      /clip again" instead of leaving a "thinking…" that never resolves.
    - **It ingests through the SAME core as `POST /api/upload`, and that is why the core moved.**
      `ingestCore` (new `internal/httpapi/ingest.go`) is §8.3 steps 5–9 — draw an id, spool to scratch,
      the ffprobe gate, `PutFile`, one transaction, hand the spool to the worker, wake it — with no
      HTTP anywhere in it; it returns a typed `*ingestError`. `upload.go`'s `ingest` is now the HTTP
      wrapper, and `writeIngestError` is the ONE mapping from a verdict to the status, code, message
      and access-log fields those routes have always written (`spoolVideo` and `probeGate` stayed as
      functions because `replace` calls them, and are now that wrapper too). The bot's `botIngest`
      maps the same verdicts onto plain SENTENCES instead. So the bot gets, by construction rather
      than by two matching lines: the account's own `ttl_days`/`unlisted` defaults
      (`applyDefaultsCtx`), erratum 60's title (the filename without its extension), the ACCOUNT's
      upload limiter (`u:<id>`, the key `router.go` uses — the bot mints no exemption), the scratch
      precheck, `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` enforced on the BYTES (an attachment that lies about its `size`
      trips the same `*http.MaxBytesError` an oversized upload body does), and the
      `CAPTURE_READY_WAIT` card-ready wait (`awaitCardReadyCtx`) — because Discord caches an unfurl
      per URL and a link posted before the card file exists would stay a bare link-out card
      (erratum 212). Not ready in time → the link goes out ANYWAY and the crawler hold (erratum 213)
      makes Discord's own retry produce the player card; the log records `card_ready=false`.
    - **Failures are one plain sentence.** `internal/notify` owns the seven of them (`SentenceFetch`,
      `SentenceTooLarge`, `SentenceNotVideo`, `SentenceBusy`, `SentenceFull`, `SentenceFailed`,
      `SentenceRestart`); anything the ingest core did not classify becomes the generic one, because an
      unclassified error is exactly the one whose text nobody has checked for a path, a bucket name or
      a credential. The operator's detail goes to the app log, scrubbed of BOTH secrets — the bot token
      and the **interaction token**, which for fifteen minutes authenticates anyone holding it to
      rewrite that reply and is therefore scrubbed exactly as the webhook endpoint is (per job, since
      it is per job).
    - **Two smaller decisions, written down because they will look arbitrary later.** The endpoint gets
      its OWN per-IP limiter (60/min, `interactionsPerMinute`) rather than sharing the `auth` bucket:
      Discord's interactions arrive from a small set of egress addresses, and a busy server would
      otherwise exhaust a 10/min bucket that login and register spend from. And the follow-up edit
      RETRIES once after a second on a 404: the endpoint's `{"type":5}` is written on the HTTP response
      Discord is still reading when the goroutine starts, so a very fast job can genuinely PATCH a
      message Discord has not created yet. **Timestamp freshness is deliberately NOT enforced** — the
      signature covers the timestamp, Discord's own examples do not check it, and a replay costs a
      duplicate upload by somebody who could already see a signed request; the E2E's fixed-timestamp
      probe is a beneficiary rather than the reason.

257. **What the harness can prove without Discord, and what only a human can** (`scripts/e2e.d/85-bot.sh`
    (new, steps 85–86), `internal/notify/bot_test.go`, `internal/httpapi/discord_test.go`,
    `internal/config/discordbot_test.go`, `internal/db/discord_test.go`,
    `cmd/clippet/admin_bot_test.go`; the live proof is the owner's).
    The E2E cannot make Discord POST an interaction, cannot fetch an attachment from Discord's CDN,
    and **must not try**: a suite that reached those hosts would be testing Discord's uptime, and the
    app's whole egress claim is that it talks to two of them and only when asked.
    - **Step 85 proves the endpoint with a keypair the harness mints itself** (`openssl genpkey
      -algorithm ed25519`, the raw key being the last 32 bytes of the DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo; the
      signature is `openssl pkeyutl -sign -rawin` over `timestamp‖body`, which is what Discord signs).
      One throwaway `compose run` container boots a second `clippet serve` on a private `DATA_DIR` AND
      a private `SCRATCH_DIR` (erratum 234's rule; without the second, that probe's boot janitor
      empties the live stack's scratch), configured with the minted public key, and curls ITSELF on
      `localhost:8080` — `curl` is in the image because the healthcheck uses it, so nothing is
      published. It asserts: a bad signature → 401 with an EMPTY body; a signed PING → `{"type":1}`; a
      signed `/clip` from an unbound guild → the ephemeral refusal; `admin users create` + `bot bind
      --no-register` + `bot ls` + `bot unbind`; and — the point of the round trip — that the SAME
      signed interaction is answered differently before, during and after the binding. Every one of
      those is answerable with no outbound call at all, which is why the bound case sends a `/clip`
      with NO attachment (the binding is read before the attachment is): "Attach a video to /clip." is
      the proof the binding was found.
    - **Step 86 proves the OFF state** on the live stack, which runs with none of the three variables:
      the route is a 404 from the catch-all, and `admin doctor` says `discord bot: off` — plus a
      probe container given ONE of the three that must exit non-zero naming all three.
    - **Everything the E2E cannot reach is unit-tested against `httptest`**, the way `internal/notify`
      has always been tested: the fetch → ingest → follow-up path, the PATCH's path and its absence of
      an `Authorization` header, the size guard on a lying attachment, the token scrub (a fake Discord
      that quotes both tokens back), `Register`'s method/path/auth/body, and the shutdown that answers
      the deferred message.
    - **What only a human can do**: creating the application in the developer
      portal, pasting `{PUBLIC_BASE_URL}/api/discord/interactions` as the Interactions Endpoint URL
      (Discord PINGs it on Save — a green save IS the first live proof), and running `/clip` with a
      real video in a real server (the card is the second). No agent can perform either, and until
      the owner does, the live half of this feature is unproven — exactly as medal #4's positive half was
      until the first live webhook run.

264. **Two copy decisions: the front door's line loses its third clause, and the link grammar is
    explained by an EXAMPLE of each rather than by a sentence** (the owner's reading of the shipped
    pages, 2026-09-11: for compact and memorable, show an example of each instead of the copy; the homepage
    tagline does not need its closing Discord clause). `web/templates/front.html`, `index.html`,
    `settings.html`, `clip.html`; `internal/urls` (`Builder.PageShort`), `internal/web`
    (`linkExamples`, `linkExamplesOf`, the two page models), `internal/httpapi/dto.go` (a comment),
    `web/static/app.js`, `internal/web/links_test.go`, `web_test.go`, `internal/urls/urls_test.go`,
    `scripts/e2e.d/80-front.sh` and `82-links.sh`, `web/STYLE.md`, DEPLOY §28 and §29, ROADMAP #35/#36.
    It amends **246(a)** (the front door's line), **250** (the control's hint) and **WITHDRAWS 251's
    owner row** — 251's other half, that an id is an address and an unlisted flip re-mints nothing,
    stands untouched. No step count, no route, no wire field and no migration changed.
    (a) **The front door reads "Upload a clip. Get a link."** The third sentence, "It plays in
    Discord.", is gone. Where a link plays is what the product does once somebody has one, and the
    door is not where that is argued; it also dated the page to one chat client, on the one page
    aimed at a stranger who may have arrived from anywhere. The slash command's own description
    (`internal/notify/bot.go`) still says a `/clip` link plays in Discord, because there it is a
    statement about THAT surface, made to somebody already in it.
    (b) **The Link control's hint is one example of each grammar, on this instance's own host.** It
    read "Memorable links read like PurpleUpdateCharacter. Easier to say, easier to guess."; it now
    reads `Compact: {host}/Xk3v9QpL2mZa · Memorable: {host}/PurpleUpdateCharacter`, both in `<code>`
    (mono is what the system gives a thing a person copies — `web/STYLE.md`). Two shapes side by side
    answer "which do I want" faster than a sentence does, and the "easier to guess" half was the copy
    the owner was rejecting. The host is the CONFIGURED one: `urls.Builder.PageShort(id)` renders the
    base's host and the id with the scheme left off — short enough for a row, and the operator reads
    the host their links will really carry — so no template holds a literal origin and the
    merge gate's URL tripwire has nothing to find. The two ids are constants in `internal/web` and
    neither is a real clip: the compact one carries digits, which no memorable word can, so `ids.Kind`
    can never read the example as the other grammar (a unit test pins both). The row grammar
    (`label | control | state`), the radios, `data-link-state`, `setupLinkState` and the "your
    default" cell are untouched, and Settings keeps the word list's credit — an attribution, not
    copy — after the examples.
    (c) **The owner's "Memorable links are easier to guess." row is withdrawn.** It was exactly the
    copy the owner named. The share page is where a clip is WATCHED; the grammar is chosen on the upload
    form and in Settings, where (b) now shows what each one looks like, and a line telling an owner
    something about a choice they already made is copy on a page that has a no-CTA rule for the same
    reason. `clip.html`'s `data-link-note` row, `app.js`'s show/hide of it (the Visibility fact it
    used as an insertion anchor now anchors on Views alone), `clipPage.LinkStyle` and `internal/web`'s
    `linkStyleOf` are gone; `internal/web/links_test.go` asserts the sentence and the element render
    for NOBODY — owner or stranger, listed or unlisted, in either grammar — and E2E step 83 keeps its
    PATCH-unlisted flow and its API assertions with the same negative checks in place of the two
    positive ones. **`ClipDTO.link_style` STAYS**: it is derived from the id, costs nothing, and is a
    wire fact a client may want named rather than re-derived. What it does NOT do any more is drive a
    page. DEPLOY §29's "What memorable costs" paragraph loses its last clause for the same reason —
    the entropy numbers and the four-words-when-unlisted rule are unchanged and still documented.

265. **A hardware decoder that refuses a source at RUN time moves the decode to the CPU instead of failing
    the clip** (2026-09-11, from the owner's first live `/clip`. Amends 216 and
    **supersedes 247 on one sentence**: whether NVDEC can decode a source is decided at plan time AND at
    run time, because the plan-time table is necessary and not sufficient).
    **Amended by erratum 289 (2026-09-16): the run-time test reads the WHOLE captured stderr and not
    the failure tail — as written here it could not see a refusal whose shutdown ran past a kilobyte,
    and the first `/clip` through the official bot was exactly that.**

    **The failure.** Clip `iGnT6cE7K85U` on the reference stack (the gpu flavour, `TRANSCODE_HWACCEL=cuda`):
    a 387 MB NVIDIA ShadowPlay recording — h264 **High, 8-bit yuv420p, 2560×1440, 60 fps, level 5.1,
    refs 1, progressive, bt709**, which is to say nothing 247's `nvdecCodecs`/`nvdecPixFmts` can refuse.
    The plan chose `light=true card_tier=light hwaccel=cuda`; the stage died in one second, exit 218:

        [h264] decoder->cvdl->cuvidCreateDecoder(&decoder->decoder, params) failed
               -> CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE: invalid argument
        [h264] Failed setup for format cuda: hwaccel initialisation returned error.
        Impossible to convert between the formats supported by the filter
               'graph 0 input from stream 0:0' and the filter 'auto_scale_0'
        ... Nothing was written into output file

    The clip was `failed` and its Discord card said "Processing failed" — about a file every other decoder
    on that machine plays.

    **What it is NOT, measured.** The host's own ffmpeg 7.1.1 (native Windows NVDEC, `-hwaccel cuda`, with
    and without `-hwaccel_output_format cuda`) prints the SAME `cuvidCreateDecoder` error on the same
    file: not WSL2, not the container, not this image. The gpu image decodes that file through the cuvid
    DECODER wrapper (`-c:v h264_cuvid`) at exit 0: the card, the driver and the stream are all fine, and it
    is ffmpeg's `nvdec` hwaccel path that will not take it. The 1080p60 proof sample of erratum 247 through
    the app's exact CUDA argv in the same image still exits 0: the environment is intact. ffprobe reports
    nothing unusual about the file. **No probe-time rule could have predicted this**, which is exactly why
    a table of codecs and pixel formats cannot be the whole answer.

    **The rule.** When an encode's ffmpeg exits non-zero with the hardware-decoder-initialisation signature
    in its stderr AND the run produced nothing — no `out_time`, no `total_size` — the stage is re-run on
    the spot with the decode off the card, and the clip never fails for this reason. It is **one attempt
    from the scheduler's point of view**: the re-run happens inside the Runner call, so the job's attempt
    counters and its transient/permanent classification (§11) are untouched (the progress stream needed
    one small guard of its own — the paragraph after this one), and only the ending of the SECOND run is
    ever reported. `internal/transcode/hwfallback.go` is the whole
    mechanism — the three stderr fragments that name the event (`cuvidCreateDecoder`, and ffmpeg's own
    `hwaccel initialisation returned error` / `Failed setup for format cuda`, matched case-insensitively;
    the British spelling is ffmpeg's), `hwInitRefusal` which returns the LINE that said so, and
    `runHWFallback` which builds the argv twice. `runInstrumented` grew a sibling returning that one extra
    fact beside the error; the "produced nothing" half is `progressTracker.wrote()`, read after `Wait()`
    when os/exec's copiers have finished. Every CUDA argv this codebase can render is built by `Encode` or
    `EncodeTiers` — no other path (poster, filmstrip, GIF, remux, copy-trim) ever asks for the card — so
    those two are the ONE place, and every hwaccel'd kind (transcode, full, light, replace, trim) inherits
    the fallback without knowing it exists.

    **The one thing that would have leaked: the progress bar.** ffmpeg prints its final `-progress` block
    whatever happened — measured in the gpu image, the refused run ends `frame=0 total_size=0
    out_time_us=N/A progress=end` — and this package reads an `end` as 100 %. §18.3's published percent is
    MONOTONE (that is what keeps a bar from going backwards mid-stage), so the refused run would have
    pinned it at the top of the encode band for the whole fallback encode. A CUDA run's report of
    COMPLETION is therefore HELD (`hwProgressGate`) until its exit status is known: released the instant
    the run turns out to have finished — before the call that would report it returns — and dropped when
    it was refused. Nothing else about the progress stream changes and a non-CUDA run never meets the
    gate. The same measurement is why "produced nothing" tests GROWTH rather than presence: that block
    carries a `total_size` of zero.

    **The shape: the decode moves, the ENCODER stays on the card** (`hwAccelNVENCOnly`, an internal third
    value of the same `accel` string that `HWAccelFor` never returns and `TRANSCODE_HWACCEL` cannot be set
    to). What NVDEC refused is the DECODER; NVENC is a different engine on the same card and is working.
    So the fallback argv is the CPU argv with the encoder swapped — the CPU filter chain (whose
    `setparams` already stamps 709), `h264_nvenc` with the tier's own calibrated `-cq`, and the
    `h264_metadata` bitstream filter; the three colour OPTIONS stay off it, because 216's trap is a
    property of an NVENC output's buffersink negotiation and not of where the frames came from. It is a
    rendering of an existing chain rather than a third pipeline: `videoChain`, `dualFilterComplex` and
    `outputArgs` each read the accel through `cudaGraph()` / `nvencOut()` and take a branch they already
    had. `EncodeArgs`/`DualEncodeArgs` keep their signatures and gain an accel-taking twin the re-run
    calls, so the second argv is exactly what this package would have rendered had the plan never asked
    for the card.

    **Proven in the gpu image**, `docker run --gpus all` on the very file (a probe container of its own,
    never the reference stack): the app's CUDA argv reproduces the failure exactly — exit 218, a zero-byte
    output — and the fallback argv exits 0 and writes a real 1280×720@30 yuv420p file probing `bt709` on
    all three colour fields. At four cpus, 30 s of that 1440p60 source into the Light tier's shape:
    **11 s on the fallback against 14 s on the plain CPU argv** (libx264 veryfast) — the 1.4–3.6× of 216
    flattened by four cores into 1.27×, worth keeping and nowhere near what a working hardware decode is.
    That gap is the price of the refusal, not of this fix.

    **One WARN, and nothing is remembered.** The transcode package knows the ffmpeg line and nothing about
    clips; the worker knows the clip and nothing about ffmpeg. So the fact travels on the job's own context
    (`WithHWFallbackSink`, installed once in `worker.withRun` — the single place every ffmpeg-running kind
    derives its context — which is the shape `internal/httpx` already uses to annotate an access-log line
    from deep inside a handler). The line names the clip, the job, the kind, the stage and the ffmpeg line
    that refused, at WARN: the §12 level for trouble that was retried. There is no per-clip hwaccel column
    to set — `hwaccel`/`hwaccel_why` are fields of the plan-time `planned` line (216) and `admin ls --stat`
    has never carried them — and a migration for one boolean nobody queries is not worth the row, so the
    log is the record and the clip is simply ready. Nothing is cached or disabled process-wide either: the
    refusal is a fact about ONE stream, and the next upload asks the card again.

    **What it deliberately does not do: cascade.** A fallback that also fails is the clip's ending,
    reported exactly as it would have been. The one case that costs is a deployment with
    `TRANSCODE_HWACCEL=cuda` and no visible device at all — `-hwaccel cuda` then prints this same signature
    ("No device available for decoder") and the fallback's encoder cannot reach the card either, so the
    clip fails as it did before. That is a misconfigured box rather than a source, the `ffcaps` boot check
    cannot see it (ffmpeg LISTS `h264_nvenc` whether or not the driver library it dlopens exists — 247),
    and DEPLOY §27 names the failure line an operator sees. Making a missing card silently transcode
    everything on the CPU forever would hide it instead.

    **Tests** (`internal/transcode/hwfallback_test.go`, table-driven, a fake ffmpeg that answers the CUDA
    argv one way and everything else another): NVDEC refuses → two runs, the second with no `-hwaccel` and
    an NVENC encoder, the encode succeeds, ONE report naming the stage and the line; the fallback fails too
    → the second run's failure, permanent, and no third run; a mid-stream CUDA failure → one run, no
    report, the ending it always had; the signature AFTER bytes were written → one run, no report; the same
    signature on a CPU run → one run, no report. Each row also counts how many times 100 % is published,
    which is the progress gate's whole contract, and the fake's refusal prints the real terminal block
    (`total_size=0`, `progress=end`) before its stderr because that is what ffmpeg does. Plus a CUDA run
    that FINISHES still reporting it, the two-output pass falling back as one ffmpeg, the argv shape (the fallback graph is character-for-character the CPU graph, and is not the CUDA one), and
    `hwInitRefusal` against six stderrs including a tail that opens mid-line. The WIRING has a test of its
    own in `internal/worker` (`TestHWFallbackWarnNamesTheClip`): nothing else would notice if the one line
    in `withRun` were dropped in a refactor — the encode would still succeed and the operator would simply
    never learn the card had stopped decoding — so `ReportHWFallback` is exported as the other half of the
    sink pair and the fake runner fires it from inside a real job. One option recorded and not built: `-c:v h264_cuvid` decodes this very file, so a refused source could keep a HARDWARE decode
    through the cuvid wrapper instead of losing it (a cleanup row).

266. **A later library page offers a way back: `Newest clips`, the un-cursored library with the filters

    `Older clips` and the browser's back button — so a page two reached from a bookmark, a second tab

    time needs a token of its own and stays ROADMAP #4's leftover, which #4 itself says "wants its own
    careful erratum".

267. **The living mark, first ship: the wordmark's eyes follow the cursor** (ROADMAP #38; the owner's
    decision of 2026-09-11: free 360° tracking on hover as the default until the roles table is decided;
    `web/static/app.js` (`setupEyes`, `setupEyesAll`), `web/static/app.css` (two rules), `web/STYLE.md`
    (one clause), `scripts/lib/visual.js` (`domFollow` and two frames); no template, no route, no
    header, no migration).
    - **What ships.** The `follow` face from the four-round exploration (`.e2e/logo/pp-alive.html`,
      gitignored): while a hovering pointer is inside the mark's TRACKING AREA both pupils enter —
      half size, 40 font units low, invisible → full size, in place, opaque, 260 ms cubic-out —
      converge on the pointer and roll after it (each pupil on a 110 × 150-unit ellipse at the
      pointer's angle from its own eye's centre, easing 18 % a frame), and leave when the pointer
      leaves (fade, shrink to 60 %, sink 30 units, 300 ms ease-in-out). After the exit every attribute
      is the injected value again — exact rest, which the DOM test compares as markup.
    - **Where.** The header wordmark (21 px: every signed-in page and the stranger's share and
      collection header), tracking area = the header BAR (`header.top`'s box), because a 360° roll
      needs room around a 46 × 40 px mark. The display wordmark (40 px) on the front door, login and
      register pages, tracking area = the auth card (`.auth`), which the cursor crosses on the way
      to the button. **Not** the embed (16 px: two-pixel pupils, and it is someone else's page) and
      **not** the message pages (`.message`: the 404, which the brief excluded by name, and the 503,
      which a healthy stack never shows) — `setupEyes` finds its area with
      `closest("header.top, .auth")` and a mark with no area gets nothing.
    - **How.** app.js injects, at boot and into each qualifying `.wordmark .pp`, one
      `<svg class="eyes" viewBox="0 -1727 2300 2000" preserveAspectRatio="none" aria-hidden="true">`:
      `.pp` is a 1 em flex item whose top is 1727 units above the baseline (ascent 1928, descent 474,
      line-height 1), so the viewBox maps font units 1:1 at any size. Inside: a `<mask>` that is the
      first p's counter path (the 600-weight outline `scripts/lib/mkcard.py`'s `WORD_PATH` carries
      since erratum 301, read back to the pp's own origin — `mkicons.py` carried it before) filled AND
      stroked white 220 wide — the counter offset 110 units outward, because the glyph's antialiased
      fringe reaches ~100 units into the ring at 16 px and a pupil pushed to the edge must be cut by
      the bowl, never sit on the ground — and two `<g mask fill="currentColor">` groups (the second
      translated 1146, the p-to-p advance) each holding one `<circle cx="628" cy="-560" r="125"
      opacity="0">`. Built with `createElementNS` and attribute writes only — no markup string, no
      style attribute, no inline script — so the CSP (`style-src 'self'; script-src 'self'`) is
      untouched; the SVG namespace string is written as two halves because `scripts/check.sh`'s
      URL tripwire reads every line. Mask ids are `eyes0`, `eyes1`, … per mark. app.css: the overlay
      is `position: absolute; inset: 0; width/height: 100%; pointer-events: none`, `display: none`
      by default and `display: block` only under `@media (hover: hover)`; app.js injects nothing
      when `(hover: hover)` does not match or `(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` does, and ignores a
      `pointerenter` whose `pointerType` is `touch`. Events: `pointerenter` / `pointermove` /
      `pointerleave` on the AREA; one `requestAnimationFrame` loop per mark while inside (entrance →
      follow → exit → rest, one state machine, re-entry during the exit tweens from wherever it is);
      a mark no longer connected to the document stops its loop on the next frame.
    - **What the exploration did that this lane did NOT carry over.** No blink, drift, glance, wink,
      smile, beam, gasp or sulk; no lids, no mouth path, no `mouthing` class, no idle timer, no hook
      on Copy link — the roles table is the owner's to decide (ROADMAP #38). The exploration's
      `mouseenter`/`mousemove`/`mouseleave` became pointer events; its Promise-and-tween storyboard
      became the state machine above (same timings, same easings, same geometry).
    - **Proof.** `scripts/lib/visual.js` gains `domFollow` (the header on a stranger's share page and
      the auth card on the front door: exactly one overlay per mark, no `style=`, the injected pupils
      at rest, opaque and off-centre and converging 700 ms after the pointer enters, the overlay's
      `outerHTML` identical to the injected one 700 ms after it leaves; zero overlays on the embed;
      zero overlays anywhere under `reducedMotion: "reduce"`) and two frames, `header-follow` (the
      library, the cursor in the bar to the right of the mark) and `front-follow` (the front door,
      the cursor over the card), both themes at 1280, each insisting the pupils are drawn and aimed
      before the shot and asserting what every frame asserts (zero console errors, zero CSP
      violations, no foreign request). `shoot()` now parks the pointer in the viewport's bottom-right
      corner before every navigation: Chromium hands a fresh page whose mouse has never moved a
      `pointerenter` at (0, 0) as it lays out, inside the header bar, and the mark would answer it;
      the corner is the page gutter on every page and width the pass shoots (the middle of the last
      row was tried first and hovered the library's collection card). The 52 rest frames are unchanged: the overlay paints nothing
      at rest and is out of flow. No E2E step: nothing server-side changed; the "no inline style"
      and "no inline script" assertions of steps 77–81 hold as they did.
268. **The Discord bot after the owner used it: the command's words point at the site, `/clip` takes a
    LINK as well as an attachment, and the follow-up says which clip it posted** (ROADMAP #33's
    wish list, written by the owner after using the bot, 2026-09-11; `internal/notify/bot.go`, `internal/notify/reply.go`
    (new), `internal/httpapi/discord.go`, `internal/urls/urls.go`, `testdata/duration.tsv` (new),
    `scripts/e2e.d/85-bot.sh` step 85, DEPLOY §30, API.md).
    **(b) — the `link` option — is WITHDRAWN by erratum 286 (2026-09-15, the owner's call); (a) and (c) stand.**
    **Amended by erratum 315 (2026-10-05):** the command is `/upload` now and its description's lead is the review's
    new sentence (the (a) clause unchanged); (c)'s two-line reply became ONE embed above the link (315(c)), its
    title rules kept; and (b)'s parser, `ParseShare`, is restored for `/clip link:` — a command of its own.
    The skeleton (errata 253–257) shipped one command deliberately, so that what to build next would be
    decided by using it. The owner used it, and found two things. **(i)** Discord refuses a too-big
    attachment in the CLIENT — "Max file size is 500.00 MB" with Nitro, 10 MB without — before a byte
    reaches this app, so the bot cannot answer that moment at all; the only two places our words appear
    BEFORE it are the command's description and an option's, and the only place after a successful
    upload is the follow-up. *"Would be cool to put something here like a link to do it on the main
    site."* **(ii)** "Clippet is thinking…" is Discord's own fixed deferred text, so the message that
    replaces it is the bot's only voice — and it was the bare link.
    - **(a) The pointer lives in the command's description, and names THIS instance.** `clipDescription`
      builds `Upload a video and get a link that plays in Discord. Bigger files: {host}` from
      `urls.Builder.Host()` (new: the base's host and path with the scheme left off — `PageShort`
      without an id, and the one caller that puts the instance inside a sentence rather than into a
      link). Discord's limit on a description is **100 characters**, and a description past it is a
      registration the API REJECTS — which would leave the server with no `/clip` at all rather than
      with a vague one — so the sentence is built to fit: a host of 33 characters or fewer is named,
      and anything longer falls back to `… Bigger files go on the site.` (81 characters, always legal).
      The description is baked into the command Discord STORES, not read per interaction, so an
      operator who changes `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` re-runs `clippet admin bot register`; `register` is a PUT
      that replaces the guild's whole command set, so re-running it is idempotent (DEPLOY §30 says so).
    - **(b) `/clip` takes a `link` instead of a `file`, and that is what makes (a) actionable.** A
      second option, `link` (STRING, type 3), beside the existing `file` (ATTACHMENT, type 11).
      **Neither is `required`**: Discord can express "this one is required" and not "exactly one of
      these two", so the rule is the endpoint's and it states both mistakes in a line each — *"Attach a
      video to /clip, or give it a link."* and *"Give /clip a video or a link, not both."* The link is
      parsed by **`urls.Builder.ParseShare`** (new), which accepts the three spellings this instance
      itself emits — `Page` (`{origin}/{id}`), `LegacyPage` (`{origin}/clips/{id}`) and `PageShort`
      (`{host}/{id}`, erratum 264's scheme-less form), plus Discord's own no-unfurl angle brackets —
      and refuses everything else: another host (matched whole, case-insensitively, port included), a
      lookalike host, userinfo, a non-http(s) scheme, `/embed/{id}`, `/c/{id}`, and any path with a
      second segment. It returns the SEGMENT, not a validated id: `ids.Valid` is the caller's check,
      made in the package where every `{id}` route already makes it (§8), which keeps `internal/urls`
      at its one import.
      **A LINK OPTION IS NOT A FETCH OPTION, and this is the load-bearing sentence of the whole
      erratum.** ROADMAP's "upload via URL" was refused as a server-side request forgery, and erratum
      254 admitted the attachment CDN only behind a closed host allowlist for exactly that reason. This
      option fetches NOTHING: `ParseShare` is a pure function over a string, the refusal happens on the
      three-second interaction response before any goroutine exists, and the job the endpoint hands
      over carries a `notify.Await` instead of an `Ingest` — a branch of `runClip` that never reaches
      the HTTP client, the attachment allowlist or the size guard, because there is no request for them
      to gate. **The §15 destination list is unchanged by this feature**, and `scripts/check.sh`'s
      call-site tripwire still finds one construction site.
      What a link may name: any clip whose watch page works. Ownership is deliberately NOT checked —
      every clip here is viewable by anyone holding its link (§9, `internal/web`'s `lookupClip`, which
      turns nobody away but a clip in `ClipDeleting`), so re-posting a link somebody already has
      discloses nothing that pasting it by hand would not, and an ownership check would break the
      ordinary case of a server where two people upload. There is no "private" clip to leak: `unlisted`
      is a noindex, not an access rule. **A missing clip and a clip on its way out answer the SAME
      line** — *"There is no such clip here."* — because two lines would be an oracle over ids that are
      unguessable precisely so that nothing enumerates them. A clip that is still ENCODING gets the
      upload path's own `CAPTURE_READY_WAIT` (`awaitCardReadyCtx`), for erratum 212's reason exactly:
      Discord caches an unfurl per URL. The rate limit on this path is the endpoint's own per-IP `bot`
      bucket (60/min, erratum 256) and nothing else — the ACCOUNT's upload bucket meters bytes into the
      library and this path adds none.
    - **(c) The follow-up is two lines: `{title} · {m:ss}` then the link.** `internal/notify/reply.go`,
      fed by `IngestResult.Title`/`DurationMS`, which the app fills from the clip row (this package owns
      no database, which is why `Ingest` was a callback in the first place). Either half may be missing —
      a link posted mid-encode has no duration yet — and a missing half is simply not printed,
      separator and all. Nothing else: no "here you go", no emoji, no instance name, no "upload more
      at"; `allowed_mentions` stays the empty parse list; a FAILED encode still gets its existing
      sentence unchanged.
      **The title is attacker-supplied text and is rendered as such.** Anybody who can upload picks
      it, and this message's whole content is a link people click, so three things happen to it before
      it is printed. Its whitespace is collapsed (a title may legally carry a newline, and the link is
      on line two). Every character Discord treats as syntax is escaped —
      `` \ * _ ~ ` | < > [ ] ( ) # - `` — which covers the ordinary case (`clip_2024_final` is an
      ordinary filename and therefore, by erratum 60, an ordinary title, and Discord would render its
      middle in italics), and also the two that are not cosmetic at all: `<@1234>`/`<#1234>` render as
      a MENTION CHIP, and `[Watch](…)` as a MASKED LINK pointing anywhere. Discord's escape rule is a
      backslash before any non-alphanumeric character, which it then swallows, so the list may be as
      wide as it needs to be without ever showing a reader a stray backslash. And a title that still
      reads as a URL after escaping — it contains `://` or `www.` — is **DROPPED ENTIRELY**, because
      no backslash suppresses Discord's auto-linker: bare text that looks like an address becomes a
      link and gets an UNFURL of its own, which would put a card somebody else chose into a message
      posted under this app's name, displacing the clip's. **The bot's reply carries exactly one link,
      and it is ours.** `@everyone` is deliberately left alone — escaping it would show a backslash for
      no gain, and the empty `allowed_mentions` parse list is what makes it inert (§17 #4).
      `formatDuration` is a second copy of `internal/web`'s (the two
      packages do not import each other and §3's graph has no edge between them), so both are pinned
      against ONE golden table, **`testdata/duration.tsv`**, exactly as nit sweep S11 pinned the three
      `humanBytes` copies after one of them had drifted in silence.
    - **What this does NOT do.** No gateway, no attachment rescue, no per-guild anything: erratum 253's
      deferred list is untouched. No new configuration variable, no migration, no new route, no
      `admin doctor` line (nothing about this can be off or misconfigured on its own), and no new E2E
      step — step 85 signs three more interactions with the keypair it already mints and proves the
      three `link` refusals on the response, with the probe given its own `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` so "a link
      of ours" reads the same on a lane stack and on the reference stack. What step 85 CANNOT cover is
      what it could not cover before: a link to a REAL clip, because the probe's database is empty by
      construction — that path is unit-tested in `internal/httpapi`, where a clip can be seeded, and
      its live proof is the owner running `/clip link:` in a real server.


269. **The parked harness nits, and the four of them that move something §16.3 wrote down.** (the cleanup list's
    34 e2e-area entries, held back on 2026-09-10 until the links and bot lanes had merged; lane `harness`,
    2026-09-11.) Most are inside the file they name and need nothing here. These do:

    **(a) A third scheduling marker, `# e2e-schedule-after: <stem>[,<stem>]`.** The exclusive phase's
    ORDER was load-bearing and nothing enforced it: 47-upload asserts the account expresses no TTL
    preference, which 55-owner's step 57 sets and clears. Name order happened to satisfy that, and a
    filtered run (`E2E_ONLY=55-owner`) dropped the precondition in silence and still printed a PASS line.
    The marker is read beside `# e2e-schedule:` and checked BEFORE any bundle runs (`dropin_check_order_`),
    against what the two phases can actually promise: an exclusive bundle may name any parallel bundle
    (the whole parallel phase finishes first) or an exclusive one earlier in name order; a parallel bundle
    may name only a bundle in its OWN lane, earlier in that lane, because two lanes run at the same time
    and nothing orders them. A contradiction is fatal; a predecessor a filter left out is fatal in a full
    run and a loud NOTE in a filtered one. 55-owner.sh is the only file that declares one today — the
    other dependency the light pass recorded (55-owner calling `probe_queue_idle`, written in
    37-library.sh) is gone, because that helper and `probe_queue_count` moved into `scripts/e2e.sh` where
    README's second convention always said they belonged. `scripts/check.sh` now ENFORCES that convention:
    a stage lists each drop-in's own `name()` definitions and fails if another drop-in calls one, over a
    copy with comments and quoted strings stripped (without that, the word "member" in an assertion
    message reads as a call to 55-owner.sh's `member()` — three such false positives, one true one).

    **(b) `has_file_f` / `lacks_file_f`.** The `has_file`/`lacks_file` pair are basic-regex greps, so `.`
    matches anything and `[` opens a character class; step 81 pinned a CSS rule with the opening bracket
    of `[data-playing]` amputated to dodge it. The `-F` pair takes the pattern as plain text and is what a
    pin on exact source should use. The regex pair stays, unchanged, for the patterns that want one.

    **(c) Three more knobs, none of them needed for the gate.** `E2E_APP_CPUS` sets the app container's
    `cpus` quota for the run, by the same shell-variable mechanism `E2E_SWEEP_INTERVAL` uses, so a lane
    stack can be timed at the cores its box has without hand-editing that checkout's `.env`; it must not
    exceed the host's `nproc` (DEPLOY §7 — a hard container-create error, not a warning), and step 1 prints
    the quota compose RESOLVED either way, because a run's timings mean nothing without it.
    `E2E_CLEAN_BUCKET=1` turns step 17's closing bucket census into an assertion (below). `E2E_SELFTEST=1`
    is not a run at all: it exercises the harness's two retry wrappers against a stub and exits.

    **(d) The retry wrappers are now tested, and the bucket is counted once at the end.** `dc` retries
    once on docker's exit 125 and `curl_` once on curl's 7/28/35; neither branch had ever fired in a real
    run, so a typo inside one would have surfaced for the first time during the failure it exists to
    absorb. Both call their tool through one indirection (`docker_`, `curl__`) that `E2E_SELFTEST=1`
    replaces with a stub failing once and then succeeding; `scripts/check.sh` runs it, and it pins what
    must NOT be retried as firmly as what must — `http()` carries the writes, a repeated write is a wrong
    assertion, so a non-125 docker failure and an exit-22 curl go straight through. Separately, step 54's
    bucket-wide `extra` assertion became a FLOOR when the bundles started running in lanes, which left a
    stray object under a clip nobody in the run owns caught nowhere; step 17 now ends with
    `admin orphans --min-age 0` after the last bundle AND after its own deletes, printing the census in
    every run and asserting `extra=0` only under `E2E_CLEAN_BUCKET=1` — a real invariant on a stack the run
    started clean, and none of the suite's business on a shared one.

    **(e) The clock is measured instead of assumed.** The Docker VM's clock runs behind this host and
    STEPS — 12–27 s behind, and backwards by 27 s inside one 25 s sleep under load. Nothing in
    the product cares, but three seconds-scale probes carry that margin implicitly and each failure cost an
    hour of rediscovering the fact. Step 1 prints `host−VM skew Ns` and the summary prints it again, with a
    NOTE when it moved; neither asserts anything. In the same spirit, step 73's second half — "the repairer
    left its own live encode alone" — is now proven from the repairer's OWN LOG ORDER (its claim line, the
    repair line, and the line that ends its own run if it has one), which is a single append-only stream
    from a single process and consults no clock at all; the `running_for` read taken seconds later is kept,
    and when the margin is lost the step says so in a NOTE instead of dying on an empty read.

    **Deferred, with the reason, because a fix that cannot be proven is worse than a recorded gap.**
    (i) Splitting the seven exclusive bundles so only the instance-wide step of each stays exclusive
    renames files (a drop-in's name IS its first step number) and rewrites this section's bundle list —
    a decision about the suite's shape that wants its own gate, and its "one step each" premise does not
    hold for 51-admin, whose step 52 also reads the instance-wide `/healthz` queue block. (ii) A retry for
    a write the app refused before reading its body cannot be built the way it was specified: the request
    id is minted server-side and reaches the client only in the `X-Request-ID` response header, which is
    exactly what is lost in the tunnel failure it would absorb, and a weaker correlation (method + path +
    a recent 4xx) cannot tell two identical POSTs apart, which is the one thing a write retry must not get
    wrong. (iii) The 503 page still has no screenshot: `clippet serve` opens and migrates its database at
    BOOT, so a `DATA_DIR` it cannot read makes the process exit rather than serve the page, and the page is
    only reachable from a per-request database failure — a database that opens and then breaks under a live
    process. The one deterministic route to the same rendered body is the crawler hold, which reuses this
    template on purpose, and it is a race against the card going ready.


270. **The storage-cost line: two optional prices, one aggregate served-bytes counter, and an estimate
    on three surfaces** (ROADMAP #39's storage-cost half; migration `0017`; branch `storage`,
    2026-09-11). The owner's frame was a storage-cost line that could be queried, for one server on a NAS
    and a friend's on a cloud bucket. **"Query" cannot mean asking the provider** —
    that is a call-home and a second credential, both on the anti-feature list — so it means the
    operator types what they pay and the app does the arithmetic on numbers it already has. What it
    needed was one number that did not exist: how many bytes this instance has SENT.

    **(a) Two optional prices.** `STORAGE_PRICE_PER_GB_MONTH` and `EGRESS_PRICE_PER_GB`, plain
    decimals in the operator's own currency per GB, parsed into millionths (`config.PriceScale`) so
    the value round-trips exactly. Currency-agnostic by construction: no surface prints a symbol,
    because the app has never been told one and never asks. Validation is a plain decimal, at most six
    fractional digits, at most `MaxPricePerGB` (10^6) before the point; a sign, an exponent, a
    separator or a currency symbol is fatal at boot naming the variable. `STORAGE_BUDGET_BYTES` is
    untouched and stays the advisory line erratum 157 made it.

    **UNSET IS ABSENT, NEVER ZERO.** With no price the cost keys are missing from `/healthz`, the
    `cost:` line is missing from `admin stats`, and the settings page's cost cells read the muted word
    `unpriced`. A `0.00` an operator never configured says "storage here is free", which is the one
    wrong thing this feature could say. A price of `0` IS a number and is honoured as one: it is how a
    friend on R2 records that egress costs them nothing.

    **(b) One aggregate counter, and nothing else** (migration `0017`, `bytes_served(day TEXT PRIMARY
    KEY, bytes INTEGER NOT NULL)`, `day` = `YYYY-MM-DD` UTC). Every byte the app hands a viewer goes
    through one `http.ServeContent` in `httpapi.serveObject` — media, posters, the Light copy a card
    fetches, filmstrips, preview GIFs — and `servedWriter` counts the body bytes of a 200 or a 206
    there. It counts what was WRITTEN, so a viewer who aborts a ranged read is charged what they
    received; an error envelope this package writes through the same writer (the 416 and 412
    `objectErrorWriter` re-answers), a 304 and a HEAD write no body and cost nothing. Static assets
    and HTML pages are deliberately out: they come from the image, not from the bucket the operator
    pays for.

    **In those words, because it must never grow:** the counter is *aggregate bytes per day and
    nothing else*. No viewer, no IP, no user agent, no session, no account, no clip, no route — the
    table has no column to join on and nothing to redact, and "private view counts are the ceiling"
    (§8.2) is not crossed for an accounting number. There is no provider API, no price lookup and no
    egress of any kind: §15's list of outbound destinations is unchanged by this feature.

    **(c) The flush window: 30 s, or 64 MiB, whichever comes first, and again at shutdown.** The media
    path adds to a map in memory (`internal/cost.Counter`) and never writes; the loop UPSERTs one row
    per day it holds. The pair is chosen from what a crash LOSES: 64 MiB at a typical 0.01 per GB is
    0.00064 of a currency unit, four orders of magnitude below the hundredth any surface prints, and
    an idle instance costs no statement at all because an empty window makes no call. **A crash
    therefore loses up to one window of served bytes, and that is an accepted cost** — this is an
    estimate for an operator, never a ledger. A write that fails puts its bytes back, so the counter
    can be late but never short. The READ path adds the unflushed window to the row, so `/healthz` and
    the settings page are exact the instant a response ends; `admin stats`, a second process sharing
    the file, is up to one window behind and says so here rather than in its output. Retention is
    `cost.RetentionDays` = 400 days, pruned by the sweeper's existing tick with one DELETE (a year plus
    a margin: the surfaces show today and this month, and the history is what makes "is this month
    unusual" answerable at all).

    **(d) The arithmetic, in one place.** `internal/cost` owns both halves — the counter and the sums —
    because they are one feature and nothing else wants either: no other package then has to know
    about UTC days, flush windows, decimal gigabytes or how a price is scaled, and the three surfaces
    cannot disagree. Stored bytes → GB at **1 GB = 10^9 bytes, the decimal unit providers bill in**
    (not the GiB the rest of the product measures files in — the 7.4 % difference would understate
    every bill) × the month price = the stored cost; this calendar month's served bytes × the egress
    price = the served cost. Amounts are integers of hundredths, rounded once, half away from zero,
    and rendered with two decimals and no symbol. It is an ESTIMATE and never a bill: the word and the
    approximation sign appear on every surface that shows one, and none of them counts an object no
    row references any more (`admin orphans` is that report, exactly as erratum 157 said of the
    budget).

    **(e) Three surfaces, and only two of them may show a price.** `/healthz` gains a `storage_usage`
    object beside `storage_budget`: `{stored_bytes?, served_today_bytes?, served_month_bytes?}` — three
    JSON numbers of bytes, and **no cost, ever**. The first cut carried the two amounts there and they
    were taken out before the feature shipped: the route is ANONYMOUS and is reachable wherever the
    origin is, so an amount printed beside the byte count it was computed from is the operator's
    configured per-GB price, one division away, and §15 says this route exposes no configured value.
    A priced instance's `storage_usage` is byte-identical to an unpriced one's, which is the property
    the httpapi test asserts. The three byte counts stay, on the precedent `storage_budget.used` set
    (erratum 157): aggregates that name no clip, no account and nobody who watched anything. DEPLOY
    §31.4 names the reverse-proxy answer for an operator who would rather even those were not public.
    Every key is optional and an absent one is never a zero — `stored_bytes` waits for the sweeper's
    first reading exactly as `storage_budget` does. **The key is `storage_usage` and not `storage`**,
    which has been the cached store-ping STRING since Phase 1 and is what the compose healthcheck and
    DEPLOY §24's alerts read; renaming that for a nicer key would break them silently.

    The costs live where the reader is known. `admin stats` prints `served:  today=… month=…` always
    and `cost:    stored ≈… /month  served ≈… this month` only when priced — that reader is inside the
    container. The settings page gains one `Storage` panel in the row grammar — `stored`, `served this
    month`, and `budget` only when `STORAGE_BUDGET_BYTES` is set — instance-wide and visible to every
    signed-in account, which is the precedent the library's budget line set (erratum 157) and the same
    reason: there is no admin role in this product, and the person who would clear space is as likely
    to be the friend uploading. **No per-account figure, no chart, no tier.**
    *Amended 2026-10-27 (erratum 349):* the panel is now the instance OWNER's (the first account); every other
    account reads its head and one sentence and no figure. The library's budget line stays on every account's page.

    **(f) One behaviour changed outside this feature.** The sweeper now publishes its storage reading
    whether or not `STORAGE_BUDGET_BYTES` is set (`sweeper.checkBudget`), because `stored_bytes` IS
    that reading and both surfaces read the cached value rather than growing an aggregate over `clips`
    — which is the rule erratum 157 set for this number, and the reason `/healthz` costs one indexed
    range over at most 31 rows of a ≤400-row table and no scan of anything. The WARNING still needs a
    budget, and the `storage_budget` object is still gated on one, so nothing the BUDGET surfaces show
    changes; the reading's new home is the `storage_usage` object above, which carries bytes and never
    a price (item (e)) — DEPLOY §31.4 names the reverse-proxy answer for an operator who would rather
    the probe were not public.

    E2E step 87 (`scripts/e2e.d/87-storage.sh`, exclusive — it asserts on an instance-wide counter)
    proves it live: two ranged reads of its own clip, `/healthz` counting them at once, the window
    reaching the database, `admin stats`' line, the settings panel, and no cost anywhere on an
    instance with no price. DEPLOY §31 is the operator's page; `config.MaxPriceFractionDigits`,
    `cost.GB`, `cost.FlushEvery`/`FlushBytes` and `cost.RetentionDays` are the numbers above, in code.

272. **The E2E cleans up after ITSELF, including after an ABORTED run — `e2e_sweep_own`, at both ends**
    (the owner's ask of 2026-09-11: make the cleanup part of the E2E, or have it reuse a fixed set;
    `scripts/e2e.sh` steps 1 and 17; `scripts/visual.sh`;
    `scripts/e2e.d/README.md`). A run that PASSED already deleted what it made, bar four accounts step
    17's prune could not reach — it carried `--older-than 1h`, so by construction it never matched the
    users of the run it was ending, only its predecessors'. A run that was INTERRUPTED left everything:
    its accounts, their clips, their objects. The only thing that had ever cleared those was a person
    typing a delete loop by hand, and on 2026-09-11 exactly such a hand-typed sweep, with an EMPTY owner
    variable, destroyed every clip on the reference stack. The harness now holds a
    standing, narrowly-scoped licence to sweep its OWN litter and nothing else.
    (a) **One function, two call sites.** `e2e_sweep_own <why> [fatal|best-effort]` lists the stack's
    accounts (`admin users`), keeps only the ones its selector matches, force-expires every clip each of
    them owns (`admin ls --owner` → `admin expire <id> --ago 2h`, the same backdating steps 15 and 19
    use, so a leftover still `processing` is past expiry + `SWEEP_GRACE` as well), WAITS for the sweeper
    to destroy them (≤ 90 s, six ticks of the run's 15 s interval, one `admin ls` per poll), then prunes
    the accounts it emptied. It runs at the START of step 1 — after `dc up -d --build`, so the run's own
    `SWEEP_INTERVAL` is already in force, and before step 3 mints the names the selector matches — where
    it is FATAL: a stack that cannot be swept is not a stack to test on, and a run that starts on
    somebody else's leftovers has a bucket census and a user inventory that mean nothing. It runs again
    at the END of step 17, after that step's own DELETEs and before the `admin orphans` census and the
    hand-back, where it is BEST EFFORT — nothing there may fail a run that has already passed. Step 17's
    old prune IS this call; there is no second prune. The wait is a small bonus there: the census that
    follows now reads a settled stack rather than one with tombstones still in flight.
    (b) **The selector is the deliverable.** `E2E_OWN_RE='^e2e_[0-9]{9,11}(_[a-z0-9]{1,3})?$'` — the
    name step 3 registers (`e2e_<epoch>`) with, optionally, one of the suffixes this suite adds to it
    (`_b`, `_c`, `_d`, `_s1`, `_s2`). It is a named constant whose comment says it is the only selector
    the function may ever use, because widening it is not an edit to a regular expression, it is a
    change to what the harness may destroy. Digits after `e2e_` are required and the suffix is at most
    three characters, so `demo_account`, `alice`, `visual_<epoch>`, an operator's own `e2e_alice`, a
    bare `e2e_` and `e2e_1789149541_long` are all outside it. Four further guards. The target list is
    PRINTED before anything is expired — `[e2e]   sweep (<why>): N clip(s) of M e2e_ account(s): <ids>`
    followed by the account names, or `nothing to sweep`, every time, so "found nothing" and "never ran"
    cannot read alike. Every id is checked against `internal/ids`' TWO grammars (`E2E_ID_RE`: twelve
    base62 characters, or three to four capitalised 3–9-letter words — §7, errata 248–251; a run mints
    both and an aborted one can leave either) AND against the count line `admin ls` prints for itself,
    so output the function cannot read ends the run instead of being guessed at. No loop body ever runs
    with an empty variable. And the account prune is still `admin users prune 'e2e_%' … --no-clips`,
    which can only ever remove an account owning no clip and no collection at all; that pattern's `_` is
    a LIKE wildcard and so is wider than the regex on its own — acceptable only because the regex
    already bounded what was EMPTIED and `--no-clips` bounds the rest. Its `--older-than` is now `1s`,
    not `1h`: at step 1 the run's own accounts do not exist yet, and at step 17 they are meant to go too.
    (c) **What it cannot clear, and says so.** `users prune` skips an account that still owns a
    COLLECTION, and a collection is removed only through its owner's session — which an interrupted run
    took with it. The sweep re-reads the inventory after the prune and NOTEs any such account by name;
    it owns no clips and no objects by then. Nothing else survives a sweep.
    (d) **Why not a fixed, reusable account set**, the other half of the owner's ask: the four parallel
    lanes inside one run already need distinct accounts, and the per-run stamp is what keeps two stacks
    and two runs apart — a fixed set would only move the question to "whose leftovers are the fixed
    accounts' leftovers". The sweep is the mechanism either way, so it is the whole change.
    (e) **`scripts/visual.sh`** runs its existing `visual_%` prune at the START as well as at the end,
    `--older-than 1s` at both, for the same reason: a pass interrupted before `visual.js`' `finally` is
    cleared by the next pass rather than by hand. It removes EMPTY accounts and never a clip
    (`--no-clips` again), so a pass whose clip survived is left exactly where it is, in
    `clippet admin users`, for a person to deal with.
    (f) **Proven without a stack.** `E2E_SELFTEST=1 bash scripts/e2e.sh` (which `scripts/check.sh` runs)
    now also pins both patterns against planted text: the name filter keeps an 11-digit stamp and 1–3
    character suffixes and drops `alice`, `demo_account`, `visual_*`, `e2e_alice`, a 4-character
    suffix and a bare `e2e_`; the id tripwire accepts both grammars and refuses an 11-character id,
    uncapitalised words, two words, five words, a count line and a path — with `BigHorse` and not
    `CorrectHorse` as the two-word case, because the latter is also exactly twelve base62 characters
    and `internal/ids` accepts it as a compact id (the overlap `New` refuses to mint into). 35 checks,
    up from 23.

273. **The display mark's tracking area is the whole page, and the eyes wait for a move** (the owner,
    2026-09-11, on the live front door: the area the eyes react to should be bigger, because on so
    minimal a page the mark itself is a small target;
    `web/static/app.js` `setupEyes`, `web/STYLE.md`, `scripts/lib/visual.js`). Erratum 267 made the auth
    card the 40 px mark's area. On the front door, login and register the mark is the only thing on the
    page, so the area is now the document itself: the eyes come out wherever the pointer moves on those
    pages and leave when it leaves the window. The header mark keeps the bar. With that, a page that
    loads under a stationary pointer would have answered Chromium's layout-time `pointerenter` and looked
    at a cursor nobody is holding (the trap 267 parked the visual pass's pointer around), so the entrance
    now waits for the first `pointermove` inside the area and never fires on the enter alone; a real hand
    always moves. Nothing else changes: the touch gate, the reduced-motion gate, the exit on leave, the
    exact rest. `visual.sh`'s pointer park still sits in the page gutter (outside the header's area) and
    its rest frames now rely on the move rule rather than on being outside the display mark's area.

274. **The living mark, second ship: every face the owner mapped** (ROADMAP #38; the owner's roles table
    and options page of 2026-09-11 — the described rarity kept, the middle of the three sizes picked;
    the go of 2026-09-13;
    `web/static/app.js` (`setupEyes`, `FACES`, `FACE_OF`, `moment`, `startAmbient`), `web/static/app.css`

    `scripts/lib/visual.js` (`domFaces`, 34 frames); no route, no header, no migration, no E2E step).
    - **What ships.** The eight faces of the exploration (`.e2e/logo/pp-alive.html`, gitignored) — `glance
      blink wink drift smile beam gasp sulk` — on the same overlay erratum 267 injects, with their round-3/4

      centred on y 703, x 242–1463, clipped from the two stems by an evenodd `clipPath` so no bow, drop or

      `drift`, `follow`; rare `wink`; meaningful `blink`, `smile`, `beam`, `gasp`, `sulk`; off none.
    - **The table.** ONE object in app.js, `FACE_OF`, maps the moments the app already knows to a face, and
      one function, `moment(name)`, plays it on every mark that has an overlay — the 21 px header mark and the
      40 px display mark alike, wherever the moment happens: `landed` (the 201 arrives, the row appears) →
      `blink`; `queued` → `smile`; `encoding` (a poll sees `processing`) → `blink`; `ready` → `smile`;
      `failed` → `sulk`; `copied` (Copy link, Copy embed, a token's Copy) → `beam`, and the FIRST copy of a
      tab (`sessionStorage`, try/catch) → `smile` instead; `saved` (Details Save, Defaults, the theme pick,
      a collection's order or clips, a password change) → `beam`; `deleted` (the clip page's Delete, a
      collection's Delete, a bulk delete) → `gasp`; `signedin` (the library after a login or a
      registration) → `smile`; `notfound` → `gasp`, which the 404 template spells as `data-face="gasp"` on its
      mark (a mark that arrives wearing a face plays it at boot). The moments a page leaves on — a sign-in,
      a delete that goes to the library, a collection save that reloads — are carried across the navigation
      in `sessionStorage` (`carry`) and played by the page that comes next; a `ready` that reloads the share
      page (or the embed) lets the smile land first (`afterMoment`, bounded at 4 s). The state moments fire on
      a CHANGE of state under the poll only, never on a page that loads mid-encode. The hover row of the owner's
      table (`gasp`) is treated as none: `follow` already answers the cursor.
    - **One state machine per mark, never two faces at once.** The follow's IN/FOLLOW/OUT gained a FACE
      mode: a storyboard is a list of steps (tweens, holds, parallel tracks) walked on the same frame loop;
      a face that arrives mid-face queues behind it, two deep and never the same as the tail (a batch of
      twenty uploads is one blink, not twenty), with a 300 ms breath between two; a face that arrives while
      the eyes are out under the pointer starts from where they are (no `enter` snap, so nothing pops); a
      pointer that moves mid-face waits, and brings the eyes out on its next move once the face is over.
      After every face: `MARK_REST`, one render, `data-face` and `sad` removed — exact rest, byte-identical
      to the injected overlay, which the DOM test compares as markup. While a face plays the wordmark wears
      `data-face="<name>"` (what the tests read; no CSS keys on it).
    - **The ambient timer.** One per open page, never on a page whose only mark is the embed's: every 45–90 s
      (uniform) a `glance` or a `drift`, alternating, and with probability 1/12 a `wink` instead (a few times
      an hour) — on every mark with eyes. It accumulates idle time on a 500 ms tick and pauses while the eyes
      are out under the pointer, while ANY face plays and while the tab is hidden (a throttled background

    - **The whole mark.** Pupil radius **150** on both marks (was 125; the owner's middle pick, one constant).

275. **The parked nits of five lanes, and the four things among them that change a contract**
    (the cleanup list's `follow`, `wish`, `harness`, `litter` and `storage` sections, held since 2026-09-11;
    the owner's go of 2026-09-13; lane `nits5`). Most
    of the twenty-odd entries are inside the file they name and need nothing here. These do.

    **(a) `clippet admin collections ls|rm` — the one leftover a sweep could not clear**
    (`cmd/clippet/admin_collections.go` (new), `internal/db/collections.go`, `scripts/e2e.sh`,
    `scripts/visual.sh`, DEPLOY §24). `admin users prune` only ever removes an account that owns
    NOTHING (erratum 86), a collection counts, and a collection was created and deleted only through
    its owner's SESSION — which an interrupted run took with it. So erratum 272(c) had to write down
    that the harness's own sweep would NOTE such an account by name at every run and no run could
    ever clear it. This is the verb it was waiting for.
    `rm` is `db.DeleteCollection`, the same statement the owner's own DELETE route calls: the
    membership rows go with it through the FK cascade and **not one clip is touched**, because a
    collection is a list of links and deleting the list deletes links. That is what makes a
    destructive verb safe to hand to a script at all — there is no data behind a collection to lose —
    and it is why this one is allowed where nothing else is. The house rules for such a
    verb are all kept anyway: `ls` finds the id, `rm` PRINTS the row (id, owner, clip count, title)
    before it removes it, an unknown id is `not found` and exit 1, and `--owner <username>` is an
    optional second selector that refuses the command when the row belongs to somebody else. `ls`
    prints in `admin ls`'s grammar — a header, one row per collection, a count line naming the filter
    — with the TITLE last and QUOTED (`%q`), so that a title carrying a space, a tab or a newline
    stays inside its own row and the listing can be read by column. `db.ListCollectionSummaries`
    (owner id, or "" for every owner) is the one new statement; there is no migration.
    **`e2e_sweep_own` gains one step, between the clips and the accounts**: for each account
    `E2E_OWN_RE` already matched (never a wider selector), `admin collections ls --owner` and then
    `admin collections rm <id> --owner`, with the guard shape of the clips beside it — the target
    list printed before anything is removed, every id checked against `E2E_ID_RE` AND against the
    listing's own count line, no loop body running on an empty variable, and output the function
    cannot parse ending the run instead of being guessed at. `scripts/visual.sh` does the same for
    `visual_<epoch-ms>` before and after a pass. A run now leaves nothing at all, and the NOTE that
