    named an unclearable account now means something the sweep did not expect rather than the normal
    ending of an interrupted run.

    **(b) `ParseShare` accepts `/embed/{id}`, and the wrappers Discord actually puts round a link**
    (`internal/urls/urls.go`; erratum 268(b) is AMENDED here rather than rewritten). **MOOT since
    erratum 286: `ParseShare` and its tests are gone with the `link` option they were written for —
    this clause is history, kept for the record.** Two of the
    verifier's notes, and both were the feature being right about the rule and wrong about the
    sentence. `msgLinkForeign` — *"That is not a clip link from this Clippet."* — was literally
    untrue of `{origin}/embed/{id}`: that is this instance's own player URL for exactly that clip,
    which this instance emitted. It is accepted now and names the same clip; the reply re-issues the
    canonical share link, as it does for every accepted spelling. `/c/{id}` stays refused, because a
    collection is not a clip and "post this clip" has no answer for a list of them. And the `<…>`
    trim became a LOOP that also takes `||…||`: Discord's own doubled `<<…>>` and its spoiler wrap
    are what a real paste carries, and one trim round refused both. It is bounded at four rounds, so
    it is still a pure function over a string with no loop a caller can lengthen. The
    protocol-relative `//host/{id}` stays refused (no scheme, so not a link of ours) and a test says
    so. **The load-bearing sentence of 268 is untouched: a link option is not a fetch option.** Every
    spelling is decided by string comparison before any goroutine exists; §15's destination list is
    unchanged.

    **(c) A read that FAILED is not a measurement that has not happened yet**
    (`internal/web/pages.go`). The settings page's Storage panel had two state words and needed
    three: `unpriced` (no price is configured), `not measured yet` (the seconds between boot and the
    sweeper's first reading) and now `unavailable` (the read itself failed). The first two go away by
    themselves and the third does not, and a panel that spelled them alike sent the operator looking
    for the wrong thing. `admin stats` has always printed `served:  unavailable: <err>`, so the two
    surfaces now say it in the same word.

    **(d) The edge-transient class: a bounded retry for a write whose EXPECTED answer is a refusal**
    (`scripts/e2e.sh` `http_refused`, `E2E_NONLOOPBACK`; the drop-ins listed below). On 2026-09-11
    three consecutive gate runs died in the same place: the tunnel dropped multipart POSTs that the
    app refuses BEFORE reading the body (steps 48 and 49), and the origin answered every one of them
    correctly in isolation. The harness retries READS on curl 7/28/35 and has never
    retried a write, for the reason erratum 269(d) states — a repeated write is a wrong assertion —
    and erratum 269's deferred item (ii) recorded that the obvious fix could not be built: the
    request id reaches the client only in a response header, which is exactly what such a failure
    loses.
    **A refused write needs no correlation, because there is nothing to correlate.** A request the
    origin refuses has no side effect to double: a repeated 401 is a 401, a repeated 403 is a 403,
    nothing was minted the first time and nothing is minted the second. `http_refused` is therefore
    http() plus one retry, and ONLY where a step asserts a 4xx and nothing else. It retries curl's
    7/28/35 and a 502 or 520–524 — an edge's own vocabulary for "I could not reach or read from the
    origin", never something this app emits — printing `retry (edge)` each time, and it does all of
    that only when `E2E_NONLOOPBACK` says something sits in front of the origin. On loopback it
    retries nothing at all, because there is no edge to absorb and a 502 there is a real answer worth
    failing on. **Every other write is still never retried**, and http() is what carries those: the
    replacement POST of step 49, the trim of step 65, every upload.
    `E2E_NONLOOPBACK` is one derivation of a question the suite already asked once inline (87-storage's
    "nothing bodyless was charged" bound, which an edge may legitimately break). The converted sites
    are exactly the ones whose only expected outcome is a refusal, and they are all in the drop-ins:
    the two multipart POSTs of step 48 and the two of step 49 that the gate actually died on, the
    bad-token upload of step 50, the read-token upload of step 35, five bulk refusals and a
    stranger's PATCH in 37-library, nine poster refusals in 43-watch, two token-mint refusals and
    two password/login refusals in 33-account, `POST /oembed`, two settings refusals,
    `theme=neon`, `POST /`, `POST /{reserved}` and the unsigned interaction of step 86 —
    thirty-two in all (5 + 6 + 9 + 5 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1, by file). A
    refusal reached through a bundle's own helper (`bulk`, `member`, `oembed`), which also carries
    successes, was left alone: the helper is the wrong place for this distinction.

    **(e) Four smaller corrections that move something written down.** `internal/config`'s
    `parsePrice` measured the LENGTH of the whole part against the ceiling, so a zero-padded
    `00000015` was refused as "above 1000000 per GB"; leading zeros are padding, not magnitude, and
    are trimmed before the check. `admin doctor` gains a **`prices`** row — the two optional prices
    as the app PARSED them (`storage 0.015/GB-month, egress unset`) or the fact that both are unset,
    and never an amount: what a price makes of your bytes is `admin stats`' business, and
    `cost.PriceString` un-scales a price in the one package that scaled it. `app.js`'s `setupEyes`
    gains an idempotence guard (one overlay per mark, whatever re-boots), and its `aim()` maps y with
    the viewBox's own height scale instead of the x scale — the overlay is
    `preserveAspectRatio="none"`, so a mark whose box is not exactly 1.15:1 stretched the two axes
    differently and tilted every aim by that much (3.3 % at the header's 21 px). `E2E_SELFTEST=1`
    ends in **`E2E SELFTEST PASS`** and never in `E2E PASS`: it touches no stack, and a caller
    greping for the suite's own pass line must not be able to read one as the other.

    **(f) What the harness now proves that it did not.** The self-test (50 checks, up from 35) pins
    `http_refused`'s asymmetry — retried through an edge, never on loopback, never on a refusal that
    arrived — and the collections listing the sweep parses, planted text and all. `visual.js`'s
    `domFollow` records the entrance FRAME BY FRAME in the page and insists the pupils were seen
    part-way between rest and settled (a build that deleted the 260 ms tween passed every settled
    assertion), and it aims the pointer BETWEEN the two eyes and below them, where the only correct
    answer is two offsets leaning opposite ways — the convergence check could not see an eye aimed
    from its neighbour's centre. Step 17's closing bucket census asserts `prefixes=` and `missing=`
    beside `extra=` under `E2E_CLEAN_BUCKET=1` (the stray it exists to catch can land in any of the
    three), and step 1 reads the APP service's `cpus:` out of the merged compose config rather than
    the first one in the file. `scripts/check.sh`'s cross-file call stage says out loud that it leans
    on running without `pipefail` and no longer needs to, and its scratch scan skips the one path
    `scripts/check.sh` rather than any file named that.

    **(g) Three calls, recorded rather than coded.** A `link:` to a FAILED clip still posts its
    link-out card (MOOT since erratum 286 withdrew the option; kept for the record): the bot's `link`
    option mirrors `internal/web`'s `lookupClip` exactly, which turns
    nobody away but a clip in `ClipDeleting`, and a second rule about which STATES may be re-posted
    would be a second answer to "what does this link name" — the owner's to change once it bites.
    The living mark's gate stays `(hover: hover)` and not `(any-hover: hover)`: erratum 267 chose the
    PRIMARY pointer deliberately, and a tablet whose primary pointer is a finger is not a device this
    should animate for because a mouse is also plugged in. And `visual.sh`'s `visual_%` prune keeps
    its LIKE wildcard: `users prune` takes the pattern straight into `username LIKE ?` with no
    `ESCAPE` clause, so `visual\_%` would match a literal backslash and quietly stop matching
    anything — the exact risk (an account named `visualX…` that owns NOTHING) is written in the
    script beside the pattern instead.

276. **A directory instead of a bucket — `STORAGE_BACKEND=fs`** (ROADMAP #37, the owner's ask of 2026-09-13:
    a local option that points at a mounted NAS, and the pick of option 1; lane `local`. New: `internal/store/fs.go` + `fs_test.go`,
    `cmd/clippet/admin_storage.go` + `storage_fs_test.go`, `compose.fs.yaml`, DEPLOY §32, E2E step 88
    (`scripts/e2e.d/88-fsstore.sh`, exclusive). Changed: `internal/config/config.go`,
    `internal/store/store.go`, `internal/httpx/health.go`, `cmd/clippet/{main,serve,doctor,admin}.go`,
    `.env.example`, DEPLOY §7/§15/§24, API.md's `/healthz`. No migration; no schema change; the S3
    path is byte-for-byte what it was.)

    ROADMAP #37 called the backend the small half and everything that assumes a bucket the real cost,
    and that is exactly how it came out: `fs.go` is one file behind an interface that already had two
    implementations, and the other nine touched files are config, doctor, stats, orphans, compose,
    backup and the docs.

    **(a) What ships.** `STORAGE_BACKEND=s3|fs` (default `s3`, everything unchanged) and
    `STORAGE_DIR`; `internal/store/fs.go` answering the seven-method contract over a directory;
    `store.Open(cfg)` as the ONE place the backend is chosen (`serve`, `admin`, `doctor` all come
    through it); `compose.fs.yaml`, the one-container flavour; `admin doctor`'s `store` row;
    `admin stats` reconciled; `admin storage migrate --to fs|s3 [--dry-run]`; `/healthz`'s `storage`
    string naming the backend that answered. **Not done, per #37's own non-goals:** no multi-node
    story, no replication, no "both at once" mode, and no second key space — `S3_KEY_PREFIX` is
    honoured on `fs` as a subdirectory, because it is a statement about the KEY SPACE and not about a
    bucket.

    **(b) The path law.** Keys become paths in ONE function (`fsStore.keyPath`), which refuses: a NUL
    or a backslash; an absolute key; an empty segment (so `clips//x` cannot be a second spelling of
    `clips/x`); a `.` or `..` segment; and — belt and braces after those four — any result that does
    not sit under the root. The empty key is the one that maps to the root itself, because `List("")`
    means "everything" the way an empty S3 prefix does; object methods refuse it through
    `objectPath`, which also refuses a trailing slash (a prefix is not something to open). It is a
    SECOND wall in front of a key space that is already safe — `internal/store/keys.go` is the only
    place a key is built (erratum 82) and the only user-influenced text in one is a sanitised
    `[a-z0-9]{1,8}` extension — which is the right number of walls for a function that turns a string
    into a path. `fs_test.go`'s `TestFSPathLaw` drives thirteen bad keys through all six key-taking
    methods and then asserts that a planted file next door to the store is untouched and that the
    store is still empty.

    **(c) Content type: NOT stored, and no sidecar.** The brief's fallback was a `.ct` file beside
    any object whose kind has no fixed extension. It is not needed and would have been worse than
    nothing, because **the `Store` contract never hands a content type back**: `ObjectInfo` has no
    such field, `GetRange` returns bytes, and every media route sets `Content-Type` from the DATABASE
    — `clips.source_content_type` for the original (§15's content-type discipline), a fixed type for
    every derived object. A sidecar would therefore have been written by this code and read by
    nothing. `PutFile` accepts the argument and ignores it; the S3 store still sends it, because S3
    stores it and an operator with `mc` in the other window can see it.

    **(d) ETag is empty on `fs`.** The S3 store reports the provider's ETag and the Fake reports the
    sha256 it holds in memory. Hashing a 4 GiB original inside `admin ls --stat` to invent one here
    would make a report cost minutes, and a cheap synthetic (size+mtime) would invite comparison with
    the sha256 the database holds beside it. So: empty, and `admin ls --stat` renders an empty one as
    `etag=(not stored)` rather than as a blank that reads like a bug. `PutFile` still returns the
    sha256 it computed on the way in, which is what the database stores and what every caller
    actually uses.

    **(e) The seven methods.** `PutFile` = copy to a `.clippet-put-*` temp file in the DESTINATION's
    own directory → `fsync` → `chmod 0644` → `rename` → `fsync` the directory, so a crash leaves a
    temp file and never a truncated object under the key the database is about to point at; progress
    is fed once per 1 MiB chunk with `done` clamped to `total`, the contract minio.go's
    `progressHook` keeps. `Download` is the reverse through `path + ".part"` and a rename, exactly as
    the S3 store does it. `GetRange` is `open` + `Seek` + `io.LimitReader`, end INCLUSIVE, `-1` =
    EOF, an end past the last byte CLAMPED and a start at or past the end an ERROR — S3's own edges,
    asserted side by side against the Fake in `TestFSGetRangeEdges`, with the one place the two
    existing implementations already disagree called out (`end < -1`: minio.go's `rangeHeader`
    refuses it, the Fake clamps it; `fs` follows the real backend). An EMPTY object therefore has no
    satisfiable range, which is also what S3 says. `Stat` is one `os.Stat`. `List` is a STRING prefix
    (S3 answers `clips/ab` with `clips/abcdef/…` too, and `admin orphans` compares key strings), with
    the walk BOUNDED to the directory the prefix names, sorted by key. `DeletePrefix` removes the
    listed objects, prunes the directories it empties up to but never including the root (S3 has no
    directories, and a store that kept an empty tree per destroyed clip would grow inodes forever),
    then RE-LISTS and returns `ErrPrefixNotEmpty` if anything is left — the contract the sweeper's
    "the objects are gone" rests on. `Ping` is: the directory exists, is a directory, and takes a
    probe file that is removed again.

    **(f) The failure vocabulary is reused, not widened.** A missing file becomes `ErrNotFound`, so
    `errors.Is(err, store.ErrNotFound)` keeps working across both backends; every other failure gets
    one of the three erratum-90 public classes; a ping failure gets one of the five erratum-31 ping
    classes, and a missing or non-directory `STORAGE_DIR` is `bucket missing` — the set is closed on
    purpose and that is its member for "the place the objects live is not there".

    **(g) The validator's rules, verbatim.** `STORAGE_BACKEND` is `l.oneOf(…, s3, s3, fs)`.
    `STORAGE_DIR` is required on `fs`, optional on `s3` (where it is what a migration would copy
    into), and validated whenever it is set — a value that would be wrong on `fs` is worth refusing
    before the operator flips the switch, not after. It must be absolute; it must be CLEAN (no `.` or
    `..` segment); it may not be `/`; and it may not BE, CONTAIN or SIT INSIDE `DATA_DIR` or
    `SCRATCH_DIR`, each refusal naming both paths. The overlap rules are the ones with teeth:
    `SCRATCH_DIR` is walked by the boot janitor and the sweeper, which REMOVE a working directory
    whose clip is gone (§12), so a media store under it would be deleted a clip at a time by the
    app's own housekeeping; `DATA_DIR` is the small precious half of the backup and the media store
    is the large one, and a deployment that cannot tell an operator which is which has lost the
    argument about what to copy where. The paths are CONTAINER paths and are therefore always POSIX,
    so the check uses `path` rather than `filepath` and does not depend on the machine a test runs on.

    **(h) On `fs` the four bucket variables are REFUSED, and that is the feature's best line.** §15's
    guarantee is "the only outbound destinations this binary has are the S3 endpoint and Discord",
    and it is enforced in the endpoint validator and the webhook allowlist because a promise an
    operator cannot check is not a promise. On `fs` the media path has NO outbound destination, so
    the sentence gets STRONGER: with the webhook and the bot unset, such an instance opens no
    outbound socket whatsoever. A leftover `S3_ENDPOINT=` line in `.env` would leave a reader unable
    to establish that by reading the file, so it does not boot:
    `S3_ENDPOINT: STORAGE_BACKEND=fs takes no S3_* variable: the media lives in STORAGE_DIR and this
    instance has no bucket, so remove the line`. All four are reported at once (erratum 104).
    `config.S3Vars` is the list, in one place, because three callers need the same one.

    **(i) The migrate verb's shape, and why.** `admin storage migrate --to fs|s3 [--dry-run]` needs
    BOTH stores configured at once, which (h) forbids. The brief offered "ignored with a NOTE unless
    migrating" or a `--from-s3-env` flag; the shape chosen is neither, because a third one is simpler
    AND stronger: `config.LoadForMigrate` is a second ENTRY POINT that relaxes exactly that one rule,
    and `cmd/clippet/main.go` routes exactly `admin storage migrate` through it. There is no variable
    an operator can set, so the relaxation is UNFORGEABLE — `clippet serve` cannot reach it, and an
    instance serving on `fs` provably has no bucket configured. `TestMainRoutesTheMigrateVerbThrough
    LoadForMigrate` pins both halves: the same environment kills `clippet migrate` naming all four
    variables, and gets the migrate verb past the loader.
    The verb's guard is the house shape for a non-destructive operation: **it never deletes from
    the source** (not on success, not on a re-run — what is left over afterwards is the operator's to
    remove, with the old store still configured and `admin stats` still able to count it), it prints
    the PLAN before a byte moves (clips, objects, bytes, both stores named, one line per clip), and
    `--dry-run` prints exactly that and stops. The source is the CONFIGURED store and `--to` names
    the other; `--to` naming the configured one is a usage error. **Every object is verified at the
    destination by the sha256 of the WHOLE object**, read back through the destination store and
    compared with what the source delivered (plus the size it reports). The first cut of this
    compared the first 64 KiB, which the verifier proved is blind to a corruption anywhere past it:
    a one-byte change at offset 1,000,000 was reported "verified". A migration is exactly the moment
    to pay one read per object for certainty — it happens once, an operator is watching it, and what
    it decides is whether every clip can be served from somewhere else from now on. A re-run copies
    what is missing, re-verifies what is there, and **copies again anything whose hash does not
    match**, so the summary's own remedy ("fix the cause and run this again") is true even when the
    failure left a same-size wrong file behind — before that fix such an object was a permanent
    failure no re-run could clear. Any failure is exit 1 and a line saying not to flip
    `STORAGE_BACKEND` yet. It carries a clip's whole PREFIX and
    not its columns (so `meta/probe.json` and a superseded rendition travel), and it does NOT carry a
    row-less prefix — that is an orphan, `admin orphans` is the verb for those, and a migration that
    copied them would make cleaning up the first thing an operator did on the new store.

    **(j) The store marker.** `clippet serve` writes `.clippet-store` in `STORAGE_DIR` at boot (and
    `migrate --to fs` writes it after a copy); nothing else does, because a verb that wrote it would
    make the absence it exists to notice impossible to observe. It holds nothing that matters — its
    ABSENCE is the signal. `admin doctor` WARNs when it is missing on a database that already
    accounts for stored bytes, which is the shape a mis-mounted share takes: an empty directory where
    the media used to be, and an app that starts happily and answers 404 for every clip it still
    lists. A WARN and not a FAIL, because an instance upgraded from a build older than the marker
    looks identical from the inside. `List` never reports it as an object.

    **(k) doctor, reconciled.** The check table gains `store` and keeps `bucket`, so the set of row
    names is the same on both backends and two runs stay comparable — **thirteen rows at the time**,
    up from twelve (§20 erratum 278 took it to fourteen; the complete pin list lives in 278(k), which
    supersedes the shorter one this paragraph used to carry and which cost a gate run when it was
    followed literally). On `s3`: `store` is one
    line naming the backend and pointing at `bucket`, which does the work — nothing about that
    backend's report changed. On `fs`: `bucket` is a `skip` with its reason on the line, `creds` says
    there is no credential to get wrong, and `store` asks the directory's own questions — exists, IS
    a directory, writable by THIS uid (a probe file created and removed, the way the bucket check
    puts and removes a probe object), free space, whether it shares a filesystem with `SCRATCH_DIR`
    (reported, never judged: both answers are legitimate and only the operator knows which they
    deployed), the marker, and §15's strengthened sentence. So a healthy `fs` instance reports
    `14 checks, 13 ok, 0 warn, 0 fail, 1 skipped` (thirteen and twelve before erratum 278's `media`
    row; fifteen since erratum 302's `login` row).

    **(l) stats, reconciled.** On `s3` the budget line (a DATABASE sum of what the bucket should
    hold) and the disk line (the container's filesystem) describe two different places, and printing
    both is the point. On `fs` they describe ONE, so the budget line APPENDS
    ` backend=fs dir=… free=… size=…` — appends, so `used=` and `budget=` stay exactly where every
    parser and E2E step 87 look for them — and the listing line becomes `store:` instead of
    `bucket:`, because there is no bucket and a line that said otherwise would be the one place this
    feature lied. `disk:` is unchanged and goes on describing the database and the scratch disk.
    `orphans` needed no change at all: `reportExtras` walks `Store.List`, which a directory walk
    satisfies — proven with a planted stray file under a live clip and a planted row-less prefix, in
    a Go test and again in E2E step 88.

    **(m) `/healthz`'s `storage` string names the backend** — `ok (fs)`, `error: unavailable (s3)`.
    It is held to erratum 31's rule: one of two words, naming no endpoint, bucket, path or
    credential, and it answers the first question anybody asks of an unwell probe. A zero
    `StorageHealth` (every test that does not care) renders exactly as before.

    **(n) `compose.fs.yaml`, and why this shape.** A compose override cannot DELETE a service, and
    erratum 247 records what happened the last time a profile was written into `compose.yaml` itself
    for a service the default path needed. So the profile is ADDED FROM THE OVERRIDE: `minio` and
    `bucket-init` gain `profiles: ["bucket"]`, which nothing ever selects, and `app.depends_on` is
    cleared with the `!reset` tag (Compose ≥ 2.24) because a dependency on a service that is not
    being started is an error. `compose.yaml` is untouched, so `docker compose up` on the default
    file resolves three services exactly as it always did (`docker compose config --services` →
    `minio bucket-init app`), and with the override it resolves one. The override also binds
    `${STORAGE_DIR_HOST:?…}` to `/media` and passes the four `S3_*` through EMPTY (compose's own
    `${VAR:-default}` would otherwise put the bundled MinIO's values back, and on `fs` any one of
    them is a boot error). `STORAGE_DIR` is `/media` and NOT `/data/media`, which the brief
    suggested: `DATA_DIR` is `/data`, and (g) refuses a media store inside it.
    **`compose.yaml` also carries the pair as ordinary passthrough rows** —
    `STORAGE_BACKEND: ${STORAGE_BACKEND:-s3}` and `STORAGE_DIR: ${STORAGE_DIR:-}` — which the first
    cut omitted, and the verifier found the consequence: the override was then the ONLY way either
    variable could reach a container, so `.env.example`'s commented lines were inert, §7's two rows
    contradicted erratum 57's "`.env` is the single place an operator sets anything", and §32.3's
    s3→fs recipe exited 2 with `STORAGE_DIR unset`. Worse, the workaround an operator reaches for
    (`exec -e STORAGE_DIR=/media … migrate --to fs`) SUCCEEDS and writes the whole media set into the
    container's writable layer, which the next recreate throws away. Both rows interpolate to today's
    values, so the default path resolves byte-for-byte as before, and `compose.fs.yaml` still wins as
    an override. §32.3's recipe is now the one that binds the destination:
    `docker compose run --rm --no-deps -v ${STORAGE_DIR_HOST}:/media -e STORAGE_DIR=/media app admin
    storage migrate --to fs`, with the fs→s3 direction spelled as the `exec -e S3_…` form E2E step 88
    already used.

    **(o) The NAS caveats DEPLOY §32.2 writes down, and how they are known.** The share is mounted on
    the HOST and bound in — a mount inside a container needs `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` and dies with the
    container, while a host mount is something the OS already knows how to retry and log. *Ownership*
    is the one that bites: the image runs as uid 10001 and SMB/CIFS does not know about uids, so
    `uid=10001,gid=10001` on the mount is what makes the files the app's, and on NFS the export
    decides; the symptom is honest and immediate (doctor's `store` row FAILs naming the uid, `/readyz`
    refuses) rather than half-written data. *Directory `fsync`* is the one the code accommodates:
    CIFS does not implement it and answers `EINVAL`, so `syncDir` treats `EINVAL`/`ENOTSUP`/`ENOSYS`
    as "this filesystem does not do that" and carries on — the rename is still atomic and what is
    lost is the share's promise about metadata reaching a platter, which is the share's promise to
    make. The alternative, failing every upload on a share that is otherwise working, is not a
    trade this feature is worth. *Amended 2026-10-27 (run 23 lane `v2-migrate`):* the file MODE gets the same
    forgiveness. PutFile's `chmod 0644` of the temp file was unconditional, so a mount that keeps no unix modes
    (vfat/exFAT answer `EPERM`, SMB without unix extensions) failed every upload; now `EPERM`/`EACCES`,
    `ENOTSUP`/`ENOSYS` and `EINVAL` from that chmod are "this filesystem does not keep modes": the write goes on,
    the object keeps the mode the mount gives it, and the refusal is logged ONCE per store (`storage: this
    directory refuses a file mode change; objects keep the mode the mount gives them`); any other chmod error still
    fails the write. Reasoned and reproduced against a test double (`TestFSPutFileOnAMountThatRefusesModes`, seen
    failing with the old unconditional chmod), not on a real FAT or SMB mount. *Case folding* is recorded rather than handled: keys are
    `[A-Za-z0-9]` ids plus fixed lowercase names, so a case-insensitive share works and a
    case-FOLDING one could in principle collide two 12-character base62 ids — a lottery nobody wins,
    written down because it is the one way the key space could bite on a filesystem and not on a
    bucket. *Latency* is noted as the shape of the I/O (ranged reads; a transcode copies to local
    scratch first), with a stall surfacing as `storage timeout` exactly as an unreachable bucket
    does. The first two are properties of the mount that this deployment DEPENDS on and are stated as
    such; the last two are stated as what they are, one bounded risk and one performance note.

    **(q) Two rules the first cut left open, both found by the verifier and both now implemented.**

    *Symlinks are never followed under `STORAGE_DIR`.* The path law is LEXICAL, which is the right
    shape for a key space `keys.go` mints — but it says nothing about what the FILESYSTEM does with
    the path, and a symlink is the filesystem's own traversal. Proven before the fix: a symlink
    planted as an OBJECT under a live clip was `Stat`-able and servable, was reported by neither
    `admin orphans` nor `admin stats` (`List` skipped every non-regular entry), and SURVIVED a
    `DeletePrefix` that reported success; and a symlinked directory COMPONENT made `PutFile` write
    and `GetRange` read outside the root. The rule now: `safePath` `Lstat`s every component BELOW the
    root and refuses the key with `ErrBadKey` naming the offending path, so `PutFile`, `Download`,
    `GetRange` and `Stat` refuse; `List` REPORTS every non-regular entry as an object, so a planted
    symlink is litter `admin orphans` sees and `--delete` clears; `DeletePrefix` uses the lexical
    path plus a PARENT-only check, because `os.Remove` unlinks a symlink without following it and
    removing litter is the point. `STORAGE_DIR` **itself** may be a symlink — pointing it at a mount
    is an ordinary deployment and the rule starts below the root. It is a check and not a
    resolution, so it is not free of TOCTOU; that is acceptable because writing into `STORAGE_DIR`
    already implies the ability to replace any object in it. The rule exists so the store's own
    reports and its path law agree with each other, not to defend a directory an attacker already
    holds. DEPLOY §32.2 states it as an operator rule: the store is the app's alone.

    *`STORAGE_OP_TIMEOUT` is honoured on `fs`.* The three storage timeouts were inert on this
    backend while §32.2 promised a `storage timeout` from a stalled share, which was the S3 store's
    guarantee quietly borrowed. A filesystem call cannot be cancelled — `os.Stat` on a hung NFS
    mount blocks in the kernel — so `withOpTimeout` runs `Ping`, `Stat` and `List` on a goroutine and
    abandons it when the deadline passes, returning the bounded TIMEOUT class. The abandoned
    goroutine is the honest cost and is written down at the call site. Transfers are deliberately
    NOT wrapped (they end on the caller's own context), so there is no `fs` equivalent of
    `STORAGE_IDLE_TIMEOUT` or `STORAGE_TRANSFER_MAX` — DEPLOY §7 and §32.2 now say which of the three
    applies rather than implying all of them do.

    *And three smaller corrections from the same pass:* `admin ls --stat` prints `store:` on `fs`
    like `stats` does (the label is one helper now, not two spellings); doctor's `webhook` row no
    longer says "opens no outbound connection but S3" two rows under `store`'s "no outbound
    connection at all"; and `S3_KEY_PREFIX` refuses a `.` segment as well as `..` — on `fs` a
    prefix of `./` loaded clean, passed `/readyz` (a ping takes no key) and then failed every
    upload, list, stat and sweep with `ErrBadKey`, which is §4's boot-time rule inverted.

    **(p) Proof.** Container Go loop green (`gofmt`, `go vet`, `go vet -tags ffmpeg`,
    `go test -tags ffmpeg ./...`). `internal/store/fs_test.go`: the path law across every method, the
    round trip with progress and mode and no temp left, atomic overwrite, the range edges against the
    Fake, a cancelled body, `NewSeeker` over the store (the media hot path's actual shape), List as a
    string prefix with a bounded walk, List reporting a crashed transfer's litter, DeletePrefix with
    directory pruning and its emptiness check, Ping's classes, the marker, one whole clip's key set
    built by `keys.go`, and a cancelled PutFile leaving nothing. One test is honestly SKIPPED under
    uid 0: forcing `DeletePrefix`'s `ErrPrefixNotEmpty` needs an unlink that fails, and root in a
    container has `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE`, so it says so instead of passing vacuously (the same contract's
    success half is asserted on every uid). `cmd/clippet/storage_fs_test.go`: doctor on `fs` (all 13
    rows, the counts, every sentence), doctor on `s3` (unchanged shape), the missing directory, the
    missing marker, stats' reconciled lines, orphans over a directory with both plants and `--delete`,
    the migrate verb's usage refusals, and a full s3→fs migration including the dry run, the re-run,
    the row-less prefix it must not carry, the source it must not touch, and a corrupted destination
    copy it must catch. **E2E step 88** (`88-fsstore.sh`, exclusive) does the whole product on a
    throwaway one-container `fs` instance with its own port, database, scratch and media directory:
    register, upload `std-720p30.mp4`, encode, serve whole and ranged, HEAD the poster, the share
    page, `admin doctor`, the boot refusal of a leftover `S3_BUCKET`, `admin stats`, `admin orphans`
    with both plants, `admin storage migrate --dry-run` (and its two refusals), then delete and watch
    the sweeper empty and prune the clip's directories. It runs on the reference stack too: it never
    touches that stack's database or store, and the only thing it asks the live MinIO is whether the
    bucket exists.

277. **Pricing presets, the quota as the headline, and the opt-in hard cap** (ROADMAP #40 parts 2
    and 3; branch `quota`, 2026-09-13; `internal/cost/presets.go`, `internal/config/config.go`,
    `internal/httpapi/ingest.go`, `internal/web/pages.go` + `web/templates/settings.html` +
    `web/templates/index.html`, `cmd/clippet/admin.go` + `doctor.go`, `internal/sweeper/sweeper.go`,
    `scripts/e2e.d/89-quota.sh`; DEPLOY §7, §25, §31.5, §31.6; no migration). The owner's picks of 2026-09-13:
    presets for the top few providers (local, AWS, Cloudflare, Backblaze, other); the quota first; and a
    question about how far from reality the price guesses would be.

    **(a) A preset is a dated copy of somebody else's list, in code.** `STORAGE_PRICING` takes
    `local`, `r2`, `b2` or `s3`; unset is the CUSTOM case erratum 270 shipped and is still the
    default. A row carries the provider's two per-GB prices in the same micros a typed price is held
    in, the currency its list quotes, the date a person read that list, and the provider's free
    allowances for storage and for egress. There is no lookup and there will not be one: "query storage
    costs" could never mean asking
    the provider (erratum 270's opening argument — a call-home and a second credential), and a preset
    does not weaken that, it only saves the typing. §15's outbound destination list is unchanged, and
    `scripts/check.sh`'s URL tripwire is why the three pricing pages are named in WORDS in
    `presets.go` and nowhere as a link.

    | `STORAGE_PRICING` | storage /GB-month | egress /GB | free storage | free egress | read | from |
    |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
    | `local` | `0` | `0` | — | — | 2026-09-13 | nobody bills a disk you own |
    | `r2` | `0.015` | `0` | 10 GB a month | — (R2 bills no internet egress) | 2026-09-13 | Cloudflare's "R2 pricing" page |
    | `b2` | `0.00695` (6.95/TB) | `0.01` | 10 GB a month | 3× the stored bytes, each month | 2026-09-13 | Backblaze's "B2 Cloud Storage Pricing" page |
    | `s3` | `0.023` | `0.09` | — | 100 GB a month | 2026-09-13 | Amazon's "S3 pricing" page, US East (N. Virginia), S3 Standard |

    **Both kinds of allowance are modelled, not mentioned** — the free storage comes off the stored
    bytes before they are priced and the free egress off the month's served bytes, so a small R2
    instance reads `0.00` because it really is free. The one allowance deliberately NOT modelled is
    AWS's S3: a new account gets a credit (up to 200 USD over six months on the read date) rather than a standing allowance, and
    an estimate that assumed a trial nobody is on would understate every bill after the first year.

    Each figure was fetched and read on 2026-09-13 while building this. Two are worth recording: B2's
    storage is **6.95 per TB-month and not the 6.00 the brief carried** — its page says "Starts at
    $6.95 / TB / mo", 16 % above the number in the brief, which is exactly the drift this table's
    dates exist for; and the S3 rate tables render client-side and did not extract, so `0.023` and
    `0.09` are the us-east-1 list prices confirmed from secondary 2026 sources rather than read off
    the AWS page itself — an operator on S3 should check theirs, and DEPLOY §31.5's accuracy table
    says so.

    **`local` is a row and not an absence.** A box with its own disks has a provider bill of zero,
    which is a measurement; the panel prints `≈ 0.00` and the hint reads `local: no provider bill`,
    which is a different statement from `unpriced`. That is the owner's call that the local preset's cost reads 0, and it
    does not breach erratum 270's "unset is ABSENT, never zero": the zero is a CONFIGURED answer, the
    same way R2's zero egress already was.

    **Currency.** Erratum 270 made the app currency-agnostic by construction because it had never been
    told one. A preset tells it one: a published list is quoted in a currency, so the row carries
    `USD` and every surface that repeats the row prints it — `R2 list prices as of 2026-09-13 (USD)`.
    The custom case still names no currency and never will, and `local` names none either, because
    nobody quotes a price for a disk you already own.

    **The override law.** `STORAGE_PRICE_PER_GB_MONTH` and `EGRESS_PRICE_PER_GB` each replace their
    half of the preset (`cost.PricesOf`); **both allowance rules stay** — the free storage and the
    free egress — because an allowance is the provider's billing rule and not a number anybody
    retyped. It is the answer to price drift without a release: an operator on a different region,
    plan or year types the number they actually pay and keeps the rules. `admin doctor`'s `prices`
    row prints which half is theirs.

    **Where the names live.** `config.PricingPresets` holds the accepted VALUES (the loader validates
    one, and `cost` imports `config`, not the reverse); `cost/presets.go` holds the rows. A test
    asserts the two lists are the same list, so a name accepted at boot with no row behind it — which
    would silently price an instance at zero — fails the build instead.

    **(b) The quota is the panel's first row, and the budget row is gone into it.** With
    `STORAGE_BUDGET_BYTES` set, `/settings`' Storage panel leads with
    `quota | 41.2 GiB of 186.3 GiB | 22 %`, and erratum 270's trailing `budget` row is that row —
    one row, not two printing the same pair. It is first because "is there room" is the question
    somebody opens the panel with, and it is the only one of the three that is actionable. Both byte
    figures are `humanBytes`, the IEC units the rest of the panel uses, rather than echoing the
    decimal `200 GB` of the `.env` line: a panel that mixed units inside one row would make the
    comparison it exists for unreadable. `admin stats` prints the same line first (`quota:`), above
    the `storage:` line, which keeps its raw `used=`/`budget=` pair untouched because four E2E steps
    and DEPLOY §25 parse it — the human/raw pair `disk:` has always printed.

    **The red.** Past the line the state cell is `--danger`. `web/STYLE.md`'s law is red = LOSS
    (delete, revoke, failed — text and a hairline, never a fill), and a full quota is a loss: of the
    next upload, refused outright when the cap is armed and unplanned-for when it is not. It is the
    exception erratum 270 anticipated for a crossed budget, drawn the way the law allows — the
    existing `.rs.danger` class, no new colour and no fill.

    **One byte, two questions.** The ROW and the CAP are `used >= budget`: a budget of N bytes is N
    bytes of room and an instance holding N has none left. The sweeper's WARN and `/healthz`'s `over`
    stay `used > budget`, erratum 157's edge, because that is what DEPLOY §24's alerts read and it
    answers a different question — "has the line been crossed". They are one byte apart and each is
    right; both are written down where they are computed.

    **(c) The cap: one variable, one refusal site, one sentence — and it is where uploads STOP, not a ceiling** (the
    clip that crosses the line is accepted whole, two uploads racing in under the line both land, a failed read lets
    an upload through and logs it; a household instance overshoots by a clip, never by a catalogue — DEPLOY §25 says so
    where a cap is armed). `STORAGE_BUDGET_HARD=0|1`, default
    0, and `1` without `STORAGE_BUDGET_BYTES` is fatal at boot (a cap of zero refuses everything,
    which nobody means by "1"). With 1, a NEW clip is refused `507 Insufficient Storage`,
    `storage_quota`, *"This instance is at its storage quota; delete or expire some clips, or raise
    the quota."*

    The site is **`httpapi.ingestCore`, at its top** (`internal/httpapi/ingest.go`, `storageQuota`) —
    the boundary "a clip is about to exist". All three creating callers run through it (`POST
    /api/clips`, `POST /api/upload`, the bot's `/clip`) and nothing else does, so a **replacement**
    (`replace.go`, which shares `beginUpload` but not this function) and a **trim** are not refused:
    neither adds a clip, both are the file behind a link people already have, and a replacement is
    usually how an operator gets back under the line. Refusing the one action that could fix the
    problem would be the worst possible reading of the variable. The refusal happens before an id is
    drawn and before a byte is spooled, so nothing reaches scratch or the bucket; the body is then
    left unread, which net/http answers by closing the read side after the reply (`doEarlyClose` +
    `closeWriteAndWait`), so the client reads the 507 rather than a reset — the shape erratum 138
    arranged for the refusals above it.

    **It reads the database, not the cache.** `db.StorageUsed` per upload, not
    `httpx.StorageBudget`'s cached reading, which is up to one `SWEEP_INTERVAL` old: a cap on a stale
    number would go on refusing for a minute after somebody deleted a clip to make room, which is
    precisely the minute it is being watched. The price is one indexed sum over `clips` per upload,
    paid only when the cap is armed — with the variable unset the function reads nothing at all. A
    read that FAILS does not refuse: the insert four steps later will fail with a 503 that names the
    real problem, and "you are out of space" would send the operator to the wrong one.

    **The bot says the same sentence**, through the same ingest error path every other refusal uses
    (`ingestFailQuota` → `notify.SentenceQuota`), and a test asserts the two constants are equal.
    Every sentence in the product that promised "no upload is ever refused because of it" now names
    the variable that lifts it — the library notice (which also says WHICH mode is on, because a
    person whose upload just failed needs that in the place they are already looking), the sweeper's
    WARN, `admin stats`' verdict, DEPLOY §7 and §25, README, `.env.example`, compose.yaml, API.md and
    DESIGN §4 and erratum 157's own title.

    **What this is NOT.** No per-user quota and no tiering (§17's anti-features): one line, one
    instance, set by whoever runs it, with nothing per account and nothing anybody can buy their way
    past. No provider API, no price fetch, no currency conversion, no invoice-side arithmetic (tax,
    request charges, minimum durations, free-storage tiers — DEPLOY §31.5's accuracy table lists every
    one of them as not modelled, with how much each is worth). `/healthz` is untouched:
    `storage_budget` is bytes only, and a capped instance's object is identical to an uncapped one's.

278. **`MEDIA_DELIVERY=redirect`: the media routes may answer a 302 to a presigned URL instead of the
    bytes** (ROADMAP #34 lane F; `internal/config/config.go`, `internal/store/{store,minio,fs,fake}.go`,
    `internal/httpapi/media.go`, `internal/httpx/middleware.go`, `internal/web/{pages.go,server.go}`,
    `web/templates/settings.html`, `cmd/clippet/{admin.go,doctor.go,serve.go}`, `compose.yaml`,
    `.env.example`, `scripts/e2e.d/90-media.sh`; DEPLOY §7, §12, §15.2, §17.3, §24.1, §31.3, §33; no
    migration). The owner's decision of 2026-09-14: the terms are not to be broken; the same R2, B2, S3 and
    S3-compatible endpoints stay supported, with a slight rearchitecture of how media reaches a viewer.

    **Why.** Cloudflare's Service-Specific Terms restrict *video* served through a proxied hostname
    from a non-Cloudflare origin on Free/Pro/Business, and on 25 Aug 2026 their video-policy page
    gained a Cloudflare Tunnel section that closes the tunnel argument in writing. clippet.gg streams
    every media byte MinIO → app → tunnel → edge, which is exactly the restricted shape. The cheapest
    compliant change is not to move the product: it is to stop the bytes crossing the CDN. In
    `redirect` mode the app keeps every gate, every URL and every card tag, and a media route answers
    **302 to a freshly presigned URL on the bucket's own origin**. On R2 the bytes are then on
    Cloudflare's own platform; on B2 or S3 they never touch Cloudflare at all. The zone carries HTML
    and a 300-byte redirect.

    **(a) The law: which routes, and where the decision sits.** The redirect is written in
    `serveObject`, which is the single funnel every media route already passes through — so the mode
    cannot change WHICH gate runs or in what order. **Three kinds carry `object.redirectable`:
    `video.mp4`, `social.mp4` and `poster.jpg`** — the player's and the card's payload, and the whole
    of what the Cloudflare rule is about. **Three never do**, each for its own reason:

    - **`/original`** is the one object with a real identity gate (erratum 207), and a presigned URL
      cannot carry one. It stays app-served in every mode, at negligible traffic.
    - **`preview.gif` and `filmstrip.jpg`** are the two media routes whose STATUS this app's own
      JavaScript POLLS with `fetch` (errata 226(b) and 227 — a HEAD, because the answer wanted is the
      status and the picture is fetched by the `<img>` that wants it anyway). A `fetch` follows a
      cross-origin 302 into a CORS check, so the response would be unreadable: the GIF button would
      poll out and the trim scrubber would never get its sheet, silently. Making them work would need
      `connect-src` widened AND the bucket serving CORS headers — exactly the "no CORS configuration"
      a BYO bucket is promised (DEPLOY §7). They are also small, on demand and owner-facing, so
      keeping them app-served costs nothing against a rule that is about video. This was found by
      reading the client, not by a failing test, and the test that pins it now exists.

    `redirectable` defaults to FALSE on purpose: a media kind somebody adds later keeps being proxied
    rather than silently acquiring a public URL.

    **(b) The gate order is unchanged, and that is the whole safety argument.** `lookupClip` (404 for
    unknown or `deleting`), the `not_ready` 409, `/original`'s 401/403 pair and `mediaObject`'s
    invariant 503 all run BEFORE `serveObject` is reached, exactly as they did. The link is therefore
    minted AFTER the decision to serve — which is why **TTL and delete stay exact**: a deleted row
    404s and signs nothing, at once. There is one bounded window `proxy` mode does not have, and
    DEPLOY §33.2 says it out loud rather than leaving an operator to find it: a link minted a second
    BEFORE the DELETE goes on fetching the object until the sweeper's next tick removes it — at most
    one `SWEEP_INTERVAL`, not one `MEDIA_PRESIGN_TTL`, because what ends it is the object's life and
    not the signature's. **Unlisted is unchanged**: `store/keys.go` already builds `clips/{12 random}/…/{8 more
    random}`, so a bucket URL is no more guessable than the share link, and §9.1 is explicit that the
    link IS the capability.

    **(c) The presign.** `Store` gains an eighth method,
    `PresignGet(ctx, key, ttl, contentType, disposition)`. minio-go's `PresignedGetObject` with
    `response-content-type` and `response-content-disposition` overrides — honoured by MinIO, R2, B2
    and AWS S3 alike — so the type still comes from the ROW and never from what the bucket happened to
    store (§15's content-type discipline survives the app no longer writing the header). **It makes no
    network call**: a query signature is HMAC over the canonical request, and `newClient` pins `Region`
    from configuration so minio-go never asks the bucket where it lives. §15's "outbound traffic goes
    to `S3_ENDPOINT` and to Discord" is therefore untouched — what changes is the VIEWER's egress, not
    the app's. `fs` answers `ErrPresignUnsupported` (a directory has no origin), which no request can
    reach because the combination is refused at boot.

    **(d) `MEDIA_PRESIGN_ENDPOINT`, and why it exists.** SigV4 signs the Host header, so a link minted
    against the origin this process uses is valid at no other. The shipped MinIO is reached by compose
    service name; a viewer cannot resolve that. So the store holds a second minio client built for the
    public origin when the two differ — it opens no connection, it only carries the host — and is the
    SAME client when they agree, which is every R2/B2/S3 deployment. Left unset it defaults to
    `S3_ENDPOINT`.

    **(e) Three refusals, in the style of errata 276 and 277.** `redirect` on `STORAGE_BACKEND=fs` is
    a boot error naming both variables: a directory has no URL, and silently proxying would leave an
    operator believing their bytes had left the box. A plain-http presign origin under an https
    `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` is a boot error naming mixed content: the viewer's browser blocks it outright
    while Discord's proxy follows it happily, so the card would work and the watch page would not —
    the worst shape a misconfiguration can have. `MEDIA_PRESIGN_TTL` is bounded `1m … 24h` and refused
    rather than clamped, because a value under the floor is somebody who meant minutes and typed
    seconds. A `MEDIA_PRESIGN_*` set while `proxy` is in force is a **NOTE** (the boot line and
    `admin doctor`'s `media` row) and not an error: it is what `.env` looks like while an operator gets
    ready to flip the switch, and "I set it and nothing happened" must have an answer that is not a
    viewer. *Amended 2026-10-27 (run 23 lane `v2-migrate`):* the NOTE fired on EVERY default stack, because
    compose.yaml passed `MEDIA_PRESIGN_TTL: ${MEDIA_PRESIGN_TTL:-1h}` and the app saw the variable set. compose now
    passes it empty unless `.env` sets it (`${MEDIA_PRESIGN_TTL:-}`; the loader's own default is still one hour), so
    the NOTE means what it says — an operator wrote the variable — and an explicit value equal to the default still
    gets it (comparing against the default instead would have hidden a setting the operator made). Pinned by
    internal/config `TestMediaNoteOnTheShippedComposeStack`, which reads compose.yaml's row and was seen failing on
    the old one.

    **(f) The TTL rule.** A `<video>` element keeps issuing ranged GETs against the SAME `src` for as
    long as its page is open. A signature that expires mid-watch therefore breaks seeking on a page
    nobody reloaded, which is why the default is an hour rather than the five minutes a signing
    library's examples suggest, and why DEPLOY §33 says so where an operator would lower it.

    **(g) What the 302 carries, and what it must not.** `Location`, `Cache-Control: no-store`,
    `X-Content-Type-Options`, and no body. **No ETag, Last-Modified, Accept-Ranges, Content-Type or
    Content-Disposition**: they describe bytes this response does not hold, which is erratum 85's rule
    applied to a third status, and a cache that stored them against this URL would be caching a
    redirect as the object. `no-store` has a second reason of its own — the Location holds a signature
    with an expiry, so a stored 302 is a link that stops working while a shared cache goes on handing
    it out. `Range` and the conditional headers are **ignored**: a 302 has no representation to range
    over, the target answers all of it, and the live Discord measurement behind this design saw the
    media proxy forward `Range: bytes=0-1023` through the hop and get its 206 back from the target.
    GET and HEAD get the same answer (Discord sent no HEAD in that measurement; answering one is
    insurance, not a requirement). `?download=1` keeps erratum 98's rule — presentation, not different
    bytes — by travelling as `response-content-disposition=attachment; filename="…"`, the only place
    the ask can travel in this mode.

    **(h) One hop, never a presigned URL in a tag.** An embed is frozen into a Discord message for
    ever (the fact errata 97 and 213 are already built on), so a short-lived signature written INTO
    `og:video` dies an hour later in every message that carries it — a lived failure in another
    project. The card tags therefore do NOT change: they point at this app's stable routes, and the
    redirect happens behind them, minted fresh on every fetch. A 2026-09-14 measurement against the
    real unfurler confirmed the hop: `embeds[0].type == "video"`, the inline player rendered, and
    Discord's media proxy fetched the redirect target's bytes (including with a query string on the
    target, and through two hops).

    **(i) The served-bytes counter's honest estimate.** Bytes leaving the bucket never pass this app,
    so the one measuring point of erratum 270 would read zero — precisely the silent lie that erratum
    wrote "unset is ABSENT, never zero" to prevent. The decision, made on purpose rather than
    discovered: **every REQUEST answered with a 302 is charged the object's whole size**. Per
    request, not per view, and the difference is not small: a `<video>` issues a fresh ranged GET on
    the same `src` for every seek — the very fact this erratum's own TTL rule is built on — so a
    viewer who seeks pays for the whole file again each time, a viewer who watches four seconds pays
    for the file, and Discord's double unfurl pays twice. A **HEAD is charged nothing**, exactly as in
    `proxy` mode, where it writes no body: "whatever follows it fetches the object anyway" is true of
    a browser and false of an uptime monitor, `curl -I` or a link checker, and bytes nobody received
    must not reach a cost line.

    Over-counting is the safe direction and it is never silent. Three surfaces read the number and two
    of them say what it is: Settings' Storage panel prints `estimated (redirect)` beside the figure,
    and `admin stats` says `bytes a viewer was redirected to fetch … — estimated (redirect): each
    request is charged its whole object` on its `served:` line plus `the served half is estimated
    (redirect)` on its `cost:` line. `/healthz`'s `served_today_bytes` and `served_month_bytes` stay
    bare integers ON PURPOSE — it is a machine surface with no room for prose and no reader to
    mislead, and DEPLOY §31.3 carries the sentence for it. The stored row and the quota are untouched
    either way: they come from the database, not from anything a viewer did.

    **(j) CSP is built from configuration.** `cspBase` stops being a constant and becomes a function of
    the media origin, with `CSPPage`/`CSPEmbed` following and `SecurityHeaders` taking it. CSP
    re-checks a redirect TARGET by host, so without this the watch page's own `<video>` — and the
    embed's — would be blocked by our own policy, silently, with nothing in the response to explain it.
    `media-src 'self' <origin>` and `img-src 'self' data: <origin>` in `redirect`, byte-for-byte the
    old string in `proxy`.

    **The origin is asked of the SIGNER, never read off `S3_ENDPOINT`** — the lane's verifier found
    the first shape wrong and this is the amendment. With virtual-host bucket lookup
    (`S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE=false`, the binary's own default and what DEPLOY §7's R2 and B2 stanzas and
    §33.3's recipe all set) minio-go prefixes the BUCKET to the host: the redirect lands on
    `clips.acct.example` while a policy built from the endpoint names `acct.example`. CSP host-source
    matching is exact, so the watch page and the embed player would have been blocked by our own
    policy — silently — on every deployment §33 exists for, while the Discord card (which does not
    apply our CSP) kept working: the exact failure shape (e) calls the worst possible. It worked only
    on the bundled MinIO, which `compose.yaml` pins to path style, which is why step 90 could not see
    it. So `store.MediaOrigin` signs one throwaway key (`MediaOriginProbeKey`, which deliberately does
    not exist and is never fetched) and reads `scheme://host[:port]` off the result; `serve` and
    `admin doctor` both fill `Config.ResolvedMediaOrigin` in from it once the store is open, and
    `Config.MediaOrigin()` answers with nothing else. A failure to resolve it is FATAL at boot in
    `serve` — the alternative is booting with the narrower policy and a player that shows nothing —
    and a WARN carrying the reason in `doctor`. Prepending `<bucket>.` here when `ForcePathStyle` is
    false was the other candidate and was refused: it duplicates minio-go's rule in a second place and
    would rot the first time the library changed it. `90-media.sh` now compares the `Location`'s
    `scheme://host` with the CSP's and with the doctor row's for EQUALITY, on a path-style boot and on
    a virtual-host one, so the harness can see it next time. The origin is still a configured value
    and never a literal: `scripts/check.sh`'s
    outbound-URL tripwire would fail the merge otherwise, and it is right to — a compiled-in bucket
    host is exactly the thing this project does not do.

    **(k) What does not change.** The card tags, the share URLs, view counting, the sweeper, `proxy`
    mode's bytes and headers (`31-nits.sh`'s full 200/206/304/416 matrix still runs on a `proxy`
    stack), `visual.sh` — **wrong, and amended by erratum 282: the visual pass reads both shapes
    too** — and `/healthz`, which still names only the storage BACKEND. `admin doctor`
    gains a `media` row — the mode, and in `redirect` the origin a viewer is actually sent to and the
    signature's life, with a WARN when that origin (or the endpoint it was signed against) is one only
    this machine can reach under a public `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` — which takes it to **14 checks**, up
    from 13 (fifteen since erratum 302's `login` row; the list below is the shape, not the count).

    **That count is pinned in nine places, and this is the complete list**, because erratum 276(k)'s
    shorter one was followed literally and cost a gate run: `cmd/clippet/doctor_test.go:133` and
    `:439`, `cmd/clippet/storage_fs_test.go:128` (the `fs` shape, `14 checks, 13 ok, …, 1 skipped`)
    and its prose at `:204`, `scripts/e2e.d/51-admin.sh:68` and its two echoes at `:107` and `:109`,
    `scripts/e2e.d/73-ops.sh:282`, `scripts/e2e.d/88-fsstore.sh:116` and its `summary_row` at `:257`,
    `scripts/e2e.d/90-media.sh`'s own `doctorsummary` assertion, DEPLOY §24.1's "Fourteen checks"
    sentence AND its table (which now carries a `media` row), and DESIGN §20 erratum 276(k)'s two
    figures. A tenth place is the row-name list itself, `cmd/clippet/doctor.go`'s `doctorChecks`,
    which every run asserts is complete. Before claiming a bump is done, grep the whole tree
    case-insensitively for the PREVIOUS count followed by the word "checks", in both spellings — the
    digits and the word — and expect zero hits, this paragraph included.

279. **The official Clippet bot: the `managed` sentinel, and the origin proof `GET /api/bot/claim`**
    (ROADMAP #34 lane A, the pilot of the `clippet-forward` repo — a Cloudflare Worker that is
    Discord's Interactions Endpoint for ONE public application and relays each signed `/clip` to the
    instance the server's admin connected; `internal/config/discordbot.go`, `internal/notify/bot.go`,
    `internal/httpapi/{bot_claim.go,router.go,discord.go}`, `cmd/clippet/{admin_bot.go,doctor.go,
    serve.go}`, `scripts/e2e.d/85-bot.sh`, `.env.example`; DEPLOY §24.1, §30.7, §30.8; API.md; no
    migration, no new dependency, no new egress). The owner's decision of 2026-09-14 (ROADMAP #34, Shape B): *"the
    official `/clip` bot is FREE for every Clippet instance — a self-hoster installs the official bot,
    claims their server (OAuth2 MANAGE_GUILD + the bot installed), pastes one token into `.env`, and
    `/clip` works."*

    **(a) Nothing on the forwarded path changes.** The forwarder POSTs the EXACT bytes Discord signed,
    with both signature headers, to `POST /api/discord/interactions`; `verifyInteraction` checks the
    same Ed25519 signature over the same `timestamp‖body` against `DISCORD_PUBLIC_KEY` — now the
    OFFICIAL application's public key — and everything after it is ROADMAP #33's code byte for byte.
    The instance's reply needs no bot token at all, and never did: the deferral is the HTTP response,
    the follow-up `PATCH …/messages/@original` is authenticated by the interaction token in the body,
    and `Register` was the ONLY caller that ever sent `Authorization: Bot …` (erratum 254). So the
    forwarder holds no secret, mints none, and re-signs nothing: the credential is Discord's own
    signature, checked twice over the same bytes. That is the whole design, and it is why the free
    product's trust model is untouched.

    **(b) The sentinel.** `notify.NewBot` returns nil on an empty token and `config.discordBot()`
    fails at boot with one or two of the three variables set (erratum 254's all-or-none rule), so an
    instance answering the official bot MUST set a third value — and the zero-code-change spelling
    would have been a 37-character token-shaped lie. `DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN=managed` is accepted BEFORE
    the charset rule (which stays exactly as strict for everything else), `DiscordBot.Managed()`
    reports it, `String()` says `token managed (the official bot)` rather than `redacted` (a word is
    not a secret, and `admin doctor`'s scrubber skips it on length anyway), `notify.BotDeps.Managed`
    makes `Register` answer `ErrManaged` rather than send the word to Discord and read a 401 back,
    and the token spellings are not scrubbed for it. `admin bot register` is refused in words, in
    the CLI, with the DEPLOY section; `admin bot bind` stores the binding, publishes nothing and
    says which; `admin bot ls` and the doctor's `bot` row say `managed`. It is a docs-and-honesty
    change, not a capability change: it removes the single worst first-run experience of the old
    spelling, where DEPLOY §30.7's table would have told a claimant "the bot token is wrong or was
    reset" — true and useless.

    **(c) The origin proof, and why it is a security invariant rather than a nicety.** In Shape B
    the forwarder POSTs to an origin the claimant TYPES. Without a consent check, anyone who
    administers one throwaway guild could point it at `victim.example` and turn the owner's Worker into
    a request relay aimed at a third party — carrying Discord API Data (the invoking user's id and
    name) to a host that never asked for it, which Discord's Developer Terms forbid. So a claim
    proves three facts server-side, in one request: A (`MANAGE_GUILD`, `ADMINISTRATOR` or owner,
    from OAuth2 `users/@me/guilds`, compared with BigInt — `ADMINISTRATOR` named explicitly, since
    that field EXCLUDES the implicit permissions an administrator holds and reads `"8"`, not every
    bit; the fix pass amended this after the verifier), B (the official application is a member of the guild,
    from `GET /guilds/{id}` with the owner's bot token) and **C — this route**: `GET
    {origin}/api/bot/claim?guild_id=G` answers **200 `{"bound":true,"app_id":"<DISCORD_APP_ID>"}`**
    only after the box's OPERATOR ran `clippet admin bot bind G <username>`, which needs a shell on
    that box; `db.ErrNotFound` is a **404 with an empty body** — one bit, no hint; a malformed id is
    a 400 naming its rule (never a 404 that would read as "not bound"); a database error is 503.
    It discloses one boolean about a guild id the asker must already know, on an origin the asker
    must already know — a fact anyone in that server learns by typing `/clip` and reading the
    link's host — plus the application id this box verifies for, which is public (it is in every
    interaction) and lets the claim page refuse "your box is set up for a different application"
    at claim time rather than at the first `/clip` (the forwarder's row 18, moved earlier). Never
    the bound username, never the user id, never a count, never a list. It is registered INSIDE the
    same `if h.discordConfigured()` block as the interactions route, under its OWN `claim` rate
    bucket (30/min per IP; clause (h) — the build had put it in the `bot` bucket), with
    `Cache-Control: no-store` (the answer changes on bind/unbind), GET only. **Inbound only**: no new egress, no new call site, no §15 change, no
    `check.sh` rule change. `/api/bot/claim` and not `/.well-known/…` because `api` is already a
    reserved first segment (erratum 248), so no minted id can collide and the router test that
    walks registered patterns needs no new word. The same endpoint is the forwarder's weekly canary
    target — "this box is still up and still consents" — with no secret and nothing beyond the
    boolean. Alternatives refused: trusting the typed origin (the relay problem above); the
    instance calling the forwarder to register itself (a call-home in the free product, a new
    egress past the tripwire); a shared secret pasted into `.env` (a fifth line, a new secret
    class, and it proves no more than C does); probing the interactions route with a bad signature
    (proves the origin is *a* Clippet, nothing about control); a DNS TXT record (the claimant may
    not own the DNS).

    **(d) What the operator sees.** DEPLOY §30.8 is the whole recipe: three `.env` lines (the
    official app's id and public key, printed on the claim page, and the sentinel), one `admin bot
    bind … --no-register` (implied on a managed instance), then the claim page. `--no-register`
    always; never `admin bot register` — there is one global command, published once by the
    application's owner. §30.7 gains the row that would otherwise have been a support question
    ("`HTTP 401` **and** `DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN=managed`" → you never register anything), and §30.8
    carries one row per sentence the FORWARDER answers on its own (rows 13–19 of its failure table:
    unclaimed, disabled, offline, the public deferral, not set up, wrong key, not available), worded
    differently from this instance's own refusals ON PURPOSE so a support question is answerable
    from the sentence alone: *"This server is not connected to a Clippet account."* is the box;
    *"No Clippet is connected to this server."* is the forwarder. The doctor's `bot` row on a
    managed instance tells the operator to paste nothing, prints the claim endpoint instead of the
    portal URL, and lists the bound servers (read from the database as `checkDB` does; never a
    verdict change). BYO application is unchanged and fully supported: §30.1–§30.7 are the path for
    anyone who wants their own app.

    **(e) A dependency the forwarder has on THIS file, written down.** `json(...)` wraps the
    interactions route in a 15 s `http.TimeoutHandler`, which BUFFERS the response until the
    handler returns; the `{"type":5}` written before `h.d.Bot.Clip(...)` reaches Discord only
    because `Bot.Clip` takes a mutex, adds to a WaitGroup and spawns. The forwarder relays that
    same response under a **two-second** deadline, so any future change that made `Clip` do work
    inline would time out every managed instance silently. `discord.go`'s package comment now
    carries it as property 5.

    **(f) What the harness proves** (`85-bot.sh`, step 85 extended — no new step number): in the
    existing probe container, `GET /api/bot/claim` is 404 (empty) before the bind, 200 with the
    boolean and the application id after it, 404 again after the unbind, and 400 `invalid_guild_id`
    for a malformed id — and the 200 never names the account. A SECOND short container booted with
    the sentinel proves the boot line says `managed=true`, `admin bot register` exits 2 in words
    with no call anywhere, `bind` without `--no-register` stores and publishes nothing, the claim
    endpoint and a signed `/clip` both follow the binding, and the doctor's row says `token
    managed`, tells nobody to paste anything, and lists the binding. The forwarder's own suite
    (67 tests in the real workerd after the fix pass) proves the other half: no malformed probe gets a 2xx, the bytes
    reach the instance unchanged and verify there, the instance's answer is relayed byte for byte,
    a silent origin gets a public deferral inside the deadline and the sweep edits it to "offline",
    a KV failure falls back to the bundle-baked map, and a claim is refused without A, without B,
    without C, or for a box configured for another application.

    **(g) Not taken, on purpose.** `verifyInteraction` still checks `ts != ""` and never that the
    timestamp is recent, so a captured valid body replays at any instance indefinitely (effect: a
    duplicate upload; the interaction token expires in 15 minutes, so the reply cannot be forged
    past that). The forwarder refuses beyond ±300 s on its own side. The instance-side fix is two
    lines — but `85-bot.sh` signs with a FIXED `BT_TS`, so it needs the harness signing with `now`
    in the same commit; it is a cleanup line, not this erratum, and it is NOT a Pass benefit (the
    instance's endpoint stays publicly reachable with the forwarder out of the path). *Amended 2026-10-27 (run 23
    lane `v2-migrate`, the review's decision: build it): TAKEN.* `verifyInteraction` now admits a request only when
    `X-Signature-Timestamp` is Unix seconds (ASCII digits, at most twelve) within ±300 s of the box's clock — the
    forwarder's own window (`DEFAULT_MAX_SKEW_S` in clippet-pass `forward/src/admit.ts`) — and the signature verifies.
    Everything else is **401 with an empty body**, the bad signature's answer: a missing or non-numeric timestamp
    logs `reject=bad_signature`; a GENUINE signature over a timestamp outside the window logs
    `reject=stale_timestamp` (checked after the signature, so only a request Discord really signed can say anything
    about the box's clock — a box whose clock is more than five minutes off refuses every interaction, and that
    log value is how its operator finds out). No nonce is held, so a replay INSIDE the window is still a duplicate
    upload, as at the forwarder. The harness signs with the clock: `85-bot.sh` (`bt_now` before every batch of
    signatures, plus a `stale` probe — a genuine signature 301 s old, 401 and an empty body), `98-form.sh`,
    `106-botsignin.sh` and `108-person.sh`; the Go helpers sign with the harness clock (`b.now()`; the package's tripwire forbids `time.Now()`). Pinned by internal/httpapi
    `TestInteractionFreshIsPlusOrMinus300Seconds` (on a fixed clock: 300 s either way inside, 301 s either way out)
    and `TestInteractionsTimestampWindow` (through the route: fresh and 240 s old admitted; ten minutes old or ahead,
    missing, non-numeric, signed and space-led refused 401, no body, the right `reject`), both seen failing with the
    window check removed.
    Same wire format, a stricter accept.

    **(h) The buckets, after the verifier (fix pass, 2026-09-14).** The forwarder pins a fixed
    `X-Real-IP: 192.0.2.1` (TEST-NET-1) on every hop, so on a box that trusts its proxy (§4's
    `TRUSTED_PROXIES`) every connected server's `/clip` shares ONE `bot` bucket
    (`interactionsPerMinute`, 60/min) — one server is fine, several busy ones are thin — and anyone
    who can reach the app THROUGH that proxy with the header set can drain exactly that bucket
    (the §4 footgun, now with a published constant as its target; without a trusted proxy the key is
    the TCP peer, which pools the same way). Two consequences, both recorded: (1) DEPLOY §30.8 says
    so in one plain paragraph, with the sentinel's value; the sentinel itself and the Worker's
    header set are unchanged — a per-guild key would need the instance to trust a header the
    forwarder invents, which is the §4 footgun again with a new name. (2) `GET /api/bot/claim` gets
    its OWN bucket, `claimLimit` / `claimsPerMinute = 30` per address (`httpapi.go`, `router.go`),
    because it is anonymous and public: a stranger's GETs must never spend the tokens the official
    bot's `/clip`s need. `TestBotClaimHasItsOwnBucket` pins both directions — draining the claim
    bucket leaves an interaction admitted, and draining the interactions bucket leaves the claim
    endpoint answering. API.md's rate table gains the `claim` row.

280. **The E2E harness is media-mode aware: one suite, two delivery shapes** (`scripts/e2e.sh`,
    `scripts/e2e.d/{31-nits,41-social,43-watch,47-upload,51-admin,62-tiers,67-capture,70-web,73-ops,
    87-storage,88-fsstore,90-media}.sh`, `scripts/e2e.d/README.md`, `compose.e2e-minio.yaml`; DEPLOY
    §33.6; **no Go change, no migration, no new step number** — 90 steps and 21 bundles, exactly as
    before).

    **Why.** clippet.gg went to R2 with `MEDIA_DELIVERY=redirect` (erratum 278) on 2026-09-14, and
    the reference stack is where every gate runs. The SEVENTH GATE's public run died at step 7 —
    `download A for the colour check: got '302', want '200'` — and the same shape was waiting in
    steps 8, 10, 21, 22, 29, 30 and seven drop-ins: everything that fetched `video.mp4`,
    `social.mp4`/`light.mp4` or `poster.jpg` and expected the app to hand back the bytes.
    `90-media.sh`'s own header said "the stack under test must stay on `proxy`", which had just
    become false. A harness that can only read one of the two shapes the product ships is a harness
    that can no longer prove the product, so the suite reads both.

    **(a) The mode is DETECTED, from the stack, once, and printed.** One anonymous GET of the run's
    first ready clip's `video.mp4`, no `-L`, body discarded, immediately after step 6: **200 →
    `E2E_MEDIA=proxy`, 302 → `redirect`, anything else is fatal there** rather than at the first
    converted site. It is never read out of `.env` and never passed in — a public run has no `.env`
    to read, and a lane's `.env` is what an operator MEANT rather than what the process booted with.
    This is the origin-dependent-assertion rule taken one step further: the suite asserts
    what the stack REPORTS, including about itself. The line it prints is
    `[e2e]   media delivery: <mode> (<host>)`, and the closing banner repeats it, because the mode
    changes what a third of the assertions above it actually asked. The detection sits ABOVE the
    `PARTIAL` guard so `E2E_ONLY` cannot change what the helpers do.

    **(b) Five helpers, and the one variable every one of them asserts.** `media_get`,
    `media_download`, `media_head` and `media_maybe` are `get`, a `curl -o`, `head_` and "a URL that
    may or may not be a media route"; in `proxy` each IS its plain counterpart, argument for
    argument, so a proxy run is byte-for-byte the run it always was. In `redirect` each asserts the
    app's 302 — signed `Location`, `no-store`, **no ETag** (erratum 278(g): a validator for bytes the
    response does not hold) — and then fetches the Location **with the caller's own extra curl
    arguments**, so a `Range:` or an `If-None-Match:` reaches the bucket, which honours both on a
    presigned GET. That is what makes a converted assertion the SAME assertion rather than a weaker
    one. `E2E_MEDIA_ORIGIN` is taken from the first Location and compared for equality on every
    redirect the suite follows: a stack that signed some links for one host and some for another
    would pass every per-request assertion and still be a stack whose CSP can only name one of them
    (erratum 278(j)). **No signature ever reaches the transcript**: every message that names a
    Location prints it through `media_redact_`, which keeps the path and replaces the query — the
    query carries `X-Amz-Signature` and the access key id, and a run's log is a file on disk.

    **(c) A media HEAD becomes a 302 plus a one-byte ranged GET.** A bare HEAD against a presigned
    URL is **403**: SigV4 signs the METHOD and the link is signed for GET. So `media_head` asks the
    object with `Range: bytes=0-0`, which every S3 implementation answers 206 carrying the BUCKET's
    ETag for that object, its Content-Type and `Content-Range: bytes 0-0/<total>`; the helper then appends ONE
    line to the header file, `Content-Length: <total>`, read off that Content-Range. `hdr()` takes
    the last match, so every `Content-Length` comparison in the suite — a card copy smaller than its
    rendition, a poster's size against the log line that fetched it, `social.mp4` equal to
    `video.mp4` under the COALESCE — keeps working with no edit at all. The status it returns is the
    honest 206 and `expect_media` is the one helper that accepts it where `proxy` answers 200; it
    widens nothing else. The APP hop of `media_head` is a real HEAD, which pins erratum 278(g)'s
    "GET and HEAD get the same answer" on every media request the suite makes and keeps erratum
    278(i)'s "a HEAD is charged nothing" true of the harness's own traffic.

    **The bucket's ETag is not this app's, and the redirect proof found the one place that assumed
    it was.** `ingest.go` stores `SourceETag: res.SHA256` — a content hash this app computed — so a
    proxied response carries a 64-hex validator and MinIO or R2 carries its own. Every ETag
    comparison in the suite is WITHIN one source and therefore unaffected; exactly one was not, and
    it is the assertion `/video.mp4 serves the upload (same ETag)` in `62-tiers.sh`, where
    `/original` (app-served in every mode) was compared with `/video.mp4` (signed in `redirect`).
    It now holds as an equality in `proxy` and stands down in `redirect`, where the length equality
    beside it still ties the two routes to one object and the `cmp` two lines further down proves
    the stronger thing in both modes: what `/video.mp4` served is byte-identical to the upload.

    **(d) Three conversion rules, and the rule that a stand-down is never silent.** (a) *The bytes
    are the point* — a download for ffprobe, a colour check, a byte count, the object's own ETag —
    and the helper follows the 302; the assertion is unchanged in substance. (b) *The APP's own
    behaviour on the media route is the point* — its 416 envelope's `Content-Range`, erratum 38's
    zero-length suffix range, erratum 44's unknown range unit, erratum 43's stale `If-Range`,
    erratum 103's `If-Match` 412, the headers a 304 does and does not carry, `Accept-Ranges`,
    `Vary`/`Cache-Control` on the object — and a 302 replaces that response entirely. Where the
