      set in `.env`. USERPROFILE is never set on Linux or macOS, so it would have refused to resolve on
      every server this file has ever run on. `scripts/fsdefault.sh` plants that exact spelling in a
      throwaway copy and asserts it fails where the shipped one resolves, so the next person to reach
      for it reads the measurement instead of repeating it.
    - **A value from `.env` arrives un-mangled**, while an EXPORTED `STORAGE_DIR_HOST=/srv/clippet-media`
      on Git Bash reaches docker as `C:/Program Files/Git/srv/clippet-media` — the MSYS quirk DEPLOY
      §32.3 already warns about for the migrate commands. `.env` is where the line belongs anyway,
      because compose reads that file itself.

    **(c) The gap the compose file cannot close, and where it is caught instead.** With NEITHER variable
    exported — a scheduler, a service account, `env -i` — the default resolves to `/Videos/clippet`, at
    the root of the host filesystem. (b) is why no compose expression can refuse that without refusing
    every Linux box, so the APP catches it: `admin doctor`'s `store` row WARNs, naming both variables
    and the fix, exactly when the DEFAULT supplied the path AND what it supplied is that path. It is a
    warning and not a refusal because the app cannot tell a deliberate `/Videos/clippet` from an
    accidental one, and because by the time the container is running the bind already exists.

    **(d) The doctor says which directory on the HOST `/media` is, and which variable supplied it.**
    The container knows only its own side of a bind mount, so this was the one question `admin doctor`
    could not answer and the one a desktop operator most needs. `compose.fs.yaml` passes two
    informational rows down beside the bind: `STORAGE_DIR_HOST` (the resolved host path) and
    `STORAGE_DIR_HOST_SET` (`1` exactly when the operator named it, from `${STORAGE_DIR_HOST:+1}` —
    the one bit the resolved path cannot carry). Neither is §4 configuration: `internal/config` does not
    read them, they are not in `compose.yaml`, and the app never joins a path from either —
    `STORAGE_DIR` remains the only path it uses. They are named in `cmd/clippet/doctor.go` beside their
    only reader, the same way `checkProxies` and `MediaNote` read raw environment. With the pair ABSENT
    the row says nothing at all rather than guessing, which is every `s3` deployment, every hand-rolled
    `docker run` and every stack older than this erratum.

    **(e) The pin is a stage, not a Go test**, because what is under test is what Docker Compose does
    with a nested default — which no Go test can observe. `scripts/fsdefault.sh` is check.sh-style, runs
    alone (`sh scripts/fsdefault.sh`), starts no container and touches no stack: six cases over
    throwaway env-files — HOME supplies it, USERPROFILE supplies it, HOME beats USERPROFILE, the eager
    `:?` proof above, `.env` wins un-mangled, this shell's own answer ends in `/Videos/clippet`, and
    `compose.yaml` ALONE still binds nothing at `/media` and carries neither row. It fails on the old
    file at its first case (`required variable STORAGE_DIR_HOST is missing a value`), verified on this
    lane. It is deliberately not wired into `scripts/check.sh`: that file is not this lane's to edit,
    and a later lane can add the stage in one line.






296. **The drop folder: a video left at the root of the media directory becomes a clip** (ROADMAP
    #42 (b), the owner's ask of 2026-09-16: a video dropped at the root of the folder gets picked up and
    made a clip, reusing the parent `Videos/clippet` folder since the clips sit in a subfolder anyway;
    lane `drop`. New: `internal/drop/{drop.go,drop_test.go}`,
    `internal/db/{drop.go,drop_test.go}` + migration `0018_drop_seen.sql`,
    `internal/httpapi/{drop.go,drop_test.go}`, `cmd/clippet/doctor_drop_test.go`,
    `scripts/e2e.d/91-drop.sh` (step 91), DEPLOY §34. Changed: `internal/config/config.go`,
    `internal/httpapi/httpapi.go`, `cmd/clippet/{serve,doctor}.go`, `internal/web/pages.go`,
    `web/templates/settings.html`, `compose.yaml`, `.env.example`, README, DEPLOY §24.1. No route, so
    no API.md change; no new dependency and no new egress.)

    **(a) One variable, off by default.** `DROP_FOLDER_OWNER=<username>` turns it on and names the ONE
    account that owns whatever arrives. Unset — the default, and every instance before this — nothing at
    the root of the media directory is ever read. It is meaningful only on `STORAGE_BACKEND=fs` and is a
    boot error on `s3`, naming the backend it needs: a bucket has no root anybody can drop a file into,
    so the line can only be a mistake, and an IGNORED mistake ends in a folder nobody is watching. That
    is erratum 276 (h)'s reasoning about a leftover `S3_*` line, pointed the other way.

    *(Amended 2026-09-18, run 2, lane `import`, and this clause's RULE was wrong rather than its
    reasoning.* "A bucket has no root anybody can drop a file into" is true of the bucket and was never
    the question: what the watcher needs is a DIRECTORY ON THIS BOX, and `s3` can have one — `STORAGE_DIR`
    is already a legal, optional value there, because it is what `admin storage migrate --to fs` copies
    into. The knob is therefore refused for the thing that is really missing rather than for the
    backend: `DROP_FOLDER_OWNER` with no `STORAGE_DIR` is a boot error naming `STORAGE_DIR`, on either
    backend. See clause (m) for what that directory is, and what it is not.)*

    **(b) An owner that names no account is a BOOT REFUSAL.** `internal/config` validates the SHAPE
    (register's own `^[A-Za-z0-9_]{3,32}$`, spelled again there because §3's import graph forbids
    importing `internal/httpapi`); whether the account EXISTS is a question for the database, which that
    package never opens. `clippet serve` resolves it right after the boot janitor — the first moment the
    database is open and the listener is not — and exits 1 with one line when it does not, exactly as a
    bad `DISCORD_APP_ID` does. A feature that is ON and silently ingests nothing for nobody is the worst
    state this could be in, and the only symptom would be somebody waiting for a clip. `admin doctor`'s
    `drop` row is the preflight for the same fact, so an operator learns it before the restart rather
    than from it.

    **(c) A POLL, and why not fsnotify.** Every 5 s, one level, no recursion, no globs. fsnotify was
    considered and did not earn its place, for three reasons in descending order of weight. **The watch
    would not fire where this feature lives**: the folder is a bind mount from a desktop (Docker
    Desktop's file sharing on Windows and macOS) or a mounted NAS share, and a host-side write generates
    no inotify event inside the container on either, while an SMB or NFS server tells a client nothing
    about what another machine wrote — a watcher that silently never fires for its own headline case is
    worse than no watcher. **The timer is needed anyway**: a file counts only once its size has been
    stable across two polls, and an event says "something changed", which is the question rather than
    the answer. **And it is a dependency**, on a binary whose dependency list is a claim §15 makes; one
    `os.ReadDir` of one directory every five seconds costs nothing beside a transcode. The interval is a
    constant and not a knob (erratum 292's lesson about knobs nobody can act on).

    **(d) What counts as a file to take**, in order, each rejection silent but for ONE `DEBUG` line per
    (name, size, mtime) — because the root of this folder is a place a person keeps things, and a
    watcher that wrote a line every five seconds about somebody's README would be the reason they turned
    it off. A dotfile (`.clippet-store`, the staging directory, whatever the OS dropped there) or a
    directory (`clips/` is one) is skipped and never logged; anything that is not a REGULAR file is
    skipped (§32's symlink rule at the front door); a `.part`, `.crdownload` or `.tmp` suffix, or a
    `.failed.txt` we wrote ourselves, is skipped; a size of zero, or a size or mtime that MOVED since
    the last tick, is still being written; a file the database has already decided about is done with;
    and last, the file must OPEN and the transcoder's own probe must accept it as a video — a
    screenshot is not one, and neither is the front of an MP4 whose moov atom has not been written
    yet. It is the last gate; what it does NOT prove is that the file is COMPLETE, which this clause
    claimed until (k) below corrected it. The ONE rejection that writes a note is the file
    that cannot be OPENED: that is not a mistake about what the folder is for, it is one thing wrong
    that the person can fix, and silence would leave them watching a folder that never empties.
    *(Amended 2026-09-17, the fix pass: the "one DEBUG line per (name, size, mtime)" above was the
    design and not the behaviour. The tick recorded only the names that PASSED the eligibility rules,
    and its housekeeping then forgot the explanation for every name that had not — so a symlink or a
    fifo at the root, the one case eligibility itself logs, was explained again on every tick for
    ever, eleven times in 55 s under `LOG_LEVEL=debug`. The tick now remembers every name it saw,
    eligible or not, and the map stays bounded by the folder exactly as before. The cleanup list's own nit
    for this described a milder symptom — "explained once rather than twice, cosmetic" — and was
    wrong about it; pinned by `TestDropExplainsAnUntouchableFileExactlyOnce`.)*

    **(e) The ingest IS the upload path.** `internal/httpapi`'s `dropIngest` is `botIngest`'s twin
    (erratum 253's ingest core, the third caller): the account's own upload budget keyed exactly as the
    upload routes key it, the scratch precheck with the size the filesystem already reported,
    `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` through the same capped reader, the storage quota, the ffprobe gate, and
    `applyDefaultsCtx` — so the clip gets the owner's own lifetime, link grammar and unlisted-or-not,
    and the title is the file name without its extension (erratum 60's rule for every other upload).
    The watcher is handed to `NewHandler` through `Deps.Drop` and gets THIS handler's ingest, once, at
    construction: a watcher with an ingest of its own would carry its own rate limiters, and "the same
    gates as an HTTP upload" would stop being true of the one gate nobody would notice. There is no
    card-ready wait, because nobody is holding a message open on this path. Every refusal comes back as
    a SENTENCE rather than a status — the note beside the file is its only reader — and every arm that
    is the person's own to act on says so, while everything else is one generic line with the detail in
    the operator's log: a filesystem error's own text names a path, and on `fs` a path is the operator's
    disk layout.

    **(f) The file MOVES, and the one place it moves to is inside the store.** On a take, the file is
    RENAMED into `.clippet-drop/` at the root of `STORAGE_DIR` — one rename on one filesystem: instant,
    atomic, out of the person's view the moment we commit to it, and impossible to pick up twice or to
    read while a capture tool is still appending. On success the staged file is removed, because the
    store now holds those bytes under the clip's own `original/` key, written by the store's own atomic
    `PutFile`. On failure it is renamed BACK to exactly where it was and a `<name>.failed.txt` names why
    in one sentence beside it. Nothing else is ever deleted: the only files this package removes are one
    it moved and one it wrote. A boot pass puts back anything a previous process left staged, and leaves
    it alone (with a WARN) when the root name has been taken since.

    *(Amended 2026-09-17, the fix pass, and this is the clause that was not true.* The boot pass's
    refusal to put an orphan back was only half a guard: the very next tick renamed the ROOT file of
    that name straight over the staged one — `os.Rename` replaces its destination silently — and the
    successful ingest then removed the result. Proven on a throwaway `fs` container: a planted orphan
    and a root file of the same name, one restart, and ten seconds later the staging directory was
    EMPTY and the account owned three clips rather than four. The lost file was somebody's only copy
    of a video an earlier run had been killed in the middle of, and all there was to show for it was
    the WARN from a boot pass that had deliberately preserved it. **The staging rename now refuses
    the collision**: the file at the root waits, the orphan is named in a WARN once, nothing is
    recorded against either file — so clearing the orphan is enough to have the root file taken on
    the next look — and neither is touched. The clause's own promise, that nothing is deleted but a
    file this package moved or wrote, is what the guard restores. Pinned by
    `TestDropNeverStagesOverAnOrphanOfTheSameName`, which ticks AFTER the boot pass; the original
    test asserted the boot pass's guard and stopped there, which is exactly where the loss began.*

    **A deviation from the brief, and the reason.** The brief asked for the file to be renamed straight
    into the store AS the clip's original. That cannot be done through `ingestCore`, which spools to
    `SCRATCH_DIR` — a different filesystem on every deployment §32.2 recommends — and "the ingest is the
    upload path" is the stronger rule of the two: a second ingest path is exactly what erratum 253
    exists to prevent. What survives of the brief's intent is what it was for: the path never leaves
    `STORAGE_DIR`, the person's root is clear the instant the file is taken, no copy is left anywhere,
    and the move is a rename rather than a copy.

    **(g) Decided ONCE, remembered across restarts** (migration 0018, `drop_seen`). The row is written
    BEFORE the staged file is removed, and that order is the whole reason the table exists: a process
    killed between them leaves a staged file that the next boot's recovery pass puts back at the root,
    and without a recorded decision it would become a SECOND clip of the same video, every restart, for
    ever. A REFUSAL is remembered exactly as firmly as a success, because a file that cannot be ingested
    stays where the person put it — without a row the watcher would retry it every five seconds and
    rewrite its note for ever. The key is (name, size, mtime), which is what a directory listing already
    knows: not a hash, because hashing every candidate on every tick would read the whole folder off a
    NAS share to answer a question that only matters at a restart. It is deliberately not enough to
    recognise a DIFFERENT file of the same name, so fixing a file and re-saving it gets it looked at
    again — which is what makes the note's own instruction true. Retention is 30 days, pruned on the
    ticks that write; the table holds no account, no path and no folder, because there is one folder and
    the name is a leaf.

    **(h) Where it reports itself.** `admin doctor` gains a `drop` row — **fifteen checks now, up from
    fourteen** (the complete pin list is erratum 278 (k)'s and every entry on it moved: `doctor_test.go`
    twice, `storage_fs_test.go` and its prose, `admin_bot_managed_test.go`, `51-admin.sh` three times
    plus its loop, `73-ops.sh`, `88-fsstore.sh` twice plus its loop, `90-media.sh`, DEPLOY §24.1's
    sentence and its table, and `doctorChecks` itself).
    The row is off-with-a-reason, or on with the account, whether that account exists, and the folder's
    state now: files waiting, files with a note beside them, anything left staged. The Storage panel on
    `/settings` gains ONE line when it is on — `drop folder | a video left in this instance's media
    folder becomes a clip owned by <owner> | on` — which names the owner and never the directory,
    because a path is the operator's disk layout and that page is read by every signed-in account (the
    same rule `/healthz` has kept since erratum 276). Each ingest is one INFO line with the clip id.

    **(i) What is NOT built: (c) watched folders.** ROADMAP #42 (c) — the same watcher pointed at
    ShadowPlay's captures folder, OBS's recording folder, a phone's sync folder — is NOT in this lane
    and nothing here anticipates it beyond making the boundary visible. That boundary, recorded so the
    next lane does not have to re-derive it: **the drop folder MOVES because that folder is ours; a
    watched folder would be READ and never written**, so it would need a high-water mark instead of a
    rename, a per-folder owner, and a rule against ever deleting, renaming or tidying anything on the
    other side. This lane's `drop_seen` table is keyed by (name, size, mtime) and by nothing else, with
    no folder column — a watched-folders lane adds one or a table of its own; it does not inherit this
    one by widening the key and hoping. The owner's own line is the test it would have to pass: a full-powered
    app, never an rsync.

    **(j) Not built either, from the brief's own questions.** No notification of a new link through the
    instance's Discord webhook: a dropped clip is announced by exactly the rule every other clip is
    (§17 #4 — a LISTED clip that becomes ready is posted, and the owner's default decides whether it is
    listed), and a second, drop-specific notification would be a second vocabulary for the same event.
    No second owner per subfolder: the brief recommended against it and this agrees — one folder, one
    account, and a subfolder is `clips/`.

    **(k) What the probe gate proves, and what it does not** (2026-09-17, the fix pass, correcting (d)
    above, DEPLOY §34.1 and this package's own doc comment). All three said the same wrong thing: that
    ffprobe accepting a file is what makes the stability rules safe, because "a half-written MP4 has no
    moov atom". That is true of an MP4 written the ordinary way and FALSE of a FASTSTART one — where
    the moov atom is deliberately at the FRONT so a player can start before the download finishes,
    which is how this app writes every rendition it makes. Measured: `head -c half` of
    `testclips/faststart-720p30.mp4` probes clean, with both streams, and dropped at the root it
    became a `ready` clip of half a video. No active writer is needed to reach it — an aborted or
    abandoned copy (a share that went away, a laptop that slept, a sync client that gave up) leaves
    size and mtime still for one tick, and still is all the stability rule asks. The **honest
    statement** is the one now in all three places: the probe catches what is not a video and catches
    half of a non-faststart one; a copy that ABORTS part-way through a faststart file can still be
    taken, and the remedy is the ordinary one — delete the clip and drop the file again. Requiring two
    consecutive stable ticks instead of one was considered and NOT done: it narrows the window for a
    copy that stalls and RESUMES, and does nothing at all for the aborted copy that is the actual
    case, at the price of doubling the delay on every ordinary drop. A real fix would be a completeness
    check this app has no way to make from outside the writer.

    **(l) A refusal about the INSTANCE's minute is a pause, not a decision** (2026-09-17, the fix pass,
    qualifying (e) and (g)). `refuse` wrote a `drop_seen` row and a `.failed.txt` for every arm the
    ingest path returned, including the two that are not about the file at all: the account's hourly
    upload budget and a momentarily full working disk. Proven with `RATE_UPLOAD_PER_HOUR=1` and three
    videos copied in at once — one clip, and two files left at the root each with a note reading "the
    file will be looked at again if you touch it", which was no longer true of them, for thirty days.
    The default budget is 60/hour and is SHARED with trims, GIFs, posters and replaces (DEPLOY.md
    §7's `RATE_UPLOAD_PER_HOUR` row), so dropping a capture folder of a hundred clips — the headline use of this feature — stranded
    forty of them behind a text file each and a human `touch`. **The ingest path now classifies**: the
    two momentary arms (and a defaults read the database could not answer) come back wrapped in
    `drop.NotNow`, and the watcher puts the file back, records NOTHING, writes nothing beside it, says
    one DEBUG line, and looks again after a minute's backoff — so a bulk drop drains at the rate the
    budget refills, by itself. Everything file-shaped stays exactly as firm as (g) describes: too
    large, empty, not a video, unreadable, past the quota. The rule, which is the one to apply to any
    arm added later: *if the answer would still be no after the person went away and came back, it is
    the file's; otherwise it is ours.* The minute of backoff is not decoration — without it a stranded
    file is re-probed and re-staged every five seconds, so forty of them would be forty ffprobes a
    tick for an hour and forty files flickering out of somebody's folder and back twelve times a
    minute. Pinned by `TestDropDoesNotDecideAgainstAFileTheInstanceMerelyCannotTakeYet` and
    `TestDropIngestSeparatesAMomentaryRefusalFromADecision`.

    **(m) The folder runs on BOTH backends, because what it needs is a directory** (2026-09-18, run 2,
    lane `import`, ROADMAP #51's second half and `clippet-pass/docs/desktop-app.md` §9 item 3; amending
    (a)). The desktop box this was built for keeps its media in a bucket and still wants somewhere to
    drop a video — that is its whole local-upload story — and the `fs`-only rule was the only thing in
    the way. Nothing in `internal/drop` changed to allow it and nothing in it asks which backend is in
    force: the watcher lists a directory, renames a file inside that same directory, and hands it to
    the ingest path, which has written through whichever store this instance opened since erratum 276.
    The staged file goes to `SCRATCH_DIR` and then to the bucket exactly as an HTTP upload's body does;
    the local file is removed only after the clip row exists, and a failure leaves it where it was with
    its `.failed.txt`, on either backend (pinned by `TestDropOnABucketInstanceIngestsIntoTheBucket` and
    `TestDropOnABucketInstanceKeepsAFileItRefuses`, which drive the real watcher over a real directory
    with a bucket-shaped store).

    **Which directory, and no new variable.** `STORAGE_DIR`, on both. On `fs` it is the media store
    itself and the drop folder is its root, which is what (a) described; on `s3` it is a folder of its
    own, bound into the container, holding nothing but `.clippet-drop/` — the clips go to the bucket.
    A `DROP_FOLDER_DIR` was considered and NOT added: it would be a second name for the same thing on
    one backend and a first name for it on the other, and it would break the one property that makes
    the pair compose — an operator who later runs `admin storage migrate --to fs` and flips
    `STORAGE_BACKEND` finds the library under `clips/` inside the folder they were already dropping
    into, and the drop folder keeps working at the same path with no line changed. The `.env.example`
    block, the compose rows and the wizard are therefore untouched; what an `s3` deployment adds is a
    `volumes:` line, which is a docker fact rather than a configuration one (DEPLOY §34.4).

    **The watcher now MAKES that directory** if it is not there (one `MkdirAll` at `Run`, before the
    boot recovery pass): on `fs` the store had already made it, on `s3` nothing else does, and a
    watcher that WARNed twelve times a minute about a folder it was allowed to create would be theatre
    (`TestDropMakesTheFolderItWatches`).
    `admin doctor`'s `drop` row reads the same sentence on both backends, which is the point — the
    backend no longer decides anything here — and `91-drop.sh` (f) asserts that row on a bucket
    instance live. The INGEST on a bucket is pinned in Go rather than in the suite: a throwaway
    container really writing into the gate stack's bucket would need that stack's credentials, which a
    drop-in may not read from `.env`, and would leave objects on R2 behind it.




297. **The first-run wizard: `/setup`, the shared store probe, and the page that prints configuration
    rather than saving it** (2026-09-17, lane `setup`, ROADMAP #45 — the scoping's "setup page",
    the reviewed setup-page design, rev 2; the owner's pick of `/setup` as the route). The free
    container's answer to "where do clips live?", at `GET /setup`, beside `/settings`.

    **(a) It collects no credential, and has no field to type one into.** It renders a `.env` block
    with the operator's own placeholders and the operator pastes it on their own machine. That one
    decision is ADOPTED AS PERMANENT here so it is not relitigated: it kills the SSRF question, the
    second-credential question and the call-home question at once, and it is the reason this page
    adds nothing to §15's list of outbound destinations. `POST /api/setup/check` takes no body and
    has no input at all. The container cannot write `.env` anyway — it lives on the host beside
    `compose.yaml` and `DATA_DIR` is a named volume — so printing is the honest mechanism rather
    than a shortcut.

    **(b) One probe, two surfaces.** `store.Probe(ctx, s, keyPrefix)` is `Ping`, put one small
    object under `{S3_KEY_PREFIX}doctor/`, delete it. **No read-back**: a GET would change what
    `admin doctor`'s `bucket` row proves and would cost a Class B operation on every press of a
    button somebody may press a dozen times while they fix their `.env`. `cmd/clippet/doctor.go`
    now calls it instead of its own inline copy, and its lines are unchanged — true only because
    `Probe` is put+delete; `*store.ProbeError` names which step failed so the row keeps its four
    sentences (the two temp-file lines became one, the probe having one way to fail at preparing a
    file). The key space is deliberately outside `clips/`, so `admin orphans` and the sweeper can
    never see a probe object.

    **(c) The bounded vocabulary, and nothing else.** `store.ProbeClass` maps every probe failure —
    ping, put or delete, whichever vocabulary it arrived in — onto the CLOSED erratum 31 set
    (`unreachable`, `timeout`, `denied`, `bucket missing`, `unavailable`). The page's state cell and
    the route's `state` field print that word and never the doctor's own sentence, which
    interpolates the bucket and the endpoint and whose `safe()` does not redact an access key id.
    `httpx.StorageHealth.State()` is `Get()` without the backend word, because the page names the
    backend on a row of its own and one fact is not printed twice.

    **(d) Who may open it.** A signed-in account — instance-wide, exactly as the Storage panel is
    (errata 270 and 277), because §14 has users and nothing else and inventing an admin role for a
    page that prints no credential would be a new concept for no gain. And, on an instance NOBODY
    has registered on yet, anybody: a first-run wizard you have to log in to see is not a first-run
    wizard, there is no owner to be yet, and the page holds nothing private. The moment the first
    account exists that door closes and an anonymous caller gets `/login?next=/setup`. A database
    that cannot answer "are there any users" reads as CONFIGURED — closed is the safe way for that
    question to fail. `"setup"` is in `ids.Reserved`; both router tests walk the mux's literal first
    segments, so omitting it would have failed on this lane's first run.
    *Amended 2026-10-27 (erratum 349):* "a signed-in account" is now the instance's OWNER — the first account created
    on it (migration 0025); any other signed-in account gets 403 and one sentence, and `Check now` refuses it. The
    first-run door (anybody, while no account exists) is unchanged — but shut, with the whole wizard, under
    `SETUP_WIZARD=off` (erratum 335 (d)).

    **(e) It is reached from ONE place in the product** — the Settings → Storage panel head, as a
    link in ink with the marker stroke — and from the docs. Not the front door, not the watch page,
    not the embed, and never as a button or a nudge: web/STYLE.md's "what may never appear" is not
    suspended for a page about storage.

    **(f) The STOP row prints no command.** With `clips > 0` and a target that is not what this
    instance is on, a row renders ABOVE the walk naming DEPLOY §32.3 and the `admin storage migrate`
    verb in words. It prints no runnable form, offers no button and blocks nothing. DEPLOY §32.3's
    correct command carries a `-v ${STORAGE_DIR_HOST}:/media` bind whose omission silently writes
    tens of gigabytes into the container's writable layer, and a `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` prefix this
    project's operator needs: a page that prints a data-moving command must print the documented one
    or none, and after 2026-09-11 (the house rule on destructive actions) it is none. A browser control that moves 45 GiB is a
    different product. Between two BUCKETS the page cannot know whether the target is the bucket it
    is already on — it prints no endpoint host and could not tell R2 from B2 if it did — so the
    sentence says so in words rather than guessing, which is the honest form of a warning whose
    precondition is invisible. The pin is that no panel renders `storage migrate --to`; the VERB's
    name stays, because an operator who is told to stop needs to know what to go and read. (The
    scoping's own E2E assertion 8 forbade the substring `storage migrate` outright, which its §3.3a
    STOP text violated; this is that contradiction resolved on the side of the reader.)

    **(g) One optional row of arithmetic, in DECIMAL gigabytes.** `10 GB is about 836 clips, at this
    instance's own average (11.4 MiB a clip)` — `db.ClipCensus`'s count and byte sum divided into
    `10^10`, which is the unit both free tiers are quoted in. The binary reading is about 7 % more
    flattering, and the flattering direction is the one a self-hosted product must not round in.
    Absent below twenty clips: an average of four clips is a guess, and an absent row beats a wrong
    number.

    **(h) No new rate limiter** (the owner's rule, ROADMAP #35). `Check now` is single-flight plus a ten
    second instance-wide cache, so a hundred presses are one probe and nobody is ever refused — a
    cache, not a limit. Two presses inside the window return the same `checked_at`, which is how a
    caller can see that.

    **(i) `Check now` RECORDS its probe in the shared `httpx.StorageHealth`** (this lane's fix pass,
    2026-09-17). It writes the outcome the way `/readyz` writes its own live ping, and it writes
    INSIDE the single-flight closure so that only a probe that actually ran counts — a cached answer
    is not a new measurement, and `checked_at` would otherwise disagree with the page's `last check`.
    Without it the one live probe on this page was thrown away: `serve.go`'s boot ping loop RETURNS
    for good on its first success, nothing polls `/readyz` (the compose healthcheck reads `/healthz`,
    which only Gets), and so panel one's state cell and `last check` were frozen at the boot ping for
    the life of the process — including `ok`, dated to boot, about a store the button had just
    watched fail. It is also what makes `web.Deps.Health`'s own comment true: the page, the probe and
    `admin doctor` cannot disagree about whether the store answered.

    **(j) The chooser's two `<select>`s are clamped** (same fix pass). `select { width: auto }` sizes
    to its LONGEST option, a flex item's automatic minimum size is that intrinsic width, and
    `min-width: auto` beats any `max-width` — so the exposure select, whose second option is the
    longest option string in the product, painted 494 px inside a 390 px viewport and took the whole
    page sideways with it (`documentElement.scrollWidth` 526 against a 390 px client width).
    `.setup .rc > select { min-width: 0; max-width: 100% }` is the durable form: the clamp survives
    any future option label, where shortening this one would only have moved the ceiling. It sits on
    the line beside the `min-width: 0` erratum 288 added for the same reason on inputs, and beside
    the one that holds the `pre` carrying the block.

    **Zero new configuration variables and zero migrations.** Pins: `internal/web/setup_test.go`
    (the no-URL law over the whole table, the total-block rule, `config.Load` accepting every block,
    the block bytes as a golden, the door, the STOP row and the refusal),
    `internal/store/probe_test.go` (three calls in that order and no fourth; the step and the class
    of every failure), `internal/httpapi/setup_test.go` (the refusal matrix, the closed vocabulary,
    ten presses being one probe, no endpoint or credential in the body, and — from the fix pass — the
    press writing its own outcome into the shared cache in both directions), E2E step 92 and one
    assertion added to bundle 88. The fix pass added two pins beside them: the `other` walk's block
    loading against a plain-http endpoint under an https instance while the same block with
    `redirect` refuses (`TestSetupOtherWalkBootsAgainstASelfHostedEndpoint`), and step 92 proving
    that same pair through `admin doctor` inside its own throwaway container.





298. **The total-block rule, `compose.nobucket.yaml`, and the two placeholder grammars** (2026-09-17,
    lane `setup`). Three decisions that make the printed block correct in BOTH directions it exists
    for, and the one new file they needed.

    **(a) A generated block ASSIGNS every variable that decides the outcome. It never instructs a
    deletion, and it never relies on a line being absent.** `COMPOSE_FILE` is read by compose on the
    HOST, is never passed into the container, and is therefore invisible to this app: the page
    cannot detect it, cannot warn about it and cannot check it afterwards. An instruction the
    product can neither observe nor verify is exactly the kind that gets skipped — and the failure
    is SILENT, because `compose.fs.yaml` hard-sets `STORAGE_BACKEND: fs` and four EMPTY `S3_*` on
    the app service, the last file's `environment` beats the first's interpolation, and empty is not
    a boot error (`config.go` tests `l.raw(name) != ""`). An `fs` operator moving to B2 by editing
    `.env` alone therefore kept booting `fs`, with no error anywhere and `Check now` saying `ok`
    about the wrong store. An assignment needs no observing: paste it and the outcome is determined.

    *Amended by this lane's fix pass (2026-09-17), which found the rule held in one direction only.*
    The same failure runs BACKWARDS through the `S3_*`, and the bundled-MinIO block — the row that
    exists so that "go back is as printable as go forward" — had left them out, with a comment saying
    `compose.yaml` supplies them on that flavour. That is true only while they are ABSENT from
    `.env`: `compose.yaml` interpolates `${S3_ENDPOINT:-…}` and, unlike `compose.fs.yaml`, sets no
    `environment` override, so a value already in the file WINS. Paste that block over a B2 `.env`
    and the app keeps talking to B2 while an unused `minio` and `bucket-init` start beside it — and
    every check the page prints CONFIRMS the wrong outcome: `docker compose ps` shows the promised
    three services, and `Check now` answers `ok`, about B2. So the block now ASSIGNS every `S3_*`
    this app reads, **empty**: compose's `:-` treats an empty value exactly like unset, so an empty
    assignment restores the bundled default where an omission lets the old one survive. It is the one
    place in this product where an empty `=` means "the bundled value" — the block says so in its own
    comment, beside the bucket walks' opposite warning — and it stays URL-free, an assignment with no
    value matching no `http(s)://` grep. The rule is now stated over all SEVEN variables the app
    reads (`config.S3Vars` plus `S3_REGION`, `S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE` and `S3_KEY_PREFIX`) rather than
    the four that are credentials, and over every block: a stale `S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE=false` breaks a
    self-hosted server and a stale `S3_KEY_PREFIX` silently moves where every object in the bucket
    lands, so the R2, B2 and S3 blocks assign the prefix too. The `fs` block assigns none of the
    seven, which is what `compose.fs.yaml` hard-sets empty and what `config.Load` refuses to boot
    with. `TestSetupBlocksAreTotal` checked only `COMPOSE_FILE`, `STORAGE_BACKEND` and
    `MEDIA_DELIVERY`, which is why nothing caught this; it now checks the whole list, in both
    directions.

    **(b) `compose.nobucket.yaml` is what makes that expressible**, and it is the only new file
    outside the page itself: ten lines, `compose.fs.yaml` minus the media bind and minus the `fs`
    environment. `profiles` on the minio pair, `!reset` on the app's `depends_on`, and NO
    `environment` block at all, so every `S3_*` still interpolates from `.env` through
    `compose.yaml` exactly as documented. It also closes a wart that predates the page: until it
    existed, an operator pointing `S3_ENDPOINT` at R2 or B2 kept running a MinIO and a `bucket-init`
    that nothing used, on a machine chosen for being small — `minio` in `compose.yaml` carries no
    profile, so removing the `COMPOSE_FILE` line STARTS it. DEPLOY §32.3's closing sentence ("leave
    `S3_ENDPOINT` pointed at R2/B2 and it never comes back at all") was not achievable as the files
    stood, and §35 corrects it to point here. Needs Compose v2.24+ for `!reset`, same as
    `compose.fs.yaml`.

    **(c) `docker compose ps` is the observable half.** Every walk ends with the service count its
    `COMPOSE_FILE` implies — one on either override, three on the bundled flavour — because that is
    the cheapest possible check that the block took effect, and it is wrong in exactly the case (a)
    describes. A Go test ties the two together so they cannot drift.

    **(d) Two placeholder grammars, decided in the design rather than by the builder.** No template
    and no Go file under `internal/`, `cmd/` or `web/` may contain a literal `http(s)://` — comments
    included; `check.sh` stage 1 greps line by line and has caught two real prose leaks — and
    `internal/web/setup.go` and `web/templates/setup.html` are both in that set. So: **paste-whole**
    for a provider that shows you an endpoint (`<paste the endpoint the console showed — whole,
    scheme and all>`) and **constructed** where none exists to copy (`<scheme>://s3.<your
    region>.amazonaws.com`, `<scheme>://<host>[:<port>]`). Neither spelling matches the grep. The
    tempting alternative — splitting `"http" + "s://"` to dodge it — defeats a tripwire and is
    forbidden in words by the repository's rules. One shared hint names the two schemes IN WORDS; region codes,
    worked examples and real endpoints live in DEPLOY §35, which is a `.md`, where URLs have always
    been allowed. The law is enforced three ways rather than promised: check.sh on the source, a Go
    test over every string the table can render, and E2E step 92 over the page as served.

    **(e) Label-independence, dated.** Each step of a provider walk is the INSTRUCTION in terms of
    the artifact and its property — true for as long as the provider offers the service — and, under
    it, a dated hint naming today's labels. Backblaze documents TWO live web consoles with different
    vocabularies and both are current; the walk carries both, because rev 1 of the scoping and its
    skeptic each read one and each concluded the other was stale. `walks read 2026-09-13` is a
    required row on the page, the same discipline `Preset.Source()` already applies to a price, and
    The cleanup list carries the yearly re-read keyed on that date.

    **(f) `MEDIA_DELIVERY` is decided by the target — except on the one walk whose endpoint may be
    private, where the EXPOSURE decides it.** *(Rewritten by this lane's fix pass, 2026-09-17; it
    read "a function of the target alone" and was wrong for the case its own walk names first.)*
    The two local options set `proxy`: `redirect` on `fs` is a boot error (erratum 278(e)) and the
    bundled MinIO has no origin a browser could reach. R2, B2 and Amazon S3 set `redirect`, because
    a hosted bucket is always an origin a viewer's browser can reach and is the one shape where the
    bytes need not cross this box at all. **"Any other S3-compatible bucket" sets `proxy`** — its
    caveat reads "MinIO on the NAS, Wasabi, Hetzner, Garage, Ceph, a LAN address" and its own step
    says "A LAN address is fine and is the NAS-with-MinIO case", and `redirect` sends the VIEWER'S
    browser to that endpoint: under an https instance a plain-http one is a BOOT REFUSAL naming
    `MEDIA_PRESIGN_ENDPOINT`, and on a plain-http instance it boots and every off-LAN viewer's player
    is 302'd to a host they cannot reach. So that walk shipped a block that could not boot for the
    case it was written for, and DEPLOY §33 says of redirect mode in so many words that "there is no
    other reason to switch". Its closing line names `redirect` and §33 for a bucket with a secure
    public origin, rather than assigning it.

    On a **Cloudflare tunnel** that same walk assigns `redirect` after all, because there the choice
    is not ours: the video may not come out of this box at all (erratum 299), which is a property of
    the EXPOSURE and not of the target. It is a whole second block rather than a line telling
    somebody to edit one, for the reason (a) gives — a block that has to be edited is the class of
    instruction this rule abolishes — and its own closing line says what the assignment now requires:
    an endpoint a viewer's browser can reach, which a LAN address or a NAS is not, so for that case
    the answer is a real bucket or one of §35.5's other ways to be reached. The table is still six
    rows and one boolean rather than a matrix: seven blocks in total, and the seventh is one walk's
    second answer.

    The bucket stays PRIVATE in both modes, and one hint under every bucket block says so: a redirect
    is a link this instance SIGNS and that expires, never public access, and it still needs no CORS
    rule and no bucket policy.





299. **On a Cloudflare tunnel the media lives in a bucket: the wizard refuses "local store +
    Cloudflare", and offers both ways on** (2026-09-17, lane `setup`; the owner's rule, which the
    scoping predates). Cloudflare's Service-Specific Terms restrict serving video through a proxied
    hostname from an origin that is not Cloudflare's on the Free, Pro and Business plans, and since
    25 August 2026 their video-policy page says in writing that a public hostname through a
    Cloudflare Tunnel is covered by the same rule (DEPLOY §33, §35). A stack that keeps its media on
    a disk at home and streams it out through a tunnel is exactly that shape, and no setting on this
    page makes it not be.

    **(a) It is a REFUSAL, not a warning.** Choose `fs` or the bundled MinIO while the instance is
    reached through Cloudflare and the walk is replaced by one sentence naming the reason — no
    steps, and NO block, because a block is an instruction to act. The bundled MinIO counts as local
    for the obvious reason: its bytes are on the same disk and this app proxies every one of them
    through the same tunnel.

    **(b) Two ways on, both doors rather than a wall.** Put the media in a bucket — any of the four
    bucket walks, every one of which sets `MEDIA_DELIVERY=redirect` ON THIS EXPOSURE (erratum 298 (f):
    the self-hosted walk prints `proxy` everywhere else, and a tunnel is where that stops being a
    choice), so the tunnel carries the page and a 300-byte redirect while the video comes from the
    bucket — which also means the bucket has to be one a viewer's own browser can reach, so a NAS on
    the LAN is not one of the four here. On R2 the bytes are on Cloudflare's own platform, which the
    rule allows outright. Or be reached some other way and keep the media here: a port forward with
    your own domain and certificate, a small relay host running a reverse
    proxy, or Tailscale for a private tailnet. Those three are ONE PARAGRAPH in DEPLOY §35 and are
    deliberately not walks — each is somebody else's product with its own documentation, and a
    half-walk would rot faster than a pointer.

    **(c) Classify the thing first, and DETECT the default.** The chooser carries a second
    `<select>` — how this instance is reached — because that is what the answer actually turns on
    (the owner's product rule). Its default is read off the request rather than asked: everything that
    comes through Cloudflare carries `CF-Ray`, which this page reads and nothing else in the app
    does. It is read for PRESENCE only and never for identity, so a forged one buys nothing but a
    refusal against the forger; the select overrides it in both directions, for somebody behind
    something else that sets it, or setting a stack up before its tunnel exists. This is the first
    place in the product that reads a request header for a page decision, and it is worth saying why
    it is not a trust decision: nothing downstream of it is a permission, and the worst a wrong
    answer produces is a person clicking one control.
    **Withdrawn by erratum 348 (b) (2026-10-27).** The owner's verdict of 2026-10-14 — name the risk, never refuse —
    replaced (a): the folder walks behind Cloudflare and on a Pass name, its block the folder block plus
    `TRUSTED_PROXIES`, its closing line the desktop app's folder-card words. (b)'s two ways are now the ways to take
    the risk away; (c)'s detection stands.

300. **Four small things the audit was right about, and the sweeper's plan** (2026-09-17, lane `misc`
    of the checkpoint-2 run — the audit's #23, #13, #25 and #29, plus the Gate 11 harness note;
    `internal/db/db.go`, `internal/db/clips.go`, `internal/worker/worker.go`,
    `internal/lifecycle/lifecycle.go`, `scripts/visual.sh`, `scripts/lib/visual.js`,
    `internal/sweeper`). Every one is XS or S and none of them changes a thing an operator asked for;
    what they have in common is that each was a shape that would be wrong the first time somebody
    leaned on it.

    **(a) `Migrate` refuses a gap-filling migration file (#23).** `Migrate` applies every UNAPPLIED
    embedded file in ascending order, so a file that fills a HOLE in the numbering — 0006, 0009 and
    0010 are holes today — runs FIRST on a fresh database and LAST on every database that already ran
    0017. Two instances of one build, two schemas, arrived at by two different orders, with nothing
    said out loud; and what follows is a migration written against a table another migration has since
    altered. The check is now made over the whole list BEFORE the first transaction: an unapplied
    version below `max(applied)` is `db.ErrMigrationOutOfOrder`, naming the file and the version it
    would have landed behind, and the operator's fix is to renumber the file above `max(applied)` —
    never to delete a row from `schema_migrations`. A fresh database has `max(applied)=0` and can never
    meet it; DEPLOY §16 ("Upgrading", under "Migrations are forward-only and automatic" — where an
    operator meets a migration at all) carries the operator's paragraph. Pins:
    `TestMigrateRefusesAGapFillingFile` (a version above every embedded file is recorded by hand, so
    every real file is a gap-filler: the refusal names `0001_init.sql` and `9999`, and `clips` does
    not exist afterwards), `TestCheckMigrationOrder`'s table, and — for free — the four "upgrades an
    older database" tests, which each build their older database as *every file but one* and now
    assert the refusal before applying that one file through `applyMigration` (`applySkipped` in
    `db_test.go`). That shape is exactly the mistake this erratum is about; no real database is ever
    in it.

    **(b) `Worker.Cancel` takes a context, and a Destroy that cannot wait leaves the tombstone
    (#13).** `Cancel(clipID)` blocked on the run's `done` channel with no bound. The run's own exit
    path is bounded by `exitBudget` for its database and bucket work, but the scratch `RemoveAll` at
    the end of it is not — so a filesystem that stopped answering held Cancel, and with it
    `lifecycle.Destroy`, the sweeper tick that called it and a DELETE's `DestroyBudget` goroutine, for
    as long as the kernel took. It is now `Cancel(ctx, clipID) bool`: a `select` on `r.done` and
    `ctx.Done()`, `false` when the context ended first, and the progress entry is evicted only when
    the run really is gone. `destroy` treats `false` the way §12 treats every failure — delete
    NOTHING, leave the `deleting` tombstone, let candidate rule (a) resume on the next tick — and
    returns `lifecycle.ErrStillRunning` at INFO, the level a cancellation already gets. An owner's
    DELETE meets its existing 202 "deferred to sweeper" path; the sweeper defers the clip, because
    Cancel returns `false` only on a dead context and the tick already reads the CONTEXT rather than
    the error (erratum 101). Nothing is orphaned by any of it: the row still points at the objects.
    Pins: `TestCancelReturnsFalseWhenTheContextEndsFirst` (a run that takes two seconds to exit, a
    caller that allows 150 ms: `false` inside the allowance, the registry and the progress entry
    untouched, and the same Cancel with room reaps it) and
    `TestDestroyLeavesTheTombstoneWhenTheRunIsStillExiting` (no store call at all, the row still
    `deleting`, the scratch dir still there, nothing logged above INFO). Both fail with the `select`
    and the branch reverted, verified on this lane.

    **(c) The visual pass is given two directories, not the checkout (#25).** `scripts/visual.sh` ran
    its Playwright container with `-v "$PWD":/src:ro` — the whole working tree, including the
    gitignored `.env` with this stack's bucket credentials — inside an image that npm-installs
    Playwright from the network on a cold build. A pass that photographs pages has no business being
    able to read a credential. It is now `-v scripts:/src/scripts:ro -v testclips:/src/testclips:ro`,
    which is everything it ever used (`/src/scripts/lib/visual.js` and the two fixtures under
    `/src/testclips/`) and keeps every path it used them at. `visual.js` asserts the mount FROM INSIDE
    before it opens a browser — `/src/.env`, `/src/compose.yaml`, `/src/internal` and `/src/.git` must
    not exist, and the harness and both fixtures must — because it is the container's view that
    matters and a mount added back by hand would be invisible from the host. `VISUAL_DRY=1` prints the
    exact `-v` arguments, so the change is provable without a browser, an image or a stack; the full
    pass is the gate's and not a lane's.

    **(d) The sweep's expiry arm reaches `clips_expires` (#29).** The candidate query was
    `state='deleting' OR (expires_at IS NOT NULL AND ((state IN (…) AND expires_at <= ?) OR
    (expires_at <= ? - ?)))`, and `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` showed why that spelling costs: the planner
    nested a SECOND multi-index OR inside the expiry arm and drove its first branch off `clips_state`,
    so every tick walked the `ready` rows of the whole instance to look at a column that index does not
    carry. Rewritten as `state='deleting' OR (expires_at <= ? AND (state IN (…) OR expires_at <= ? -
    ?))`, `expires_at <= ?` is a top-level term of that disjunct and drives `clips_expires`; the
    tombstone arm still drives `clips_state`, once. The two forms select the same rows — `expires_at
    <= ?` is false for NULL, which is what the `IS NOT NULL` guard it replaces said, and `expires_at <=
    ? - ?` implies `expires_at <= ?` for any non-negative grace — and SQLite proves the partial index's
    own `WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL` from the comparison. The rest of AUDIT #29 stands refuted and
    nothing was added: no `clips(expires_at, state)` index, no change to the claim. The statement is a
    constant, `sweepCandidatesSQL`, so a test can EXPLAIN the exact query (erratum 84's method, and
    erratum 100's). Pins: `TestSweepCandidatesUsesTheExpiryIndex` (one `clips_state` search, a
    `clips_expires` search, no bare `SCAN clips` — and the old spelling is EXPLAINed beside it and must
    show two, or the pin would be decoration) and `TestSweepCandidatesRewriteSelectsTheSameRows` (both
    spellings over a fixture holding every shape §12 distinguishes, compared id for id, in order).

    **(e) This package's wall-clock deadlines are scaled for the build (Gate 11 harness).** The
    eleventh gate's first `check.sh` failed in `TestStartBlocksAndTicks` — "Start never destroyed the
    expired clip", a 20 ms-interval sweeper given five seconds for one clip — and the same test passed
    alone, in 247 s, on the same tree. The box was carrying two lane builders and a third container's
    `go test`, and `-race` instruments every one of the sweeper's operations. It is not a product fault
    and it may not be fixed with a product change, so what moves is the allowance and not one
    assertion: a build-tagged `raceDetector` constant (two `_test.go` files, so the product is
    untouched) and `deadline(d)`, which multiplies by 12 under `-race`.
    `TestDeadlineScalesUnderRaceOnly` pins both halves, and `check.sh` runs this package in both
    builds, so both are executed on every gate. The better answer is still a fake clock, and it is
    written down as one: `Start`'s loop would have to take an injectable ticker, which IS a product
    change and belongs to whoever wants it.
